The Great Chapter on the Pervasion of the Yoginī Tantras and so forth: Saurāṣṭra, Kāśmīra, Suvarṇadvīpa, and Upamelaka—among these are Luṭṭhaḍḍhya and Siṃhala;
the cities of the Nāyikās, Mahendraśaila, the land of Sindhu, and Kirātaka.
The cremation ground (śmaśāna) is of four kinds: *jhij*, *chu*, *clu*, and *su*; their presiding goddesses (*nāyikā*) are Marudeśa, Gahvara, Kulatā, and Samala.
Likewise, the secondary cremation ground (*upaśmaśāna*) is said to consist of *clu*, *chra*, *jjha*, and *eṣu*; their presiding goddesses are [the same].
Caritra, Harikela, Vindhya, and Kaumārikāpurī— these four are known as Pīlava; likewise, Ghigṛ, Khukla, Upaveśma, Virajā, Koka, Tripurī, and Śrīhaṭṭaka.

These twelve leaders among the *kḷ*, *khū*, and *gṛdhya* [families] are declared to be fourfold; the sixteen beginning with *kā* are the female messengers (*dūtī*) who are the leaders of the empty maṇḍalas,
and the four beginning with *hā* are in the external cremation grounds.
A, Ā, Aṃ, Aḥ, Ha, Hā, Haṃ, Haḥ—these are the messengers (dūtīs) upon the lotus petals;

likewise, there are eight skull-cups (kapālas). The principal goddesses (nāyikās) reside in the pericarp (kaṇikā) and the shield (kheṭa), through the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination and the obstruction of the support of the ascendant (lagna).
In ultimate reality, the twelve stages (bhūmis) are known as the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and so forth; conventionally, they follow the sequence of ignorance (avidyā) and the rest.
In the signs beginning with Capricorn, they follow the reverse order of the archer (Sagittarius) and the rest; these are old age, death, and so forth.
By virtue of the unobscured nature, they are the ḍākinīs and the elements of the body.
It is taught that there are seventy-two types based on the divisions of the pure Dharma;
these mantra-siddhas, who exist conventionally, are the female leaders (nāyikās) in the temples and other locations.
Now, their seed-syllables (bījākṣara) arise from the primary seats (pīṭha) and so forth.
Thus, for example: *kā jāpū o* in the *pīṭhas*; *iti pī ṭheṣu go rā de mā* in the *upapīṭhas*.
A-mu-o-kā in the fields (kṣetra), tri-ka-ko-lā in the secondary fields (upakṣetra),
and ka-ha-ca-la in the chandohas.
*Kāṃ koṃ hi ne* in the *upachandoha*s;
*mā pra ko gṛ* in the *melāpaka*s; and *so 'kā su siṃ* in the *upamelāpaka*s.
"Na ma siki" in the cremation grounds;
"ma ga ku sa" in the secondary cremation grounds;
and "ke vi ko" in the thickets.
Vi, Ko, Tri, Śrī—thus in the *upapīlava* [sections];
likewise, in the sixteen cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*), at the Vāyavya gate, on the left and right, are Kaṃ, Ka, La, La, Kaṃ; thus, Ko, La, Ha, La, La, Ko; and then Ka, Kā.
In this way, [it applies] to both the foul-smelling and the stainless.
O Lord, the Leader, you are the one who bestows joy.
and the seed and the sprout.
O,
sir! Ka!
And indeed,
in the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the bite of a snake: "He [is located] at the western and northwestern gates."

Then, *na* and *nā* are at the northern gate; *bā* and *mṛ* are for the death of children; *ī* and *śva* are for the Lord (*Īśvara*); then *ma* and *mā* are for the cremation ground; *śā* and *gha* are for terrible battle;
then *ṇa* and *ṇā* are at the southern and southwestern gates; *śū* is for piercing with a trident; and *u* is for the leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*).
Then, here at the eastern Āgneya door, on the left and right of the Āgneya door: Bhīme is *bhī*, and Bhayaṃkare is *bha*.
Then, on the left and right of the Īśāna door: Ṅa and Ṅā; Hahākāre is *ha*, and Aṭṭāṭṭahāse is *ā*.
Then, on the left and right of the Nairṛtya door: Raudranāde is *rau*, and Phetkāre is *phe*.
Now, *kṣa-kṣā* are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the sixteen cremation-ground goddesses.
Thus, the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, as taught for the purpose of introducing the ignorant through worldly conventions, should be examined;

for [in reality], sacred sites (*pīṭha*) such as Kāmarūpa and Jālandhara are false, since it is stated that there are millions of villages within even a single region, each presided over by its own deity.

Likewise, because [the dūtīs] are not mentioned among the ninety-six regions such as Bhoṭa, Cīna, and Mahācīna, nor among the millions upon millions of villages presided over by deities, the dūtīs would be non-pervasive;
therefore, it was stated by the Blessed One in the Root Tantra as follows:
"Pūrvavideha shall be the Pīṭha, and Jambūdvīpa in the south."
In the west is Aparagodānīya, and in the north is Uttarakuru;
there are secondary islands in the intermediate directions, and likewise on the surface of the earth are the upapīṭhas and all the fields (kṣetra) within the enclosures of the oceans.
Thus,
whatever contradiction there may be in the Lord’s previous and subsequent statements regarding the *Tricakrasaṃvara* and the *Hevajra*, it is for the sake of liberating beings from their fetters;

for here, those places such as the *pīṭhas* and *upapīṭhas* which are mentioned in the *Cakrasaṃvara* are taught in the *Hevajra* as the *kṣetras*, *upakṣetras*, and so forth, though presented in a different order.
Just as even the mundane accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*) do not occur for yogins in external seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth,

one should understand that the twelve zodiac signs (*lagna*) within the internal self are the twelve limbs beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*), which are restrained through the cessation of old age, death, and so on by means of the bow and other [weapons]. In those seats and so forth, the coming and going of the elements— the aggregates, constituents, and sense-bases (*skandhadhātvāyatana*)— which are the pure aspects of the Tathāgatas, has occurred in the past, occurs in the present, and will occur in the future, according to the distinctions of authority (*adhikāra*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and dissolution (*laya*).

Furthermore, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), in the *Tricakrasaṃvara*, the authority (*adhikāra*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and dissolution (*laya*) of the twenty-four goddesses—divided by way of the junctions (*sandhyā*), watches (*prahara*), and half-signs (*lagnārdha*)—have been taught.
Here, in the *Ṣaṭcakramahāsaṃvara*, through the flow of the mandala of the signs (*lagna*), there is authority, enjoyment, and dissolution.
In this context, "authority" means the presiding over the vital breath (*prāṇādhiṣṭhāna*); that itself is understood as enjoyment, sovereignty, and dissolution—the station of the goal.

The authority and dissolution [of the breath] upon the back of the Goddess occurs here in front, by means of the nature of the five elements: in the northwest (Vāyu) and northeast (Īśa), below the southwest (Daitya) and southeast (Agni), in the south (Yama) and northwest (Yakṣa), and in the others;

in the crown (Uṣṇīṣa), the heart region, the throat and head, and having gone to the wheels at the navel and the secret place. In each eight-spoked wheel, from the bottom upwards, every day, within the interval of two signs starting from Capricorn, the authority and dissolution upon the back of the Goddess occurs here in front by means of the nature of the five elements, and so forth, as it is elaborated.

Here, in the Capricorn ascendant consisting of five *daṇḍas*, during the first *daṇḍa*, the earth mandala [is situated] in the right channel at the navel; within the twelve petals, the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has jurisdiction over the western sector of the Capricorn petal, and the conceptualization here is that of the wind element (*vāyu*).
And here, *slṛ*...
O Wealthy One,
what has been done here?

And in the *Yoginītantra*, in the Great Chapter on the Emanation [of the Deities] beginning with Capricorn as the Ascendant: "When the Goddess Prāṇaśakti has her domain and abides in the Earth-maṇḍala, then she is dissolved in the Central Water-maṇḍala."

The taking of rebirth is the cessation of the former and the arising of the latter; as in the examples of the recitation of scripture or a lamp, so too here, regarding the phenomena of the limbs of death and rebirth:

there is authority over the earth-mandala and dissolution into the water-mandala; authority over the water-mandala and dissolution into the fire-mandala; authority over the fire-mandala and dissolution into the air-mandala; authority over the air-mandala and dissolution into the void-mandala; and authority over the void-mandala and dissolution into the gnosis-mandala—thus it is in Capricorn (makara).
Then, as for that movement which occurs in the middle [channel] at the *kumbha*-petal, it is said to be upward in the wheel;

thus, when there is authority (*adhikāra*) in the *avadhūtī* within this *jñānamaṇḍala*, then there is dissolution (*laya*) in the space-maṇḍala in the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*). When there is authority in space, then there is dissolution in wind; likewise, when there is authority in wind, there is dissolution in fire; when there is authority in fire, there is dissolution in water; when there is authority in water, there is dissolution in earth; and when there is authority in earth, there is dissolution in the *avadhūtī* within the *jñānamaṇḍala*.

Thus, in the mandalas of Pisces and Aries, as well as in those of Taurus and Gemini, Cancer and Leo, Virgo and Libra, and Scorpio and Sagittarius—these being the sixty mandalas—the authorities over enjoyment and dissolution are to be understood as fourfold at the end of the three ascendants in the middle [channel].

Likewise, in the wind-sector, in the Daitya, Vahni, Ghora, Adhas, Kha, Sura, Yāmya, Yakṣa, and Aparā mandalas—ten mandalas in total—and by the word "ca" (and), also in the knowledge-mandala, in Capricorn and Aquarius; thus it is for the others as well.
Now, the channels of the support-wheels (ādhāracakra) beginning with Capricorn are described: "The crown" (uṣṇīṣa), and so forth.
Here, in the first circle of the crown wheel, there are four channels, with one in the center;
likewise for the wheels of the heart and so on.

Therefore, in the *uṣṇīṣa*-wheel, there is the movement of the crocodile (*makara*) and the pitcher (*kumbha*) starting from the northwest spoke; because of the purity of space in the eastern wheel, there is the vajra symbol, and thus in the mandala, in the space-wheel (*ākāśacakra*), there is the vajra-garland (*vajrāvalī*). Likewise, by virtue of the nature of the heart, in the wind-wheel (*vāyucakra*), there is the sword-garland (*khaḍgāvalī*) in the Pisces and Aries [signs]. Similarly, by virtue of the nature of fire, in the throat-situated fire-wheel (*tejaścakra*), there is the jewel-garland (*ratnāvalī*) in Taurus and Gemini.
In the head, due to the nature of water, there is a row of lotuses in the water-wheel during Cancer and Leo;
in the navel-wheel, due to the nature of earth, there is a row of wheels during Virgo and Libra;
and in the secret wheel, due to the nature of gnosis, there is a row of daggers during Scorpio and Sagittarius.
In these wheels, each having eight spokes, the yogi must understand this daily movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) starting from the sign of Capricorn (*makara-lagna*), both below and above.

Here, wherever the *prāṇa* exercises its authority, there one should recite, by means of the flow of the *prāṇa* and not with a rosary, one foot of the forty-eight-foot mantra of the Blessed One together with the name of the presiding deity of that mandala. Likewise, one should recite one foot of the sixteen-foot mantra together with the names of the cremation-ground goddesses; and [one foot] of the eight-foot mantra together with the eight goddesses of the lotus petals, as will be described hereafter.
Thus, the movement of the wheel occurs every ten *daṇḍas* within each pair of zodiacal signs beginning with Capricorn (*makara*).
In this way, by means of sixty *daṇḍas* in a single day and night, the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs across sixty circles.

Likewise, on their respective days, the movement of the Yoginīs occurs within their own respective circles for the demons (*danuja*), humans, spirits (*bhūta*), gods (*deva*), asuras, and so forth; this movement is the cause of creation and dissolution. Mahāmāyā, the Great Fierce One, is the one who effects the destruction of all beings.
In whatever way he himself is the agent and the remover, he is remembered as Vajradhara; both in the beginning and in the middle.
In the center,
O Mahāhi, within the mandala of the space-mandala.
"O, it is so," [he replied]. "O Dan-po-la, there is none in the first stage."
In the *Vajrāvalī*, [the section on] the wind-wheel (*vāyucakra*) does not exist;
"there" does not exist.
Of each word, O venerable one, there is one word for each step.
On a red lotus petal.

O Maṇḍalatu, O Bho, O Lus-las-skyes-pa’i-phra-mo, O Evam-anutanuja Vimalaprabhā! The Perfection of Wisdom is neither an agent nor a creator; the Buddha is neither a slayer nor a destroyer. For the followers of the Buddha, it has been taught that there is no physical, verbal, or mental action performed by embodied beings.

"By one who speaks the truth, the being experiences the fruit of what is auspicious or inauspicious; there is no other agent for anyone"—this is the rule of the Blessed One. (36) The syllable *Bha* is the lotus; *Sarva-vajra* is the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*). By means of the *maṇi-gati*, the imperishables (*akṣara*), and the drops (*bindu*), there is all-bliss (*sarvānanda*) everywhere, the abode of equal bliss for the Vajrin at all times. That which enters into the lunar fluid within that [lotus] by way of the Guru’s mouth is Kālacakra himself. This is the wheel of Ḍākinīs, which is the "time" of the Māras—freed from time—that causes the fear of death. (37) "'The syllable *Bha*' and so forth..."

The movement of the Yoginīs through the six cakras, beginning with the uṣṇīṣa, occurs by means of the letters starting with *ka*. Therefore, the "lotus of the Lord" is the central lotus in the maṇḍala; it is [described] as being "by all vajras," meaning by the four imperishable syllables consisting of four drops (*bindu*). The lotus situated within the *kuliśa-maṇi* (the jewel of the thunderbolt) is the "all-bliss" (*sarvānanda*), the abode of universal bliss on all sides because of the non-emission (*acyutatva*) of the Vajrī. Consequently, it is the producer of bliss for the Yoginīs at all times.
Thus, the rule is that he who enters into that imperishable bliss—the liquid moon—through the mouth of the Guru, the mouth of gnosis (*jñāna-vaktra*), is indeed the Kālacakra yogī.
Thus, this wheel is said to be "time," which means it is explained as the phenomena beginning with ignorance;

this *ḍākinī*-wheel causes death-fear for the four Māras, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), and is liberated from all obscurations—it is not some other imagined host of deities. By means of the syllables of wisdom and method, according to the power of both families, the names *ḍākinī* and *ḍāka*—together with the other words via the three vajras—are divided into beginning, middle, and end.

The mantra (*jāpya*) is presided over by the vital breath (*prāṇa*); indeed, by virtue of both [the upward and downward] movements, those who have entered the movements of the *rasa* (mercury/nectar) quickly attain accomplishment according to their respective karma—the *ḍākinīs* and *vajra-ḍākas*. Regarding "wisdom and means" (*prajñopāya*), and so forth:

here in this *Kālacakra*, by means of the syllables of wisdom and means—here, wherever there is a short seed-syllable of wisdom, then for the means it becomes long by virtue of its family; when there is a long syllable of wisdom, then for the means it is short.

Thus, by virtue of both lineages, there are the names of ḍākinīs and ḍākas, such as Śivavajrā and Slavajra; likewise, Slavajrā and Śivavajra are Earth and Wind (*yū*), respectively, through the distinction of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*).

Thus, for water and fire, it is *ṣṛ-vajrā* and *vajra*; likewise, as before, it is *bṛ-vajra*. This is the name to be recited for all the *ḍākinīs* and *ḍākas*, consisting of the three vajras together with the subsequent words, divided into beginning, middle, and end.

At the beginning is the syllable *oṃ*; in the middle is the first word of the garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*); then the seed-syllable of the Vajradūtī together with the *vajraḍāka*; then the short *huṃ* is the mind-vajra, the long [syllable] is the speech-vajra, and at the end is the syllable *phaṭ*.

Then follows the garland mantra (*mālāmantra*) consisting of seventy-two words; in those [sections], according to the *Mahoddeśa* on the radiation of the *Yoginītantra* and so forth, among the seventy-two words, eight words at the beginning are to be recited together with the goddesses of the lotus petals, sixteen words together with the goddesses of the cremation grounds, and forty-eight words together with the names of the heroes (*vīra*) and heroines (*vīreśvarī*) of the six wheels are to be recited.

Here, the eight syllables of the four charnel ground squares are to be recited during the twelve entries in the center; they are empowered by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) at the time of the transits (*saṃkrānti*) beginning with Capricorn. As for the remaining sixty syllables, through the empowerment of the five mandalas, the *mālā-mantra*—together with the presiding deity of that mandala empowered by the vital breath—is accomplished by yogins. They attain accomplishment quickly through the differentiation of the flow, having entered the movements of the *rasas*, and having entered the six states of existence. This is the rule regarding the Blessed One’s "Vajra of All Ḍākinīs and Ḍākas."
Here, according to the conventional [truth], the placement of the *makara* and so forth corresponds to the *ka*-group and so forth in the *devīmālā-mantra*.
In that regard, there are twelve transition (*saṃkrānti*) steps as follows:
*oṃ āḥ hūṃ hoḥ haṃ kṣaḥ haṃ kṣamalvya kālacakre vajre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. During the *makara* transition, there is a recitation (*japa*) of fifty-six and a quarter breaths.
Thus, during the transit into Aquarius (Kumbha): *oṃ durdānta e damaka jātijarāmaraṇāntaka svā vacce huṃ huṃ phaṭ*;
during Pisces (Mīna): *oṃ trailokyavijaya haḥ vacce huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*;
and during Aries (Meṣa): *oṃ mahāvīreśvara aḥ vacce huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Oṃ vajrabhairava haḥ vace huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus in Taurus;
Oṃ vajrakāya aḥ vace huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus in Gemini;
Oṃ vajragātra haṃ vace huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus in Cancer.
Oṃ vajranetra aṃ vajre huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus at the Leo [transit];
oṃ vajraśrotra hā vatre huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus at the Virgo transit;
oṃ vajraghrāṇa aḥ vatre huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—at Libra.

Oṃ vajrajihva kṣā vace huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—this is for Scorpio. Oṃ vajradanta kṣa vatre huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—this is for the transit of Sagittarius. One should recite these together with the breath; thus is the mantra-recitation of the Knowledge-Mandala for the twelve transits.
Oṃ vajranakha klū vacce ghi vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus, one should perform three hundred and forty-nine recitations on the Makara-Earth mandala.
Likewise, in all cases, for the sixty mandalas:
Oṃ vajrakeśa khū vacce gṛ vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus [one recites] over water.
Oṃ vajraloma gṛ vastre khu vastra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus in fire.
Oṃ vajrābharaṇa ghī vajre kla vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus in wind.
Oṃ vajrahāsa 'dā vatre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus in the space-maṇḍala. In the cremation ground, the Blessed One is the Means (upāya); therefore, there is an absence of a second seed-syllable.
Thus it should be understood everywhere in the space-mandala.
*Oṃ vajragīte 'da vastre huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is the breath-recitation (*śvāsajāpa*) in the jar-space-mandala.
*Oṃ vajranṛtya ghi vajre kla vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is for the wind.
*Oṃ vajrāyudhaka gṛ vajre khū vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is the breath-recitation (*śvāsa-jāpa*) for fire.
*Oṃ vajrakrodhādhipate khu vatre gṛ vastra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is for water.
*Oṃ vajraḍāka kḷ vastre gho vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is for the earth mandala.
Thus the *ka*-group is concluded.
Then, in the sign of Pisces (*mīna*), on the earth mandala, one performs the breath-recitation (*śvāsajāpa*) with: *oṃ vajraḍākinījālaparivṛta clū vace jhi vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
In the water [mandala], [one recites]: *oṃ śīghramāgacchāgaccha chū vatre nṛ vastra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

Oṃ! By the command of Vajrasattva, all Māras, obstacles, and Vināyakas; Kinnaras, Kiṃpuruṣas, Garuḍas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Pretas, Kumbhāṇḍas, Apasmāras, Kṣetrapālas, Vetālas, Pūtanās, wicked Nāgas, Grahas, and so forth—those who cause minor calamities through all fevers and all diseases, and who delight in harming all sentient beings: Jaḥ! Having quickly drawn them in again and again with my hook, Ja vastre chu vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ! [They are cast] into the fire-maṇḍala. Oṃ! Those who have gone to the upper direction—Oṃ 6 10 15 20.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, [regarding the section on] Knowledge: "JHĪ VAJRE CLA VAJRA HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ"—thus, in the wind [mandala], for those who have gone to the eastern direction:

"OṂ [draw them] repeatedly, Ā VASTRE HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ"—thus, in the cremation ground within the space mandala. Then, for ARIES (Meṣa): "OṂ [draw them] repeatedly, TRA VACCE HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ"—thus, in the cremation ground within the space mandala, for those who have gone to the southern direction.

Oṃ, having drawn in again and again those who have gone to the northern direction, *jhivatre c vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—thus [it is] in the wind. Oṃ, having drawn in again and again those who have gone to the western direction, *nṛ vatre chū vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—thus [it is] in fire. Oṃ, having drawn in again and again those who have gone to the northwestern direction, *chu vajre jū vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—thus [it is] in water.

Oṃ, having repeatedly drawn in those who have gone to the direction of Īśa: *cla vajre jhī vastra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Thus, the breath-recitation (*śvāsajāpa*) is performed upon the earth mandala. Then, at the moment of the Taurus ascendant (*vṛṣalagna*): Oṃ, having repeatedly drawn in those who have gone to the direction of Nairṛti: *ṭla vastre ḍhi vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Thus, the breath-recitation is performed upon the earth mandala. Oṃ, having repeatedly drawn in those who have gone to the direction of Agni: *ṭhū vatre ḍṛ vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Thus, [the breath-recitation] is performed in water.
Oṃ, having drawn in again and again those who have gone to the downward direction: *ḍṛ vajre ṭhu vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—thus [it is] in fire.
Oṃ, having drawn in again and again those who have gone to the mandala of space: *ḍho va ṭḷ vastra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—thus [it is] in wind.

Oṃ, having drawn in again and again those who have gone to the mandala of wind: *ṇā vajre huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—thus [it is] in the mandala of space, in the cremation ground; this is the breath-recitation (*śvāsajāpa*).
Then, in the sign of Gemini: *oṃ tejomaṇḍalagatān ākṛṣyākṛṣya ṇa vajre huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is the breath-recitation (*śvāsajāpa*) in the cremation ground within the space-mandala (*ākāśamaṇḍala*).
In the sign of Cancer: *oṃ udakamaṇḍalagatān ākṛṣyākṛṣya ḍhi vajre ṭḷ vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is [the recitation] in the wind.
In the sign of Leo: *oṃ pṛthvī...* [recitation].

Having repeatedly drawn in those situated in the maṇḍala with *ḍṛ vajre ṭhū vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, [one recites] *oṃ kāmadhātugatān ākṛṣyākṛṣya ṭhu vastre ḍa vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ* over the fire; *oṃ rūpadhātugatān ākṛṣyākṛṣya ḍḷ vaje ḍho vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ* over the water; and [the recitation of breath] over the earth-maṇḍala. This is the breath-japa.
Then, in the Cancer ascendant (*karkaṭalagna*): *oṃ arūpadhātugatān ākṛṣyākṛṣya plū vastre bhi vastra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is the breath-recitation (*śvāsajāpa*) on the earth mandala.
*oṃ kāyadhātugatān ākṛṣyākṛṣya phū vastre bṛ vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is in the water.
*oṃ vāgdhātugatān ākṛṣyākṛṣya bṛ vacce phu vastra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is in the fire.
Oṃ cittadhātugatān ākṛṣyākṛṣya bhī vatre pla vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ—this is the breath-recitation in the wind [mandala], at the cremation ground in the lion [position].

Oṃ pañcaskandhagatān ākṛṣyākṛṣya mā vatre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ—this is the breath-recitation in the space mandala, at the cremation ground in the lion [position]. Oṃ pañcadhātugatān ākṛṣyākṛṣya ma vastre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ—this is the breath-recitation in the space mandala, at the cremation ground in the lion [position].

Oṃ, having drawn in and drawn in those who have entered the five sense faculties—bhi vajre plu vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus in the wind. Oṃ, having drawn in and drawn in those who have entered the five objects of the senses—bṛ vajre phū vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus in the fire.
Oṃ, having drawn in and drawn in those who have entered the five organs of action—phu vastre bṛ vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus in the water.

Oṃ, having drawn in and drawn in those who have gone to the objects of the five sense organs—*bṛ*, *kṛṣyākṛṣya*, *pḷ*, *vastra*, *bhī*, *vajra*, *huṃ*, *hūṃ*, *phaṭ*—this is the breath-recitation (*śvāsajāpa*) upon the earth mandala. Then, at the maiden ascendant (*kanyā-lagna*), Oṃ, having drawn in and drawn in those who have gone anywhere at all—*tula*, *vastra*, *dhi*, *vastra*, *huṃ*, *hūṃ*, *phaṭ*—this is the breath-recitation upon the earth mandala.

Oṃ, in the great cremation ground, on the ground blazing with vajra-fire, cause them to fall, cause them to fall—*thū*, *vajre*, *dṛ*, *vastra*, *huṃ*, *hūṃ*, *phaṭ*—this is [the recitation] in water.
Oṃ, with the vajra-noose, bind, bind all [the enemies] in their arms; *dṛ vastre 'thu vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—thus, in the southeast.
Oṃ, with the vajra-chain, restrain, restrain all [the enemies] in their feet; *ghī va la vastra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—thus, in the northwest.

Oṃ, you who delight in causing minor afflictions to the body, speech, and mind of all sentient beings, O Great Wrathful One, pulverize, pulverize them with the vajra; *nā vacce hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—thus, in the cremation ground within the mandala of space.

Then, at the Libra ascendant (*tulā-lagna*), one performs the recitation of breath (*śvāsajāpa*) in the cremation ground within the mandala of space with the mantra: *oṃ vajrakhaṅgena nikṛntaya nikṛntaya na vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
In the wind [mandala], [one recites]: *oṃ vajratriśūlena bhedaya bhedaya dhi vastre tla vastra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
In the fire [mandala], [one recites]: *oṃ vajrakartikayā hana hana dṛ vajre thū vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Oṃ vajrabāṇena bindha bindha thu vatre dṛ vajra huṃ huṃ phaṭ—this is the breath-recitation (*śvāsajāpa*) over water.

Oṃ vajrakīlakaiḥ kīlaya kīlaya va vastre ghī vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—this is the breath-recitation over the mandala of the earth. Then, at the moment of the scorpion ascendant (*vṛścikalagna*): Oṃ vajramudgareṇā-koṭayākoṭayasla vastre śi vastra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—this is the breath-recitation over the mandala of the earth.

Oṃ vajracakreṇa chedaya chedaya—pū vastreṣu vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ; thus for water. Oṃ vajrakuntena bhindha bhindha ṣṛ vajre—pūvajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ; thus for fire. Oṃ vajradaṇḍena tāḍaya tāḍaya śī vajre sla vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ; thus for wind.

*Oṃ vajraparśunā chinda chinda kā vajre huṃ huṃ phaṭ.* Thus, one performs the breath-recitation (*śvāsajāpa*) in the cremation ground within the sphere of space (*ākāśamaṇḍala*). Then, when the sun enters Sagittarius (*dhanurlagna*), [one recites]: *Oṃ, having divided [the earth] into three and a half crores of fragments, offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to all the spirits (*sarvabhūta*) upon the ground of the cremation ground! Ka vajre huṃ hūṃ phaṭ.* Thus, one performs the breath-recitation in the sphere of space in the cremation ground. *Oṃ, by means of the vajra-hand-drum (*vajraḍamaruka*), O Vajra-Ḍākinī, cause [them] to come, cause [them] to come! Śi vajre slū vastra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ.* Thus, [one performs it] in the wind.

Oṃ vajraḍākinībhyo mārakāyikānāṃ rudhiraṃ nivedaya nivedaya bṛ vajre-pūvajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus in fire. Oṃ pañcāmṛtahāriṇībhyaḥ pañcāmṛtaṃ nivedaya nivedaya-pu vajre-ṣu vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus in water. Oṃ sarvavajraḍākinīsahitaḥ sarvasattvānāṃ śāntikaṃ pauṣṭikaṃ rakṣāvaraṇaguptiṃ kuru kuru sla vastre-śī vajra huṃ hūṃ phaṭ—thus on the earth mandala; this is the breath-recitation (śvāsajāpa).

Thus, one should recite the *mālā-mantra* every day a number of times equal to the breaths of the wheel (*śvāsacakra*). Now, the *Sarvabuddhasaṃvara* is described by means of the avadhūtī breaths and the five wheels of body, speech, mind, and gnosis:

"Here, those breaths which existed in the central channel at the time of birth—sixty-four thousand and six hundred—by groups of three, there arise the goddesses situated in the middle of the gates through the power of the sky (space).

With one foot, the Mother of the Three Worlds is born, holding a curved knife and a scalpel; Kālacakra, embraced by the digit of nectar-bliss, stands in the *ālīḍha* posture upon the sun and moon. (39)
Regarding the passage beginning with "ye śvāsā" (those breaths):

here, at the time of birth, those breaths of the child which occurred in the central channel (*madhyamā*)—namely fifty-six and a quarter breaths, or five hundred and sixty-four—constitute the eight wheels (*cakras*). By virtue of the earth and sky, they are located at the centers of the gates [in the sequence] 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 6, and 10, as stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*.

Among these breaths, there are eight breaths possessing the nature of body, speech, mind, and gnosis (*jñāna*), distinguished by wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*); these are the eight goddesses on the petals of the womb-lotus.

In this context, there are no skull-bowls; rather, there are eight heroes through the purification of form in the earth-wheel, eight through the purification of perception in the water-wheel, eight through the purification of feeling in the fire-wheel, eight through the purification of mental formations in the air-wheel, eight through the purification of consciousness in the space-wheel, and eight through the purification of primordial wisdom in the eight cremation grounds.
Thus, there are forty-eight [heroes] in the six wheels of the secret place, navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown.
Thus, there are two in the nostrils, two in the eye-apertures, two in the ear-apertures, and two in the apertures of the tongue, mouth, and crown—this is the host of goddesses.

Thus, fifty-six [deities] are produced by the remaining single foot; she is the Mother of the Universe, the progenitor of the three worlds, holding a curved knife and a conch-shell in her hands. Embraced by her, who stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture as the digit of nectar, the Blessed One Kālacakra stands upon the sun, moon, Māra, and the afflictions, embraced by her in the *ālīḍha* posture as the supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*).

The seed-syllables (*bīja*) of these breaths are to be stated by the passage to be spoken later, beginning with "the eight measures starting with *la*," and for that reason they have not been written here.

The meaning of *nīna* here is as follows: at all times, the yogi should cultivate the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the central channel; through its entering and exiting, until it becomes stable and enters the state of retention (*kumbhaka*) at all times, the yogi then becomes a possessor of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) through the recitation of the breath (*prāṇajāpa*). This is the rule of the Blessed One.
Thus, one should recite the mantra whose limbs are inseparable and which is joined with the breath; this is the previously mentioned *vajrapada* in all tantras, namely, "the mind."

Although the recitation of breath (*prāṇajapa*) is devoid of the utterance of mantras and the counting of beads, it is nevertheless called *japa* because of the inhalation and exhalation of the vital breath. || 39 ||

Now, the purification of the seats of the deities (devatāsana) is described, both externally and internally: The five [elements], the three [qualities], the moon, and the sun; the days of the week, the seven [planets], and the full [moon]; according to the influence of the objects and qualities, these are the seats. Furthermore, there are other seats consisting of the four oceans and the movements, as well as the sun and the moon.

Other seats consist of the black [night] and the white [day], the seven planets, the sun, and the full moon. The doors, the seven, the sun, and the full moon are the seats of the sun and the moon in their even and odd positions.
Regarding "five" and so forth:

here, for the Solitary Hero (*ekavīra*), the seat is the moon; the parrot is the sun; and passion (*rajas*) is [the fifth]. Since these five elements possess the nature of wisdom (*prajñā-dharma-svabhāva*), they are the five objects which are the qualities of the moon; these are the moon-seats of Locanā and the others, extending up to the space element (*ākāśa-dhātu*).

Due to the influence of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*), there are three sun seats for Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi, which constitute the great form (*mahārūpa*) consisting of the four elements. Because Vairocana is the abode of the four constituents (*caturdhātu*), he has a moon seat; because he is of the nature of gnosis (*jñāna*), he has a sun seat. As for the formlessness (*arūpitva*) of feeling and the other [aggregates], it is according to the statement: "Thus there are five moon mandalas and four sun mandalas, through the distinctions of the equality of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*."

Thus, the *Samāja* consists of nine aspects by virtue of being the support for the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), qualities (*guṇa*), and sense objects (*viṣaya*). Just as in the womb there are the consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) and so forth of one born, so it is likewise with the deities. Furthermore, there are four wrathful seats (*krodhāsana*) known as the "movements of the waters" (*abdhicāra*). Due to the increase and decrease of debt and interest regarding the sun’s *ravikādhana*, these are the solar seats of the wrathful ones.

Thus, with the spies of the wrathful deities (*krodha*), the *Samāja* consists of thirteen elements. Likewise, there are seven days (*vāra*) as the seats of the sun (*sūryāsana*), and twelve full [days] as the lunar mandalas (*candramaṇḍala*); this third *Samāja* consists of nineteen elements. There are twelve dark full-moons (*kṛṣṇapūrṇā*) which are new moons (*amāvāsyā*) each year, and twelve white full-moons (*śvetapūrṇā*) which are full moon days (*paurṇamāsī*); thus, there are twenty-four seats of the sun and moon for the Leader (*nāyaka*). Depending on his family (*kula*), he is either the Moon or the Sun;
thus, the *Samāja* of the deities consists of twenty-five elements according to the distinction of their supports (*ādhāra*).
Furthermore, among those, seven other seats are added, making thirty-two seats;

these consist of the five aggregates (*skandha*), the four elements (*dhātu*), the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*), and the eleven wrathful deities (*krodha*). Thus, the *Samāja* consists of thirty-two aspects.

Again, regarding the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) on even and odd steps: the departure is the sun-seat (*sūryāsana*) and the arrival is the moon-seat (*candrāsana*); by this, the *Samāja* consists of thirty-four aspects.

Thus, the *Ṣaṭkāra* (Sixfold) is so called because, according to the principle that just as in the womb there is a meeting of the elements (*dhātu*) as the support and the supported, so too is there a gathering of the deities; thus, the *Samāja* is sixfold. (40) Now, the purification of the seats (*āsanaśuddhi*) in the *Tricakrasaṃvara* is described: The spokes are the movements of the moon and sun; the lotus petals, the four doors, and the corners are the seats. Furthermore, the spokes are doubled, and those very seats consist of the sun and moon. The spokes are full when the spokes are equal or unequal; the seats are the movements of the four oceans, whether in the sun or in the full moon, according to the family (*kula*), or in the *saṃpuṭa*. (41)
Regarding "the spokes" and so forth:

here, in the three wheels (*tricakra*), there are twenty-four spokes. These are the previously mentioned lunar movements—the elements, the Vedas, the qualities, the hands, and the moon—which amount to twenty-five. Of these, twenty-four become the spokes of the three wheels;
the twenty-fifth belongs to the deity of the lotus garland (*padmavala*) and is the seat of the *preta*.

The spokes (*ārā*) are eleven, namely the six tastes (*rasa*), the two [Yugas], and the moon; among them, three are located on the petals of the lotus in the womb (*garbha*), while the remaining eight abide in the form of corpses (*śava*) in the eight cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*). "Spokes" refers to the supports (*ādhāra*), and "corpses" refers to the vehicles of the Goddesses.
Thus is the *Tricakrasaṃvara*.
Furthermore, by dividing them into former and latter [groups], the movements (*cāra*) are doubled, resulting in seventy-two seats for the goddesses in the *Mahāsaṃvara*.
Thus is the *Ṣaṭcakrasaṃvara*.

In the *Māyājāla*, there are twenty-four full [movements] as the white and black lunar and solar seats; likewise, the seven days (*vāra*) are the seven solar seats, and the eleven solar movements (*arkacāra*) are the eleven solar seats.
Now, regarding the moon seats according to the division of states (*bhāvabheda*): thus, there are thirty-three and forty seats;

some [count] the moon and sun seats as before by way of even and uneven [divisions], making forty-five seats. In the second [section], "the movements of the oceans" (*abdhicāra*), there are four sun seats or moon seats according to the division of *ravikā*, which arise through the division of the state of the body (*kāyabhāvabheda*).
Thus, there are forty-nine seats for the deities in the third *māyājāla*.
Just as the elements (*dhātavaḥ*) serve as the support for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of a child in the womb, so too are they established externally and in the supreme state (*para*).
Such is the rule regarding the purification of the *samāja*, *māyājāla*, the three wheels (*tricakra*), the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*), and the *saṃvara*.

In those tantras, the Leader (nāyaka) resides in the sun because his nature consists of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), or he resides in the moon because his nature consists of wisdom (prajñā). Vairocana resides in the lunar mandala within the dharma of compassion (karuṇā) according to his family (kula); thus, by the power of wisdom and compassion, he is the Leader. Alternatively, in the union (saṃpuṭa) of non-dual wisdom and compassion, he is established as Kālacakra and so forth, the Primordial Buddha (Ādibuddha), because he is without parts (niranvaya). || 41 ||

Now, the purification of the faces of the deities beginning with Vāyu is described: for Vāyu, there is one face consisting of touch; by the power of the subsequent qualities, there is a second face consisting of the organ of sealing (mudraṇāsya); and for Śikhin (Agni), there is a third face consisting of both form and touch, as well as a face consisting of sealing. For Payas (Varuṇa), there is a fourth face consisting of touch, form, and taste, as well as a face consisting of sealing. For Avani (Earth), there is a fifth face consisting of the qualities beginning with smell and ending with touch, as well as a face consisting of sealing. ||42||
Regarding the passage beginning with "of the wind-knowledge" (*jñāna-vāyoḥ*) and so forth:
here, the faces of the deities such as Wind are twofold; one is through the purification of the objects (*viṣaya*), and the second is through the purification of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*).

Among these, for the element of wind, one face consists of the quality of touch (*sparśa-guṇa*), while the second is the seal (*mudraṇa*) consisting of the quality of sound (*śabda-guṇa*). By that, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is the seal of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Thus, for air, there is one face consisting of touch, while the second is a face of sealing located on the head due to the influence of another quality, not merely in the place of the mouth. Similarly, fire has two faces according to the nature of its objects, form and touch; by that same quality, it has a third face of sealing through sensation (*vedanā*), which is also the sealing of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Likewise, the three faces of water consist of touch, form, and taste; the fourth face is sound, characterized by space, which is the seal (mudrā) of that [water]. Thus, by way of this designation, the sealing of consciousness (*vijñāna*) occurs through the quality of the objects—smell, taste, form, and touch—which constitute the four faces of earth.
Therefore, it is established that for the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is the seal. || 42 ||
The void is fivefold, and the face of space is the sixth, being the seal of the [other] faces. Thus, by the power of qualities, there is one face of the gnosis element through the six voids;
mixed with four, it bestows the fruit of equal bliss; with five, it is wisdom and method in three and two; with ten faces, it is fourfold by the power of the three types of qualities. (43)

Because of the statement, "The fivefold void is the great void of five syllables," the face of the space element (ākāśadhātu) is the sealing of the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha); thus, by the power of its qualities, it becomes the sixth face of the knowledge element (jñānadhātu). Therefore, by means of the six voids, that [knowledge element] possesses six faces, and its sealing is the aggregate of consciousness; such is the rule of the seals (mudrā), which is pure by virtue of the qualities of the elements and objects.
Now, one [element] is mutually mixed with four, bestowing the fruit of equal bliss; the pentad is mixed with two and three.

In this context, when the wind element—which consists of the single quality of touch—is conjoined with the earth element—which consists of the four qualities beginning with smell and is sealed by the quality of space—then there arises the yoga consisting of wisdom and method, which bestows the fruit of equal bliss.

Likewise, fire, which consists of the two qualities of touch and form and is sealed by the quality of space, and the water element, which consists of three qualities and is sealed by the quality of space, become a pentad when mutually combined;
thus it is a pentad for both earth and wind.

Thus, the elaboration regarding wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), which are the front and back, or the left and right, joined with one another, has been explained in this internal chapter by such statements as: "Wisdom and means are bone and flesh, along with water and blood; fire is indeed urine," and so forth. This is the rule. Furthermore, the division of the three other qualities is stated by the verse beginning with "threefold," etc.

In this context, all elements (*dhātu*) possess the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. By means of these, all the elements—the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) from smell up to the *dharmadhātu*—are the faces of the elements; thus they have six arms.

In this way, by virtue of the threefold qualities, there are twelve faces and fourfold wisdom and method, [arranged] front, back, left, and right. [The rule is: the right [face] is above. [Note: The Sanskrit text contains several lacunae and corruptions. The Tibetan translation provided here clarifies the intended meaning. **Yoginītantra-ādi-sphuraṇa-mahoddeśa**, Chapter [X], Verses 42–44. * "Qualities" (*guṇa*) is not present in the Tibetan version. * "And in this way" (*evaṃ ca*) is not present in the Tibetan version. * "Fourfold" (*caturdhā*) is not present in the Tibetan version. * "Body and mind" (*kāyacitte*) is missing! * [Fragmentary notes regarding textual variants]. **Translation:** In this regard, all elements possess the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Through these, all the elements—the six objects of the elements, beginning with smell and ending with the *dharmadhātu*—constitute the faces of the elements; therefore, they have six arms. Thus, by the power of the threefold qualities, there are twelve faces and a fourfold arrangement of wisdom and method, [distributed as] front, back, left, and right. The rule is that the right [face] is above.

In the *Samāja*, the sign for all [deities] is as follows: through the purification of the white channel (*śukranāḍī*) and the bone, the vajra, lotus, and wheel are on the right; while the dust (*rajas*), blood, and flesh are represented by the vajra-bell, jewel, and sword on the left. This is the rule of the *Samāja*: here, whichever deity’s own sign appears on the palm of the first right hand, in its place the vajra-sign takes its position.
Thus is the convention of the *Samāja*.
Just as in the assembly, when the Buddha who enters the center goes to the place of Akṣobhya, such is the rule regarding the symbols as well.

Thus, between the five-faced and six-faced [deities], there is the eleven-faced; between the consciousness and gnosis elements, there are the five-faced and six-faced; and between the five-syllable Great Void and the dot-void six-syllable, these two are again mutually dependent, resulting in the thirty-two-faced assembly—this is the rule. (43)

Now, the purification of the faces and so forth according to the division of time is described: due to the division of the junctions (*sandhyā*), there are four [faces]; the threefold face is due to the division of the ascendant (*lagna*); it is of three colors according to the value of the ascendant; the division of the arms occurs from the half-ascendant (*lagnārgha*); even the unequal embrace becomes equal in body and mind during the limbs of the junction; on the front and back, there is the embrace of the three faces, the flavors, and the arms; the union with Wisdom (*prajñā*) occurs in the middle limb; for even the laughter and so forth constitute the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) at the junction of the watches (*yāma*). ||44||
Regarding the passage beginning with "sandhyā" and so forth:

according to the rule that "in this system, the Lord Vajrī is proclaimed as day and Prajñā as night," the Lord is four-faced and eight-armed through the division of the watches (*prahara*) and the junctions of the watches (*sandhyā*), from midnight until midday; likewise, Prajñā is also four-faced and eight-armed from midday until midnight.

The embrace is equal during the day and night at midday; it is also unequal during the morning and evening twilights due to the decrease or increase of day and night. In that regard, in certain instances, the Lord has five faces and ten arms while the Goddess has three faces and six arms due to the increase of day;
due to the increase of night, the Goddess has five faces and the Lord has three faces, as established by such [traditions]. This is the first purification of Kālacakra.
Thus, the second is stated, beginning with "threefold," etc.

Here, there are twelve zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn (*makara*). Among them, the signs of Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces have faces that are black, red, and white respectively—due to the divisions of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*—and possess three colors according to the distinction of the ascendants (*lagna*) for the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*). Likewise, the faces of Aries, Taurus, and Gemini have red, white, and black colors due to the divisions of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas* for the Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajra*). And the faces of Cancer, Leo, and Virgo have white, black, and red countenances due to the divisions of *sattva*, *tamas*, and *rajas* for the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*).

The ascendants beginning with Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius—distinguished by the qualities of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*—are of yellow, red, and white colors, respectively, according to the Wisdom-Vajra.
Due to the meaning of the ascendant, there is a division of arms into three colors;
for each pair of the six [faces], they correspond respectively to the left and right, starting from the root face.
Thus, the Lord Kālacakra alone has twelve faces and twenty-four arms.

Here, regarding the union of the previously mentioned deities—whether with one face, four faces, and so forth—the embrace that occurs between those with unequal or equal [faces] is the meeting (*melāpaka*) of the preceding twilight with the subsequent twilight at the junction of the limbs (*sandhyāṅga*). As for the mutual embrace of those with three faces and six arms, that occurs at the junction of the limbs in the middle, namely the midday twilight and the midnight twilight.

Thus, "in body and mind" (*kāyacitte*) uses the locative case in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*), because of the distinction between the state of the body and the state of the mind (*bhāvabheda*).

Thus, at the morning and evening twilights, there is an embrace in the Yoginītantra through the union of the dissimilar (*viṣamasamāpatti*), whether it be between the one-faced and four-faced [deities], or the one-faced and eight-faced, and so forth; whereas in the Yoga[tantra], there is an embrace between those with equal faces and arms during the equal times of day and night—this is the rule according to specific times. Thus: "O, there is no watch (*prahara*) nor darkness born from the interval; there is no [time] of the midnight twilight. In the *Vimalaprabhā*, he is the knower of auspicious and inauspicious, the knower of time, the knower of the pledge (*samaya*), the pledge-holder (*samayin*), and the all-pervading lord.
"Knowing the faculties of sentient beings, knowing the proper time, and skilled in the three liberations"—this is the rule regarding the Blessed One’s *Nāmasaṅgīti* [of Knowledge].
Now, the Action Tantras (*kriyātantra*) are explained: "Wisdom," and so forth.

Here, the union with wisdom (*prajñāsaṅga*) is the Yoginī Tantra; the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) is also in the Yoga Tantra. The union of the preceding and following junctions—the conjunction at midday and midnight—is established in both Tantras. The laughter and so forth occur during the junctions of the watches (*yāma*).

In this context, the *tantra* intended for the first watch [of the night] is the *hasita-tantra* (the tantra of laughter); that intended for the third watch is the *īkṣaṇa-tantra* (the tantra of gazing); at the junction of the fifth watch is the *stana-sparśa-tantra* (the tantra of touching the breasts); and at the junction of the seventh watch is the *pāṇigrahaṇa-tantra* (the tantra of taking the hand). Thus, the *tantra* is fourfold. For what reason?
Because here, for those who have mastered the totality of wind (*vāyu-kṛtsna*), the bliss of vibration (*spanda-sukha*) arises merely through the laughter of wisdom (*prajñā-hasita*).
For those who have mastered the totality of fire, happiness arises from liberation; for those who have mastered the totality of water, happiness arises from the touch of the breast;
for those who have mastered the totality of earth, happiness arises from taking the hand in marriage.
Thus, there are sixteen levels of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), from Akaniṣṭha down to the Brahmakāyika; their detailed exposition will be explained in the forthcoming *Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*.
Therefore, the established tenet (*siddhānta*) is that the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) consists of sexual union (*dvandvayoga*).
The abiding of those free from passion occurs everywhere in the formless realm. || 44 ||

Now the entry into the nature of the body is described: the nature of Kālacakra necessarily enters into the red and yellow limbs of Prajñā; the nature of Prajñā [enters] into the white limb of the Vajrin, which resembles a dark cloud, starting from the left and the front.

By means of the nature of Prajñā, the excellent body becomes divided: the left and front limbs are gentle, while the right and rear limbs are fierce; thus is the nature of the Supreme Lord of Jinas divided.
Regarding the phrase "the limb of wisdom" (*prajñāṅga*) and so forth:

here, when one enters the red element of fire, which is the limb of wisdom, or the yellow element of earth, the nature of Kālacakra necessarily arises as the union of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*). This is because that wisdom which exists in meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) is what grasps the state of means, and that means is what grasps the state of wisdom. Through that grasping of the state, bliss arises; by that, the white water-element of Kālacakra enters into the red limb of fire and becomes of equal flavor (*samarasa*).
Thus, on the earth element, the black [wind] becomes equal in taste with the yellow-bodied wind;
likewise for the deities in the south and west.
Thus, the state of wisdom (prajñā) enters into the white-bodied water element as the state of passion (raktabhāva).
In the left side of the Vajrins, within the dark-colored wind element of the deities, there is the yellow earth-nature which enters from the east;
likewise, there is the mutual conjunction of green and blue [elements] above and below.

Thus, it becomes divided by way of the nature of Prajñā in the excellent body of all beings: the left and eastern parts are gentle (*saumya*), while the right and rear parts are fierce (*raudra*). In the same way, the state of the Supreme Lord of Jinas is divided; thus it is established that the upper part is gentle and the lower part is fierce. || 45 ||

The preeminent family of the Victor’s assembly, inseparable from wisdom (*prajñā*), attains a dual nature; and when separated from the Lord of Wisdom, the group of Yoginīs is likewise fixed in the intermediate directions.

[In this] chapter, [there is] the great exposition on the radiation of the *Yoginītantra* and so forth: the pair consisting of the right and left, as well as the east and west, by means of the forms of the Sun and Moon; and likewise black, yellow, blue, and green, situated in the sky and the underworld. (46)

Thus, "the preeminent assembly of the Victor’s family, born of wisdom, consists of the white element (śukradhātu), characterized by water, wind, and space; that which, through the division of the body, becomes the dust-element (rajodhātu) divided by its states of being, having the nature of earth, fire, and gnosis (jñāna)—thus the preeminent assembly of the family has two natures. This host of deities is both red and white, and it is also left and right, yellow and black, and east-west and up-down, blue and dark green.
In this way, the group of the Wisdom Consorts (prajñā) possesses a dual nature divided according to their status as consorts; they are fixed in the intermediate directions:
in the south-west and north-east they are white and red, while in the north-west and south-east they are black and yellow—this is the rule for their dual nature.

Likewise, the assembly of Means (upāya) is situated in the cardinal directions, and the assembly of Yoginīs consists of Locanā and the others, as well as Tārā and the others, situated in the intermediate directions.

Thus, there is a pair on the right and left, and likewise on the front and back, consisting of the sun and the moon; and black, yellow, blue, and green, situated in the sky and the underworld—such is the rule for the host of deities.

The Prajñās are red for those of the white family, white like the moon for those of the red family, likewise yellow for those of the yellow family, black for those of the excellent golden (yellow) family, and dark blue for those of the black family; furthermore, they are multicolored for those of the blue family and green for those of the green family, and are said to be likewise blue. Thus indeed, the deities of the goddesses should be known as situated in the direction of their own respective families. ||47||

Therefore, from embracing a family of another, the wisdom-consorts (*prajñā*) of white means (*upāya*) become red; the wisdom-consorts of red means likewise become white like the moon; the wisdom-consorts of yellow means are black in color; the wisdom-consorts of black means are like excellent gold; and the wisdom-consorts of blue means are multicolored (*viśvavarṇā*). Furthermore, the rule is that the wisdom-consorts of green means are blue, and so it has been stated.

The accomplishment of the ritual action (*kriyā*) arises from embracing a woman of another family; there is no accomplishment of the ritual action through embracing one of one's own family, because of the contradiction of an action directed toward oneself. Indeed, for those whose nature is the female organ (*bhaga*), pleasure is not produced by contemplating the female organ; likewise, for those whose nature is the male organ (*liṅga*), pleasure is not produced by contemplating the male organ.
Therefore, in the *Kālacakra*, women of one's own family do not serve as the Wisdom (*prajñā*), because of the contradiction of an action directed toward oneself.
Now, regarding the mind’s grasping of its own nature by way of the principle of a reflection in a mirror, that very point is examined here:

in this case, the reflection of a man in a mirror does not resemble [a woman] possessed of breasts and hair, nor is the reflection of a woman devoid of breasts and the female organ; therefore, there is no self-nature [in the reflection], and likewise, there is another contradiction.
In this case, whatever marks are on the left arms of the original image (*bimba*) are found on the right arms of its reflection in the mirror;
likewise, that which is the left face becomes the right. (The reading "uttara" should be understood according to the Tibetan version.)

"O, Re Sig" (some say)—this additional phrase is found in the *Vimalaprabhā*. That [the deity] has the same color as oneself (*svābhā*) does not occur; therefore, the meditation on the maṇḍala circle is performed through the embrace of another family (*parakula*), according to the system of the *Kālacakra*. Furthermore, in another tantra: "By whatever state the minds of men are joined, they attain identity with that, just as a gem assumes all forms. [This is because] those words which have their hands scattered about are not capable of critical analysis.

Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), in the cultivation of the image of emptiness, there is no conceptualization of a formal image (*rūpabimba*). Therefore, there is no "self-luminous" [nature] whatsoever;

in every aspect and every color, there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) for either cognition (*jñāna*) or the cognizable (*jñeya*), as both are devoid of the conceptualization of atoms or substantial entities.

Consequently, the cultivation of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is the task regarding things such as pots, cloths, carts, and armies; it is not partial, being free from all worldly conventions. This is the Madhyamaka tenet established by reasoning in the *Tattvapaṭala* of the Mantra system. || 47 ||

For the Lord of Jinas proclaims the Prajñātantra from the eastern face, and again from the western face he speaks the Yogatantra permeated by yoga; from the left face he speaks the Kriyā and so forth, and indeed from the eastern face he speaks the Yogācāra;
again from the western face he speaks the entire Madhyamaka, and from the white face he speaks the pure Vaibhāṣika. (48)

The Lord of Jinas proclaims the Ṛgveda from his western mouth, the Yajurveda from his left face, the Sāmaveda from the right face in the lineage of the Supreme Hari, and the Atharvaveda from his eastern face;

furthermore, from his front face he proclaims the Kola-tantra, from his rear face the Gāruḍa and Bhūta-tantras, from his left face the Siddhānta, and from his right face, which resembles the rising sun, the Viṣṇu-dharma. (49)

From the back [face] arises Sadyojāta; from the supreme white face, Vāmadeva; from the left, Pratiṣṭhā; and from the right, Aghora is Vidyā. Furthermore, from the wind-faced [face], Māruta and Brahmaśānti arise; from the empty-faced [face], Śūnya and Īśa. These were expanded by the Lord of the Three Worlds for worldly purposes as the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and the other, Kali Yugas, according to the distinctions of the back face and so forth. ||50||

The Great Chapter on the Pervasion of the Yoginī Tantras and so forth: From the eastern face, the Lord of Jinas proclaims the Sarvāstivāda; from the southern, the Sāmmitīya; from the western face, the Sthāvira; and again from the northern face, the Mahāsāṃghika. From the eastern face, humans are emanated; furthermore, from the other [northern] face, animals are emanated. From the southern face, the spirits and gods are emanated; and from the supreme white face, the hell-beings and asuras are emanated. (52)

The radiation also proceeds from the heart-cakra through the eastern face, from the navel-cakra through the western face, from the enjoyment-cakra through the right face, and from the innate-cakra through the left face; it occurs everywhere.

From the center of the faces of the cakras, existence within the body reaches its dissolution, as does the entire threefold world, through the various aspects of the mouth of this progenitor of the Victors. (53)

For just as water flows from the moon-stone toward the moon due to its non-conceptual nature, so too does the Dharma of the Omniscient One flow into the world by relying upon the body of the Lord of Jinas.

Just as that water, the Dharma, becomes of a single taste within the receptacle of the seed-element, it becomes manifold among sentient beings through the purification of their minds, owing to the power of their previous karma. (54)

In this abode of the three worlds, there is no lack of the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) that accomplishes all aims; yet, due to the power of unwholesome fruits of their karma, sinful beings do not perceive it residing within their own minds.

It is not the fault of the wish-fulfilling gem that all beings experience both inauspicious and auspicious results; rather, when a being is pure, he becomes the Lord of Victors (Jinendra)—what need is there for any other Victor?
That sprout which is born proceeds toward destruction from the state of having been born; once it has perished, that very seed-king becomes its progenitor once again.

As for that which was prior, the statement that "it has died" is due to its having become something else, not because it has been born in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Since he has come from the Void, the One Endowed with Ten Powers (*daśabala*) proceeds upon the earth by means of that moment of bliss.

In this world, a moment of innate bliss is attached only to bliss; it is not attached to any other state. Therefore, those aggregates (*skandhas*) that have arisen from it become its progenitors for that moment of bliss once again.
From that pure [moment] arises another dharma, and from that yet another, until the pure [result] emerges—just as roots, branches, flowers, and fruit grow from a seed planted in fertile soil. (57)

Earth, water, fire, and air, as well as the subtle particles (*aṇu*) of taste and supreme taste, are of six types; [the first five] are each lacking one of the sense objects beginning with smell, while the last is devoid of sense objects and is perceivable by gnosis.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the forms of desire are formless; Yama, Yami, and the Moon, and finally the *dharmadhātu*, are always present in all their aspects, serving everywhere as the support for the innate, imperishable bliss. (58)

Mutually becoming aggregates, the objects and subjects are one another's enemies; these ignorances are fivefold, mutually attached, and immersed in the movement of flavors within a moment of pleasure and pain.

Existing in every form on all sides, they do not delight in the virtues of others; established as indivisible vajras, there is again the mutual striking of earth and the other elements, and thus other states have returned to their primary condition. (59)

And by means of those [elements], the Great Kālacakra manifests his manifold emanation-activities through the radiating vajra-flames for the sake of asuras, gods, and humans dwelling in the desire realm;

through the enjoyment-forms in the sky for the sake of the sons of the Victors and the Arhats; through the portions of emptiness, the entire triple world is the totality of emptiness; and through the winds, it is the totality of wind. (60)

By means of the expanded portions of fire, the entire world becomes water; by the portions of water, the entire world becomes earth; and through the elements arising from the sphere of the earth, it becomes the intrinsic nature of all things.
One should perceive this [world] as a single self, equal on all sides to space, upon the pure ground. Thus, the body of the Buddha does not die, because it has the nature of singular bliss. (61)
From these five aspects, which are in fact one, this perfect awakening consists of twenty aspects; furthermore, from that, it takes on the nature of manifold illusions.
Its single moment bestows the fruit of equal bliss, having no other nature of karma; herein, the means is the non-emitted moment, which is the innate state for entering the *dharmadhātu*.

The infinite Buddha-fields, the elements with their immeasurable qualities beginning with space, the threefold existence consisting of arising, persistence, and destruction, all sentient beings within the six realms of rebirth, the Buddhas, the wrathful deities, the gods and others whose hearts are compassionate, and the Bodhisattvas together with their consorts—this entire wheel belongs to each and every Śambhu, the Victor who is venerated by the three worlds. (63)
Therefore, from the forty-eighth verse up to the sixty-third verse, sixteen verses are easy to understand. || 48–63 ||

The Great Chapter on the Pervasion of the Yoginī Tantras and so forth. Now, the purification of the ten aspects within the body is described: Hair, skin, blood, flesh, as well as sinews, bones, marrow, and the channels; within those [channels] are the winds such as *prāṇa* and the others, with the movement of the sun and moon throughout the center of the wind.

Consciousness is in the center of the moon, embraced by all phenomena like a stainless jewel; it is the state of supreme nectar, the pervasive unstruck sound (*anāhata*), characterized by the non-duality of existence and non-existence. (64)

"Body hair," and so forth. Here, body hair and head hair are the space element (*ākāśadhātu*); skin and flesh are the wind element (*vāyudhātu*); blood is twofold and is the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*); sweat and urine are the water element (*toyadhātu*); bone and marrow are the earth element (*pṛthvīdhātu*); and the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*), such as the *prāṇa* and others, are the gnosis element (*jñānadhātu*). Rāhu’s tail is the gnosis-vajra (*jñānavajra*); Rāhu is the mind-vajra (*cittavajra*); the sun is the speech-vajra (*vāgvajra*); and the moon is the body-vajra (*kāyavajra*).
The movement of these four occurs everywhere within the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Consciousness is in the center of the moon, in the center of the semen; like a stainless jewel or crystal, it is embraced by all phenomena through the application of proximity.

The non-duality of existence and non-existence is like an illusion, the reflection of emptiness; herein lies the imperishable bliss, the state of supreme nectar, the pervasive unstruck sound (*anāhata*)—this is the rule.
There is tenfold purity regarding the body. || 64 ||

Now, those elements are purified by means of the ten stages (bhūmis): the ten stages beginning with *loma* (hair) and ending with *candra* (moon), which pervade the entire body, have been taught; likewise, the other six groups beginning with *la* (the labial class) always bestow the fruit of equal bliss upon yogins.

Therefore, for the sake of liberation, yogins who have taken refuge at the feet of their Guru must seek this [truth]; there is no other Buddha whatsoever who, being devoid of a body, is all-pervasive and the giver of liberation. 65.

Regarding "hair and so forth": here, hair and body hair are Pramuditā; skin and flesh are Vimalā; blood is Prabhākarī; lymph-fluid is Arciṣmatī; bone and marrow are Sudurjayā; the channels and vital breath are Abhimukhī; the fire of time and the element of passion are Dūraṅgamā; Rāhu is Acalā; the sun is Sādhumatī; and the moon is Dharmameghā. Through the nature of passion, darkness, and dust, there is the conventional entry [into the path]. Thus, from hair up to the moon, these are present throughout all things and have reached the state of being free from obscuration.
Regarding those ten stages (*bhūmi*) which have been taught, they are further said to consist of six groups (*ṣaḍvarga*) of consonants and vowels.

Among them, the *ka*-group is the Joyous (*pramuditā*). Likewise, in numerical order, there are the six groups: *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ta*, and *sa*; and [the vowels]: *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, *ha*, *aḷ*, *o*, *ar*, *e*, *a*, *la*, *u*, *ṛ*, *i*, *a*, *haḥ*, and *am*.
In this way, even in reverse order, the groups beginning with the long vowels are the stages of wisdom (*prajñā-bhūmi*).
These always bestow the fruit of equal bliss upon yogins.
Therefore, it is the Lord’s injunction that they must be sought by yogins who have taken refuge at the feet of their guru and who move within the *avadhūtī*, for the sake of liberation.

There is no other Buddha whatsoever who, being free from the body, is all-pervasive and the bestower of liberation; rather, in this context, the elements of the body, when unobscured, are the givers of Buddhahood and the givers of liberation. || 65 ||

Sentient beings are Buddhas; there is no other great Buddha here in the world-system, for their immeasurable existence is severed through the propitiation of them. Because they are free from conceptual construction, they belong to the three realms. In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said: "A yogi who commits an act of hostility toward the Gnosis indeed goes to the great Raurava hell and others; therefore, even when one's own mind is pure, one should not act in opposition to those people who are ignorant or wise. (66)

O King, when one has attained a connection with sentient beings, there may arise for those wandering in saṃsāra either a virtuous mind such as pure loving-kindness and so forth, or a mind of hatred, passion, and the like. Even the bodhicitta—whether it be of two kinds, that which is moving or that which desires to move—is always a demonic mind if it lacks the setting out toward liberation and is devoid of the vow.

The Māras cause unrest within the abode of the three worlds, while the Bodhisattvas bring peace; yet even the Lord of Māras, when devoid of wisdom, becomes a source of supreme terror, whereas the one endowed with wisdom is the sole Teacher. The Māras perceive the intent of others as their own demonic purpose, while the Protectors perceive it as the thought of bliss. Therefore, through the power of the Buddhas, the entirety of the three worlds endures for infinite time.
Even that measure of the world-system which has been described by the Victors is for the sake of human beings who possess knowledge;
for the Buddhas, there is no fixed measure due to the power of their innate body, which is indeed one yet manifold.
They always manifest a measure according to the capacity of sentient beings in the field of karma; if the gods were to say, "This is my own desire-measure," they would be called atheists.

By which the Lords of Jinas are born, by the power of which they emerge from the womb day after day, and by which they become perfected in an instant, free from flux and devoid of vibration or non-vibration—having abandoned that Buddha-activity which is devoid of equal bliss, whoever meditates upon another emptiness as Buddhahood, for him even the innate bliss remains far away for many millions of aeons. (70)

One does not obtain grapes from a neem tree, nor ambrosia from poison; one does not find a lotus from a Brahma-tree, nor the bliss of nirvāṇa from emptiness. Accomplishments do not arise from virtue or non-virtue, nor heaven from the slaughter of living beings in sacrifice.
The supreme state of Śiva is not attained by the restraint of the senses, nor is the immovable bliss of the syllable spoken by the Omniscient One obtained from the Veda or from an impure mind.

O King, the evil mind of sentient beings arises when they are possessed by the hosts of Māra; yet even that which is devoted to merit and wisdom and bestows happiness is always possessed by the Bodhisattvas.

Because they proceed toward Nirvāṇa through the power of the blissful samaya, having struck down the Māras of the afflictions, the Māras therefore create manifold obstacles for them at every moment of the day. (72)

First, the *karmamudrā* should be served for the purpose of increasing this innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) of the Victor; she who is complete in body, face, feet, crown-protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*), and all limbs, and fully endowed with the marks and minor characteristics [as described in verses 66–76 of the *Yoginītantrādispharaṇamahoddeśa*].

Therefore, she is of the nature of the sun, resembling a flash of lightning, the mother who generates unchanging bliss (*acyutasukha*), illuminating the *vajra*, and having her body pervading the three worlds; thus, she exists as the *dharmadhātu* at all times in everything. (73)

These four mudrās, which grant the fruit of imperishable bliss, should be cultivated by the yogin. Through the application of the path of worldly passion for the celestial consort (*surataratigati*), whether in a village, a forest, a cremation ground, an impure or pure dwelling, a brothel, or a temple, and through the practice with women of high or low caste, by means of physical strength, pleasure, food, drink, and so forth—from this point, the nine stanzas following the sixty-fifth up to the seventy-fourth are easy to understand. || 66–74 ||

Now, when the image of emptiness has been seen, the attainment of the moments by yogins through the cessation of the vital winds is described: By the winds striking together, the lightning-flame melts the moon at the crown of the head. Whichever drop (bindu) has melted from that [moon] goes to the throat and heart; it is then obstructed at the navel and the secret place.

That vibration and fluidity of the drop which has reached the jewel of the vajra is completely obstructed at the tip of the banner. If that bestows the moment of the wisdom of Prajñā through the non-emission of the stream of drops, [that is the goal]. (75)

"By the winds," and so forth: when the primordial image (*prāgbimba*) has been seen, there occurs a collision of the ten winds through *prāṇāyāma*. By means of those ten [winds], such as *prāṇa* and *apāna*, which are colliding at the navel-center (*nābhikaṇikā*), the *caṇḍālī*—which is like a flash of lightning fire—arises; its crest is a ray of light. That crest causes the moon—the *bodhicitta* located in the place of birth—to melt at the head, that is, the forehead.

Whichever drop of *bodhicitta* flows from this [place]—having gone from the forehead to the throat, the heart, the navel, and the secret place—becomes arrested; by the power of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, the action-drop (*kāryā-bindu*) is arrested at the secret place. Likewise, the speech, mind, and gnosis drops (*vāk-citta-jñāna-bindu*) are arrested at the navel, the heart, and the throat. From this drop, that which is the clear fluid and the throbbing fluid is spoken of; therein, the fluid of the action-drop, having been arrested at the secret place, is firmly blocked at the tip of the vajra, at the mouth of the *liṅga*.

If one says that the blissful vibration of the moment of wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna) is caused by the non-emission of the stream of drops (bindu), then it is established that the knowledge of the action-seal (karmamudrā) is not the wisdom-knowledge. || 75 ||

Therefore, the Dharmadhātu bestows here the innate moment of bliss free from movement; having drawn in all the Māras of the afflictions who have entered the paths of the vital fluids, and having destroyed them, the yogi—having entered the path in this very life—attains supernatural powers, the stage of omniscience, and the status of a Guru of the three worlds, or else, through that very grasping, he passes away at death to another birth.

Therefore, from that cause which is the state of non-falling, the *dharmadhātu*—the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)—bestows here the moment of perfected bliss; by means of that, there is the supreme unchanging bliss of *mahāmudrā*, as well as the bliss of the *karmamudrā* and *jñānamudrā*, which is vibration, transitory, and the bliss of skillful means (*upāya*). This vibration is transitory and consists of the "child" (*bāla*) and the "mature" (*prauḍha*), just as mercury is "child," "youth," "old," and "bound. Likewise, the semen (*śukra*) is also "child," "mature," "old," and "obstructed" through the destruction of all obscurations.
Obstruction is called "impurity.

When that very *bodhicitta* moves upward and reaches the forehead, then that mind becomes a *tathāgata* just as it came. Having drawn [the mind] by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one [withdraws] all the two hundred and twenty [channels] that have entered the courses of the tastes and reside within the six mandalas of earth and the other elements.

Having thus destroyed the Māra of the afflictions, [the practice] bestows upon yogins who possess vigor in this life the twelve supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of the Omniscient One, as well as the glories of the twelve stages (*bhūmi*) to be described hereafter—the status of being the Guru of the three worlds, namely omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and so forth.

Therefore, when one who has attained yoga dies while having entered the path, he attains everything again through that very grasp or the force of his latent impressions (*vāsanā*) by means of another human birth; even if he lacks vigor, the rule is that he will attain knowledge by the end of seven births, provided he does not abandon his cultivation. || 76 ||

Now, the arising through the empowerment of the Bodhisattvas is described: The body-seal (*kāyamudrā*) is of two kinds: that which is devoid of qualities and of little being, and that which is free from sense objects; it is colored by passion for him and is a treasury of qualities. Furthermore, the speech-form (*vāksvarūpa*) is of two kinds:
black and white. The mind-seal (*cittamudrā*) is of two kinds: colored and delighting in the qualities of sense objects. [Their years] are clearly eight, two, five, five, two, and forty-five. (77)

Regarding the passage beginning with "she who is devoid of qualities" (*nairguṇyā*): here, the maiden who is "devoid of qualities" (*nairguṇyā*) is one who lacks the qualities of the *dharmadhātu* because she has not undergone emission (*acyavana*). She is of "limited nature" (*alpabhāvā*), meaning her body-element (*kāyadhātu*) is incomplete; she is one whose teeth have not fallen out, and this is the rule for an eight-year-old.
Thereafter, the second [type] is one whose teeth have fallen out, and this is the rule for those up to ten years of age.
