Thus, the body-seal (*kāyamudrā*) is one with an intact womb;

from the age of eleven years up to fifteen years, she is devoted to passion (*rāgānuraktā*). Another, a treasure-house of qualities (*guṇanidhi*), is the speech-seal (*vāṅmudrā*) of two kinds, lasting for another five years each—thus for eight years and two years, and then five years each.
Then, after forty years— meaning from the age of ten onwards for another forty years—
the mind-seal (*cittamudrā*) alone is devoted to the black state;
thus, she is a sixty-year-old woman.

Furthermore, another [type] is "empty of knowledge" (*śūnyaveda*); for forty years she is devoted to the white state (*śvetabhāva*), and having become old with wrinkles and grey hair, she remains so until the end of a hundred years. Thus, among these three, the body-seal (*kāyamudrā*) is extremely young, the speech-seal (*vāṅmudrā*) is extremely mature, and the mind-seal (*cittamudrā*) is extremely old.

Having avoided these three, an eleven-year-old girl who is complete in all auspicious marks should be protected by the royal preceptor, or by the consecrated king, or by other lords who have been consecrated. || 77 ||

As long as Ratneśa remains, the Mother of the Supreme Victor must be protected by yogins. At the time when Ratneśa has arisen, having drawn the mandala—the treasury of all qualities—the Great Chapter on the Emanation of the Yoginī Tantras and so forth proceeds. Through mantras empowered by the Buddha, he creates equal bliss; having established protection in the secret [lotus], one should taste the bodhicitta situated at the jewel of the vajra, together with the mantra. (78)
As long as Ratneśa exists, there is no passion (*rajas*) such that one might say "let it not exist"; therefore, she must be protected.

When the time has come for Ratneśa, having drawn the *maṇḍala* of Kālacakra—the treasury of all qualities—and having first thoroughly trained her, having consecrated her therein with the mantras of the Buddha’s empowerment and the six-syllable mantra through the Mañjuśrī-samādhi, and having likewise perfected that Prajñā, he emits the bodhicitta of equal bliss during the flow of the right channel. One should cause it to expand within her secret lotus together with the mantra, accompanied by the mantras of body, speech, mind, and gnosis.

Then, having performed the protection of her secret place with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the yogi should savor the *bodhicitta* located at the jewel of his own vajra; he gives that also to her, and taking from her lotus what is to be taken—the [fluid]—with his ring finger and thumb, he should savor it for the sake of all protection; this is according to this procedure. || 78 ||
In that [mandala], he who is the son of the Conqueror’s progenitor is Mañjuvajra; due to his preeminence in wisdom, he sometimes manifests as a daughter and is certainly the Mother of the Buddhas.

From him, by means of other three flowers, there is Jambhala holding a white lotus, Vajrapāṇi, and the other eight wrathful kings (krodharāja) possessing great supernatural power, who are located in the cardinal and intermediate directions with their respective eight flowers. || 79 ||

In that consecration (*ādhāna*), the son who arises is Mañjuvajra due to the predominance of wisdom (*prajñā*); if, however, a daughter arises due to the predominance of passion (*rajas*), then she becomes the locus of Viśvamātā.
Therefore, she is certainly the Mother of the Buddhas;
such is the ritual procedure for the empowerment of Mañjuśrī as Viśvamātā.
Therefore, regarding the phrase "with three other flowers":

if no embryo has been produced during the first menstrual period, then by drawing the mandala again and again with each subsequent appearance of the menses, one should emit the *bodhicitta* through other samādhis.
In this way, in the second [period], there is the manifestation of Lokeśvara as the "Bearer of the White Lotus."

In the third [circle] is the emanation of Jambhala; in the fourth is Vajrapāṇi. Regarding the sons and daughters, there is the empowerment of the sounds of Pāṇḍarā and Vasudhārā, as well as the Vajra.
Beyond those, there are eight wrathful kings (krodharāja) of great supernatural power, each situated in one of the eight directions, accompanied by their respective retinues.
Here, in the previous empowerment of Jambhala, there is the empowerment of the Uṣṇīṣa through the Uṣṇīṣa-samādhi;
in the place of Vāgvajrapāṇi, there is either Atinīlā, Śumbharāja, or Raudrākṣī.
Then, in the fifth dust-layer, Vighnāntaka is with Anantavīryā; in the sixth, Prajñāntaka is with Jambhī; in the seventh, Padmāntaka is with Māninī; and in the eighth, Yamāntaka is with Stambhī.

Then, in the ninth [petal], Mahābala; in the tenth, Mārīcī; in the eleventh, Acala and Cundā; in the twelfth, Ṭakkirāja and Bhṛkuṭī; and in the twelfth, Nīladaṇḍa and Vajraśṛṅkhalā—thus, in the intermediate directions, through the *samādhi* of the wrathful ones, there is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the wrathful deities within the womb.
Then, the thirteenth is the dust-element (*rajas*), which is again the first, just like the member beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*). || 79 ||

In that month, the menstrual flow (*rajas*) which arises indeed originates from Mañjughoṣa; for thirty years, with each flow, a Bodhisattva of great courage (*mahāsattvika*) manifests, though slightly diminished in his essence (*sattva*).
Then, for another thirty years, [beings] arise who are empty of the Vedas; and thereafter, other beings of little vigor (*alpavīrya*) appear once more. (80)

For during that month, whatever *rajas* (menstrual blood) arises, that very *rajas* originates from Mañjughoṣa. Thus, by taking that as his object of focus (*ālambana*), the yogin should emit the *bodhicitta*; that becomes the support for the embryo for twenty years. During each successive period of *rajas*, when there is a Bodhisattva—whether one, two, or more—he becomes a great vessel for the mother, though he is slightly deficient in the constituent elements of a sentient being (*sattvāṃśa*) until the forty-year mark, [the mother’s] up to twenty years.
And again, from that [state], another self of little vigor arises;
thus, for eighty years, there is the presiding over the embryo according to the divisions of the mother’s *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

Therefore, because the passion (*rajas*) in the womb has not obstructed the sense objects, there is no emission (*seka*) due to its destruction; according to the word of the Lord of Jinas, the consecration of wisdom (*prajñābhiṣeka*) should be given to one whose seed is not lost.

By seeking the qualities of earth, water, fire, wind, and space within those [consorts], this service to the Bodhicitta—which resides in the limbs of the Jina—becomes a performer of the welfare of sentient beings and yields great fruit. (81)

Therefore, the *rajas* in the womb is not obstructed regarding its function as the site for the embryo; without that, there is no infusion (*seka*) due to the absence of the seed of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). "Seed" refers to that which sprouts. However, the consecration of knowledge (*jñābhiṣeka*) should be given by the words of the Lord of Jinas to one whose seed is lost and who is aged, just as it is given to a monk; likewise, it is also given to a woman of wisdom (*prajñā*), just as it is to a nun. Thus, women of twenty years are excellent for the purpose of consecration and empowerment. In the same way, the qualities of the earth element are [perfected] over twenty years each; likewise, the qualities of water, fire, wind, and space are to be sought through the limbs of people until the age of one hundred.
This service to the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), through the generation of the bodhisattva, becomes one that accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings and yields abundant fruit. || 81 ||

Now the drinking of nectar is described: That fly which drinks the blood of the most excellent gods and men is *Amṛtekā*. [The nectar] has entered from the mouth of the secret organ (*chadi*) into the jewel of the vajra, not into the center of the lotus;

feces, urine, blood, and flesh have entered into the midst of the vomit as the supreme state of equal flavor (*samarasa*). This is the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*), taught by the Lord of the Three Worlds in all the tantras. (82)
Regarding the passage beginning with "the drinking of blood" and so forth:
here, in the external sense according to the *neyārtha* (interpretable meaning), it refers to a fly that drinks blood; however, according to the *nītārtha* (definitive meaning), it is the *avadhūtī*.
That which drinks the element of *rajas* at the time of emission for the most excellent gods and men is the immortal fly, the singular *avadhūtī*; the meaning is that she is "obstructed."

That which is the "used skin" externally is, in the definitive sense (*nītārtha*), the vomit that is the bodhicitta. From the secret mouth, it is the doctrine of the vajra-jewel; it has not entered the external lotus of wisdom.
Thus, the non-falling feces, urine, blood, and flesh—being of supreme equal flavor (*paramasamarasa*)—enter into the midst of the vomit without flowing. Being restrained, they become unobscured.

This is the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*), the non-falling five nectars, taught by the Lord of the Three Worlds in all tantras. It is not taught that external excrement and so forth lead to accomplishment. This is the rule regarding the nectar. || 82 ||

Now, the protection and consumption of the outer *samaya* is described: Whatever bliss has fallen into the *prajñā-dharmodaya* must be protected with effort; by means of that, any being whatsoever becomes a Bodhisattva in the family of the Victors (*jinakula*).

Therefore, the Rākṣasas who have become Māras consume him at every daily occasion. They teach that what is consumed, when joined with the flower of wisdom (*prajñāpuṣpa*), bestows the fruit of auspicious bliss. ||83||
Regarding the passage beginning with "wisdom" (*prajñā*) and so forth:

here, when a yogin performing the cultivation of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), if his unconfined *bodhicitta* falls into the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) of wisdom, then even though it has fallen into the source of phenomena of wisdom, that bliss must be protected with effort.
For what reason?

Whoever is released by that bodhicitta-samādhi becomes a bodhisattva indeed within the family of the Victors, increasing the lineage of the Sugatas; therefore, those Māras and Rākṣasas who consume semen as food devour that bodhicitta daily at the appointed time for those followers of the Sugatas who lack protection and are not in meditative equipoise. Furthermore, even men under the pretext of being yogins teach others—that is, to foolish people—that it should be consumed when joined with the "flower of wisdom" (prajñāpuṣpa) as a means to bestow the fruit of the bliss of Śiva, so that they may go to hell. || 83 ||

When the non-manifestation of the thunderbolt from the lotus has reached supreme bliss, and there is no contraction whatsoever until the empowerment of the Buddha occurs, then indeed the accomplishment of desire arises.

At that time, having entered through the thunderbolt and the lotus, the wheel of gnosis (jñānacakra) enters one’s own heart; having filled this dual body with rays of light, it makes it take the form of a wheel. || 84 ||

Then, by the Bodhisattva-mantrin, from the navel down to the vajra [tip], until no contraction occurs, the empowerment of the Buddha manifests in this way: when the accomplishment of desire arises, then indeed, having entered the heart of the Means (upāya) by the vajra-path and entered the heart of Wisdom (prajñā) by the lotus-path, one causes the circle of deities that has entered the heart of one's own *kulīśa* to take the form of a wheel; having filled these two bodies with rays of light, [one performs this]. || 84 ||

If this accomplishment were not present within the vajra-jewel situated in the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) endowed with wisdom, one would have to establish the entire family of the Victors in that which is joined with wisdom; furthermore, it is stated again: "Whosoever, being deceitful, desires the destruction of this Buddha-body, he shall be slain by the Vajra-holder. (85)
If this accomplishment were not to occur, then one should take the *bodhicitta* residing in the *vajramaṇi* with the ring finger and thumb and consume it.
Likewise, that very [substance] which has come outside the lotus of the *prajñā* should be consumed by both.

Furthermore, for the sake of protection, one should establish the entire family of the Victors (*jinakula*) within the *dharmodaya* of the *prajñā*; one should place the six syllables on the forehead and other parts, and the six limbs on the heart and other parts.
"Endowed with wisdom" means endowed with passion (*rajas*). When the bodhicitta, which is the goal, is protected, great merit arises.
Furthermore, it is stated: "This bodhicitta is the Buddha-body;

whoever, being a deceitful partisan of Māra, desires its destruction, shall be slain by the Vajrī, that is, by Heruka. This is the rule for the protection and consumption of the *samaya* of bodhicitta. || 85 ||
Those many mantras of a cruel nature that were proclaimed by the Lord of the Three Worlds—may they all never cause fear or the destruction of the faction of Māra for living beings.

Furthermore, those other heretics who delight in the field of battle against the Smṛtis and act as destroyers [of the Dharma], may those [mantras] be employed by the Son of the Supreme Victor for the protection of living beings. || 86 ||

In this Mantra system, those many mantras of a cruel nature that have been proclaimed by the Lord of the Three Worlds—all of them generate fear for the destruction of the faction of Māra among living beings;

they are never [meant] here for Māras who are the authors of the Smṛtis and are devoted to the field of battle, nor for other heretics who are slayers. These [mantras] are to be employed by the supreme sons of the Jina for the protection of living beings against that faction, because it is the cause of fear for the destruction of their Dharma, and not for the purpose of taking their lives. (86)

The ḍākinīs preceded by Vajra are not to be petitioned by the wise for the destruction of animal-like beings; they were emanated by the Lord of the Three Worlds for the sake of protecting sentient beings.

Therefore, they protect [the practitioner] at every daily occasion and cause hatred toward the one to be subdued (sādhya). Indeed, through the power of the ritual action, the sādhya goes to his death; this is the Māra of the practitioner. ||87||
In this *Yoginītantra*, those Vajraḍākinīs are not to be invoked by Buddhist scholars for the purpose of slaying ignorant, ordinary people;
why?
Because they were emanated by the Lord of the Three Worlds into the world-system for the sake of protecting sentient beings.

Therefore, those who possess supreme compassion protect the worlds, yet they cause hatred toward the practitioner who deceives the world. Now, if when an act such as killing has been performed, the victim dies through the power of that rite, the practitioner—due to the conceit of thinking, "This Māra was slain by me"—goes to hell because of that minor action. Thus, being free from possessiveness and free from the conceit of "I," one does not perform minor actions; one regards all sentient beings just as one regards oneself. (87)
O Master!

[In the *Mahoddeśa* on the radiation of the *Yoginītantra* and other systems, verses 85–89: The minds of men are entirely enamored with trivial spells (*kṣudravidyā*) due to the power of inauspicious fruits. With a mind seized by the hope, "This spell will bring the entire triple world under my control in a single instant," they enter hell, having abandoned the gift of knowledge. Wealth remains behind, and one's own wife falls under the power of another—alas, what a practice of false dharma! (88)

In this world, the minds of transmigrating beings are everywhere enamored with base sciences due to the power of unwholesome fruits; their hearts, seized by the hope that "this science will bring the entirety of the three worlds under my control in a single moment," enter hell, abandoning the gift of knowledge. When death arrives, the wealth becomes subject to others, and one's own wife becomes subject to others, becoming attached to another man.
Alas! How perverse is the engagement with unrighteousness among those wandering in saṃsāra! || 88 ||

Thus ends the first chapter, the Mahoddeśa on the Emanation of the Yoginītantra, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the *Mūlatantra*.

(2) The Mahoddeśa on the Determination of the Purity of the Four Bodies: Having bowed to the Body of Great Bliss, which is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither; which is completely free from the four extremes.
Extracted by Mañjuvajra from the *Ādibuddha* which is without lineage,
the characteristics of the four Buddha-bodies are here set forth.

This Sahaja-body is the Dharmakāya; it is neither wisdom nor means. This Sahaja-body is indeed the very nature of wisdom and means; free from darkness through the distinction between gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is this Sambhogakāya, which, like a reflection, performs the welfare of manifold beings. Furthermore, for the sake of maturing sentient beings, it becomes the Buddha-Nirmāṇakāya. || 89 ||
Regarding "not wisdom" and so forth:
here, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the white fortnight consisting of fifteen digits (*kalā*); the black fortnight, which is the waning of the lunar digits, is the means (*upāya*).
Thus, the white is night and the black is day.

Therefore, the sahajakāya is neither wisdom nor method; this sahaja-body of the Buddhas is thus neither existent—the white side—nor non-existent—the black side, which is the absence of parts. Because existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory, there is no union between them, nor is it of the nature of neither. Furthermore, without these two sides, the white and the black, that innate bliss does not exist.
Thus, the sixteenth digit, purified of the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), is emptiness; it neither exists nor does not exist.

By the words "Prajñā" and so forth, it is called the *sahaja* body possessing the nature of gnosis (*jñāna-dharminī*) in the *Vimalaprabhā*, because for yogins it is characterized by the outflow (*niḥṣyanda*) from the imperishable fourth state (*turya*).

Thus, it is established that the neuter is the innate body (*sahajatanu*). Here, the perfection of one's own welfare becomes the *dharmakāya* for the sake of the perfection of the welfare of others, through the cessation of deep sleep;
and that indeed consists of wisdom and means, being free from darkness due to the distinction between gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

In this context, "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the apprehending mind of the yogi, while "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is the knowledge of others' minds, which is the object of apprehension characterized as the knowable.

Thus, the apprehending mind is wisdom (*prajñā*) because it is free from conceptual construction; for yogis, the means (*upāya*) is the non-apprehended mind, which is the imagined nature characterized by compassion.
Through this distinction between the apprehender and the apprehended, the Dharmakāya—whose very essence is wisdom and means—is the performer of the welfare of others.
And that [sound] arose from the innate (*sahaja*);

thus, the outflow (*niṣyanda*) is the innate at the navel, while the maturation (*vipāka*) is at the heart in the wheel of dharma (*dharmacakra*). This very body of dharma (*dharmakāya*) is the body of enjoyment (*saṃbhogakāya*), acting for the benefit of many sentient beings like a reflection for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others.

Here, whatever past or future form is seen by the divine eye as having the nature of a reflection and being translucent, the sound that issues forth therein is the echo, which is the *saṃbhogakāya*, the very essence of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*).
Through the divine ear, divine cognition is the grasper, and the echo is the grasped;

by means of that, one knows the enumeration of past and future times—namely, "in such-and-such an eon, such-and-such an age, such-and-such a year, such-and-such a month, such-and-such a fortnight, such-and-such a day, and so forth, such-and-such a being arose, and such-and-such will arise.

By this, beings are to be disciplined. Through the exhaustion of the dream state, the effort of the person (puruṣakāra) is at the throat; it is the Saṃbhogakāya for those whose vital energy flows upward.
For the sake of maturing sentient beings, this [Buddha] becomes the *saṃbhogakāya* and again the *nirmāṇakāya*, consisting of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*).
Although it is one, it appears as many through the display of various emanations for the sake of sentient beings;

thus, through the perspective of ultimate reality (*vivṛti*), there is the union of the one and the many as wisdom and skillful means, while through the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), there is the contradiction between the one and the many.

And that [body], through the exhaustion of the waking state, is the stainless *nirmāṇakāya* at the forehead, the great jewel *Ratnaketu* who displays all forms (*aśeṣarūpasandarśī*)—thus, according to the *Nāmasaṃgīti* (9.24), there is one innate [body]. That very same [innate body] is fourfold as the *dharmakāya*, *sambhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya*. || 89 ||

That single Vajrasattva became Heruka, resembling a cloud at the end of an aeon, for the sake of maturing the fierce ones; he became Ratneśa, the Victor of the Samaya, for the sake of the happiness of the deluded; he became Kamaladhara for the sake of passion in those who suffer; and he became Amoghasiddhi, with a sword in his lotus-hand, for the sake of destroying obstacles. (90)
That very same one previously mentioned, this unique Vajrasattva, resembling a cloud at the end of an aeon, black Heruka, became *vaṃ*;
by means of the nature of non-falling (*acyutadharma*), that other consciousness becomes Heruka,
and he is the emanation of Vajrasattva for the sake of maturing the fierce ones.

And that Vajrasattva became Vairocana, the Victor of the Samaya, for the sake of maturing those who are deluded; he became Ratneśa, the Source of Jewels, in another form, for the sake of giving to those who suffer. And that Kamaladhara became Amitābha, the Delighter, for the sake of passion in those possessed of passion, through the non-falling dharma—that other sensation which removes all suffering. Through the non-falling dharma, that other perception is the giver of non-falling bliss.

And he became Amoghasiddhi, with his lotus-hand holding a sword, for the purpose of destroying obstacles; those other formative factors (*saṃskāra*) which, through the quality of being unshakable (*acyuta-dharma*), render the mind free from obscuration and utterly destroy the obstructions of Māra and so forth, are the purification of the five Buddhas. || 90 ||
Furthermore, O friend, there is no "graspable.
Moreover, O friend, there is no "other-conceived" (*parakalpita*).
Furthermore, O friend, there is no "divine" (*divya*).

[Chapter on] the Determination of the Purity of the Four Bodies, etc., verses 89–91. Now the five elements are described: From Hatred she became Viśvamātā, resembling the fire of universal destruction; from Delusion she became she known as Locanā; through Supreme Compassion she became Māmakī;

from Pride she became she known as Pāṇḍarā, a treasury of all virtues; and from Jealousy she became Tāriṇī. These two, Viśvarūpā and [Viśvamātā], along with the objects and subjects, and all others, came into being. || 91 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "from hatred" (*dveṣāt*) and so forth:

here, through the destruction of ordinary hatred (*prākṛtadveṣa*), the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)—which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the Mother of the Universe (*viśvamātā*) in all her aspects—became Vajradhātvīśvarī, the Vajraḍākinī.

Likewise, through the destruction of delusion (*moha*), Locanā arose from great delusion (*mahāmoha*) by means of supreme compassion; and Māmakī arose from the destruction of pride (*māna*) for the sake of great pride (*mahāmāna*).

From the destruction of passion (*rāga*) through Great Passion (*mahārāga*), she became Pāṇḍarā, the treasury of all qualities and the Savior; from the destruction of envy (*īrṣyā*) through Great Envy (*maheṣya*), she likewise became [Locanā]. Thus, the element of space is one, the element of earth is another, the element of water is another, the element of fire is another, and the element of wind is another. This definition of the elements is established as the "unfallen bliss" (*acyutasukha*) from the perspective of the unobscured image (*nirāvaraṇabimba*). These two, the Universal Form Kālacakra and the Universal Mother, are Wisdom and Means, become a single fusion (*ekalolībhūta*).

All others became objects and subjects: the odors and so forth were those objects (*viṣaya*), while the ears and so forth were those subjects (*viṣayin*); the speech, hands, and so forth were others, as were the actions of the organs of action and so forth.
Thus: "It has hands and feet everywhere; it has eyes, heads, and faces everywhere;
it has ears everywhere in the world, and stands encompassing all. This is Vajrasattva.
Thus: "He who knows himself and knows others, who is all, belonging to all, the foremost person, who has transcended worldly comparisons, the supreme lord of knowledge—he is to be known.
Likewise: "Siddhārtha, whose resolve is accomplished, who is free from all conceptual constructions."
"The non-conceptual, inexhaustible realm, the supreme, undecaying dharmadhātu"—this is the rule concerning the characteristics of the Gnosis Body (*jñānakāya*) in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*. (91)

O, from the *Satyataḥ* (bDen Pa Las), in the *Vimalaprabhā*: Now, the various dwellings of the Buddhas according to the inclinations of sentient beings are described—[the Buddha] dwells by means of compassion within the wombs (*bhaga*) of the Vajra-women, whose nature consists of the five aggregates of gnosis, for the sake of maturing those beings who have not established the rules and are devoid of merit;
as for why the Blessed One dwells in Śuddhāvāsa and other such realms, it is for the sake of providing a sign (*nimitta*) for the Śrāvakas.
The stability in the syllable *mevaṃ* is for the purpose of establishing those who are supremely disciplined in the higher [state]. ||92||
"Five," and so forth.

Here, that which is the descent into the womb, the grasping of the five aggregates, and the movement for the sake of birth within the female womb by those free from the obscurations of afflictions and the like, is for the purpose of maturing ordinary people—who lack merit and have not observed the prescribed rules—out of compassion.
As it has been said: "That which is the impermanence of the Buddhas, whose bodies are the vajra-body..."
What concern can there be for other beings, who are like the core of a plantain tree?
By such statements as these, those who hold to the doctrine of impermanence are brought to maturity.
Furthermore, regarding the arising [of Buddhas] in the Pure Abodes and other realms, this is for the sake of destroying the ego-clinging of those Śrāvakas who have attained the state of gods;
they are brought to maturity through the teaching that this state of godhood involves great suffering at the time of death.

The state of abiding in the syllable *evaṃ* within emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the teaching of the fourth body (*caturthakāya*) for the sake of establishing those of supreme discipline—such as Maitreya and others—as well as good servants and so forth, in the state of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambuddhatva*).

Emptiness is the nature of being empty; here, the knowable (*jñeya*), both past and future, is empty. The perception of that [emptiness] is the state of emptiness. It is profound because of the non-existence of the past and future, and it is vast because of the perception of the past and future.
Thus it is said: "The proponent of emptiness is the bull, whose roar is profound and vast."
The great-sounding conch of Dharma, the great drum of Dharma, the great battle-cry.
He is the one whose nirvāṇa is non-abiding, the Dharma drum resounding in the ten directions;
formless yet possessing form, supreme, with manifold forms that are not made of mind.
"The glory of the manifestation of all forms, the bearer of all reflections"—this is the rule concerning the Blessed One in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*. (92)
Of sentient beings.
For the sake of maturation, the threefold movement—distinguished as body, speech, and mind—arises invariably at all times for the Vajrī, both internally and externally.

Externally, it occurs in various locations; within the excellent body, it is the movement of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*); and on the mandala of the earth and other elements, it arises in the womb of the Vajra-lady of the All-pervading Lord. (93)
O Noble One!

[In the *Paṭala*, verse—] This is the Great Chapter on the Determination of the Purity of the Four Bodies and so forth: That mind which does not go toward sound and other objects, nor toward anything else, likewise remains in the syllable EṂ within the state of supreme bliss; this is the momentum of body, speech, and mind.

The one Vajrin is threefold, enveloped by objects and subjects as well as by the elements; he dwells in the three times and the three places, and has entered the three realms of existence for the sake of the welfare of manifold sentient beings. || 94 ||

In the Tantras, the statement "Thus have I heard" means that it has been understood by me as follows: The Vajrī [Vajrasattva], beginning with the melting of the moon, resides in the head, the lotus of the throat and heart, the navel, and the secret place;

he is in the bhaga of the Vajra-women. Having entered the Buddha-field via the three emissions of the drop (*bindu*) upon reaching the other's lotus, that Blessed One should be recognized here by the yogins. || 95 ||

By the power of his vows and qualities, through states such as tranquility and freedom from passion, and by the force of latent impressions produced in previous births, they see him as one and yet as many, situated within the mandala.

With a single purpose expressed in infinite languages, he enters the hearts of living beings according to their respective natures; situated in the mandala, he goes for alms to wander among those who remain stationary, for the sake of their merit. (96)
Proclaiming at all times the threefold true Dharma—pertaining to the past, future, and present—for the hungry ghosts, asuras, nāgas, gods, humans, and those of noble India, Tibet, and so forth;

establishing the entire triple world upon the path through their respective languages, this speech of the Omniscient One bestows the fruit of equal bliss, whereas the language of the gods (Sanskrit) would not do so. 97.
Even for the Buddhas, she is unapproachable; yet the illusory emanation of the Buddha, possessing immeasurable qualities, manifests herself within the abode of the three worlds like Indra’s net.

Distinguished by various states, she enters the respective minds of the Victors, gods, and humans. Among these, the phenomena that arise are like the sky reflected in water; their appearance here is born of delusion. (98)
For the Vajra-body of the Victor is in every aspect inaccessible to objects and sense-faculties; the Vajra-speech accomplishes the Dharma through the sounds of the hearts of all sentient beings;

and the Vajra-mind of the Vajra-holder, which is the nature of the consciousness of sentient beings pervading the entire earth and the grasper of phenomena, is that very same Jñāna-vajra, like a stainless gem. (99)

The six beginning with generosity and the four are the ten powers said to bestow the fruit of equal happiness; their pure means are the supreme tenfold [perfections] at the end of the jar, which is the full mind.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*: "The destruction of the māras of knowledge and the afflictions is indeed 'intoxication' (*madana*); Hara, Vajravṛndra, Drumā, and so forth are the six mudrās; the six voids are the progenitor of the three worlds; knowledge and discernment are one. (100)

The wheel is transparent on all sides; "the three worlds" is bliss; the jewel is passion for that very [bliss]; the lotus is the destruction of the afflictions; the vajra is the body of great gnosis, for it is indeed indivisible; the sword is the cutting away of ignorance. Furthermore, those six families which are produced by these [five] should be understood in this way: the aggregates, elements, sense-faculties, and so forth, are of equal taste like space. (101)
That in which the form of birth reaches its end is called the Great Form; that in which the suffering of saṃsāra reaches its end is called Great Sensation;
that in which the perception of saṃsāra reaches its end is the Great Vajra-perception; and that in which the increase of saṃsāra reaches its end is indeed the Vajra-conditioning. 102.
That in which the states beginning with waking reach their dissolution is called *vijñāna*; that in which the state of ignorance reaches its dissolution is the very *jñāna* of the Sage.

These supreme and excellent Victors, Vairocana and the others, are sixfold as the six families (*ṣaṭkula*); others are the divisions of the six elements: earth, fire, water, wind, space, and peace. (103)
That Locanā in whom all delusion goes to its destruction is the Earth; that Māmakī in whom all pride goes to its destruction is Water;
that Pāṇḍarā in whom all attachment goes to its destruction would be Fire; and that Tāriṇī in whom all envy goes to its destruction is Wind. (104)
She in whom all hatred goes to its destruction is Vajradhātvīśvarī; she in whom all envy goes to its destruction is the Imperishable Mother of the Universe.
He who perceives form, both seen and unseen, in the mind and indeed in the sky, possesses the eye [of the Buddha]; he who hears sound clearly from afar possesses this great ear of the Jina. (105)
That beautiful nose of the Lord perceives every scent that produces supreme bliss; and that tongue always tastes the nectar of its own moon, which bestows happiness.
[In the *Paṭala*:

"The Great Chapter on the Determination of the Purity of the Four Bodies and so forth"—] That Vajra-body faculty always removes the touch of the vajra from all sides; and that mind which enters into equal bliss through the application of wisdom and means—that is his *dharma*. (106)

These Bodhisattvas, divided into six types, are the objects and subjects; all these excellent Victors, together with their consorts, are the sixfold objects beginning with form (rūpa) and so forth, pervading everywhere. They are transparent, unborn, unceasing, producers of supreme bliss, untainted, and accessible through gnosis. Within the three realms, there is no other object of apprehension; they are accessible through the doors of the sense faculties of the entire world. (107)
Therefore, the fifteen stanzas following the ninety-second are easy to understand. (93–107)

Thereafter, that very hidden account is expanded upon: In this regard, the exceedingly powerful Jambha performs the summoning of knowledge (*jñānākṛṣṭi*) and its entry; Stambha effects its binding through the power of supreme bliss, as well as the honoring of pride (*māna*).

Vajravega brings about the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) within the wheel of knowledge (*jñānacakra*). Thus indeed are the Vajra goddesses established in their fixed roles within the body of the Tantra for the yogins. (108)
"Jñāna," and so forth.

Here, indeed, in the meditation on the mandala circle, having first accomplished the *samayasattva*, the practitioner of mantra must then perform the attraction, entry, binding, and pleasing of the *jñānacakra* (wisdom-circle), bringing it into a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*).

The attraction is performed with the "vajra-hook" using the syllables *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*; the entry with the "vajra"; the binding with the "vajra-noose"; and the pleasing with the "bell. [This is done] in the east, south, and—

Regarding the fact that in the Yoginītantras it is proclaimed everywhere that the Wrathful Kings stationed at the western and northern gates [perform their functions] with the Vajra-Ḍākinīs, that very point is now explained in terms of the internal (adhyātman): "He performs the summoning of gnosis here in the body, and again, he is exceedingly powerful. In the context of the young woman, "gnosis-being" (jñānasattva) refers to the semen; its "summoning" is spoken of in the language of intentional terminology (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*). He effects the piercing of the multitude of winds, such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and brings the *bodhicitta* to fullness at the crown of the head—this is the meaning.

Regarding its entry: *Jambha* (the subduer) causes the entry of that [fluid], which has been transformed into radiant energy (*tejas*), into the throat, heart, navel, and secret lotus in the form of a drop of liquid;
thus it is called *stambha* (paralysis), as the earth element (*pṛthvīdhātu*) binds that drop and does not allow what has arrived to depart with excessive speed due to the power of supreme bliss.

*Mānaka* (the measurer) is the water element (*toyadhātu*); the clear fluid of the drop, having reached the secret lotus and the *vajramaṇi*, is called *spanda* (vibration). Due to the power of unchanging bliss (*acyutasukha*), the water element brings satisfaction and produces coolness in the body—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, for the sake of ascending from that place, Locanā and the others awaken that very outflowing bliss (*niṣyanda-sukha*) by means of the previously mentioned vajra-songs.

Then, for the sake of the outflow, Locanā impels it at the navel; Māmakī, for the sake of maturation (*vipāka*), at the heart; Pāṇḍarā, for the sake of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), at the throat; and Tārā, for the sake of purity (*vaimalya*), at the head.
Great bliss, thus aroused by these and other means, having attained purity, renders all the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields free from obscuration.

Thereupon, the state of omniscience arises for yogins; it does not arise through a conceptualized maṇḍala nor through the songs of the yoginīs. This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) found in all tantras, both in its concealed (*saṃvṛti*) and its revealed (*vivṛti*) forms. || 108 ||

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated: "Nīladaṇḍa performs the striking of the Māras of the Jñānakula within the abode of the three worlds; Acala, like the fire at the end of an aeon, performs the binding; the exceedingly powerful Ṭakki performs the pinning; Stambha himself performs the immobilization that brings their power to the ground; and Uṣṇīṣa performs the destruction of their magical powers (*ṛddhi*). Thus the wrathful goddesses are revealed as fixed in their respective roles, as before. (109)

Then, for the sake of maturing the *pretas*, there was an emanation; likewise, for the protection of Indra and the other gods in the cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as for the maturation of the *nāgas*, the entire family of hooded serpents was projected by the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (*vajrin*); and for the maturation of the *daityas*, there was also an emanation of those with the faces of great dogs and so forth. (110)

Then Nīladaṇḍa and the others perform the activities of the action-faculties, such as coming and going in space, having performed the striking and so forth of Māra and his hosts; thus, having conquered all the members of Māra’s army by means of the power of the four forms of fearlessness, the Tathāgata sets the Wheel of Dharma in motion—this is the rule regarding the previously mentioned characteristics. (109–110)

Everything for the sake of the benefit of sentient beings, possessing various excellent qualities, as well as whatever else exists—the pervasive emanation of the Lord extending to the end of the elements—should be understood as being within one’s own body.

Thus, the tantras and mantras belonging to the various families arise from the distinction between the yoga of the yoginīs; and therein, both these two types—the mundane and the supramundane—exist by virtue of the qualities of the child (the disciple). 111.

Thus, whatever emanation exists other than unobscured bliss—even within the terrifying maṇḍala extending from the elements (*bhūtajā*) up to the limit of three and a half crores, and within the internal self from the hair-pores to the end of the body—it should be understood as the unobscured collection of constituents (*dhātusamūha*), possessing these various excellent qualities for the sake of all sentient beings, right here in one’s own body.

Likewise, the tantras and mantras belonging to the various families, the yogas of the yogins through their various divisions, and the worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*)—these constitute the two types of initiation (*seka*) in this Kālacakra: the worldly, according to the qualities of the novice, and the unsurpassed, according to the qualities of those who desire the unsurpassed path; such is the rule. (111)

Now, the meaning of the mundane and supramundane consecrations is stated: The touching of the breasts of the Prajñā, the tasting of the supreme nectar, the embrace, and that which occurs during union with the Prajñā—the fourth moment, the attainment of nectar when the bodhicitta has melted—all this is indeed mundane, shown through supreme compassion for the sake of the path. The supramundane consecration is that which is the attachment to the divine mudrā of the Supreme Lord of Jinas. (112)

By the words beginning with "wisdom" (*prajñā*) and so forth, it is stated here that the fourfold initiation—consisting of the master (*ācārya*), secret (*guhya*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and knowledge (*jñāna*) initiations—is described in the *Samāja* and other tantras as laughter, gazing, joining hands, and union (*dvandva*). Furthermore, the word "likewise" (*tathā*) refers to the fourth [initiation].

In the chapter on the determination of the purity of the four bodies and so forth, the section concerning the flask and other implements constitutes this initiation; however, it is merely a convention for the sake of performing the role of a master according to relative truth (*saṃvṛti*), not the ultimate reality (*tattva*). This is because of the statement: "Having initiated [the disciple], one should reveal the reality. Thus, the fourfold initiation consisting of laughter, gazing, joining hands, and the yoga of union is not the reality itself.
In this context, when analyzed, the non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*)—the reality free from dualities that has arisen through the cause of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*)—does not exist.
If here the bliss of the means (*upāya*) were to arise through the cause of wisdom (*prajñā*), then the gnosis of the means of wisdom would arise through the cause of the means;
if this were so, there would be two distinct gnoses due to the differentiation of both types of gnosis.
Therefore, there is no non-duality;
and because of the absence of non-duality, there is an absence of Buddhahood.
Alternatively, if "prajñājñāna" is understood as the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñā*), that too is flawed; rather, it is established that "upāyajñāna" is the knowledge of skillful means (*upāya*).

Therefore, the pleasure of the means (*upāya*) is twofold—transient (*kṣara*), being either that of the child or the mature; the pleasure of vibration (*spanda*) of wisdom (*prajñā*) is the grown; and when there is the non-vibration of those two by way of the *mahāmudrā*, it is free from the two organs and non-dual (*advaya*).
Thus, the worldly [act] of touching the breast of wisdom and so forth is shown for the purpose of introducing one to the path;
the supramundane consecration (*seka*) is that which is the attachment to the divine consort (*divyamudrā*) of the supreme Lord of Victors, and that alone is so called. || 112 ||

That which is a mere appearance of the mind, produced within one's own intellect and resembling a reflection in a mirror, should be cultivated by the lords of yogis; and that which has been cultivated by all the sons of the Victors becomes the blazing flame of wisdom for the Buddha.
Through the yoga of constant practice, it burns away the entire host of Māra along with its objects, and bestows upon the bodies of the yogis the supreme bliss for a year. (113)
The verse beginning with "In the mere appearance of the mind" and so forth is easy to understand. || 113 ||

Wisdom (*prajñā*), gnosis (*jñāna*), and mind (*citta*)—of which there are ten kinds—are its very manifestation; immersion into this is the *sekha* (consecration). That which is like the reflection of a stainless moon in a mirror is indeed [the state];

therefore, that from which the bliss of nirvāṇa does not fall away, which is innate (*sahaja*) and imperishable (*akṣara*), is the fourth. He in whose heart and mouth this face of the Buddha resides is the glorious Guru. || 114 ||

"Wisdom (*prajñā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*)" and so forth are explained here as follows: wisdom is the apprehending mind (*grāhakacitta*), and knowledge is that tenfold object of apprehension (*grāhya*)—consisting of smoke and so on—which appears like a reflection in a mirror or a prognostic image (*pratisenā*) belonging to that apprehending mind; thus, "knowledge" means the apprehended mind (*grāhyacitta*).
In this way, just as one's own eye is reflected in a mirror, the eye is apprehended by itself; such is wisdom and knowledge.

"Immersion (*seka*) in this" means that here, the entry of the perceiving mind (*grāhakacitta*) into the perceived mind (*grāhyacitta*), which is the non-engagement with external objects, is called immersion by means of the six limbs: withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), meditation (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*).

From that immersion, there arises the innate (*sahaja*), imperishable (*akṣara*) fourth bliss, which does not fall away from the bliss of nirvāṇa; it is the supreme among the movements of the child, the mature, and the emission, transcending worldly analogies and free from the conduct of the three worlds—this is the meaning.

Free from laughter, gazing, touch, embracing, holding hands, and union; free from the causes of the *karmamudrā* and *jñānamudrā*; characterized by emptiness appearing in all its aspects—this is the "Buddha-face," the "Wisdom-face. That master in whose heart this has been meditated upon and become his own direct experience (*svānubhava*), and who exists at all times for the purpose of imparting it to disciples as something present in his own mouth—he is the glorious Guru Vajradhara;
none others are those who understand through the pleasure of the two organs. || 114 ||
And "the wisdom-knowledge" does not exist,
O Dehi Tse, at that time.

And since the "mouth of ignorance" does not exist in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the entry of this very mind into its own reflection is now described: for one whose mind is unattached to space and whose eyes do not blink, having entered the vajra-path from emptiness, there appear smoke, a mirage, a clearly manifest stainless firefly, and a lamp.

The flames, the moon, the sun, and the vajras are seen as the supreme digit (paramakalā), and in their center is the bindu; therein is the Buddha-image, the manifold saṃbhogakāya free from sense objects. || 115 ||

With the words beginning with "space" (*ākāśa*), it is taught that here in the Mantra Vehicle and the Pāramitā Vehicle, the practice of yoga is twofold: the practice of yoga in space and the practice in an open area. He who attains yoga in space, having fixed his mind on space at night in a windowless room in total darkness, beholds the signs beginning with smoke; with unblinking eyes, he has entered the Vajra Path. Here, having entered the central life-force (*madhyamā-prāṇa*), with a mind fixed on space from within emptiness and with unblinking eyes, he has entered the Vajra Path from emptiness. From emptiness, he beholds by means of the night-yoga: smoke, a mirage, a clearly manifest stainless firefly, and a lamp.
Then one sees the cloudless sky;
then from that sky, at the conjunction of the deities, there is seen a flame in the cloudless sky according to the verse: "The self-arisen one born of space, the great fire of the wisdom of insight.

Likewise: Vairocana, the great radiance, the illuminator of the light of wisdom; the moon-like appearance; the sun, the lamp of the world; the vajra-Rāhu, the torch of wisdom; the one of great splendor, the luminous one, the supreme flash of lightning; and the King of Knowledge, the Lord of Supreme Mantras, the Bindu.

Thus, the Blessed One has stated in the *Samāja* that the sign (*nimitta*) is tenfold through the practice of night (*rātriyoga*), and in the *Nāmasaṅgīti* through the practice of day (*divāyoga*). Therefore, [it is said]:
"The King of Mantras accomplishes the great purpose. This refers to the vision of the image (*bimba*) in all its aspects, such as cloth-paintings, pots, and so forth.

In the center of that [image], within the drop (*bindu*), is the Buddha-image, which is devoid of sense objects due to the absence of substantiality and the absence of conceptual construction; it is the manifold Enjoyment Body (*sambhogakāya*).
Then, through the yoga of the reflection (*bimba*), that very sound of the unstruck (*anāhata*) is heard;
thus, the *nirmāṇakāya* is from the appearance of form, and the *saṃbhogakāya* is from the appearance of sound—this is the meaning. || 115 ||
The yogi should gaze at the sky, free from clouds, with a steady vision, until a black line appears within the channel of time (kālanāḍī), shimmering and pure-rayed.

Within that [line], one’s own mind—devoid of objects, omniform, possessing all colors, and like the sun in water, unclouded—is seen as the image of the Omniscient One; it is nothing other than consciousness itself. 116.

In this regard, during the daytime yoga, the sky— free from clouds— should be gazed upon by the yogi with a fixed gaze in the forenoon and afternoon, keeping one's back to the sun; otherwise, darkness arises from the rays of the sun, and due to that obstruction,
one should observe daily until a black line, the size of a hair, shimmering and pure-rayed, is seen within the bindu.

The reflection of the Omniscient One, which is entirely contained within the *Avadhūtī* known as Kālī, is the entire threefold realm—like the sun in water—possessing all colors, possessing all forms, one’s own mind free from objects; it is not another mind, for that which is one's own mind does not become another's mind, because there is no knowledge of another's mind [as stated in the chapter on the determination of the purity of the four bodies, verses 115–119].

In this context, first the appearance of one's own mind is seen by the Tathāgata with the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*); through the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and so forth, the knowledge of others' minds is seen. Thus, the five eyes of the Blessed One were described in the *Dharmasaṃgraha*.

In this manner, through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanābalena*), there will arise in sequence the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the Buddha-eye, the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*), and the gnosis-eye (*jñānacakṣus*).
Consequently, for the Omniscient One, there is nothing whatsoever that remains unseen. || 116 ||

When the image is seen, one should perform the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) at every daily occasion, until a circle of light rays, revolving and encircling one’s own body, becomes visible; after six months, that path-consciousness (*mārgacitta*) of the practitioners—which is devoid of touch and reaches the blissful state beyond passion and non-passion—increases for the Lord even for a moment by the number of his breaths.

Then, once the image (*bimba*) has been seen, one should perform the retention of the vital wind (*prāṇa-vāyo-nirodha*), known as *kumbhaka*, at the time of every day, until a wheel of rays (*raśmi-cakra*) is seen revolving, encircling one's own body, from the aforementioned image within the internal self.

Then, after six months, for ascetics who are beginners and celibates, the path-consciousness (*mārga-citta*)—which is the consciousness of the image of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bimba*)—proceeds to the immutable bliss (*akṣara-sukha*) of equal pleasure, which is devoid of touch and free from the duality of the two sense organs.
Then follows the moment of awakening characterized by a single instant (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodhi-lakṣaṇa*), the instant that is beyond the extremes of passion and dispassion.

"Passion" (*rāga*) refers to the white fortnight; its "end" is characterized by the sixteenth digit (*ṣoḍaśī-kalā*). "Non-passion" (*arāga*) refers to the black [fortnight]; its "beginning" is characterized by the time of perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*), which has not yet entered the black fortnight. That very moment increases by the number of breaths—namely, the count of twenty-one thousand six hundred. Thus, it increases from the tip of the secret jewel (*vajramaṇi*) by thirty-six hundred moments. Having caused the vital winds (*prāṇa*) to cease for that same number of moments, one reaches the secret lotus (*guhyapadma*); by that, the two stages (*bhūmi*) are attained.
Thus, there are four, six, eight, and ten stages respectively at the navel, heart, throat, and forehead;
and twelve at the crown of the head through the exhaustion of all vital breaths. || 117 ||

Oḍrā, nidrā, ghūrma, and abhisandhi; that bliss which arises from the union of the vajra and lotus in the state of the couple—by means of the guru’s instructions and observances, one should cause its increase. It increases here; there is nothing surprising in this. Having destroyed the afflictions and the Māras through the yoga of the year, the excellent yogin enters the Lord of Jinas.

Between the flames, in the midst of *virama* and *sahaja*, and between knowledge (*jñāna*) and realization (*vijñāna*), the *oḍā* has arrived at the secret place; between *virama* and *sahaja*, it is at the navel; the union of sleep and agitation is at the heart; and between knowledge and realization, it is at the throat. In the form of the drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, mind, and gnosis, that bliss which has come from the forehead through the union of the couple—by means of the Guru’s instruction and the previously mentioned restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), that bliss of the seminal essence increases as it moves upward; there is nothing marvelous in this reaching up to the forehead.

Having thus slain the afflictions and the Māras, the master of the Jinas enters [the central channel]; having killed the vital breaths moving through the left and right, the master of the Jinas enters the image of emptiness.
Through the union with *vaṣaṃ*, the excellent yogin, abiding in the *avadhūtī*, generates the moment of great bliss by means of the *kumbhaka* and increases that bliss—this is the rule. || 118 ||

Now the characteristics of the image (*bimba*) are described: It has the form of earth, yet it is not solid; it is not liquid like water due to its lack of fluidity; it has the form of fire, yet it is not fire; it is motionless, though its body is like the moving wind, yet it is not the wind; it has the form of emptiness, yet it is visible; it possesses all colors—white, green, and the great universal color—but it is not a [mere] color; and though it possesses every form, it is invisible due to the power of the Māras and the afflictions that defile one's own heart. || 119 ||

By the words "of the earth" and so forth, it is shown that here the appearance of emptiness is seen as the form of earth, yet it is insubstantial and not solid; the form of water is like a mirage, yet it is not water because it lacks the nature of water;
likewise, the form of fire is not fire.
That which has a body moved by the wind and yet remains motionless due to its fluidity is not the wind;
it is not a substance and is of the nature of emptiness. Nevertheless, it is perceived like a city of illusion (māyānagara), appearing endowed with colors such as white and so forth;
yet, because it is not a substantial entity, it is not a color, and though it possesses all forms, it is invisible to children at all times.

For what reason? The rule is that it is due to the influence of the Māra of the afflictions (*kleśamāra*), which arises from the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the left and right channels (*nāḍī*). || 119 ||

Now the locus for the movement of the channels is described: Sound (nāda), the drop (bindu), the digit (kalā), and gnosis (jñāna) reside in the state of immortality; the channels are bound together like a chain, with the paths of prāṇa and apāna. The vajra, together with the lotus, is joined with the lotus;
in the midst of the collision of the two winds is the exit and entry of the objects and subjects, as well as the grasping of the signs such as smoke and so forth—all this is the secret. || 120 ||
By the words "nāda" and so forth,
it is meant that here, in the heart, the *nāda* is the *cittabindu*, which generates the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*);
and as for the *bindu*, it is the *kāryābindu* in the forehead, which generates the waking state (*jāgrat*).
"Ka" is at the throat, the bindu of speech that generates the dream state;
"Jñāna" is at the navel, the bindu of knowledge that generates the fourth state (turyā);
thus, those who have reached the plane of immortality [perceive] the channels bound together like a chain.

The "Amṛtapada" (Place of Nectar) is the forehead; those who have gone there are the "Amṛtapadagatas," namely the Lalanā, Rasana, and Avadhūtī. Bound by chains, they form a triple-path (*tripatha*) between the navel and the heart. Then, having pierced the heart-center (*hṛtkanikā*) within the Avadhūtī, the Lalanā proceeds by circulating through the right and left petals [of the heart]. From there, having formed a triple-path between the heart and the throat, it proceeds again. Likewise, having formed a triple-path between the forehead and the throat, and a triple-path between the uṣṇīṣa and the forehead—thus having formed four triple-paths—the Lalanā proceeds through the left nostril to the "Supreme Place" (*parapada*), the "Twelfth End" (*dvādaśānta*), the "End of the Kalā" (*kalānta*). (As stated in the *Adhyātmapaṭala* of the *Kālacakra-tantra*).
The *rasanā* goes by way of the right [nostril] and the *avadhūtī* simultaneously through both apertures;

thus, having formed a triple path below between the navel and the secret organ (*guhyamadhye*), the *viṇmūtranāḍī* (feces and urine channel) goes by the left and right. The *śaṅkhinī* is in the middle; within the secret lotus, below the secret lotus, the feces channel is situated in the center, the urine channel goes to the left toward the penis or the vulva, and the semen channel goes to the right. This is the movement of the channels, as described in the previously mentioned Adhyātmapaṭala: "Thus, the three paths of prāṇa and apāna" refers to the upward paths of the left, right, and middle for the *prāṇa*, and the downward paths of feces, urine, and semen for the *apāna*.
The lotus with the vajra is the womb of women; because it throbs, it is like a jewel-vajra, and because it flows, it is joined with the lotus and thus expands.
This occurs in the center of the union of the two winds at the navel, in the object located in the center of the union of the prāṇa and apāna; this is a word without a case ending (*avibhaktika*).
Regarding the objects of the sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth, their emergence and entry into the channels occurs at the navel;
that alone is what was previously described,
whereas for the smoke-like channels and others, there is no such [emergence or entry].

[Chapter, Verse: The Great Chapter on the Determination of the Purity of the Four Bodies and so forth. The grasping of the signs occurs through the door of the *avadhūtī*; by the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that this very [process] takes place at the navel.
This entire secret must be concealed from childish people—this is the rule. || 120 ||

Now the conclusion of the yoga is stated: The entry of the vital breath into the center; the binding of the mind as it moves through the sun and moon in the right and left [channels]; the attainment of supreme bliss during the application of the mudrās; the awakening of the vajra and the sound of the vajra within the lotus; the splashing of one’s own hand-water for the sake of pleasure; the abandonment of the seed along with bliss—this is the mouth of the glorious Guru, which removes the fear of death. (121)

Regarding the passage beginning with "In the middle, the vital breath" (*madhye prāṇa*), here first the yogin must effect the entry of the vital breath into the middle channel, the *avadhūtī*, by which he perceives the sign. Thus, one is called the "Body-Vajra" (*kāyavajra*) of the venerable Guru who has bound [the winds]; from that, the rule is that there is a binding of the vital breath together with the sun moving through the right path and the moon moving through the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*). This is the second, the Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajra*), which is breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

When the mind is attached to the image during the application of the mudrā, the bodhicitta melts; this is the third face of the mind, which has attained supreme bliss and is the awakening of the vajra. Now, if bliss does not arise through the door of the image, then the sound of the vajra should be made gently within the lotus. If a woman is not obtained, then one should perform the stirring with the lotus of one's own hand for the sake of increasing bliss, not for the sake of emission.

Thus, the abandonment of the seed-syllable, accompanied by bliss, removes the fear of death; this is the fourth garment of the illustrious Guru, namely the garment of knowledge—this is the rule regarding the practice of yoga. || 121 ||

Now the destruction of the five mandalas is described: Earth dissolves into water, and fire likewise into water; fire dissolves into wind, and wind into space; and space indeed dissolves into the tenfold sign, and the sign dissolves into the omniform, imperishable, supreme bliss, the unstruck gnosis-body (jñānakāya).
From that gnosis, O Lord of Men, supernatural powers and accomplishment arise for men in this very life.
With the words beginning "earth" (*pṛthvī*) and so forth:

here, when the yogin becomes one whose eyes do not blink, having fixed his mind upon the void with a wrathful gaze, then—whether on the left or the right—"earth" is merely an illustration. When the yogin performs meditation at the time of the flow of earth on the right, this is the procedure; it is not, however, [the procedure] for the time of the flow in the left channel according to the sequence of the mandalas of space and so forth.
Therefore, whichever mandala the vital breath (*prāṇa*) flows through, whether on the left or the right, that very mandala is so called because it is characterized by that [flow].
By that [process], the vital breath (*prāṇa*) moves from the earth-mandala into the fire-mandala via the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*).
In this way, it proceeds through the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*) starting from the space-mandala (*ākāśa*) up to the gnosis-mandala (*jñāna*).

Thus, it enters the ninefold signs (*nimitta*), beginning with smoke; from the sign, it enters the image (*bimba*) possessing all aspects; from the image, it enters the imperishable bliss (*akṣarasukha*). That very thing is "this" (*idaṃ*).
O, there is no fifth;
and the ground is thus:
knowledge is the perfection of wisdom.

From knowledge comes supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), such as traveling through the sky, and accomplishment (*siddhi*), which is sovereignty over the three realms; O Lord of Men, this occurs for men in this very life—this is the rule for entering the path. || 122 ||

Now, the sixteen subdivisions of the four bodies are described: The emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) arises from desire; its speech is certainly complete, its flame is the emanation-mind which produces supreme bliss, and its frown is gnosis itself.

Bliss is the enjoyment body (*bhogakāya*); it is his supreme bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*), and in sequence, his speech and mind become the gnosis-vajra—this indeed is the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) of this Śambhu. (123)
"Desire," and so forth.
Here, from the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), wherever there is one body, there are also others, such as speech and mind.
"Desires" refers to the fact that through the cessation of bodily bliss (*kāyānanda*), the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddha becomes certain.

Regarding that emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the cessation of the bliss of speech is speech itself, which is full. The flame is the emanation mind; "flame" is the cessation of the bliss of mind. The wisdom-vajra that produces supreme bliss is the emanation's *oḍrā*, which is the cessation of the bliss of gnosis (*jñāna*).
Thus, there is the fourfold emanation (nirmāṇa) as well as the fourfold enjoyment (saṃbhoga).
Bliss (ānanda) is the enjoyment body (bhogakāya), which is the cessation of the supreme bliss of the body; it is, in sequence, the supreme joy of cessation (viramānanda).
Supreme bliss (paramānanda) is the speech of enjoyment (saṃbhogavāk), [attained] through the exhaustion of the supreme bliss of speech.
Cessation-bliss (*viramānanda*) is the mind of enjoyment (*saṃbhoga-citta*), the cessation of the supreme bliss of the mind.

Thus, speech and mind are the knowledge-vajra; co-emergent bliss (*sahajānanda*) is the cessation of the supreme bliss of knowledge for this Śambhu of enjoyment. Therefore, from that [cessation] arises the fourfold Dharma of enjoyment. || 123 ||

Kampā is indeed the Dharma-body, bowed to by the three worlds; from it arises Speech (Vāg). Ghūrmā is indeed the Dharma-mind, which destroys the fear of existence; Sleep is its Gnosis. Varṇā is indeed the Pure Body (Śuddhakāya); the vowels, devoid of *kalā*, *bindu*, and *nāda*, are respectively Speech, Mind, and the Gnosis-vajra of Śambhu’s Pure Body, which pervades the threefold existence. 124.

*Kampa* is indeed the bliss of the cessation of action (*kāryaviramānanda*); its cessation is the *dharmakāya*, which is honored by the three worlds. From that *dharma*, the emergence of speech occurs; thus, the cessation of the bliss of the cessation of speech (*vāgviramānanda*) is [the *sambhogakāya*]. *Ghūrma* is indeed the cessation of the bliss of the cessation of mind (*cittaviramānanda*); the *dharmacitta* is the destroyer of the fear of existence, the knowledge of *dharma*. Its sleep is the cessation of the bliss of the cessation of knowledge (*jñānaviramānanda*). *Varṇa* is indeed the innate bliss of the body (*kāyasahajānanda*); its cessation is the pure body (*śuddhakāya*).
"Kalā, bindu, and nāda, devoid of vowels, in that order": "Kalā" is the cessation of the innate bliss of speech, which is pure speech;
"bindu" is the cessation of the innate bliss of the mind, which is pure mind.
*Nāda* is the cessation of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) through gnosis; it is pure gnosis.

Thus, the *jñānavajra*—which exists in three ways within phenomenal existence (*bhava*)—belongs to Śambhu, the Vajrasattva of the pure body. It is differentiated by the divisions of sixteen joys (*ānanda*), according to the statement: "The knower of reality in its sixteen aspects" (*Nāmasaṃgīti* 9.15).

Reality in its sixteen aspects is the great immutable bliss (*mahākṣarasukha*) in its expanded sense (*vivṛtyā*), while in its conventional sense (*saṃvṛtyā*), it consists of twelve aspects for both Buddhas and transmigrating beings.

Through that cessation of the twelve links and the destruction of the vital breath, the Vajra-Sun is the Great Light (*nāmasaṃgīti* 8.33); it possesses the meaning of the truth in its twelve aspects (*nāmasaṃgīti* 9.15). [The term] *buddhatvaṃ* is added; the Tibetan version lacks the word *kāya*. [In the chapter, verse: This is the great section determining the purity of the four bodies and so forth.

By means of the cessation of the sixteen digits of semen (*śukra*), [he] possesses the stainless radiance of the moon; as it is said, "the knower of reality in sixteen aspects" (*Ṣoḍaśākāratattvavit*)—thus the Blessed One Kālacakra is perfected. || 124 ||

Now, the cessation of the waking state and the others is described: Furthermore, this other [state], which has the nature of waking and dreaming, as well as the nature of deep sleep and the fourth (turya), moves through objects while residing in the body and merged with the breath; it becomes motionless when merged in the mind. When one is established in knowledge, even for a moment due to sexual union, and when the *bodhicitta* is melted, the vajra-mind certainly arises in four ways through the sequence beginning with the emanation (*nirmāṇa*). || 125 ||
"Awakened," and so forth.

Here, for transmigrating beings, the *bodhicitta* situated in the body—that is, located in the head—is characterized by the state of waking (*jāgrat*). When it has entered the throat, being absorbed in the breath (*śvāsa*), it takes the form of dreaming (*svapna*). In both these states, it "wanders through objects.
Furthermore, when it is motionless, absorbed in the mind, and located in the heart, this is the third state of consciousness, which has the nature of deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
"Abiding in gnosis" does not mean abiding in the navel; rather, it refers to the nature of the fourth state (*turya*), characterized by the moment of emission resulting from sexual union.
When the *bodhicitta* has flowed, that very mind—having ceased its fourfold [activity]—becomes for the Buddhas the characteristics of the Nirmāṇa, Sambhoga, Dharma, and Sahaja bodies.
Therefore, through the sequence beginning with the Emanation body, the Mind-Vajra necessarily arises within the four [bodies]. (125)

Thus, the mind—which exists in four ways within the threefold existence of living beings—is to be guarded by the lord of yogins within the *bindu*, for it bestows the fruit of equal bliss, is all-pervasive, and is the cause of liberation.

If the *bindu* is released, where is there liberation? It is the seed of birth for yogins once supreme bliss has departed; therefore, this moment of worldly pleasure must always be avoided here by ascetics. (126)

Thus, the mind characterized by waking and the other states belongs to transmigrating beings who have entered the three realms of existence in four ways; yet that very *bodhicitta* resides within the *bindu* at the center, in the support of *bodhicitta*. That alone must be protected by the lords of yogins for the sake of liberation—it is all-pervasive and bestows the fruit of equal bliss and the fruit of imperishable bliss. If there is emission of the *bindu*, it falls from its support; where then is the liberation of the supported *bodhicitta*? When the support has reached supreme bliss, it becomes the seed of birth for yogins.
Therefore, this moment of the flow of saṃsāra must always be avoided here by those who strive for liberation.
In this context, the Blessed One’s injunction is that the perishable— the momentary vibration— is to be abandoned.
The yogi must perform [the practice] upward by means of the outflow (*niṣyanda*) and so forth, until stainlessness (*vaimalya*) is attained.

"Just as it came, so it went"—this rule for the arising of the supreme immutable bliss is to be explained in detail in the following verse beginning with "oneness" (*ekatva*) and so forth, once the realization of the supreme immutable knowledge (*paramākṣara-jñāna*) has been established.
Therefore, this concludes the section here.

Thus ends the second major chapter, the Determination of the Purity of the Four Bodies and so forth, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghu-kālacakra-tantra-rāja* following the *Mūla-tantra*, within the Chapter on Gnosis.
O! He analyzes (vidhārayati).
And the Lord of Serpents.
This is the great chapter entitled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of the Supreme Unchanging" from the Vimalaprabhā. Homage to the glorious Vajrasattva.
Homage to Mahāmudrā, the supreme immutable bliss!
Homage to the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas!
Homage to the Wrathful Kings, Vāḍākas, Vajras, and Ḍākinīs!

Now, because the realization of the phenomena consisting of the conceptualization of the form, color, arms, and posture—arising from the transformation of the *hūṃ* syllable upon the lotus and sun-moon seats of the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*), which is the innate body (*sahajakāya*) born of the imperishable—is indeed [attained], therefore the accomplishment of the Blessed One’s supreme imperishable gnosis is described as follows: "The unity of the vowels and consonants is the seat of the Moon and Sun for the Vajra-holder; no other sign transformed by the *hūṃ* syllable is desired as a form of color. This belongs to the one who has reached the end of the perishable, whose divine senses have arisen through the imperishable, who is the drop (*bindu*) possessing all aspects, the supreme Lord of Jinas, the bearer of universal illusion. (127)

By the phrase "oneness," and so forth: for oneness belongs to the initial vowels (*ādikācau*). The "beginning" (*ādi*) refers to the group of vowels starting with *a*, as well as the letter *ha* (the Moon), both individually and collectively. The "beginning" (*ādi*) refers to the group of consonants (*vyañjana*) starting with *ka*, as well as the letter *kṣa* (the Sun), both individually and collectively.
Of those two, the moon and the sun, represented by the letters *ha* and *kṣa*, or alternatively by the letters *a* and *pa*,
their oneness— their unification— is the seat (*āsana*), the support.
The lotus consists of the consonant *pa*.
The lunar disc consists of the syllable *a* or *ha*, and the solar disc consists of the syllable *ra* or *kṣa*.

Regarding the "Vajrin" (the Wielder of the Vajra) who is the supported (*ādheya*): the "vajra" is the unbreakable gnosis of supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*) which is non-falling (*acyuta*); he is the "Vajrin" because that [gnosis] exists within him. Of that Vajrin, who is the supported; "not" (*na*) means that the seat (*āsana*) has been rejected as the support (*ādhāra*).

Likewise, it is not accepted that the sign of the vajra is produced from the syllable *huṃ*, nor that the body of the deity produced from the sign of the vajra possesses the nature of being conceptualized through its color, arms, and form as something characterized by a substratum (*ādheya*).
Why?
Because it would have the characteristic of dogmatic attachment (*abhiniveśa*) and the nature of the perishable (*kṣara*).

In this context, vowels such as *a* and so forth, and consonants such as *ka* and so forth, which are perishable (*kṣara*) and dependently originated, are called "syllables" (*akṣara*) by those learned in the treatises.
As it has been said: "It does not perish (*na kṣarati*), it does not move, and it does not go to another place; therefore, a vowel is called a 'syllable' (*akṣara*) by means of this word.
Consequently, a foolish practitioner, being deluded, grasps a collection of vowels or a collection of consonants as being the syllable itself.
From the perspective of ultimate truth, the collection of vowels and consonants is not the syllable (*akṣara*).

By the word "syllable," one means the gnosis of supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*), which is Vajrasattva. Likewise, because it serves as the protection of the mind, mantra is also called the gnosis of supreme immutability.
Likewise, the inner science, the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), is called by the Victors the "innate body" (*sahajatanu*):

it is the naturally luminous Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) whose nature is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*); it is the state of fullness, the non-fluctuation of the *dharmadhātu*. These two are beyond the range of the sense faculties produced through dependent origination, yet they are the range of the divine faculties; they are the Mother of the Buddhas and Vajrasattva; their intrinsic nature is supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*); they transcend the nature of atoms; they are like a mirror-image, a prognostic vision, or a dream; and they are the very essence of supreme immutability.
Here, "syllables" refers to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; these five syllables, being free from obscuration, are said to be the great emptinesses (*mahāśūnya*).
Likewise, the elements of earth, water, fire, air, and space are free from obscuration. [In this context,] there is no *bho*, nor is there the letter *ya*.
And the letter *ya*.
[In the chapter on Passion, verse 127: The great instruction titled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of the Supreme Syllable" states that the five syllables have also been taught.
The six syllables are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, free from obscuration and devoid of grasping at their respective individual objects;
likewise, the spheres of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are also said to be the six syllables, free from obscuration.
When these aggregates, elements, and sense-bases have become of one single flavor, they become the drop-void (*binduśūnya*).
And that drop (bindu), being non-emitted, is called the supreme syllable (paramākṣara).

The supreme syllable is also the letter A; the letter A is the source of the Perfectly Awakened One (samyaksaṃbuddha), who is Vajrasattva, consisting of wisdom and means, the neuter state, and is called the Innate Body (sahajakāya), consisting of gnosis and the object of gnosis, because of the inseparability of cause and fruit.

And that Blessed One Kālacakra is said by the Blessed One in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, in the first verse of the *Vajradhātumahāmaṇḍalastava*, to be the state of supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukhapada*): "Thus: the Blessed One is the Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, born from the syllable A; the syllable A is the foremost of all letters, of great significance, and the supreme unchanging."
Thus it was stated in the second verse of the *Kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñānastava* as follows:
"The great bindu, which is without syllables, is the progenitor of the meaning of all mantras."
The five-syllabled is the great void; the six-syllabled is the void of the bindu. (Nāmasaṃgīti 5.1)
Thus it is also stated in the *Mūlatantra*: "The union of the vowels and consonants is intended as the seat (*viṣṭara*) of Vajrasattva" (*Nāmasaṃgīti* 10.2).
Thus,

for the body arisen from the syllables, the moment of emission characterized by the state beginning with the syllable *Hūṃ* has come to its end; that which has reached its conclusion is called "time," the supreme unchanging moment of non-emission,
and that itself is the Vajra-knowledge.
