At that time, the wheel of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases is without obscuration; the oneness of the three realms is to be known as being without obscuration.

That very thing is called the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajra Realm (*vajradhātu-mahāmaṇḍala*), which possesses all forms and all faculties, is the nature of the drop (*bindu*), the sustainer of universal illusion (*viśvamāyādhara*), the body of the Blessed One, and consists of wisdom and means (*prajñopāyātmaka*). Thus it was said by the Blessed One: "Time, the beginning of the universe, the Vajra, the incomparable Person, all-pervading, free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), immovable, with ears, nose, mouth, eyes, and head, and with hands and feet everywhere."

I pay homage to Kālacakra, the end of all beings, the lord of beings, the upholder of the supreme boon of the three worlds, the cause of causes, the primordial knowledge, attainable through yoga, and the state of supreme bliss.

Thus, in the *Vimalaprabhā* (Kālacakra-tantra 5.245): "The Veda, together with its limbs of knowledge (*jñānāṅga*), along with the Smṛtis, the Mīmāṃsā, and Logic, as well as the philosophical systems (*siddhānta*) and other treatises composed in this world by poets such as Vyāsa and Vaiśvānara—these are not 'knowledge' (*vidyā*).

Rather, that which is called 'knowledge' here in this world by the sages is the science of the inner self (*adhyātmavidyā*), the syllable [Oṃ], wherein the entire triple world exists, O King, and wherein it is dissolved once again. [187b]

Thus (Kā0 Ta0 2.96), that very same Blessed One Kālacakra, whose nature consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), is described here in terms of the relationship between the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the knowledge (*jñāna*);
herein, the supreme unchanging gnosis (*paramākṣarajñāna*), which is the cause for the destruction of all obscurations, is called "Time" (*kāla*), and this is the means (*upāya*).
The knowable—the three realms characterized by infinite phenomena—is the wheel; that very [wheel] is wisdom, the unity of knowledge and the object of knowledge, which is called the Kālacakra.
This was stated by the Blessed One in the fifty-third verse of the fifth chapter of the *Tantrarāja*, concerning the wheel of the Kālacakra.

Namely: infinite Buddha-fields; elements such as space, which possess immeasurable qualities; the threefold existence consisting of abiding, arising, and destruction; all sentient beings within the six realms of rebirth; the Buddhas; the wrathful deities; the gods and others who possess compassionate hearts; and the Bodhisattvas together with their consorts—this is the single wheel of the Jina Śambhu, who is venerated by the three worlds.

Thus, according to the sequence stated [in Kālacakra-tantra 5.63], the wheel characterized by the object of knowledge belongs to Time, which is of the nature of gnosis; the unity of these two—gnosis and the object of knowledge—is the *Kālacakra*.
By this means, that very Lord Kālacakra, who is the syllable *Evaṃ*, Vajrasattva, is celebrated in all tantras by the Victors.
It was said by the Blessed One in the fifth chapter of the *Mūlatantra*: "Knowledge that is indivisible in every respect is designated as 'vajra.
The oneness of the three realms of existence is the *sattva*; thus he is remembered as Vajrasattva."

Therefore, for the sake of attaining the Mahāmudrā-siddhi, no relationship of support and supported is asserted for this bindu—the Sahaja-body, the Lord of all Victors, who arises from the syllable, possesses all aspects, and sustains the universal illusion.

Just as the relationship between the substratum and the contained is accepted for the sake of accomplishing worldly attainments (*laukikasiddhi*), so too it is for the yogi who delights in the means for achieving supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*). Such a practitioner—having received the instructions of a true guru, having abandoned association with the wicked, having cultivated the signs such as smoke and so forth, being a beginner purified by the middle [path], whose mind is bound by supreme affection toward all sentient beings as if they were an only son, who relies upon both the mundane and supramundane truths, who is indifferent toward his own body, children, wife, and the like, who does not partake in the property of monasteries, hermitages, or gurus, who relies on the path of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who dwells in the four sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*) of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, who is free from the desire to achieve worldly attainments such as rites of pacification (*śāntikarma*), who wishes to ascend to the state of omniscience, and who has abandoned the conceptual meditation on the mandala circle and so forth—perceives all phenomena as unarisen, like reflections in a mirror within the space of all-aspect emptiness (*sarvākāraśūnyatā*). And here, a Tibetan commentary is provided. The numbers given in the *Mātṛkā* (index) are maintained in the notes (*ṭippaṇī*).
Thus it is in every case, even at the beginning.

The Great Chapter titled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of the Supreme Immutable" [from the chapter on the investigation of phenomena consisting of an aggregation of atoms, verse 127]: By one whose mind is like a dream, appearing as the manifestation of the radiance of one's own mind; by one who has distanced himself from the emptiness of nihilism (*uccheda-śūnyatā*); by one who is devoted to the dharma that is blissfully self-cognized within; by one who has abandoned the dharma of pleasure cognized by the external senses; by one whose nature consists of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*); by one skilled in stabilizing the *bodhicitta*; by one who has obtained the instruction on the path of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*) which is the great bliss of the supreme immutable (*paramākṣara-mahāsukha*); it is held that the dharma of conceptualizing the deities of the mandala—including their supports and supported, their signs, colors, arms, and postures—is not desired.
Now, why is it that the maṇḍala-circle has no existence apart from the conceptual mind? Because it is characterized by arising and ceasing,
the yogi should meditate upon the Leader at this very moment of its manifestation.
At that moment, there is the absence of the deities of the east and so forth;
at the moment one should meditate upon the eastern deity, at that moment there is the absence of the central lord and the others.
In this manner, there is the absence of all the deities in succession.
When one meditates on the blue face, at that time there is an absence of the red and other faces; when one meditates on the red face, at that time there is an absence of the blue and other faces;
in this manner, there is an absence of all the faces in succession.
At the very moment one meditates on the vajra symbol, at that moment there is an absence of the sword and other symbols;
at the time one meditates on the sword symbol, at that time there is an absence of the vajra and other symbols.
In this manner, there comes about the absence of all symbols in succession.

How so? Just as when the cognition of a jar has ceased, the cognition of a cloth arises, so too, when the cognition of the Lord of the Mandala has ceased, the cognition of the previous deity arises. Thus, there is non-existence due to the cessation of what has been produced, and non-existence due to the non-production of what has not been produced. Since there is non-existence of both production and non-production, there is the non-existence of everything.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining Mahāmudrā, the yogin should not engage in the cultivation of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

And it was said by the Blessed One in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, in the hymn to the perfectly pure wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, in the fifteenth verse, as follows: "Siddhārtha, one whose resolve is accomplished, free from all conceptual constructions, non-conceptual, the inexhaustible element, the supreme and imperishable *dharmadhātu*."
Thus, even the ego-identification with Vajrasattva (*vajrasattvāhaṅkāra*) should not be performed;
for it was stated by the Blessed One in the twelfth verse of that very hymn: "The Sugata, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the knower of the world, the supreme..."
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, he stands firm in the principle of the two truths.
Therefore, according to the word of the Tathāgata, even the conceptual cultivation of the pride of Vajrasattva should not be performed by a yogin who relies upon ultimate truth.
Indeed, has it not been stated by the Blessed One, the Knower of Reality, the Tathāgata, in all the kings of tantras, that one should first of all cultivate the protective wheel?

Then, having meditated on the seed-syllable of the deity within the moon-maṇḍala of one’s own heart, and having performed the purification through the gates of liberation and so forth, the mantra-practitioner awakens the Tathāgatas in the expanse of space with rays from the wisdom-seed-syllable; having made offerings to them, he performs the confession of sins, the rejoicing in merit, the going for refuge in the Three Jewels, the surrendering of his own body, the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), the taking of the path, and the focal point of emptiness.

Thereafter, he should visualize the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), whose intrinsic nature is the element of space, and in its center, [he should visualize] that which is transformed from the syllable *HŪṂ*.

O, Trayodaśa! [In some versions] "should meditate" (*bhāvayet*) is not present. [The sequence is as follows: Oṃ, Haṃ. Then, according to the intention of the Prajñātantra, one should visualize the mandalas of wind and so forth upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, followed by a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) or a vajra-fence (*vajrapañjara*).
Thereafter, one should visualize the mandala transformed from the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*), complete with all characteristics and provided with seats of the moon and sun.

Then, in the center, one should meditate on a lotus transformed from the syllable *paṃ*, a moon mandala transformed from the syllable *a*, or a sun mandala transformed from the syllable *ra*. Above that, by means of the seed-syllables of knowledge consisting of the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*), one should visualize the form of the deity, which is composed of the five wisdoms: the mirror-like, the equality, the discerning, the all-accomplishing, and the perfectly pure dharma-realm wisdoms. Then, melted by the passion of wisdom, the vajra of body, speech, and mind is awakened by the goddesses with vajra songs; it is again empowered by body, speech, and mind, and is perfected through its own insignia.

Then, the practitioner of mantra should visualize himself as the form of Vajrasattva’s ego-identity, endowed with the vajra crown and ornaments, having performed the dismissal of the host of deities from the mandala, the summoning of the wisdom-circle (jñānacakra), its entry, binding, and pleasing, its unification in equal flavor with the pledge-mandala (samayamaṇḍala), and his consecration by the goddesses of all the Tathāgatas.

Regarding this, some may have the following intention: "How can the meditation on the mandala-circle here be called 'conceptual meditation,' given that it is a negation of the Tathāgata’s word? Therefore, it is said: Indeed, this is true; however, the Blessed One, the Knower of Reality, relying upon conventional truth (*lokasaṃvṛtisatya*) and out of consideration for the dispositions of sentient beings, has taught that knowledge which is dependently originated and within the range of dependently originated faculties—being partial and capable of only partial purposeful action—for those of dull intellect, inferior vigor, who do not examine ultimate reality, whose minds are terrified by profound and vast wisdom, who delight in the performance of rites such as pacification (*śāntika*), who are attached to the enjoyment of sensory objects, and who desire the accomplishment of mundane attainments (*siddhi*) such as the sword, pills, collyrium, alchemy, and elixirs. Thus it was spoken.
Therefore, because it is capable of performing limited purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), this word of the Tathāgata is based upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

However, just as the Tathāgata has taught, even for those things that are limited yet capable of performing limited purposeful action— such as conceptualizations, meditations, mantras, jewels, stones, swords, pills, elixirs, and alchemical substances— their power is nonetheless immeasurable.

And so it is observed here: he who possesses white meditation (*śukladhyāna*) performs peaceful rites (*śāntikarma*) in a tranquil form, but does not perform rites such as killing; likewise, black meditation (*kṛṣṇadhyāna*), which is fierce in form, performs killing, but does not perform [rites] such as subjugation (*vaśya*);

likewise, red meditation (*raktadhyāna*), which is passionate in form, performs subjugation, but does not perform [rites] such as immobilization (*stambhana*); likewise, yellow meditation (*pīta-dhyāna*), which is rigid in form, performs immobilization, but does not perform [rites] such as pacification (*śāntika*).

In this same way, poison is also to be understood: white meditation (śukladhyāna) renders poison non-poisonous in the form of a drop on the forehead; red meditation (raktadhyāna) causes the agitation of poison; black meditation (kṛṣṇadhyāna) effects the transfer of poison; and yellow meditation (pītadhyāna) effects the immobilization of poison. Thus, localized conceptual meditation performs a localized purposeful action. Likewise, jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs are to be understood in this manner.
Here, even a mantra, once accomplished, performs pacification but does not perform rites such as killing.
He who performs killing does not perform subjugation and so forth;
he who performs subjugation does not perform immobilization and so forth; he who performs immobilization does not perform pacification and so forth.
Therefore, mundane knowledge is not capable of performing the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) of a supramundane omniscient one;
thus, it is established that even though [substances] such as the sword and so forth exist, they were not spoken of by the Blessed One [in this context].
[One might ask: "If even a single mantra, when accomplished, performs all ritual actions (*sarvakarmāṇi*), how can it be partial (*prādeśika*)? Here, the intention of someone might be as follows:
Therefore it is said: "In this world, even a single mantra, once accomplished, performs all rites. Is this alone the authority? Why? Because of the difference in ritual action (*kriyābheda*).
Here, even for a single mantra, there is a distinction based on the difference in ritual action; and that was taught by the Tathāgata.

For instance: in rites of pacification (*śāntika*), the mantra recitation ends with *namaḥ*; in rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), it ends with *svāhā*; and likewise in attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*). [In the chapter on] the Great Instruction named "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of the Supreme Syllable," it is stated that [the mantra] ends with *vauṣaṭ*. In rites of inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), it ends with *hūṃ*; in subjugation (*vaśya*), it ends with *vaṣaṭ*; and in killing (*māraṇa*), it ends with *phaṭ*.
Thus, even in the performance of fire-offerings (*homakārya*), a distinction is taught according to the different types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*).

In this context, a mantra offered into a circular (*vṛtta*) fire-pit with fuel-sticks of milky trees such as the *udumbara*, along with *dūrvā* grass and milk, effects pacification (*śānti*); it does not perform rites such as nourishment (*pauṣṭika*).

When offered into a square (*caturasra*) fire-pit with the aforementioned fuel-sticks, grains, and clarified butter (*ājya*), it performs nourishment; it does not perform rites such as killing (*māraṇa*).
When offered into a bow-shaped (*cāpākāra*) fire-pit with bone fuel-sticks, human flesh, poison, and blood, it effects killing; it does not perform rites such as eradication (*uccāṭana*).

In a five-cornered sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), when an oblation is offered with crow feathers, human marrow, and *rājikā* mustard seeds, it effects expulsion (*uccāṭana*); it does not effect subjugation (*vaśya*) or other rites.

In a seven-cornered sacrificial pit, when an oblation is offered with fuel-sticks of *kiṃśuka*, red flowers, or water, it effects attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*); it does not effect subjugation or other rites. In a three-cornered sacrificial pit, when an oblation is offered with fuel-sticks of *khadira*, sweat, and *bilva* flowers, it effects subjugation; it does not effect immobilization (*stambhana*) or other rites.

In a hexagonal sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one who is struck with fuel-sticks of *vilva*, jasmine garlands, and phlegm performs immobilization (*stambhana*); it does not perform enchantment (*mohana*) and so forth.

In an octagonal sacrificial pit, one who is struck with fuel-sticks of the sun-plant (*arka*), golden flowers, and wine performs enchantment; it does not perform pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth.
Thus, the distinction has been stated according to the different types of colored powders (*rajas*).

White powder is used for rites of pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭika*); black powder for rites of killing (*māraṇa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*); red powder for rites of subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*); yellow powder for rites of immobilization (*stambhana*) and delusion (*mohana*); and green powder for the rite of revivification (*pratyujjīvana*). Furthermore, distinctions are stated according to the types of rosaries (*akṣasūtra*).

For pacification (*śāntika*), the mantra recitation is performed with a crystal rosary; for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), with a rosary of pearls; for killing (*māraṇa*), with a rosary of human teeth; for expulsion (*uccāṭana*), with a rosary of camel teeth or donkey teeth; for subjugation (*vaśya*), with a rosary of *putrajīva* seeds; for attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), with a rosary of lotus seeds or red sandalwood; for immobilization (*stambhana*), with a rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads; for delusion (*mohana*), with a rosary of *ariṣṭa* seeds; and for reviving (*pratyujjīvana*), the mantra recitation is performed with a rosary of emerald beads.

Thus, even for those substances accomplished through mantras, medicinal herbs, jewels, swords, elixirs, alchemy, and so forth, there exists only a localized quality; they do not possess the quality of the knowledge of the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara-jñāna*).

Just as the Blessed One, within these three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-systems of Buddha-fields, simultaneously performs the welfare of sentient beings through many emanation bodies and various sounds, likewise, a yogin—even by means of these localized accomplishments—is unable to perform the welfare of all sentient beings because of their localized nature.
It was stated by the Blessed One in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, in the Praise of Discriminating Wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), within the first three verses, as follows:

"Namely: Suchness (*tathatā*), true selflessness (*bhūtanairātmya*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the syllable-less (*anakṣara*), the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyatāvādī*), the bull (*vṛṣabha*), whose roar is profound and vast."

When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of these four nutriments? “Contact, monk, is the cause, contact is the condition for the arising of these four nutriments. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of contact? “The sixfold sense base, monk, is the cause, the sixfold sense base is the condition for the arising of contact. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of the sixfold sense base? “Name-and-form, monk, is the cause, name-and-form is the condition for the arising of the sixfold sense base. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of name-and-form? “Consciousness, monk, is the cause, consciousness is the condition for the arising of name-and-form. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of consciousness? “Volitional formations, monk, are the cause, volitional formations are the condition for the arising of consciousness. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of volitional formations? “Ignorance, monk, is the cause, ignorance is the condition for the arising of volitional formations. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of ignorance? “When asked ‘What is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of ignorance? it would not be fitting to answer anything other than: ‘Ignorance has no known origin; it is without limit in terms of its beginning. For what reason? Because, monks, this chain of dependent origination is deep and difficult to see. It is because of the exhaustion of craving, through dispassion, that there is cessation of clinging; through the cessation of clinging, there is cessation of existence; through the cessation of existence, there is cessation of birth; through the cessation of birth, aging and death cease, as do sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this way, monks, this dependent origination is profound and appears profound. Yet, monks, it is through not understanding, not penetrating this Dhamma—that is, this dependent origination—as it really is, that this generation has become like a tangled skein, like a knotted ball of thread, like matted rushes and reeds, and does not pass beyond the plane of misery, the bad destinations, the nether world, and saṃsāra. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘In this way, monks, this dependent origination is profound and appears profound. “It is so, Ānanda, it is so! This dependent origination is indeed profound and appears profound. Yet, Ānanda, it is through not understanding, not penetrating this Dhamma—that is, this dependent origination—as it really is, that this generation has become like a tangled skein, like a knotted ball of thread, like matted rushes and reeds, and does not pass beyond the plane of misery, the bad destinations, the nether world, and saṃsāra. But when, Ānanda, a noble disciple understands, penetrates as it really is this dependent origination and its conditions, then he is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those monks rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. And how, monks, is there the cessation of these four nutriments? Through the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; through the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; through the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; through the cessation of name-and-form, the sixfold sense base ceases; through the cessation of the sixfold sense base, contact ceases; through the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; through the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; through the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; through the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; through the cessation of existence, birth ceases; through the cessation of birth, aging and death cease, as do sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this way, monks, there is the cessation of these four nutriments. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Venerable Sāriputta and said: “Friend Sāriputta, just now the Blessed One spoke thus: ‘Monks, there are these four nutriments... [as above] ...Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this way, friend, there is the cessation of these four nutriments. Now, friend, what is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of these four nutriments? “Friend, contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the arising of these four nutriments. “But, friend, what is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of contact? “The sixfold sense base, friend. “What is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of the sixfold sense base? “Name-and-form, friend. “What is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of name-and-form? “Consciousness, friend. “What is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of consciousness? “Volitional formations, friend. “What is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of volitional formations? “Ignorance, friend. “But, friend, what is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of ignorance? “When asked ‘What is the cause, what is the condition for the arising of ignorance? it would not be fitting to answer anything other than: ‘Ignorance has no known origin; it is without limit in terms of its beginning. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having delighted and rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Sāriputta, rose from his seat and approached the Blessed One. Having paid homage to him, he sat down at one side and reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had had with the Venerable Sāriputta. “It is so, Ānanda, it is so! This dependent origination is indeed profound and appears

Thus, just as here the omniscient body, speech, mind, and gnosis are non-conceptual and capable of performing all purposeful actions in every aspect, so too, even when accomplished through conceptual meditation, mantras, and the like, these do not become capable of performing the purposeful actions of an omniscient one for yogins;
likewise, even the totalities (*kṛtsna*) such as earth and so forth, though directly realized by those free from passion, remain limited.
Why? Because of the limited radiation of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).

Here, one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) and realizes the "earth-totality" (*pṛthvī-kṛtsna*) may radiate that earth-totality, but he is not capable of radiating the water-totality (*toyādi-kṛtsna*) and so forth;
this should be understood for each individual totality, up to the "space-totality" (*śūnya-kṛtsna*).
In this regard, one who emanates the *samāja* mandala within this [particular] mandala is not able to emanate the *cakrasaṃvara* and so forth;
and one who emanates the *cakrasaṃvara* is not able to emanate the *samāja* and so forth, because they are limited in scope.

Now, someone might have the following intention: "When a single mandala-circle is directly realized here, all mandala-circles and even the threefold world (*traidhātuka*) are directly realized. There is no other threefold world apart from the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and mandala-circles."

Therefore, it is said: Here, if upon the direct realization of even one [totality]—whether it be the totality of the elements (*dhātu-kṛtsna*) or the mandala-circle—the realization of the elements were to occur, and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and so forth were to be attained, then there would be no such thing as the "direct realization" of omniscience, knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of the aspects of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) for the sake of attaining the state of an omniscient one. Furthermore, if upon the direct realization of even a single [totality] such as earth, or upon the direct realization of the mandala-circle, perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambuddhatva*) were to occur, then there would be no such thing as the attainment of the states of a Śrāvaka, a Pratyekabuddha, or a Siddha.

In this regard, as the word of the Blessed One is heard in the three vehicles: "In such-and-such a buddha-field, in such-and-such a world-system, in such-and-such an eon, there was a Tathāgata—the son of such-and-such [a person], born in such-and-such a family—who possessed the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and was adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics; he possessed the six superknowledges, attained perfect enlightenment in such-and-such a place, dwells in such-and-such a place, turns the wheel of Dharma, teaches such-and-such a Dharma through various sounds to beings of diverse inclinations, and having manifested the great display of the elements in such-and-such a place, has entered final nirvāṇa."

Having seen the extraordinary and magnificent miracles of these relics, gods, asuras, and humans worship them; yet they do not [worship] in the same way [the memory of] a certain Buddha in a certain buddha-field, a certain world-system, in a certain eon—how he was born as a yogi endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics, possessing the six superknowledges; how he attained perfect enlightenment in a certain place, dwelt in a certain region, turned the wheel of Dharma in a certain location, taught various Dharmas through various sounds to beings of diverse inclinations, simultaneously displayed his physical miraculous powers throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems, and finally entered parinirvāṇa after manifesting the great relic at a certain site.
Regarding the great pervasion of those elements—the Great Chapter titled "The Accomplishment of Supreme Unchanging Gnosis" (Chapter 56, Verse):
Having seen [this], the elements are worshipped by gods, asuras, and humans;
therefore, a yogi does not become a perfectly awakened one merely upon the direct realization of a single maṇḍala-circle.
Why? Because there is no turning of the wheel of Dharma [by him], and because there is no prophecy from a Tathāgata.

Just as here Maitreyanātha was prophesied by the Tathāgata that he would become a Tathāgata in a future time, and others such as Bhasmeśvara were prophesied by the Tathāgata that they would become perfectly awakened ones (samyaksaṃbuddhas), the Blessed One does not prophesy in the same way for any yogin who has directly realized a single maṇḍala circle that he will become a perfectly awakened one.

However, the meditation on the maṇḍala circle was taught by the Blessed One according to the dispositions of sentient beings for the sake of attaining worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*), such as the sword, the pill, the collyrium, and the elixir.
Therefore, through the direct realization of the deities of the maṇḍala circle, accomplishments such as the sword are achieved by the practitioner; yet omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is not achieved.

If omniscience were achieved by the power of meditating on the maṇḍala circle, then for what purpose would the accomplished ones (*siddhas*) here set forth the words of the Blessed One in their own treatises?

Therefore, mundane supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) do not bestow the qualities of omniscience, because they are limited and lack the speech of an omniscient one; furthermore, because the manifestation of supernatural power occurs through a body possessed of obscurations, a yogi who has directly realized a dharma that is still obscured does not become omniscient. Consequently, it is when the unobscured dharma is directly realized that the yogi becomes omniscient, due to the characteristic of the unobscured dharma.

The All-Knowing One possesses the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, recollection of past lives, all supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), and the destruction of all outflows (*āsrava*). He possesses the power of knowing what is possible and impossible; the power of knowing the ripening of karma; the power of knowing the various elements, both single and manifold; the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties; the power of knowing the various inclinations; the power of knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering; the power of knowing affliction and purification; the power of knowing the details of many births; the power of knowing all supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*); and the power of knowing the destruction of the outflows.

Likewise, there is the stage of Universal Radiance with the splendor of the great solar orb; the stage of Nectar Radiance, luminous like the great moon; the stage of Sky Radiance, as firmly established as the sky; the delightful stage of Vajra Radiance; the stage of Jewel Radiance, established through consecration; the stage of Lotus Radiance, which is stainless due to the purity of the nature of phenomena and is free from grasping; the stage that performs the deeds of a Buddha; the incomparable stage; the stage of Similes, which is realized through the penetration of all similes; the unsurpassed stage of Wisdom Radiance; the stage of Omniscience, which is of great luminosity; and the stage to be personally realized, which fulfills the knowledge of yogins.

The Tathāgata has no stumbling, no shouting, and no loss of mindfulness; he has no unconcentrated mind, no perception of diversity, and no equanimity lacking discernment; there is no decline in his zeal, no decline in his vigor, no decline in his mindfulness, no decline in his concentration, no decline in his wisdom, and no decline in his vision of the knowledge and liberation.

In the past time, unimpeded, unattached, and wishless knowledge and vision proceed; in the future time, unimpeded, unattached, and wishless knowledge and vision proceed; in the present time, unimpeded, unattached, and wishless knowledge and vision proceed.

All bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge; all vocal action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge; all mental action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge.

Therefore, because he is perfectly established in equanimity at all times and in all places, and because he has fully realized emptiness, the Tathāgata is one whose wisdom is utterly pure; due to his characteristic of being without obscuration, he is not someone with obscurations. It is not that some single deity of the maṇḍala circle—purified through the conceptualization of number, color, arms, and shape, and through the radiation of [emanations]—becomes Vajrasattva, the One Endowed with Ten Powers. Rather, there is no "speech" (vacana) and there is no "element" (dhātu).
There is no *dharma*.

(20, 20, 25, 30, T 437, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 90, 68) In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the knowledge of the path of the Omniscient One: being overcome by false ego, he thinks, "I too am Vajrasattva, I am the one possessing the ten powers (*daśabala*).
This one is not the possessor of the ten powers; he lacks the power of the ten powers, being a partial, great fool.
The unprecedented Buddhahood of this yogin, which is a great marvel arising from the removal of all obscurations,

was spoken by the Blessed One in the ninth verse of the *Nāmasaṃgīti*’s *Pratyavekṣaṇājñānastava*: “Pacifier of the suffering of the three types of suffering, reaching the end of the limit and the liberation of infinite space, liberated from all obscurations, he has attained equality with space.”
( *Nāmasaṃgīti* 8.9) Therefore, according to these words of the Blessed One, a yogin does not become omniscient through the power of meditating on conceptual forms.

Now, one might object: "Has the Tathāgata not stated in the *Sarvatantrarājas* that the five aggregates are the Buddhas such as Vairocana; the elements are the goddesses such as Locanā; the six sense faculties are the Bodhisattvas such as Kṣitigarbha; the objects of the senses are the goddesses such as Rūpavajrā; and the wrathful kings such as Yamāntaka are Mohavajra and the others?
Consequently, the body of sentient beings is the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddha"—such might be the intention of some.

Therefore it is said: regarding that which is asserted here by the foolish—that the body of sentient beings is the emanation-body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Buddha—this statement is not the word of the Tathāgata. For if one examines it, it falls apart when considered in light of ultimate truth; if the body of sentient beings were the emanation-body of the Buddha, then all sentient beings dwelling within the three realms would have previously been perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
If [the self were eternal], then the activities of hearing, reflecting, meditating, giving, and so forth for the sake of Buddhahood would be in vain; prior to the attainment of perfect enlightenment,
there would be no arising or ceasing of all sentient beings,
and there would be no afflictions such as pleasure, pain, hunger, or thirst within saṃsāra.

The six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and other such manifestations of the Buddha's qualities would not exist; yet this has neither been seen, heard, inferred, nor prophesied by the Tathāgata. Therefore, due to the absence of the Buddha-qualities, sentient beings do not become Buddhas because they are firmly established in *saṃsāra*.
Thus it was stated by the Blessed One in the thirteenth verse of the *Suviśuddhadharmadhātustava* within the *Nāmasaṃgīti*:

That is to say: "He stands at the far shore of saṃsāra, established on the ground where all that is to be done has been accomplished, immersed in the realization of absolute knowledge (kaivalya-jñāna), armed with the weapon of wisdom, and a destroyer [of afflictions]. (Nāmasaṃgīti 6.13)
Therefore, based on that statement of the Tathāgata, the body of sentient beings is not the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of a Buddha.

Yet, might it not be someone’s intention [to argue] that the Tathāgata has stated that through the power of the practice of cultivation, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth, will take the form of the maṇḍala wheel, and by that very means, Buddhahood is attained? To this it is said: Here, indeed, what is to be stated by the ignorant is that the Tathāgata has taught that through the power of cultivation, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth, will take the form of the maṇḍala wheel, and by that very means, Buddhahood is attained.
That is not so, because of the absence of the accumulations of merit and wisdom.

For here, if for yogins—without the accumulations of merit and wisdom—the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth were to take the form of the mandala-circle through the power of practicing meditation, and if perfect buddhahood were to arise through the power of practicing conceptual meditation, then anyone else who lacks material wealth [would also achieve it]. (Note: The word "five" does not appear in the source text.)
2. ca. ‘Sukha’ is not present. 3. Bho. ‘Yataḥ’ (Because) is added. 4. Bho. ‘Buddhatvam’.
5. O, one of meager merit (*puṇyahīna*).
[From the *Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*, Chapter on the Great Summary (*mahoddeśa*), verse 127.]
One might think, "I am a king," and by the power of that habituation, he too will become a king;

however, this is not seen to occur without a store of merit (*puṇyasambhāra*). Just as one who lacks a store of merit will not become a king through the power of habituation to false conceptualization (*mithyāvikalpa*) over many eons (*anekakalpa*), so too, a yogi who lacks merit and wisdom (*puṇyajñāna*) does not become a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*samyaksambuddha*) over many eons through the power of habituating to conceptualization, because of the absence of merit and wisdom.
This was stated by the Blessed One in the sixteenth verse of the *Suviśuddhadharmadhātustava*:
That is to say: he is possessed of merit, the accumulation of merit; he is knowledge, the great source of knowledge;
he is possessed of knowledge, the knower of the existent and non-existent; he is one who has gathered the two accumulations.
From these words of the Blessed One, it follows that one devoid of merit and wisdom does not become a Buddha through the power of practicing the cultivation of conceptual forms.

Now, if the cultivation of form is conceptual, then since a yogi [would consist of] conceptualization, he will not become a Buddha; in that case, what is the purpose of this statement of the Tathāgata that "this body must be purified by the hosts of deities of the maṇḍala-circle"? Such might be the thought of someone.

Therefore it is said: This is true here; by means of the *samaya*-language, the Tathāgata has designated each one as Vairocana and so forth. However, this is not according to the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) in its own nature, like the words "pot" or "cloth"—such that the female organ is the lotus, the male organ is the vajra, feces is Vairocana, urine is Akṣobhya, blood is Ratnasambhava, semen is Amitābha, and flesh is Amoghasiddhi. Rather, the designations for the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) have been stated by means of the names of the five Tathāgatas, but they are not deities according to the logic of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, it cannot be said that the body of the deity is a putrid body because it is devoid of essence;
so it was stated by the Blessed One in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, within the "Praise of the Wisdom of the Utterly Pure Dharmadhātu," in the three verses beginning with the twentieth, as follows:
"Of singular solid essence, having the nature of a vajra, the Lord of the World, newly born."
Born from space, self-arisen, the great fire of the wisdom of insight;
Vairocana of great radiance, shining with the light of gnosis;
the lamp of the world, the torch of wisdom, of great splendor, and luminous.
The King of Vidyās, the foremost Lord of Mantras, the one who accomplishes the great purpose of the King of Mantras;
the Great Uṣṇīṣa, the Wondrous Uṣṇīṣa, the All-Seeing, the Lord of the Sky.
( *Nāmasaṃgīti* 6.20–22) Therefore, from these words of the Blessed One, it follows that the Buddha-body is not a localized body (*prādeśikakāya*).

Now, if the Tathāgata is not possessed of form (*rūpin*), then how [can there be] the descent into the womb, the childhood play, the demonstration of all arts, the departure from the inner apartments, the sitting at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the destruction of Māra’s host, the descent of the deities, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), and the bow-length halos? 1. ca. daśamena | 2. ca. 'tadyathā' is not present.

3. Furthermore, there would be no "knowledge" (*jñāna*). [In the absence of such knowledge,] activities such as the four modes of conduct (*catur-īryāpatha*), traveling through space, coming and going, and performing deeds for the benefit of sentient beings would not exist;

likewise, the Blessed One’s accomplishment of the community of disciples (*śrāvaka-saṃgha*) would not occur, nor would the Great Parinirvāṇa, the display of great miraculous powers (*mahātiśaya-prātihārya*), or the manifestation of the relics (*dhātu-saṃdarśana*).
Some may hold the view that since the emanation of relics— such as hair, teeth, flesh, and bone— is worshipped by the inhabitants of the three worlds,
and since other such marvelous miraculous displays of the Tathāgata belong to the Blessed One who possesses form and not to one who is formless,
therefore the accomplishment of the Blessed One’s form-body (*rūpakāya*) is not false.
Therefore it is said: whatever is stated here regarding the accomplishment of the Blessed One’s form-body (*rūpakāya*) for the sake of ordinary people is not false; yet this alone is not the truth.
Why?
Because it possesses the nature of arising and perishing.

For here, if this manifestation of the womb of the Blessed One, his activity of coming and going for the sake of all sentient beings, and his display of the realm of great parinirvāṇa exist only from the perspective of ultimate reality, then the accomplishment of the Tathāgata would be fruitless.
Why?

Because even though the form-body (*rūpakāya*) of the Blessed One is accomplished through the display of the realm of the body (*kāyadhātu*) and the great parinirvāṇa, it remains as if unaccomplished.

How can that which is an arisen body, having perished and been accomplished, produce for the practitioner an inexhaustible body? This is a contradiction: how will that which is itself unaccomplished accomplish another? Furthermore, if there is the manifestation of relics characterized by great excellence—since in this manifestation of relics the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor marks, and the halos of light have now perished from the body that has become a mass of relics due to the absence of the prior body—then the Vajrasattva-body does not exist within the mass of relics.

In the absence of the body, there is no accomplishment of another Vajrasattva; here, due to mutual contradiction, those who do not realize the reality have perished. Since [Vajrasattva] possesses the nature of arising and ceasing, for the sake of accomplishing a Vajrasattva characterized by the qualities of production and destruction, the Perfection of Wisdom, emptiness, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the limbs of enlightenment, the path, the truths, the meditations, the immeasurables, the formless attainments, the doors of liberation, the superknowledges, the concentrations, the dhāraṇīs, the powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha would be in vain.

Taking the three refuges, the confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, the generation of the bodhicitta, the accumulations of merit and wisdom, and the various practices of awakening would be in vain;
the wisdom consisting of hearing and reflection would be no different from ignorance;
and the methods consisting of wisdom and skillful means would become flawed methods.
In the ultimate truth, there would be non-comprehension of the profound and vast Dharma, even though it is being comprehended.

In the conventional truth of the world, for the sake of accomplishing worldly siddhis, [the practice] is encompassed by the vajrakīla, the armor, the vajra-fortress, the vajra-cage, the protection-wheel, and so forth; it is described as the empowerment of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and body, speech, and mind; it is performed through the placement of the gatekeepers, the entry of the one possessing gnosis, the initiation, and so on; and within the fivefold fortress, the mandala of radiant light, and the emanated world-realms, the accumulation of all offerings and the gathering of the provisions for the welfare of beings—those sentient beings to be trained therein—would at all times be entirely in vain, and yet it is not so.
Therefore, qualities such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses do not arise in Vajrasattva, who is subject to the nature of arising and perishing.

Furthermore, if the Blessed One were here possessed of form (*rūpin*), then, being situated in a single location, he would not be capable of performing beneficial actions for sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in many mountain ranges within world-systems as vast as the sands of the river Ganges, because of his having a physical body (*rūpakāyatvāt*).

Now, as for the statement of those with immature intellects— that even by means of the form-body (rūpakāya), having gone to one world-system and performed beneficial activity for the sentient beings residing there, it then goes to another world-system, and from there proceeds elsewhere—
that very thing is not logically tenable; why?

Since even in a single directional sector there is no measure to the world-systems, how much more so for the infinitely infinite sentient beings residing in the world-systems situated in all ten directions? It is impossible to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings by going again and again with one's form-body over many eons—
[for] O,
there is no limit to the realms (*dhātu*).
O! The Conduct of the Bodhisattva. O! There is no "gnosis" (*jñāna*). O! There is no "armor" (*kavaca*).
O, there is no "going. [End of] the chapter, verse: the great instruction named the Accomplishment of the Knowledge of Supreme Unchanging Syllable (*paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*).

Now, by the power of meditation and mantra, having summoned the sentient beings residing in various Buddha-fields and world-systems and established them before him, he performs the teaching of the Dharma for them.
Having established them on the path, one would dismiss them to their respective world-systems;

that indeed would be exceedingly contrary [to the purpose], for it would be impossible to manifest oneself before even a single atom's worth of countless sentient beings with form who reside in various world-systems within the hollow of the entire sky.

Furthermore, even by means of this form-body (*rūpakāya*), he performs the work of benefiting sentient beings residing within a single buddha-field—that is, throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-systems—for those of immature intellect. However, when this statement is examined through ultimate reasoning, it is devoid of meaning; it is like the word of Īśvara, established merely by his command and lacking both logic and valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
According to the scriptures of the authoritative ones, Īśvara is partless and the creator of all things.

And as for the ritual action: here, the five nectars beginning with *vairocana*, the edible portions of cow dung and so forth, which are taught by the Tathāgata to be pure by nature—it is said that by consuming these, the body will become free from old age and death, and even Vajrasattva will become a granter of boons.

"Otherwise, living beings are to be slain by means of the *krodharāja* samādhi in the Vajra family; one must speak the truth by means of the Amoghasiddhi samādhi in the Khaḍga family; the property of others is to be taken away by means of the Ratnasambhava samādhi in the Ratna family; another's wife is to be taken by means of the Amitābha samādhi in the Padma family; and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are to be consumed by means of the Vairocana samādhi in the Cakra family. Furthermore, the other ten paths of unwholesome action (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*) are to be performed by the yogin through the yoga of the deity. Thus, taking the words of such corrupt teachers as authoritative, they perform the ten paths of unwholesome action; they consume [substances] that have not been purified, not awakened, not ignited, and not transformed into nectar (*amṛta*).

One might have the following thought: "Those five nectars (pañcāmṛta), even when consumed, do not bestow the qualities of Buddhahood upon those who eat them, because they lack understanding of the Tathāgata’s words. Surely, in all the Kingly Tantras, the Tathāgata has stated that the five nectars are to be consumed by the yogin; why then is there this prohibition here?"

Therefore it is said: "In this regard, that which is to be stated by the foolish—that the five nectars and so forth were taught as foods by the Tathāgata in all the king-tantras—is true; however, [this applies] to yogins, not to ordinary beings."

By the power of their mantras or the power of their meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), poisons that have been purified, awakened, ignited, and rendered immortal become poisonless; liquors become milk; harmful poisonous waters and the like, which bring death to sentient beings, become elixirs (*rasāyana*); bones become flowers; teeth become pearls; skulls become lotuses; flesh becomes *putrakeśa*; blood becomes *sihnaka*; urine becomes musk (*kastūrikā*); semen becomes camphor (*karpūra*); excrement becomes the "fourfold equal" (*catuḥsama*); and body hairs become saffron filaments (*kuṅkumakeśara*).

In this way, various harmful substances—purified, awakened, ignited, and transformed into nectar by abandoning their harmful nature—are declared by the Tathāgata to be pure by nature; they are not [pure] by not abandoning their harmful nature.
Furthermore, those poisons and so forth, being pure by nature and transformed into nectar, when consumed by yogins, become providers of great strength and nourishment to the body.
Excrement and the like, being pure by nature, when smeared upon the body, exude a divine fragrance.

Therefore, these have been spoken by the Tathāgata for yogins, and not for others—those who have not accomplished the mantras of the deities, the fools in the assembly who pride themselves on being scholars, those who possess the deceit of a crane, those who covet the property of monasteries and temples, those bound to rebirth in the realms of hungry ghosts and hell-beings, those fallen from their own and others' welfare, those who teach meanings contrary to the meaning declared in the tantras, and those great Mārakāyika demons who prey upon unexamined people; thus they were spoken by the Blessed One.

Even though those poisonous substances and corrupt materials were purified, awakened, ignited, and turned into nectar by those whose minds were bitten [by ignorance], they did not abandon their corrupt nature throughout many eons; because they did not abandon their corrupt nature, they did not become pure by nature.

Therefore, as long as a son of noble family, a daughter of noble family, a monk, a nun, a layman, a laywoman, or a beginner is unable—either through the power of meditation or the power of mantra—to remove the evil nature of those corrupt substances, he must not be given the rule regarding the eating and anointing with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth by his Vajrācārya teacher, whether that teacher be a beginner or one endowed with the power of mantra. This is the Great Chapter on the Accomplishment of the Knowledge of Supreme Unchanging [Bliss] (*paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*). If one eats impure poison and the like, death occurs; if one anoints oneself with impure substances, public censure arises. From self-inflicted death and public censure, hell results. This is because bad counselors abandon the intentions of sentient beings. Thus it was said in the fifteenth verse of the *Adhyeṣaṇā* section of the *Nāmasaṃgīti*: "I shall reveal [the teachings] for sentient beings according to the distinctions of their inclinations."
"For the destruction of all afflictions without exception, for the abandonment of all ignorance without exception" (Nāmasaṃgīti 1.15).

Therefore, according to these words of the Blessed One, the Vajrācārya must bestow the precepts upon his disciples in accordance with the dispositions of all sentient beings, so that beginners do not suffer death by their own hand or incur the censure of the world.

Now, if it is the case that hell results from being censured by the world here, then since all philosophical systems (*darśana*) mutually censure one another, would it not follow that all philosophical systems would go to hell due to this mutual censure?

If this were so, one might think that the treatises on logic (*pramāṇaśāstra*) are contradictory, as are all established doctrines, and that everything such as vows and moral conduct (*vrataśīla*) would be rendered useless. Therefore, it is said: what is asserted here by the ignorant—that all the treatises on logic and so forth are contradictory—is not the case. Why? Because for those who have minds intent on investigating reality (*tattva*), there is no fault in those mutually opposing views; for their minds are based on the investigation of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they lack any intention to harm any sentient being, and possess the intention to benefit all sentient beings.

Furthermore, in this context, the consumption and anointing with poisons and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth belong to worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*), not to the investigation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Poison, the five nectars, and so forth are not the ultimate truth (*tattva*), such that by investigating them no faults would arise even from the world’s censure.
Therefore, the teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhists is according to the dispositions of sentient beings; it is not devoid of the dispositions of sentient beings.

The disposition (*āśaya*) of sentient beings also arises according to their country, family, and social conventions; therefore, the Vajrācārya should teach the worldly dharma to them by means of the worldly conventional truth (*laukika-saṃvṛti-satya*) according to their country, family, and conventions.
However, supramundane gnosis (*lokottara-jñāna*), which is common to both truths, is that very same [gnosis], and for it there is no grasping at what is edible and what is inedible.

For what is edible and what is inedible is merely a matter of filling the stomach; it is not the purification through the four gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and lack of volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Therefore, a beginner should determine what is edible and inedible according to the local customs of their own country. Furthermore, regarding visiting families or non-families: in some regions purity is achieved with the skull-water of the Kāpālikas; in some regions cow-meat is to be eaten; in some regions horse-meat; in some regions dog-meat; in some regions elephant-meat; and in some regions human-meat is to be eaten.

In this same way, other meats as well may be eaten by all castes and non-castes according to local custom; for instance, in some regions the drinking of liquor is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas, in some regions it is prescribed for Śūdras, and in some regions it is prescribed for both the noble-born and the low-born.

In some regions the remnants of a dog's meal are to be eaten; in some regions there is no ritual sipping of water (ācamana) after eating; in some regions the meat of a pig is to be eaten, in some regions the meat of a buffalo, and in some regions the meat of a goat.
In this same way, other types of meat as well should not be eaten by those of high or low caste according to the local customs of the region.

In some places, *caṇḍālas* are disciples (*śrāvakas*); in some regions, the practice of the four castes prevails; in some regions, the practice of a single caste for all prevails; in some regions, when the husband has died, the son takes his mother as a wife; in some regions, there is marriage between brothers and sisters; in some regions, there are relations with maternal uncles; in some regions, members of noble and ignoble families have sexual intercourse with one another; and in some regions, Brahmin women engage in the profession of courtesans.
Thus, through the practice of visiting various regions, the yogi should engage with families that are both those whose food is permitted and those whose food is forbidden.

Likewise, regarding family deities (*kuladevatā*): in some families the deity is a serpent (*nāga*), in some a goat, in some a pig, in some a buffalo, and in some an owl; likewise, other animals may also be the family deities of others. These must neither be killed nor eaten.

Likewise, for some the family deity (*kuladevatā*) is the *palāśa* tree, for some the *arka*, and for some the *aśvattha*; similarly, other trees may also be the family deities of others. These must not be cut down nor damaged;
in this regard, even worldly conviction is observed.
Why?
Because of the affliction of one's own family and the benefit of one's own family.

In this world, whichever deity is propitiated by someone bestows benefit, while when opposed, it causes great affliction; therefore, one who is devoted to the practice of mantra, meditation, and sādhanā conducts himself according to the local customs and traditions of those [deities], until the attainment of the mantra or the attainment of knowledge occurs.

Then, by his own will, he determines what is edible and inedible, who is approachable and unapproachable, and what is drinkable and undrinkable; no one is able to cause him any obstruction. When such a mantra has been accomplished, the practitioner becomes a *yogī*.

He is a perfected one (*siddha*) because of his ability to traverse the sky, having expanded the *maṇḍala-cakra*. He becomes omniscient (*sarvajña*) because of the exhaustion of the obscurations of the afflictions (*kleśa*), the maras, and the knowable (*jñeya*); because of the manifestation of the perfection of miraculous powers in all their forms; and because of his turning of the wheel of Dharma through the teaching of the entire collection of the aggregates of phenomena (*dharma-skandha*) in the language of the Omniscient One.
It was stated by the Blessed One in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, within the first three verses of the forty [stanzas] of the *Pratyavekṣaṇājñānastava*: "The yoga of wisdom and gnosis is as follows:

the great exertion of the *Māyājāla*, the supreme lord of all tantras; he who sits cross-legged upon the entirety of vajras, the bearer of the entire body of gnosis; Samantabhadra, the one of excellent intelligence, Kṣitigarbha, the sustainer of the world."
"The Great Passion of all Buddhas, who holds the wheel of manifold emanations; the supreme essence of the nature of all things, who upholds the essence of the nature of all things;
whose nature is non-arising, whose purpose is the universe, who upholds the essence of the nature of all phenomena.
Thus it is also stated in the *Tantrarāja*, in the fifth chapter, by the two verses beginning with the sixtieth:

Indeed, by means of those [elements], the Great Kālacakra manifests through manifold emanations: with vajra-flames radiating for the asuras, gods, and humans dwelling in the desire realm; with the enjoyment bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*) for the sons of the Victors and so forth in the form realm; and with the emptiness-totalities (*śūnyakṛtsna*) through the empty [space] for the Arhats in the sky; the wind-totality through the winds; the fire-totality through the portions of fire; the water-totality through the waters expanded throughout the world and the portions of water; and the earth-totality through the portions of earth. Thus, through the assembled objects, he reveals the nature of all things.
One should perceive this single self as being entirely equal to space on the pure stage; thus the body of the Buddha exists, for it does not die, because its nature is singular bliss.
Thus ends the Yoga of Non-dual Gnosis (*advayajñānayoga*).
O Asura, there are fifty-nine [verses] in this;
and throughout this [section], in place of the word "aṃśaḥ," the word "maṅgaḥ" occurs everywhere.

In this chapter, the Great Exposition titled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of Supreme Unchanging [Bliss]": From these words of the Blessed One, it may occur to some that a yogi does not become a perfectly awakened Buddha through the power of consuming the five nectars, reciting mantras, or meditating on the conceptualized mandala-circle.

They might think: "Has it not been stated by the Blessed One that when the mandala-circle is directly realized, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā occurs for yogis? Therefore, how is it that here, even when the mandala-circle is directly realized, the yogi does not become omniscient? This will be the intention of certain individuals here.
Therefore it is said: Here, it was previously stated that the mandala-circle is a web of conceptual construction, limited and granting only limited fruits of accomplishment.

Now, this is merely a delusion of the ignorant: that by taking hold of a karma-mudrā, or by the power of pills, the power of mantras, the power of seven-fold recitations, the power of the sword and so forth, or by the power of meditation or the power of accomplishing the mandala-circle, one becomes invisible; [they think] one does not become the Blessed One Vajrasattva, who is omniscient and liberated from all obscurations.
It was said by the Blessed One in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, in the hymn to the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajra Realm, regarding the bearer of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*):

"For example: he who abides in the samādhi of great meditative concentration, who bears the body of great wisdom, who possesses great power and great skillful means, and who is an ocean of the knowledge of vows."

Thus, from these words of the Blessed One, it follows that this accomplishment of Mahāmudrā is the Mahāmudrā characterized by the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in all phenomena, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Mother of the Buddhas; she is also designated by the term *dharmodaya*.
Therefore, from that *dharmodaya*, the arising of all phenomena occurs by way of their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Phenomena—such as the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*)—are devoid of intrinsic nature. The *dharmodaya* is the source of their arising; it is the Buddha-field, the dwelling place, the place of delight, and the place of birth for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. It is not, however, the *dharmodaya* in the sense of being the arising of blood, urine, and semen, for this field of passion and dispassion belongs to those in cyclic existence (*saṃsārin*), and not to the Tathāgatas.

Therefore, the Source of Phenomena (*dharmodayā*), whose nature is the *dharmadhātu*, is the Mother of the Universe (*viśvamātā*) embraced by the Blessed One in the *Kālacakra*; she is eternally free from all obscurations.
Here, "passion" (*rāga*) is the time of arising, and "emission" (*cyuti*) is the time of cessation; the union of these two is the time of the imperishable (*akṣara*).

Its "wheel" (*cakra*) is the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajra Realm (*vajradhātumahāmaṇḍala*); thus, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, when free from obscuration, are called the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajra Realm.
By this arising from the syllable, she—the unarisen Mahāmudrā—is embraced.

Whoever, by virtue of the latencies of merit from previous births and through the instruction of a true guru, directly realizes and embraces this Mahāmudrā—who is free from the conceptualization of all phenomena, a mere manifestation of one's own mind, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, the Great Emptiness that gives birth to innate bliss—for many days and nights, day and night, has attained the siddhi of Mahāmudrā and is called the omniscient Blessed One.

Therefore, an initiate (*ādikarmika*) must not perform the deeds of a yogi; a yogi must not perform the deeds of a perfected one (*siddha*); and a perfected one must not perform the deeds of an omniscient one (*sarvajña*).

In this way, according to the previously mentioned rule, an initiate must observe what is edible and what is inedible, and so forth. Now, regarding the speech of those with sinful minds—the Daityas whose dharma consists of the instructions of false gurus—it has been stated here by the Tathāgata in the *Tantrarājas*: "All commitments (*samaya*) are to be consumed with a mind free of conceptual construction."

Therefore, first of all, we shall consume the five nectars and so forth; subsequently, by the power of that practice, the accomplishment of the pledge (samayasiddhi) will arise. By the power of the accomplishment of the pledge, things such as poison, which are normally unfit for consumption, will become edible, and foul-smelling things such as excrement will become fragrant—such is the statement here regarding the pledge-seal (samayamudrā).
O, there are no fragrant things to be eaten.
Furthermore, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, there is a supreme contradiction:

how could it be that first one must enter the fire, and later, through the power of practice, the fire will be arrested? It is not so. Here, if those who are greatly wicked, deceivers of others, mockers of the teaching of the Omniscient One, violators of the great commitments (*mahāsamaya*), destined for the Avīci hell, and impure in mind—were their minds purified, then why would they not perform the duties of a yogin?

In this world, the yogi with a purified mind enters fire but is not burned by the fire; he paralyzes a rutting lordly elephant but is not intoxicated by the rutting elephant; he mounts lions, tigers, and the like, but is not torn apart by lions, tigers, and the like; he enters a river so full that it can be drunk from by crows, but is not carried away by the current of the river; he consumes poison but does not become unconscious from the poison; he consumes swords and other weapons but is not cut in the mouth by the weapons;
likewise, he makes edible what is inedible and performs the transformation of his own and others' forms.
Thus, these manifold forms of yogic activities are not performed by a beginner.

The Blessed One has stated that there is a tenfold classification of yogis: first, the yogi who has generated the thought of awakening (*cittotpādika*); then, those who have become like children (*bālabhūta*) and those who have become like youths (*kumārabhūta*); the beginner practitioner (*ādikarmaka-yogācāra*); one born from [the practice of] yoga (*janmaja*); one perfected in application (*prayoga-sampanna*); one perfected in intention (*āśaya-sampanna*); the non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*); one who has attained consecration (*abhiṣeka-prāpta*); and one bound to only one more birth (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*).

From that, there are ten masteries of the Bodhisattva: mastery over life, mastery over karma, mastery over requisites, mastery over resolve, mastery over aspiration, mastery over miraculous power, mastery over rebirth, mastery over the Dharma, mastery over the mind, and mastery over knowledge;

these correspond to the ten stages (bhūmis), namely: the Joyous, the Immaculate, the Luminous, the Radiant, the Difficult to Conquer, the Facing, the Far-Reaching, the Immovable, the Excellent Intelligence, and the Cloud of Dharma.

In this way, the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) become fulfilled—namely, the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and knowledge.
Thus the practitioner becomes a Bodhisattva.
This was stated by the Blessed One in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, in the *Suviśuddhadharmadhātustava*, in the third and fourth verses: "Attainer of the ten perfections, Abode of the ten perfections."
He is the purity of the ten perfections, the method of the ten perfections; he is the Lord, the master of the ten stages, established upon the ten stages;
his self is purified by the ten knowledges, and he upholds the purification of the ten knowledges.
Thus, it is said by the Blessed One that the yogi, the Bodhisattva of purified mind, [should practice] here in this Mantra Vehicle.

However, some—by means of the Heroic Method (*vīrakrama*) or the Self-Consecration Method (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*)—entering a cremation ground at the dead of night for one year, two years, up to twelve years, or even until death, are unable to directly perceive the Blessed Lord Heruka through the power of mantra recitation and meditative concentration. Likewise, they are unable to [perceive] deities such as Samantabhadra in secluded places such as mountains, gardens, rivers, and seashores.

Having little diligence and acting for the sake of their own and others' worldly interests, they perform the recitation of mantras, fire offerings (*homa*), ritual oblations (*bali*), meditations, and the visualization of mandala wheels within their own homes regarding the domain of ritual action; yet, due to the influence of improper place and time, their mantras remain unaccomplished and their minds become alienated from the deity. Likewise, having fallen away from the path of Mahāmudrā meditation through the process of purification, being devoid of the instructions of a true guru, and having fallen into the Great Nihilism (*mahoccheda*), these wicked gurus will teach the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to those of childish intellect who fail to examine the profound and vast Dharma.

The Great Chapter entitled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of the Supreme Unchanging. As it was said by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "All phenomena are free from conceptual construction; all phenomena are empty; all phenomena are signless; all phenomena are wishless; all phenomena are devoid of formative activity; all phenomena are devoid of arising; all phenomena are beyond syllables; all phenomena are empty of causes; all phenomena are inconceivable."

Therefore, for the sake of attaining the fruit of omniscience, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be indifferent toward all phenomena; he should not abide in the aggregate of form, nor in feeling, nor in perception, nor in mental formations, nor in consciousness. He should not abide in the earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element, nor in the space element. He should not abide in the eye element, nor in the form element, nor in the eye-consciousness element; nor in the ear element, nor in the sound element, nor in the ear-consciousness element; nor in the nose element, nor in the odor element, nor in the nose-consciousness element; nor in the tongue element, nor in the taste element, nor in the tongue-consciousness element; nor in the body element, nor in the tactile object element, nor in the body-consciousness element; nor in the mind element, nor in the mental object element, nor in the mind-consciousness element. Thus should he not abide.
Thus, the Blessed One has stated that the perfection of wisdom is the inconceivable gnosis of the Tathāgata for the sake of attaining perfect enlightenment.
Why is it inconceivable? Because its intrinsic nature is the absence of both passion (*rāga*) and dispassion (*virāga*).

For when conceptualization arises in sentient beings here, there is passion toward desirable objects and dispassion toward undesirable objects; thus, passion and dispassion become the causes of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

Furthermore, when the Tathāgata’s wisdom is free from conceptual thought (*niścintana*), there is no attachment toward desirable objects and no aversion toward undesirable objects. Due to the very absence of these two, there is an absence of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); and because of that absence, perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbuddhatva*) occurs. Therefore, the means for attaining Buddhahood is the Tathāgata’s wisdom free from conceptual thought, and not some other conceptual construction or meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Thus, those who are unawakened and yet desire this non-conceptual wisdom will say, having fallen into a great nihilism (*uccheda*).

Therefore it is said: If, in this context, non-conceptual cognition were the bestower of Buddhahood, then why have all sentient beings not become Buddhas? For even in their deep sleep, non-conceptual cognition occurs in them, yet they possess neither attachment toward desired objects nor aversion toward undesired objects.

Therefore, in that state of deep sleep (*suṣuptāvasthā*), passion and its absence would not exist; nor did all sentient beings become perfectly awakened Buddhas by means of that thought-free cognition (*niścintana-jñāna*). Consequently, thought-free cognition is not the Tathāgata-knowledge, because in the *Samādhipaṭala* of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) were taught by the Blessed One, among which is the absorption named "Jewel Lamp" (*ratnapradīpa*).
If, in this context, there were no contemplation of the Jewel Lamp, nor even its appearance, then how could it be the absorption named "Jewel Lamp"?

In this way, other meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) as well do not constitute "beyond-thought" (*niścintana*), because they possess the characteristic of being self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*) and because they are states of insentient emptiness.

Now, there is this objection from the ignorant: "If this Tathāgata-knowledge is self-cognizable, then how was it stated by the Tathāgata that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)?

To this it is replied: Here, Tathāgata-knowledge is indeed the realization of the lack of intrinsic nature in all phenomena; it does not have the characteristic of a total non-existence like the mind in deep sleep.

It is stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "There is that mind which is no-mind," meaning it is called naturally luminous (*prakṛtiprabhāsvara*). If this self-cognizable Tathāgata-gnosis did not exist, then the teaching of the Dharma by the Tathāgata would not occur in accordance with the dispositions of sentient beings, because all phenomena would remain unawakened due to the absence of such self-cognition.

If [the Tathāgata's gnosis] were self-cognizable by means of the sense faculties (*indriya*), then it would not be partless (*niṣkala*), all-pervading, or omnipresent, because of the obstruction of all [senses].

Therefore, the Tathāgata’s gnosis is self-cognizable, knows the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-svabhāva-jña*), is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), and is beyond the senses (*anindriya*).

This was stated by the Blessed One in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, in the *Pratyavekṣaṇājñānastava*, by way of the three verses beginning with the twentieth: "In the *Vimalaprabhā*: Nirvāṇa, cessation (*nirvṛti*), peace (*śānti*), excellence (*śreya*), departure (*niryāṇa*), and the end-maker (*antaga*)."
The culmination that brings an end to pleasure and pain is dispassion and the complete destruction of the afflictions.
Unconquered, incomparable, unmanifest, without appearance, stainless, partless, all-pervading, omnipresent, subtle, the seed, and free from outflows.

"Free from dust, stainless, immaculate, with faults cast out, free from affliction, perfectly awakened, one whose self is fully enlightened, the all-knowing, the all-perceiving, the supreme. Thus it is stated in the thirteenth verse of the *Kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-stava*: "He who knows himself and knows others, who is everything, who is more beneficial than all, for he is the foremost person (*agrapudgala*)."
"He who has transcended all comparisons is to be known as the supreme Lord of Gnosis.

Thus it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*, in the ninety-ninth verse of the fifth chapter: "The Body-Vajra of the Jina is indeed omniform and inaccessible to [ordinary] objects and subjects; the Speech-Vajra is that which accomplishes the Dharma through the sounds of the hearts of all sentient beings;
