the Mind-Vajra of the Vajrin is the nature of the consciousness of beings, pervading the entire earth; and the Gnosis-Vajra is that very same [Mind-Vajra] which, like a stainless jewel, is the grasper of all phenomena."

Therefore, the Tathāgata’s gnosis is devoid of sense faculties and is self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*). [Objection to the term *jñāna*]: Now, if the Tathāgata’s gnosis is self-cognizable, then it cannot exist because of the absence of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). It has been stated by the Blessed One in the *Tantrarājas*: "In the absence of the aggregates, the gnosis of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*) is not perceived. At the time of the emission of the *bodhicitta* from the union of the two organs, in the interval between the *sahaja* (innate) and *virama* (cessation) moments, there is a single moment consisting of three drops (*bindu*); this alone is called the Samantabhadra gnosis of great bliss, and it is described as being self-cognizable.

In this regard, some may have the following intention: "How can there be the gnosis of great bliss (*mahāsukha-jñāna*) which is Samantabhadra, devoid of the drops (*bindu*) of bodhicitta and lacking sense faculties, when it is being analyzed as being as useless as a sky-flower smelled by the son of a barren woman?

Therefore, it is said: "This is not so; for the Tathāgata has stated that the drop of bodhicitta is the bliss of emission (*kṣarasukha*), which is Samantabhadra, the great bliss, and the gnosis of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*). This is because of the prohibitive statement: 'That fourth is again like that.'"

In this context, if the third [joy], the bliss of emission (*kṣarasukha*), were the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), and the fourth were the all-pervading goodness (*samantabhadra*) of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), then there would be a designation for that which has already been designated;
however, this is not logical. Why?
Because it would entail the fault of redundancy (*punaruktadoṣa*).
Just as when "hand" has already been said in a chapter, to say "hand" again, or likewise to say "curd" again—
this is the speech of children and madmen, not that of the wise.

Therefore, because of the statement "the fourth," it is not the third; yet because of the statement "that again is such," that very thing is the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*). Consequently, those who do not understand the word of the Blessed One will say here that they are ruined: "The third was spoken of by the Blessed One with the words 'that again is such' as being the fourth; there would be no such thing as a 'fourth' [distinct from the third].

Herein lies the engagement in non-dharma among the foolish—those who desire the melting bliss produced by the two organs and have fallen away from the knowledge of the great immutable bliss (*mahākṣarasukha*).
Therefore, the bliss of the emission of the bodhicitta is not the fourth [dhyāna], which is the all-pervading Samantabhadra, the gnosis of great bliss.

This was stated by the Blessed One in the third verse of the *Kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñānastava* within the *Nāmasaṃgīti*: "Having all forms yet formless, holding the sixteen, the half, and the quarter-bindu; transcending conceptualization, he holds the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna."

It is also stated in the *Tantrarāja*, in the fifty-sixth verse of the fifth chapter, as follows: "Thus, the fourfold mind of living beings residing within the threefold existence must be protected by the lord of yogins within the center of the *bindu* for the sake of liberation, as it bestows the fruit of equal bliss and is all-pervasive.

If the *bindu* were liberated, where would there be liberation for yogins who have attained supreme bliss? It is the seed of birth; therefore, the momentary pleasure of saṃsāra must always be avoided here by ascetics.
Therefore, the fourth is not the third.

In this context, if the drop (*bindu*) were the third [joy], namely the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), and that same [drop] were the fourth, then the Blessed One would not be the holder of the sixteen half-and-half drops. If the fourth were the cessation (*virāma*), then he would not be the holder of the pinnacle of the four meditative absorptions—joy, supreme joy, cessation, and the innate (*sahaja*).
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s gnosis is beyond the senses and self-cognizable;
for this reason, the yogin must protect the *bodhicitta* very firmly and must not let it be emitted.

Furthermore, there are no other drops—such as urine, water, and so forth—either within the body or externally that are devoid of the drop of *bodhicitta* and yet will bestow the fruit of Buddhahood; such is not the case. If the fourth, the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*), does not exist without the third, and the Blessed One is the "Bearer of the Drop" (*bindudhṛk*), then some might ask here: "What will become of the wisdom of insight in light of the statement 'that again is thus'? Therefore, it is said: In this Vajrayāna, relying upon the mundane and supramundane truths, the Blessed One has taught threefold wisdom (*prajñā*)—namely, the action seal (*karmamudrā*), the knowledge seal (*jñānamudrā*), and the great seal (*mahāmudrā*)—by way of a single designation.

Among these, for the yogin, there is the bliss of the *karmamudrā* and *jñānamudrā*, characterized by vibration (*spanda*), and the bliss of the *mahāmudrā*, characterized by non-vibration (*niḥspanda*).

Here, if the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñā*) is "wisdom-knowledge" (*prajñājñāna*) characterized by emission (*cyuti*), produced as the fruit of the means (*upāya*) through the cause of wisdom, then that which is produced as the fruit of wisdom through the cause of the means becomes "means-knowledge" (*upāyajñāna*) for the yogin. Thus, for the sake of attaining the accomplishment of *mahāmudrā*, there are two kinds of knowledge because they are mutually dependent.

Thus, when there is knowledge of each of the two individually, there is an absence of the knowledge of non-duality; and due to the absence of the knowledge of non-duality, even Buddhahood becomes non-existent, because of being devoid of the pure, supreme, immutable gnosis (*paramākṣarajñāna*).

Now, if "gnosis of wisdom" (*prajñājñāna*) means the gnosis of wisdom, then likewise "gnosis of means" (*upāyajñāna*) would mean the gnosis of means; in that case, the same fault as before would apply.

This was stated by the Blessed One in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, in the hymn to the Gnosis of Discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), in the thirty-sixth verse and those following: "The supreme immutable gnosis is purified of duality."

Namely: the Perfectly Awakened One, seated in the vajra posture, the upholder of the Dharma of the Buddha’s assembly, born from the lotus of the Buddhas, the glorious one, the bearer of the treasury of omniscient wisdom.

"The King who holds the universal illusion, the great holder of the Buddha-vidyā, the diamond-sharp, the great sword, the pure, the supreme syllable"— thus it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*, in the chapter on Sādhana, by two verses beginning with the one hundred and ninety-ninth, regarding the characteristics of Mahāmudrā: "Having abandoned this Karmamudrā whose heart is defiled and the imagined Jñānamudrā, one should meditate upon the Divine Mudrā (Divyamudrā), the Mother of the Supreme Victor, for the sake of perfect enlightenment."

Untainted, changeless, as vast as the great void, all-pervading, attainable through yoga, immutable, the splendor of knowledge, the remover of the impurities of worldly existence, and interwoven with the Wheel of Time.
The Mudrā conforms to illusion; she appears as a form in the sky, in the mind, and in a mirror. Illuminating the three worlds, she flashes with many rays resembling lightning and fire.

Unchanging within external bodies, devoid of sense objects, and existing merely as a manifestation, she resides in the ether and embraces the mind consisting of consciousness. She alone is the one [reality] of the world’s manifold forms.
Thus it is also said in the Mūlatantra: "Having abandoned the Karmamudrā and the conceptualized Jñānamudrā..."
"One should visualize Mahāmudrā through the yoga of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*).

According to this rule of the Blessed One, the bliss of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) is not the all-good (*samantabhadra*) bliss of the supreme unchanging; likewise, the bliss of wisdom (*prajñā*) conceptualized through the meditation on the mandala-circle is not the all-good bliss of the supreme unchanging, because of the non-abandonment of conceptual construction.

Now, having fallen away from the knowledge of Mahāmudrā due to the instructions of false gurus, they act like cattle; there is no Buddhahood for them, because of the absence of the knowledge of Mahāmudrā.
The non-abiding gnosis of Mahāmudrā cannot be imparted by a false guru who is devoid of the path.
As for the path itself: "That fourth is likewise."

Thus, if one is not awakened by the fourth consecration, all consecrations would be meaningless. Now, if Samantabhadra is the supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*), and that itself is the fourth knowledge of Mahāmudrā which is not devoid of Mahāmudrā,
then for what purpose did the Blessed One teach this cultivation of great bliss through the union of the two organs?

Through this meditation, the attainment of Buddhahood and the state of Vajradhara in this very life has been stated; such may be the intention of someone here. [From the *Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*, the Great Chapter titled "The Accomplishment of Supreme Unchanging Gnosis," it is said: Therefore, it is stated: "In this regard, that which was spoken by the Blessed One regarding the means of accomplishing great bliss through the union of the two organs is true; for the Blessed One, in the fifth chapter of the *Tantrarāja*, in the one hundred and ninety-ninth verse, stated: 'By that passion through which sentient beings have gone to destruction, the Protectors (Tāyins) are liberated.'"
Whatever beings protect at every moment of the day, the Protectors give that back;

whatever beings liberate—the happiness residing in their own hearts—that the Victors protect. Therefore, this conduct of the Supreme Victor would be difficult even for gods, nāgas, and asuras to perform.
Thus it is said:

"In this world, by which passion sentient beings, when it has fallen away, undergo dissolution and death; by that very same [passion] when it is un-fallen and has become the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), the Protectors, the Buddhas, become liberated.
That which sentient beings protect, such as children, wife, and so forth, the Protectors give away."

That great bliss which sentient beings seek to liberate, the Buddhas protect. For that reason, the conduct of the Tathāgatas—which is difficult for gods, asuras, humans, and nāgas to perform—is their miraculous transformation (*vikurvita*). Therefore, the yogin must ensure that the *bodhicitta* does not fall away, in order to accomplish the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*) through the sequential stages.
Thus, what is taught as the cultivation of bliss through the union of the two organs refers to the state [of realization], not the state of the emission of *bodhicitta*.
This habitual tendency toward emission (*cyutivāsanā*) is, for sentient beings, by nature an adventitious stain from beginningless time; through it, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) occurs.

By that very attachment to the seal (*mudrā-saṅga*) through which the habitual tendency toward emission arises, by that same [attachment] there will arise the habitual tendency toward non-emission (*acyutivāsanā*), like the fire of mercury (*sūtaka*).

It was stated by the Blessed One in the *Tantrarāja*, in the chapter on Sadhana, in the 224th verse: "The fire is the enemy of mercury; without fire, the binding of mercury never occurs. Without being bound, it cannot produce gold; and for those who argue otherwise, there are no enjoyments devoid of gold."
Thus, for men, the bond of the mind with women is never absent; when unbound, it pierces the body and bestows supreme bliss here upon one whose body has been pierced.
Thus:

Just as mercury (*sūtaka*) flees from the touch of fire but is bound by that very fire through a specific method, so too the *bodhicitta* flees from the touch of the *dharmodaya* but is bound by it through a specific method.

Just as mercury, when bound by fire, transforms all base metals into gold, so too the *bodhicitta*, when bound by union with the *dharmodaya*, renders the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇa*).
Therefore, the inconceivable power of mercury and the *bodhicitta* cannot be deliberated upon by the foolish.

Consequently, even in the context of the *karmamudrā*, the visualization of the deity is taught for the purpose of stabilizing the *bodhicitta*, just as the heating, digestion, and so forth of mercury are prescribed.
The Tathāgata did not teach the consumption of the *bodhicitta* once it has entered the lotus of the animal-like ritual act.

The Blessed One has taught the accomplishment of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) and so forth in the *Tantrarāja*, in the seventy-third verse of the fifth chapter. As follows: [Verse 32]: "O Victor, for the sake of increasing this innate bliss (*sahajasukha*), the action-seal (*karmamudrā*)—beginning with the one to be served—is of the nature of the sun, complete with face, hands, feet, crown-protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*), and all limbs. In the *Vimalaprabhā*: "The action-seal, beginning with the one to be served, is for the purpose of increasing this innate bliss of the Victor; therefore, she is of the form of the sun, complete with face, hands, feet, crown-protrusion, and all limbs."

Resembling a bolt of lightning, generating the bliss of the Infallible One, complete with all the marks and limbs, and illuminating the three worlds, that which has its body pervading the three realms is therefore the Dharmadhātu.
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, what is that which is described here in this thirteenth chapter by the one hundred and thirteenth verse? "The mere appearance of the gnosis-mind (*jñānacitta*), produced within one's own mind like a reflection in a mirror, should be cultivated by the lords of yogins and served by all the sons of the Victors.
That flame of gnosis, once awakened, burns away the entire host of Māras along with their objects, and through the yoga of the year, it bestows equal bliss upon the bodies of yogins."
Thus [it is asked]:

"O Blessed One, according to your rule, even through the union of the two organs, this Mahāmudrā—which is a mere reflection of one's own mind—should be meditated upon by the yogin until the end of enlightenment, having abandoned the leaking bliss produced by the external organs. Is it not true that the Tathāgata has stated that in the absence of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) devoid of the union of the two organs cannot be self-cognized, because it is non-emitted (*acyuta*)?

How does the yogi, having formed an attachment to the manifestation of his own mind by means of his own mind, render his own mind free from obscuration and enjoy the gnosis of great immutable bliss, given the absence of a body composed of an accumulation of atoms?

The opposite of this would be like saying, "Devadatta, having mounted his own shoulder, goes to the village"—such might be someone's intention here; therefore it is said: what is to be stated here by the foolish is that the self-cognized wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) does not exist through mind-only (*cittamātra*) apart from the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields (*skandhadhātvāyatana*) which consist of a collection of atoms; that is not so. Why?
Because of the power of adventitious mental latencies (*vāsanā*).

In this context, what are called the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) are the adventitious mental impressions (vāsanās). Through their influence, feelings of pleasure and pain enter the mind; yet when investigated from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), these do not belong to the body through its own minor afflictions.
Here, the body—which consists of a collection of atoms—remains as if fallen into a dream-state; it possesses no minor affliction whatsoever by which suffering could enter the mind.

This is well-known in all the worlds: in that very state, another body consisting of mental impressions (*cittavāsanā*), devoid of a collection of atoms, appears as it travels to another place. When that body traveling to another place is afflicted by thieves and the like, suffering enters the mind through that affliction, and because of that suffering, one cries out.
This is a great marvel:
even without a physical body and without thieves and the like, a cognition of suffering arises for the mind, which is directly experienced by itself (*svasaṃvedya*).

Thus, when mental bliss enters through the enjoyment of great desire in a dream, that itself is a marvel; for even without a body and without the enjoyment of desire, a self-cognizable knowledge of bliss arises in the minds of sentient beings.

This very point cannot be deliberated upon by the learned, who possess only limited knowledge; how much less can the wise conceive of the all-pervading, great immutable bliss-knowledge of the yogi, which is self-cognizable, transcends the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of saṃsāra, and arises from the latent impressions of nirvāṇa?
[End of chapter, verse]

The Great Chapter entitled *The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of the Supreme Immutable*. Now, this is the statement of those heretics of sinful intellect who are devoted to the reality of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*): "In this state of dreaming, within the body composed of an aggregate of atoms, there is exhalation and inhalation; by the power of these two, exhalation and inhalation, the three states occur, not in the absence of exhalation and inhalation."

This very point is investigated: for if, in this world, there were no state of dreaming in the mind without inhalation and exhalation, then how could the appearance of the mind persist for as long as one watch (three hours) without inhalation and exhalation during the states of death and fainting? [In these states] the body appears to be led by the messengers of Yama, and by the command of King Yama, the city of Yama appears. Within that city of Yama, King Yama himself also appears.
That Yama conducts an investigation into the merits and demerits of that deceased body.
Having reflected on this, he says: "In such a way that his life-span is not exhausted here, therefore lead this being quickly to the world of mortals while his body has not yet perished.
Such is the rule for the messengers of Yama;
by that rule, those messengers of Yama cast his body into the world of mortals.

When it has been cast there, by the power of mental impressions (*vāsanā*), that dead body again experiences inhalation and exhalation. Then, by the power of other impressions, the waking state occurs.
In that state, due to the awakening of the mind, it relates to its circle of kinsmen the narrative concerning King Yama.

Therefore, even in the absence of a body and in the absence of inhalation and exhalation, the adventitious latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless mind arise for sentient beings due to the power of non-rebirth; they are not inherent.

If this samsaric tendency were inherent, then there would be no such thing as the Buddhahood of sentient beings. Because it is adventitious, its destruction occurs; through that destruction, Buddhahood is spoken of by the Tathāgata.
Thus, when examined in these various ways, this saṃsāra is nothing other than the mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of one's own mind; it is not anything else.
Furthermore, the latent impression of saṃsāra is a moment characterized by transition (*cyuti*), not the imperishable (*akṣara*);
whereas the latent impression of nirvāṇa is a moment characterized by non-transition (*acyuti*), not the perishable (*kṣara*).
And it was said by the Blessed One in the *Tantrarāja*, in the chapter on the Inner Self (*adhyātmapaṭala*), in the one hundred and second verse:

"O King, whoever has entered into the midst of whatever [element], delighting in vows and observances, and bound by the fetters of karma—by his own nature within that, he comes to belong to that family through its influence.

As long as there is existence for a lifetime, due to the power of the threefold state of being, there is sensation, whether pleasure or pain; for so long, O King, is there wandering here in the terrible cycle of existence, whether in heaven or below."

Furthermore, in that same chapter, the ninth-seventh verse describes the purification of yoga (yogavāsanā): If a lord of yogis who has not yet attained yoga should meet death while his mind is still wavering, he is born in this glorious human world into a family of eminent sages, endowed with yoga.
By means of that previous practice, he again acquires the vast yoga of knowledge; once knowledge is attained, he proceeds to the imperishable supreme state, where one is not born again.

Thus, by the power of mental impressions (*cittavāsanā*), the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) becomes self-cognizable, and not from the experience of a body composed of atoms. [As stated] in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "Now, when sexual intercourse occurs during the state of dreaming, does the emission (*cyuti*) occur in the sleeping body, or in the dream-body [which is the body of mental impressions]?"

"Therefore, great bliss is self-experienced through the power of this body, and not from the body of mental impressions (*cittavāsanā*). Such will be the statement of certain people who desire the pleasure of the two organs (*dvīndriyasukha*). To them it is said: "In this regard, what is asserted by the fools—that falling away occurs from a body consisting of an aggregation of atoms, and not by virtue of the body of mental impressions—is not valid. Why? Because of the falling away from the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*)."

For in this case, if there is no death without a body composed of an aggregation of atoms, and if there is no cyclic existence (saṃsāra) without death, and if there is no attainment of great bliss (mahāsukha) without cyclic existence, then how will those belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) undergo rebirth for the sake of Buddhahood without death? Since they lack a body composed of an aggregation of atoms, those who are formless have no physical body; and since they lack a body composed of an aggregation of atoms, there is no emission of semen (śukracyuti); and due to the absence of the emission of semen, they possess neither bliss nor cyclic existence.

And this was indeed stated by the Blessed One in the second chapter on the internal [body], in the third verse, regarding the body consisting of an aggregation of atoms and the imperishable gnosis (*akṣarajñāna*), as follows:

"In this body, the entire collection of elements arises from food and drink of the six tastes; and from the primary elements (*bhūta*) come the six tastes. The collection of elements is clearly and invariably manifested from the space-element (*khadhātu*).

In the void (*śūnya*), gnosis becomes blended, of equal taste (*samarasa*), imperishable, and eternal. Thus, one should know that which is peaceful and abiding within the elements—pervading the threefold existence—to be present within one's own body."

Regarding this body—that is, the body of animals or humans for which there is the drinking and eating of food consisting of the six tastes—this body is "one possessing the drinking and eating of the six tastes.

Within it, the "aggregate of constituents" (*dhātuvṛnda*) occurs; that is, the confluence of the constituents of hair, skin, blood, flesh, bone, marrow, and semen constitutes the aggregate of constituents.

Why? Because of the consumption of food and drink possessing six tastes (*ṣaḍrasa*). The intention is that these six tastes—bitter, sour, salty, pungent, sweet, and astringent—attain the nature of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) such as the hair and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the six tastes from the elements" (*bhūtebhyaḥ ṣaḍ rasāḥ*):

the elements (*bhūta*) are the constituents of earth, water, fire, air, and space, which exist in the form of atoms of solidity, fluidity, heat, motion, and taste. From these, when conjoined with their respective seeds, the six tastes beginning with bitter arise.
The intention is that the elements (dhātavaḥ) attain the nature of taste (rasasvabhāvam).

It should be stated that they arise from the primary elements (bhūtebhyaḥ) by virtue of the dispositions of sentient beings (sattvāśayavaśāt); however, from the perspective of ultimate analysis (paramārthavicārataḥ), even the elements become tastes, not through a relationship of produced and producer (janyajanakasambandhāt).

The collection of elements arises from the space-element (khadhātuḥ); that is, the collection of elements arises from the space-element, which is the phenomenon of emptiness (śūnyadharma), like a sprout from a seed.

Just as a sprout does not arise from a seed that has perished, nor does it arise from a seed that has not perished, so too [phenomena do not arise] by abandoning their own nature, nor from an insentient element, nor from a void of annihilation.

Thus, all phenomena arise from the void; "knowledge is blended within the void" means that there is an absence of arising and cessation for void phenomena, which are but the manifestation of one's own mind. Knowledge is the awakening to that [manifestation], which is imperishable bliss. When there is no arising or destruction in that manifestation of one's own mind, knowledge is "blended"; in the manifestation of one's own mind, one becomes of one taste (*samarasa*), not through a relationship between knowledge and the object of knowledge.
This very syllable is "eternal," meaning it is the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*).
Being thus situated within [the body], it is "peaceful.

In this manner, by this sequence, the yogin should understand and know that the syllable residing in the elements of the body is present within the threefold existence—that is, within the existences of desire, form, and formlessness—within his own body.

Therefore, for animals and humans, the seminal seed (*śukrabīja*) is the cause of the body's origination; it is the great instruction named "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of Supreme Unchanging Wisdom" (*paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*). That very seed, having become the constituent elements (*dhātu*) within the body through the six tastes, consists of an aggregation of atoms of earth, water, fire, air, and space, and is composed of smell, form, taste, touch, and sound; it is the element of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*). From this nature of the seed, the body born of karma arises, and at the time of death, that same fivefold seed ceases and departs.

Furthermore, like the body in a dream, the body of latent impressions (*vāsanā-kāya*) is empty, devoid of an aggregation of atoms, and unceasing. By means of that very unceasing body of latent impressions, which has arisen from the latent impressions of karma, one again takes up a body consisting of an aggregation of atoms. Upon taking up this body consisting of an aggregation of atoms, the latent impression of the previous body is abandoned, and the latent impression of the present body arises in the mind.

For that reason, from the empty aggregates of mental impressions (*cittavāsanā-skandha*), the adventitious aggregates and phenomena arise; and from the adventitious aggregates and phenomena, the empty aggregates of mental impressions arise. Therefore, not even a single atom goes to the next world. Why? Because, even upon the abandonment of the previous aggregates, there is the grasping of subsequent aggregates. Thus, according to the sequence described, at the time of death, from the body composed of the five elements that consumes the six flavors, a seed born of karma consisting of the five elements emerges; the mental impression (*cittavāsanā*) also becomes composed of the five elements for those who consume the six flavors.
Furthermore, for the gods, there is no body composed of the five elements that consumes food of six tastes, because of the absence of such six-tasted food.

For those gods belonging to the six classes of the desire realm, such as the Moon and Sun, the body consists of a collection of water, fire, air, and space; it possesses the four qualities of form, taste, touch, and sound, but is devoid of the quality of earth-smell. Because of its lightness, even their semen (*śukra*) is of that same nature, and even their mental impressions (*cittavāsanā*) are of that nature at the time of emission.

The body of those possessing a form-body (*rūpakāyika*) consists of an aggregation of fire, wind, and essence-atoms; it is composed of the three qualities of taste, touch, and sound, and is devoid of the qualities of earth, water, smell, and taste. Semen (*śukra*) is also composed of the three qualities, and at the time of emission, the mental impression (*cittavāsanā*) likewise consists of those [qualities] for these sixteen [beings]. For those without a form-body (*arūpakāyika*), the body consists of the element of emptiness (*śūnyadhātu*); it is merely the mental impression and consists of the quality of sound. Semen, too, is devoid of the qualities of earth, water, fire, wind, smell, taste, form, and touch.

In these primary qualities of earth and the other elements, there exists only a secondary quality; otherwise, without the combined qualities, the latent tendencies of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra-vāsanā*) would not arise from the manifold qualities for the four [classes of beings]. Thus, within these three realms of existence—namely, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin—there are eleven [classes] of the desire realm.

The Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahmā, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha—these are the sixteen realms of form (rūpa).

Then there are the four formless realms: the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana), the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana), the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcanyāyatana), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).

Thus, at the time of death for those in the desire, form, and formless realms, the semen issues forth according to its sequence as consisting of five, four, three, and one quality respectively; it is by the power of mental impressions (*cittavāsanā*) and not otherwise that the wandering in *saṃsāra* occurs.
For this reason, it was said by the Blessed One in the fifty-eighth verse of the fifth chapter of the *Tantrarāja*:

Namely: earth, water, fire, and air; and the six types of atoms consisting of taste and supreme taste, each progressively lacking one quality starting from smell; the final [atoms] are devoid of objects and are perceivable by gnosis.

As for the kāmas and rūpas, they are both with form and without form; the final one is the dharmadhātu, which is of all aspects and always serves as the support for the innate bliss of the immutable throughout.
(The word "prāk" does not exist).
O, form (rūpa) indeed.

Seven. In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said: "For that reason, by the power of the inclinations of sentient beings, the Tathāgata taught the Dharma as follows: the Vaibhāṣika, the Sautrāntika, the Yogācāra, and the Madhyamaka. Among these, the Vaibhāṣika is the treatise that reveals the factors of logical proof; the Sautrāntika is the treatise that reveals the meaning of the sūtras; the Yogācāra is the treatise that reveals consciousness-only; and the Madhyamaka is the treatise that reveals the ultimate reality. These were spoken by the Blessed One according to the inclinations of sentient beings—from the minds of those who are distant and unfit, to those who are near and fit."

In this world, beings who from beginningless time have been non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), devoted to the doctrines of gods, spirits, and asuras, have lost the path to omniscience. Relying on the four castes or a single caste, they desire the enjoyment of the fruits of heaven; they are proponents of a creator and of a self. Among them, those who propound sound rely on the doctrines of gods and spirits; those who propound Īśvara and those who propound a self, as well as those who propound birth, are Mlecchas who rely on the doctrines of asuras. These include proponents of a creator, proponents of a life-principle (*jīva*), and those who are devoid of the doctrine of birth.
These Mlecchas hold a dual grasp: the grasp of an aggregate of atoms (*paramāṇu-sandoha*) and the grasp of a person (*pudgala*) consisting of the factors of rebirth (*upapatty-aṅgika*).

This is their intention: "If there were no person consisting of the factors of rebirth within a body that is an aggregate of atoms, then once the body—an aggregate of atoms—has perished, who would take up another body? Therefore, a spontaneously born person (*upapāduka-pudgala*) exists; by establishing this, the fruit of heaven and the fruit of nirvāṇa are attained."

Thinking that there might be nothing called Nirvāṇa other than the fruit of heaven, the Blessed One, the Knower of Reality, having understood their intention in their own minds at the time of their inquiry into reality, said: "There is a person who carries the burden; I do not say he is eternal, nor do I say he is non-eternal.

According to these words of the Blessed One, this truth implies that in the state of dreaming, the person consisting of mental impressions (*citta-vāsanā-pudgala*) cannot be said to be either non-eternal or eternal.

By this word of the Tathāgata, having abandoned the Mleccha-dharma, they became Buddhist Vaibhāṣikas; then, hearing the supramundane Dharma being taught, some Bodhisattvas here relinquished the grasping at a person (*pudgalagraha*) and took refuge in the path of the Perfectly Awakened One— thus [are] the Sautrāntikas, who furthermore possess the grasping that [the self] consists of an aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*).

The intention of these proponents of figurative meaning (arthavādin) is as follows: if the world of moving and non-moving beings existing within the hollow of space did not exist, then that which is called the "three worlds" would not exist; in the absence of cyclic existence (saṃsāra), there would be no higher or lower realms of rebirth, and likewise, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would not exist, nor would there be supreme nirvāṇa, nor even the manifestation of the relics (dhātu) of the Blessed One, because of the absence of objects existing within substantial entities.

Thus, at the time of their inquiry into reality, the Blessed One, having understood the intention of their minds, said: "There exists a final body composed of an aggregation of atoms, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, by whose grace there arises the state of Perfect Enlightenment and the Great Parinirvāṇa; that alone is the truth. Upon hearing of the power of such a body composed of an aggregation of atoms, and having abandoned the doctrine of birth, the doctrine of sound, the doctrine of Īśvara, and the doctrine of a creator, they became Sautrāntika Buddhists.

Furthermore, having heard the Bodhisattvas’ teaching on the supramundane armor (*lokottaravarman*), some abandoned that very grasping at objects and took refuge in the path of the Perfectly Awakened One.

However, for those practitioners of yoga (*yogācārin*) who are proponents of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*), there remains a grasping at consciousness. Their intention is as follows: the entire realm consists of mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*) through its sixfold division of limbs; thus, what is called an "atom" (*paramāṇu*) does not exist.

Just as in the state of dreaming, purposeful activity proceeds by means of an object that is merely a mental appearance even though there is no substantial atom (paramāṇu-dravya), so too in the waking state an object appears through a non-existent object, like the floating hairs, gold, or conch-shell seen by one whose vision is impaired by cataracts. Thus, at the time of their inquiry into reality, the Blessed One, having understood their mental disposition, said: "The triple world is consciousness-only; there is no saṃsāra other than consciousness. Through the cessation of worldly consciousness, the seed of existence itself ceases, and from that comes nirvāṇa."
This alone is the truth:
from the non-inert (ajaḍa) arises the manifestation of pleasure and pain, not from the inert (jaḍa).
That which is called pleasure and pain is indeed saṃsāra; the absence thereof is called nirvāṇa.
Having heard these words of the Blessed One and abandoned the doctrine of a self consisting of the ear, [the disciples] practiced yoga.

Just as in a dream, disciples see their preceptor and ask about their doubts, and the preceptor, for the sake of the disciples' doubts, renders them free from uncertainty; yet in that case, the preceptor is not a manifestation of the mental impressions (*vāsanā*) of the disciples' minds—likewise, for meritorious beings, the Blessed One is a manifestation of their own minds, neither arisen nor ceased.

For this reason, by the power of the mental impressions (*vāsanā*) of the four Buddhist schools, the Blessed One taught the cultivation of the impermanent person (*pudgala*) for the *Pudgalavādins*; the cultivation of the totalities (*kṛtsna*) of earth and so forth for the *Arthavādins*; the meditative absorption of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra-samādhi*) for the *Vijñānavādins*; and the cultivation of non-dual knowledge, which is like a dream and beyond syllables, for the *Mādhyamikas*.
Thus [are established] the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).

For the Vaibhāṣikas, Sautrāntikas, and Yogācāras, there is *sopadhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder); for the Mādhyamikas, there is *anupadhiśeṣa-apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder, non-abiding), because of the cessation of cause and effect. It is devoid of the states of deep sleep and waking, and is like the fourth state (*turya*) of dreamless sleep;
thus it was said by the Blessed One in the tenth verse of the *Pratyavekṣaṇājñānastava*:
"Completely liberated from all substrates (*upadhi*), he is well-established on the path of space."

"He is the holder of the great wish-fulfilling gem, the all-pervading lord, the supreme among all jewels. Thus, [one might ask: is it not the case that for the Perfectly Awakened One (samyaksambuddha), there is a nirvāṇa without remainder that is free from the grasping of conceptual positions? Indeed, in the state of dreaming, the appearance of non-insentient [objects] is seen even without insentient phenomena; however, in the waking state, by the power of mental impressions (cittavāsanā), the appearance of non-insentient [objects] is not seen without insentient phenomena, like a reflection in a mirror.

In that state, even the manifestation of the yogin’s meditative cultivation appears in two ways: like the moon in water, while the substratum exists, the attributes [appear]. In that state, the yogin perceives in the sky non-material attributes—which are dream-like, unconstructed, unarisen, non-empty, and non-mental—devoid of material attributes. Why is this very thing not well-known? Because it is through the investigation of attributes that the substratum exists.
The Tathāgata has stated that things are like an illusion.
It might be the intention of some here [to argue] that a non-inert appearance is not perceived through meditative absorption (*samādhi*) without inert phenomena;

therefore, it is said: Here, indeed, that which must be addressed is this: for those who delight in the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of an inert mind, it is claimed that in the waking state a non-inert appearance is not seen without inert phenomena—but that is not so. Why? Because in a mirror-image (*pratisenā*), a non-inert appearance is seen even without inert phenomena.

Just as a young girl sees the non-inert appearance of past, future, and present phenomena in a mirror-image divination (*pratisenā*) through the power of the empowerment of the mantra-deity, yet those [phenomena] of the past, present, and future do not exist, so too there is no "mind" (*citta*). [This is] the performance of activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*) by the power of intention (*abhiprāyavaśena*).
Inert phenomena exist facing a mirror, yet without those inert phenomena there would be no appearance of the non-inert in the mirror; nor are those phenomena merely imagined by a young girl.
In the same way, through the power of the empowerment of his own mind, the yogi—having pierced the sky—sees the three realms as non-inert appearances even without inert matter.

This was stated by the Blessed One in the *Sādhanāpaṭala* in the one hundred and ninety-eighth verse: "The mudrā, resembling an illusion, appears in the mind and in the sky like a form in a mirror; illuminating the three worlds, it flashes with many rays of light resembling lightning and fire."

"Externally, within bodies, she is undivided, devoid of objects, a mere appearance situated in the sky; consisting of consciousness, she embraces the mind, and she alone is the one [reality] behind the world of manifold forms. Thus, from these words of the Blessed One, it follows that the yogi perceives the manifestation of non-inert phenomena even in the absence of inert properties. Now, as for the question: why is it that the young girl perceives a manifestation in the mirror of *pratisenā* through the grace of the teacher? It is because the teacher has performed the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the mantra-deity upon the young girl.

In this case, the preceptor has performed the empowerment of the mantra-deity upon the young girl; by virtue of that empowerment, the young girl perceives the reflection in the mirror of *pratisenā*, but one who is devoid of the empowerment of the mantra-deity does not.

Therefore, by the grace of the guru’s command, the yogi perceives the threefold world as mere appearance within the element of space. Here, someone who is unbound by [the guru's] command might have this thought; therefore it is said: "In this matter, what the fools claim—that through the grace of the guru’s command there occurs the empowerment of the mantra-deity in the *kumārikā*—is not so. Why? Because in the mirror of the *pratisenā*, there is no appearance of the teacher."

In this regard, if the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the mantra-deity occurs in the maiden by the grace of the teacher’s command, then why does that same empowerment not also occur for the teacher? For if he were to empower the maiden and then inquire about the knowledge of the past, future, present, and the imperceptible, she would herself speak after seeing the reflection there in the mirror of *pratisenā*, provided he himself possessed that empowerment. But such is not the case; therefore, it cannot be said that the empowerment of the mantra-deity occurs in the maiden through the grace of the teacher. The same applies to the yogin as well.

However, there is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the mantra-deity within the maiden; this is for a specific reason. Because the maiden does not experience the bliss of emission (*cyuti-sukha*) resulting from the friction of the two organs, for that reason there is empowerment.

This is also well-known in the world: "Just as [there is no emission] in the sexual union of a maiden," for that reason, by the power of the empowerment of the mantra-deity, the maiden perceives a reflection in the *pratisenā*-mirror, whereas another young woman does not perceive such bliss from the two organs.

Just as in the case of the empowerment by a deity of a youth (*kumāra*), where a young woman sees a youth and a youth also sees a young woman, so too yogins—by virtue of practicing the bliss of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara-sukha*) and through the renunciation of the bliss of external emission—attain the state of a "virgin" (*kumārikā*) and perceive the past, future, and present through the power of the empowerment of their own minds, not by the grace of a guru’s command.

[Objection: But surely many who are not celibate (*abrahmacārin*) teach liberation (*kaivalya*) even without the practice of the supreme unchanging bliss; therefore, the empowerment of the mantra-deity occurs even without celibacy.
Otherwise, how could they teach liberation? O Amala, O Āsaktasya, [this is] the two-hundredth [verse].

And they say in the chapter [of the *Śrīparamādya-tantra*], in the great instruction (mahoddeśa) titled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of Supreme Unchanging Syllable" (*Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*), verse [X]: "The intention of some may be as follows: 'In this world, the blessing of the mantra-deities occurs for those who do not practice celibacy (*abrahmacārin*'); that is not so. Why? Because the manifestation of the objective occurs through the power of practicing the luminosity (*jyotis*)."

For here, that very knowledge which is absolute (*kaivalya*) is the limb of light, common to all beings; by means of instruction and by means of calculation, it makes known lost horoscopes and the like. Just as when *karṇapiśācikā* (ear-demons) are propitiated by others, they speak whatever flashes in their minds, so too when *kṣetrapālas* (field-protectors) are propitiated by others, they speak whatever flashes in their minds.

By others, Mothers (*mātaraḥ*) are propitiated; having entered the bodies of others through possession (*āveśita*), they speak. By others, Nāga kings are propitiated; having entered the bodies of those bitten by the black snake (*kāladaṣṭa*), they speak. By others, servants (*ceṭaka*) are propitiated; at the command of the practitioners, they enter the bodies of beings and cause them to behave like fools. By others, Ḍākinīs, Rākṣasas, and so forth are propitiated; they drink the blood of sentient beings. By others, Bhūtas are propitiated; having entered the bodies of beings, they depart after causing sounds, trembling, and the like. By others, Vighnas and Vināyakas are propitiated; they create obstacles for sentient beings. By others, gentle deities (*saumyadevatā*) are propitiated; they provide protection for sentient beings. By others, Kāma-deities are propitiated; they cause madness from lust and the discharge of semen in sentient beings. By others, various other malevolent deities are propitiated; some perform paralysis (*stambhana*), some delusion (*mohana*), some expulsion (*uccāṭana*), some enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), some killing (*māraṇa*), and some even the uprooting of trees and phallic emblems (*liṅga*). In this way, they perform many such minor harmful acts in an invisible form.

Those by whom these wicked deities belonging to the host of Māra have been mastered, and who—by means of these petty, superficial cognitions that produce immediate conviction—act as teachers for fools, perform religious instruction, and proclaim a "knowledge" whose essence is mere conviction regarding those who are unstained by the poison of desire: he who possesses no command over desire, no command over the poison of the unstained, and no command over the piercing [realization] of the individual (āṇava), the Śāmbhava, and the Śākta—whether manifest or non-manifest—even if he is learned, he is a beast;
though devoted to the welfare of all beings, he wanders for alms, dwelling alone without a companion, having fallen from his own true purpose.
This is also well known in the world: "Indeed, the loss of one's own welfare is foolishness.
Therefore, this command of supreme sovereignty, which bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation, has come down through the sequence of lineage and is obtained by the grace of the Guru.
Thus it was said by the omniscient Supreme Lord: "There is no mother equal to the Guru; there is no father equal to the Guru."

"He who enables one to cross the great and most terrible ocean of saṃsāra, so difficult to traverse"— thus it is said that when a guru bestows initiation (*dīkṣā*) upon a disciple even from a distance of a hundred *yojanas*,
that initiation which grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation is the giver of final release (*mokṣa*). Thus [it is taught].

Thus, having awakened those great fools—who are overcome by great greed and possess only meager understanding—by means of various methods, he bestows favor upon them and imparts that command. They too become greatly delighted, thinking: "By the grace of our Guru we are liberated;

now we shall do everything! We shall eat the impure, we shall engage in sexual intercourse with women of low caste, we shall commit the taking of life, false speech, taking what is not given, drinking liquor, and so forth.
In this way, they perform various kinds of demonic deeds (*mārakarman*) here for the sake of attaining *siddhi*.

Nor does the perfection of their bodies arise through the grace of the command of supreme sovereignty; nor do they know the past, future, or present; in the end they undergo death, and their body is consumed by fire or devoured by dogs, birds, and other creatures;
neither the *jīva* becomes Śiva, nor does consciousness become a *vajrī*.
Thus, all such successions of empowerments by minor mantra-deities belong to the Māras.
These should be investigated by yogins who delight in the knowledge of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara-jñāna*).
Through these [practices] based on inferior mantras, the vajra-entrance (*vajrāveśa*) does not occur;
and this was stated by the Blessed One in the seventh verse of the *Ādarśajñānastava* within the *Nāmasaṃgīti*:

Namely—namely: Vimalaprabha (Stainless Light), Vajrajvālākarālākṣa (Fierce-Eyed One with Vajra Flames), Vajrajvālāśiroruha (One with Vajra Flames for Hair), Vajrāveśa (Vajra-Possession), Mahāveśa (Great Possession), Śatākṣa (Hundred-Eyed), and Vajralocana (Vajra-Eyed).

Thus, it is stated regarding the entry into the body (*kāyāveśa*) and so forth in the *Tantrarāja*, in the chapter on consecration (*abhiṣeka*), by the eighty-ninth verse: "By the entry into the body, the yogi performs bodily actions through the power of the qualities of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*); by the entry into speech (*vāgāveśa*), he becomes a debater who conquers the three worlds of gods, nāgas, and asuras;

by the entry into mind (*cittāveśa*), everything residing in the hearts of others—past and future—is known; and by the entry into gnosis (*jñānāveśa*), one becomes a Buddha, a teacher of teachers, and a wise, unique instructor."

Thus, because there is an absence of the descent of the Vajra, the descents of minor deities do not bestow the fruit of Buddhahood; let alone Buddhahood, even the state of being a sovereign of the three worlds is not attained through these partial descents. Furthermore, even [attainments such as] the sword, elixirs, and alchemical potions (*rasāyana*) are not accomplished by these. Why?

Because the Guru, who bestows the command of supreme sovereignty, is one who plunders the wealth of others, if indeed by the grace of the Guru’s command even great fools were to attain the kingdom of the three worlds and the state of omniscience in this very life, then for what reason does the Guru suffer the misery of poverty and not even possess the state of a perfected alchemist (*rasasiddha*)? When considered in these various ways, it is clear that the state of omniscience does not exist for one devoid of the two accumulations of merit and knowledge from previous lives; therefore, for the sake of accumulating merit and knowledge, one must act for the benefit of sentient beings.

The Blessed One stated in the sixty-sixth verse of the fifth chapter: “Beings are Buddhas; there is no other great Buddha here in the world-system. By propitiating them, immeasurable existence is severed through non-conceptuality. For the yogi who commits an act of malice toward them goes to the great Raurava and other hells. Therefore, even when one’s own mind is pure, one should not act in opposition to those people who are ignorant or wise.”

Therefore, for the sake of the accumulation of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*), one must perform service to sentient beings; and for the sake of the accumulation of gnosis (*jñānasaṃbhāra*), one must practice the meditation on supreme unchanging gnosis (*paramākṣarajñāna*).

Without benefiting sentient beings, there is no accumulation of merit; and without the meditation on supreme unchanging gnosis, there is no accumulation of gnosis—this is the heart-essence of the Tathāgatas.

It was stated by the Blessed One in the *Tantrarāja*, in the seventy-second verse of the fifth chapter, as follows: "O Lord of Men, the sinful mind of sentient beings arises when it is possessed by the hosts of Māras; yet even that which is devoted to merit and wisdom and bestows happiness is always possessed by the Bodhisattvas.

Because they go to Nirvāṇa through the power of the blissful *samaya* having destroyed the Māras of the afflictions (*kleśa*), therefore the Māras daily create many obstacles for them during that very *samaya*. [End of] the Great Exposition entitled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of Supreme Unchanging [Bliss]."

Thus, from these words of the Blessed One, a yogi must perform the practice of his own mind through the yoga of the Great Seal of the Supreme Syllable for the sake of liberation; otherwise, liberation does not occur by the command of the Guru alone—
why is that?
Because the Blessed One is the instructor of the path,
the phenomena that move according to his command bestow liberation upon living beings; for in some cases,
the Victor is the giver of liberation through the instruction of the path by means of his command.
If liberation for embodied beings were to occur solely through the grace of the guru’s command,
then the compassionate one would not teach liberation through meditative absorption.

Therefore, for the sake of liberation, a yogin should not perform the practice of external deities and mantras for the sake of attaining worldly accomplishments (*laukika-siddhi*). In this context, external deities cause minor disturbances; even when propitiated, they seek out the vulnerabilities of the practitioner. By their power, the practitioner causes minor disturbances through other fierce deities. When the practitioner is seized by them, those propitiated malevolent deities become his enemies. At the time of death, they say nothing [to help him], and the practitioner, dying in a state of non-concentration (*asamādhi*), goes to hell.
Then, once they have been accomplished, what will they give? Like accomplished poor women, they say: "O practitioner!
We shall perform all your observances."
If a practitioner says, "Please bind the King and bring him here," then those minor deities offer an excuse, saying, "We are not capable in this matter.
Thus, when such minor deities have been propitiated, they offer excuses regarding the subject of the Omniscient One.

Therefore, what is the purpose of propitiating wicked deities for those who desire the state of the Omniscient One? And by the command of the Guru, which consists of the true nature of the phenomena of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

The Blessed One stated in the Root Tantra: "Just as the principle of Śiva, the principle of desire, and the principle of poison circulate according to one's command and become a source of conflict for men, so it is not with the principle of Buddhahood."
The mind, when defiled by passion and other afflictions, is subject to decay and is the cause of saṃsāra;
when purified through separation from those [afflictions], it is pure and naturally stainless.
Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything to be added by command; nothing is to be given and nothing is to be taken away—the pure reality is the Great Imperishable.
For one who possesses the pure reality in its entirety, there is no giver, no taker, and no teacher;
even the Omniscient Lord himself is powerless over those who lack the accumulation of merit.
For persons, the supreme accumulation of merit arises from benefiting others;
from that [merit] comes the accumulation of wisdom, and from those two comes the supreme state of Buddhahood.

The piercing (vedha) occurs in three ways— in the principle of Śiva, the principle of Kāma, and the principle of Poison— and through the command of the Guru, it brings about for men the bliss of the supreme imperishable (paramākṣara).
and by virtue of supreme bliss.
And by the king and the queen.
And the piercing (vedha) may be of the individual (āṇava), the divine (śāmbhava), or the empowered (śākteya) nature, occurring through the Command (ājñā).
Through the piercing of mind, speech, and body, one experiences sleep, dreaming, and waking.
Poison is known as the Śiva-principle by the command of the guru for the ignorant; for embodied beings, the agitation of mind, speech, and body is the emission of semen.
By the grace of the guru’s command, it is known as the principle of desire (*kāmatattva*);
they call it "poisonless," yet poison is indeed poison.
By the grace of the Guru’s command, the ritual action regarding both the immobile and the mobile is known as the "Principle of Poison" (viṣatattva), which produces immediate conviction.

The bliss of the three principles (tritattva) that is imperishable cannot arise for all embodied beings except through the grace of the Guru’s command; therefore, the observer of vows should meditate upon that.

It is said in the *Jñāna*: "When I, the Lord of the World, was entering hell for the sake of sentient beings, the guardians of the night said: 'We bow to those Buddhas who, though liberated from the bonds of existence, take up existence for the sake of sentient beings; who do not abandon the fruit of their actions over time because they are messengers of the meaning of emptiness; whose mental impurities have been burnt by the fire of true cognition; who are always moistened by perfect compassion; and who delight in inconceivable conduct for the sake of sentient beings.'"
Thus,
O Great Beings (*mahāsattvānām*); the term "of the Great Beings" is added.
O,
Right Vision!
O!

In the *Mārakāyika* chapter, verse [number], the Great Summary titled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of Supreme Unchanging [Reality]": Thus, for those possessing manifold virtues who have burned away the obscurations of the afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), there remains a mere fragment of an obscuration of the afflictions consisting of the performance of activities for the sake of sentient beings, for the purpose of taking birth; otherwise, there would be no teaching of the path for sentient beings.
Without the path, there can be no emergence of sentient beings from beginningless saṃsāra, due to the absence of association with bodhisattvas;
therefore, in this context, bodhisattvas have previously made the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) very firm.
This bodhicitta has two types of bonds: through detachment from wisdom (prajñā-virāga) and through passion for wisdom (prajñā-rāga).

Just as there are two types of bound mercury (*sūtaka*): one by means of the yoga of sweating and renunciation (*svedasaṃnyāsa-yoga*), and a second by means of the yoga of the combination of *viḍa* and the fire for digesting (*jāraṇā*) iron and other metals;
of these two, that mercury which is bound by the yoga of sweating and renunciation remains only slightly when blown with a fierce fire and mostly flees away.

However, that which is bound by the fierce fire through the digestion of all metals and gems, when blown with a fierce fire, never flees away; rather, by virtue of further stages of digestion of its "food" (*grāsa-jāraṇā*), it undergoes a change of state.
Namely: smoke, the hissing sound "ciṭiciṭi," the frog-leap, trembling, and motionlessness—these are the five stages of the taste.

Likewise, through the power of the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there occurs a successive state of the *bodhicitta* according to the distinctions of weak, middling, intense, and extremely intense.

That which is the binding (*bandha*) by means of the yoga of the "sweat-release" (*svedasaṃnyāsa*) is the binding of the *bodhicitta*. This occurs through the force of cultivating the impermanent person (*pudgala*), through the direct realization of the totalities (*kṛtsna*) such as earth and so forth, and through the detachment of wisdom (*prajñā-virāga*).
Just as even in the yoga of the "sweat-release," there is the consumption of the metal-bite of mercury (*rasa*) after some time, and by means of that consumption—

Just as a change of state occurs, so too, through the cultivation of the impermanence of the person (*pudgala*) and the cultivation of the totality of earth and the other elements, there occurs a change of state due to the exhaustion of the insentient aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;
this "change of state" is called the attainment of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Here, the stages are twofold: the stage of one free from passion (*vītarāga-bhūmi*) and the stage of the perfectly enlightened one (*samyaksambuddha-bhūmi*).
By the power of the stages (*bhūmi*), supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is of two kinds: supernormal power of a single form and supernormal power of all forms;
likewise, there are the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) and the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Similarly, there is the vision of the number of objects and the vision of the number of all objects.

Likewise, speech is of the nature of the enumeration of sentient beings and of the nature of the enumeration of all sentient beings; likewise, the teaching of the Dharma has the characteristic of the enumeration of sentient beings and has the characteristic of the enumeration of all sentient beings;
likewise, there is nirvana with remainder and nirvana without remainder.

Likewise, the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*), the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), the cultivation of the four noble truths, and the samādhi of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of the non-existence of all phenomena—
thus, through the distinctions of the stages (*bhūmi*), the performance of the welfare of sentient beings occurs in two ways.

In this context, through the attainment of the first bhūmi, there is the manifestation of objects not previously perceived as far as one world-system; through the attainment of the second bhūmi, as far as a second world-system in each of the ten directions; through the attainment of the third bhūmi, as far as a fourth world-system in each of the ten directions; through the attainment of the fourth bhūmi, as far as an eighth world-system in each of the ten directions; through the attainment of the fifth bhūmi, as far as a sixteenth world-system in each of the ten directions; through the attainment of the sixth bhūmi, as far as a thirty-second world-system in each of the ten directions; through the attainment of the seventh bhūmi, as far as a sixty-fourth world-system in each of the ten directions; through the attainment of the eighth bhūmi, as far as a hundred and twenty-eighth world-system in each of the ten directions; through the attainment of the ninth bhūmi, as far as two hundred and fifty-sixth world-systems in each of the ten directions; through the attainment of the tenth bhūmi, as far as five hundred and twelve world-systems in each of the ten directions; and through the attainment of the eleventh bhūmi, there is the manifestation of objects beyond perception as far as one thousand and twenty-fourth world-systems in each of the ten directions.
Thus, the two-thousandfold and three-thousandfold world-systems are characterized by their enumeration.

The so-called "Single-Thousandfold" Sahā world-system consists of one thousand [worlds] in each direction—upward, downward, below, above, east, west, north, south, southwest, northeast, northwest, and southeast;
in this manner, there are the two-thousandfold and three-thousandfold [systems].
Beyond that is the so-called Mahāsāhasra [world-system], extending to the limits of a great incalculable world-system (lokadhātu), O "Nothing-at-all" (akiñcit); and there is nothing further.

And there are no elements of primordial wisdom (*jñānadhātu*) in the *Vimalaprabhā*; among those, the manifestation of the unseen object occurs for the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksambuddha*) due to the attainment of the twelve stages, but not for those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*).
The attainment of these stages of the Tathāgata occurs through moments of great imperishable bliss arising from the passion of wisdom (*prajñārāga*).
The first attainment of a stage occurs when one hundred and eighteen moments, characterized by non-falling (*acyuta*), are attained.

By this reckoning, up to the twelfth stage, there are twenty-one thousand six hundred moments of protection; through these moments of protection, the attainment of the twelve stages occurs, culminating in the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination.

From the cessation of the twelve zodiac signs (*lagna*), there is the cessation of the twelve astrological houses (*rāśi*); from the cessation of the twelve months, there is the cessation of three hundred and sixty days; from the cessation of three hundred and sixty days, there is the cessation of twenty-one thousand six hundred *ghaṭikās*.

Thus, just as it is externally, so too within the body is there the cessation of the breaths that correspond in number to the *ghaṭikās*. From the cessation of the breaths comes the cessation of the body by means of the moments of the immutable bodhicitta. Just as quicksilver (*sūtaka*), once processed, consumes metals and gems and, having taken up their great passion (*mahārāga*), remains, no longer possessing the nature of an inert element.

By that great passion (*mahārāga*), whatever metals it touches become free from tarnish, and stones become jewels; likewise, the cultivated bodhicitta, having consumed the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) along with their vital breaths, remains having grasped their great passion. Through that passion, by the power of merit, in whichever sentient beings one bestows empowerment, they attain the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), but not perfect buddhahood (*samyaksaṃbuddhatva*). Just as for metals transmuted by mercury, there is an absence of tarnish, yet no absence of the nature of being a dull element.
The state of being an inert element will cease to exist when the processed metals attain oneness with the mercury (*rasa*);

therefore, through their mutual conjunction, the elements no longer possess the nature of elements, and the mercury no longer possesses the nature of mercury, because of the abandonment of their former intrinsic natures.

Likewise, when the elements of the body have become one with the mind, they no longer possess the nature of elements, and the mind no longer possesses the nature of mind, because of the absence of the prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, it was said by the Blessed One: "There is that mind which is no-mind.

Thus, according to the sequence stated here, the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) are to be understood as belonging to the lords of the eight stages and to the gods such as Īśvara; however, the five superknowledges do not belong even to the Bodhisattvas or to the sages (*ṛṣi*) such as Vaśiṣṭha and others. Why? Because of the authority of the *Rāmāyaṇa* and the *Mahābhārata*.
In this *Rāmāyaṇa*, it is heard in the words of Vālmīki that at the auspicious moment (*lagna*) provided by Vasiṣṭha, Prince Rāma performed the marriage ceremony with Sītā.
By the grace of the auspicious moment granted by Vasiṣṭha, Rāma was deprived of his kingdom and entered the forest, and Sītā likewise remained constantly in sorrow;
nevertheless, it has been said: "The fruit of past actions must be experienced; the [positions of] planets and lunar mansions are useless."
Jānakī has become a vessel of sorrow because of the wedding hour appointed by Vasiṣṭha.

Thus it is heard in the words of Vyāsa in the *Mahābhārata*: "Those among the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas who enter Kurukṣetra on the new moon day shall be victorious. Having heard these words, the Pāṇḍavas entered on the thirteenth lunar day, while the Kauravas entered on the new moon day.
Among them, those who entered on the thirteenth day became victorious, whereas those who entered on the new moon day met their death.

Now, as for the statement of the wicked sages that "on this thirteenth day, the new moon occurred due to the conjunction of the moon and the sun," that itself is not tenable. Why? Because there is no waning of the fifteen digits of the moon;
here on the thirteenth day, the waning of the fifteen digits of the moon does not occur.
Because a new-moon day might occur on the same weekday and under the same lunar mansion as that on which the thirteenth day occurred,
for this reason their reliance on astrology is not a manifestation of reality through the five supernormal knowledges;
likewise, the ancient dharma [is rejected] by those whose minds are characterized by false and sinful views.

As it has been said: "During the time of King Bali, while churning the ocean of milk, Uccaiḥśravas, Airāvaṇa, the Kaustubha jewel, the Pārijāta tree, the Apsarases, Lakṣmī, the Moon, nectar, and the Kālakūṭa poison emerged"—so indeed it is stated in the section on the Purāṇic Dharma.
[This is] verse 95, from the Great Chapter titled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of the Supreme Syllable.
If this were so, then during the reign of Andhaka alone, there would be no lunar day, weekday, month, asterism, or season, because of the absence of the rising and setting of the moon and the sun.

If the moon were situated in the ocean, there would be no enjoyment of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), and thus the phases beginning with the first day (*pratipad*) could not be perceived; likewise, the sun’s rising and setting, as well as the seven-day cycle of the planets beginning with Mars, would not occur. Indeed, in the kingdom of Hiraṇyakaśyapa, there was an absence of days and so forth; it was in that lineage that Bali was born by the power of time.
Then [the opponent argues]: "The ocean was churned by the gods and asuras;

therefore, this is not the moon, but rather the moon upon the head of Īśvara. However, that very statement is inconsistent. It is false that Andhaka met his death out of longing for that very moon, and it is false that the Kālakūṭa poison emerged from it. Furthermore, Īśvara was not blue-throated (Nīlakaṇṭha) from the beginning, because he consumed the Kālakūṭa poison during the time of King Bali.

Likewise, [the claim] that Airāvaṇa, Uccaiḥśravas, Lakṣmī, the Kaustubha jewel, and the nectar emerged [from the ocean] is false, because in the battle with Andhaka, all the gods possessed their respective emblems and their respective vehicles. Furthermore, [the claim] that the wicked sages entered the ocean due to Indra’s downfall caused by the curse of Durvāsas is false, for there was no loss of prosperity for the other gods due to Indra’s curse.
If it were as stated in this sequence, all the dharmas of the Purāṇas would be rendered futile.

The Blessed One stated in the one hundred and eighty-second verse of the fifth chapter that the ancient religious systems are in vain, as follows: "If Lakṣmī, the horse Uccaiḥśravas, the celestial tree, the lord of elephants, the Apsarases, the Kaustubha gem, and the nectar of immortality had been present in the sky during the time of Bali’s sovereignty while he churned the ocean; yet, in the absence of the moon, there were no lunar days (*vāra*), lunar dates (*tithi*), or groups of seasons (*ṛtugaṇa*) in the kingdom of Andhaka. He too met his death through greed for the crescent moon of Śiva; after him came that very Bali."

Thus, when examined by this reasoning, the worldly Purāṇas are seen to be false. Now, as for the wicked words of the Brahmanical sages: "In this world, the Vedic Dharma was innate; later, the Dharma taught by the Omniscient One became artificial."
Therefore, the Vedic dharma is the elder.
To this it is said: Let the Vedic dharma be the elder, and the dharma of the Omniscient one come later;
what contradiction is there in this?

First there was the great innate darkness that did not illuminate the path to omniscience; subsequently, for the purpose of destroying it, the light of the thousand-rayed sun appeared, illuminating all paths.
Between these two—the great darkness and the light—the innate darkness, though elder, is not dear to those who possess eyes.

Likewise, first there was the innate and elder Vedic dharma, which did not illuminate the path to Nirvana; subsequently, for the purpose of destroying it, the younger dharma of the Omniscient One appeared, illuminating the path to Nirvana.

Between these two—the Vedic dharma and the dharma of the omniscient—one is not the Vedic dharma; it is not innate, nor is it the elder [path], nor is it dear to the wise, being like a great darkness to those with eyes.
Therefore, between the elder and the younger, the younger is superior.
Consequently, liberation occurs through the means of the knowledge of the supreme imperishable, and not through the latent impressions of emission (*cyuti-vāsanā*) found in the Vedic dharma.
In this way, even the Matsya Purāṇa and others, when examined up to the point of Kalki, are found to be meaningless;
for they state that this Blessed Buddha is Vāsudeva, the ninth incarnation, and Kalki is the tenth.

In the Kali age, the Buddha will, under the guise of a great illusion (*mahāmāyā*), corrupt the religion of sacrifice; he will corrupt the religion of war, ancestral rites, the doctrine of caste, the taking of life, false speech, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, harsh speech, slander, idle chatter, covetousness, malice, and wrong view; he will corrupt all harm toward sentient beings, the destruction of one's own lineage, the duty of the warrior class (*kṣatradharma*), and the words of the great seer Vyāsa—the *Bhārata*, the *Gītā*, and the Vedic scriptures—which are said to bestow the fruit of heaven.

Then, having corrupted them, he taught to the Śūdras and others a perverted doctrine as follows: "The perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of skillful means, the perfection of aspiration, the perfection of power, and the perfection of knowledge—these ten perfections are to be fulfilled by a Bodhisattva."

A mind of loving-kindness must be cultivated toward all sentient beings; a mind of compassion must be cultivated; service to all sentient beings must be performed. The ten unwholesome paths of action—killing, false speech, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, harsh speech, slander, frivolous chatter, covetousness, malice, and wrong view—must not be committed. Having awakened the Śūdras and others through these contrary teachings on the Dharma, he will have them shaved and make them monks wearing saffron robes.

Those who formerly stood on the side of the Dānavas and were not slain by Vāsudeva in battle—those who, having brought defilement upon the Brāhmaṇas, go to hell—it was for their sake, as well as for the sake of the Śūdras and others who previously stood on the side of the Dānavas, that this illusory form of Buddha (Buddhamāyā) was created by Viṣṇu, so that they might go to hell.
Such is the descent of Buddha.

Furthermore, Kalkī, having been born as the son of the Brahmin Yaśas in the region of Sambhala, will become Vāsudeva; mounting a horse made of stone and slaying all the Mlecchas with arrows made of Darbha grass, he will perform a sacrifice of much gold and once again make the earth consist of Brahmins.
Thus, many such inconsistent statements were composed by wicked Brahmins at the time of the Buddha's appearance; they did not exist previously in the recitation of the Vedas.

Here, at the time of the teaching of the *Ādibuddha*, the Tathāgata spoke in the section on astrology within the chapter on world-systems (*lokadhātu-paṭala*): "When the dharma of the Mlecchas arises, there will be the destruction of the Siddhāntas, and abbreviated calculations (*laghukaraṇa*) will prevail upon the earth. Furthermore, six hundred years after I have passed into nirvāṇa, Mañjughoṣa will become the Kalkī named Yaśas in the land of Sambhala, born in the Śākya clan as the son of Sureśāna from the womb of Queen Vijayā."

For example: Six hundred years from the first year, King Yaśas will appear in the land called Sambhala. Then, indeed, after eight hundred years, the Mleccha religion will prevail in the land of Makha. At that time, humans on earth must understand that the clear and concise astronomical calculation (*laghukaraṇa*) [will arise], and due to the conjunction of time, the destruction of the established tenets (*siddhāntas*) will occur throughout the entire surface of the world.
Thus [it is said]:
Mañjughoṣa has been prophesied by the Tathāgata;
and he, together with three koṭis of brahmin seers headed by Sūryaratha, will establish a single vehicle with the intention of the Vajrayāna.
Therefore, he shall be Mañjughoṣa by the name Kalkī, not by being established as one born of the Brahmin caste.

If Kalkī were the son of the Brahmin Yaśas, then by what means would he be Kalkī here? Without wealth, how could he be a "wealthy" one (*dhanī*)? *Kalka* is the mixing together of the castes and non-castes; he who possesses that *kalka* is Kalkī, and not without *kalka*. He alone is Kalkī.

Furthermore, at the end of the age (*yugāvasāna*), having seen the extreme unrighteousness of the barbarians (*mleccha*), he will become as immovable as a mountain; through the supreme horse-samādhi (*paramāśva-samādhi*), he will multiply infinite supreme horses and, having caused the minds of those barbarians to melt away, he will establish them in his own Dharma.
He will uproot their [wrong] Dharma, but not their lives.
This was stated by the Blessed One in the forty-eighth verse of the *Adhyātmapaṭala*: "O Goddess, from the womb of Viśvadevī... (*mātā viśvadevīgarbhe*).
O you who possess [it]!
O four ages! [End of] the chapter, verse.

The Great Chapter entitled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of the Supreme Unchanging" (*paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*): The Lord of the Wheel (*cakrī*), the Lord of Speech (*vaṣtrī*), and the Sovereigns of the Gods—these twelve limbs are restrained within one's own body. Indeed, Kalkī is perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). The elephants, horses, chariots, servants (*kiṅkara*), and the Noble Ones (*ārya*) are the means of cognition (*apramāṇa*).

Each possesses the name of Rudra. Hanuman prevails over the disciples (*śrāvaka*) and the sins of living beings; he whose mind is intent on his own path of virtue destroys the wickedness of the barbarian kings who inflict suffering.
