The battle with the Mlecchas was prophesied by the Tathāgata in such passages as "kā ta" and so forth, which were stated in the first chapter: "Kalkī shall slay the Mlecchas with mountain-like horses. This was for the purpose of undermining the minds of those wicked ṛṣis; otherwise, if doubt had first arisen in their minds, they could not have been awakened. Therefore, the Blessed One said to the Bodhisattva: "One must possess skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*). Consequently, the ancient doctrines (*purāṇadharma*), when examined, are found to be meaningless.

Then the wicked sages spoke these words: "The Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstra of Manu, the Veda with its auxiliary branches, and medical science—these four are established by authoritative injunction; they are not to be undermined by logical reasoning."
He who declares the words of Manu, Vyāsa, and Vasiṣṭha— which are in accord with the Vedas—
to be without authority, shall indeed be a slayer of Brahman.
Thus [it is said].
This very statement of the wicked sages, devoid of inquiry, is intended merely to establish their own school and serves to delude the ignorant.

Now, if the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for passion and emission in sentient beings is beginningless, and cyclic existence proceeds by its power, then for what purpose did the Blessed One teach the twelve-linked dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), wherein the factors such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth are subsumed under afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering (*duḥkha*) respectively?
From affliction (*kleśa*) arises karma; from karma arises suffering (*duḥkha*); and from suffering, once again, affliction arises.
This very wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) is the cause and the fruit of the entire world.
There is no other sentient being whatsoever.
Phenomena arise from what is empty, and they are also empty of those very phenomena.
This is to be understood through such examples as the practice of recitation and so forth.

Therefore, this habitual tendency toward transmigration does not constitute the wheel of saṃsāra; yet, someone here might have this intention, and for that reason it is said: "In this context, that which is called by the ignorant—the twelvefold dependent origination consisting of afflictions, karma, and suffering—that alone is the wheel of saṃsāra. That is not so. Why?

Because the Blessed One is the holder of the supreme immutable gnosis (*paramākṣaravidyādhara*). For here, the Blessed Lord Vajrasattva is the holder of the supreme immutable great gnosis, having transcended the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); by contrast, worldly beings are holders of mutable gnosis, seized by the latent tendencies of cyclic existence. Therefore, the supreme immutable is the great passion (*mahārāga*) which is gnosis; whereas for sentient beings, ignorance (*avidyā*) consists of the beginningless latent tendencies of passion, through which the activity of passion arises. Furthermore, passion is mutable, and from the mutable comes dispassion (*virāga*).
Dispassion (*virāga*) is indeed hatred; fainting (*mūrcchā*) is of the nature of hatred; and fainting is delusion (*moha*).
Thus, ignorance (*avidyā*), which consists of passion, hatred, and delusion, is not like a garland of flowers in the sky.

Ignorance is called an affliction (*kleśa*); from ignorance comes formative action (*saṃskāra*), which is karma; from formative action comes consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is suffering—this is the first subtle measure (*udumātrā*) consisting of body, speech, and mind.

From consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is affliction (*kleśa*); from name-and-form, the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is karma; from the six sense-bases, contact (*sparśa*) is suffering (*duḥkha*). This is the second medium degree of body, speech, and mind. From that contact, sensation (*vedanā*) is affliction; from sensation, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is karma; from craving, grasping (*upādāna*) is suffering. This is the third intense degree of body, speech, and mind. From that grasping, becoming (*bhava*) is affliction; from becoming, birth (*jāti*) is karma; from birth, old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) is suffering. This is the fourth intensely intense degree of body, speech, and mind.

Thus, there are four measures (*mātrā*) consisting of body, speech, mind, and gnosis, corresponding to the three signs beginning with Capricorn (*makara*) within the divisions of the womb, the door, and the exterior. Among these, for human beings, the first month of conception is Capricorn, which is ignorance (*avidyā*) as the womb; the second month is Aquarius, which is mental formations (*saṃskāra*) as the door; and the third month is Pisces, which is consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the exterior. These three months constitute the soft measure (*mṛdu-mātrā*) for those born from a womb. Then, the fourth month is Aries, which is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as the womb; the fifth month is Taurus, which is the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as the door; and the sixth month is Gemini, which is contact (*sparśa*) as the exterior. These three months constitute the medium measure (*madhya-mātrā*).

Then the seventh month is Cancer, the womb of sensation (*vedanā*); the eighth is Leo, the door of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); the ninth is Virgo, external grasping (*upādāna*). This triad of months constitutes the third [level], the intense (*adhimātra*). Then the tenth month is Libra, the birth of the womb; the eleventh is Scorpio, the door of becoming (*jāti*); the twelfth is Sagittarius, external aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). This triad of months constitutes the intensely intense (*adhimātrādhimātra*). Thus, through the division of body, speech, mind, and gnosis, that which is the first mild level (*mṛdumātrā*) of gnosis should be understood as the fourth [level] of the body.

It was said by the Blessed One in the fifth Knowledge Chapter of the *Tantrarāja*, in the one hundred and seventieth verse: "From karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) suffering arises, and from that [suffering] affliction itself arises; thus this wheel of saṃsāra revolves. The cause is like the fruit, and there is no other sentient being.

Furthermore, here the aggregates and phenomena arise from the voids, and at the end of death they are known to be void again—just as [sound arises from] recitation, a lamp, water, and flowers, or [fire from] a sun-crystal, acid, and seeds."
Thus, by these examples beginning with the study of sacred texts (svādhyāya), the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (skandhas) should be understood:
just as through the studies of one [disciple], there is neither the exhaustion of the teacher's knowledge nor the non-attainment of it by the disciple.
Thus, from a lamp comes the emergence of another lamp;
likewise, the moon [is reflected] in water,
and fragrance [arises] from a flower in a cloth.
Fire from the sun [is produced] in the sun-crystal; an echo from sound;
the flow of saliva from sourness; and a sprout from a seed.
Likewise, the underlying intention regarding the aggregates (skandhas) is due to the influence of the latent impressions (vāsanā) of perishable passion;
therefore, according to the word of the Blessed One, the wheel of saṃsāra consists of perishable passion and ignorance.
Thus, when perishable passion is destroyed, one becomes the supreme imperishable (paramākṣara).
The supreme syllable is great passion;
from great passion, dispassion is lost;
that which is called dispassion is in fact hatred.
From the destruction of hatred, great hatred arises;
from great hatred, the delusion called "fainting" (mūrchā) is destroyed;
and from the destruction of that delusion, great delusion (mahāmoha) arises.
From great passion, great hatred, and great delusion, ignorance—which consists of passion, hatred, delusion, and pride—is destroyed;
through the destruction of ignorance, great wisdom arises.

Thus, from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact; from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; and from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of old age and death. Such is the cessation of the twelve links.

By way of contrast, it should be understood that the limbs of the Blessed One are without obscuration. Now, one might think: "If the Buddhahood of yogins arises through the destruction of perishable passion (*kṣararāga*), then for what purpose was the destruction of the four—death, the aggregates, the afflictions, and the son of the gods—performed by the Tathāgata?

Therefore, Buddhahood does not result from the destruction of perishable passion. Such might be the intention of someone here. [End of chapter, verse: The Great Instruction titled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of Supreme Unchanging [Bliss] (*paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*). 99.
Therefore it is said: "In this regard, what is stated by fools—that the external Māras were destroyed by the Tathāgata—is not so. Why?
Because of the contradiction between the preceding and the following.
For if Buddhahood occurred first and the defeat of Māra later, then the Buddha would lack freedom from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*), due to the affliction caused by Māra."
Now, if the defeat of Māra occurs first and Buddhahood afterwards, then why do other transmigrating beings not also effect the defeat of Māra without attaining Buddhahood?

Or, if the defeat of Māra and [the attainment of] Buddhahood occur simultaneously, that is not the case; for at the very moment when Māra exists, Buddhahood would not exist, because the mind is still possessed of obscurations.
And at the very moment when Buddhahood exists, Māra is not present, because all obscurations have been exhausted.
Therefore, for sentient beings, the four Māras consist of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance regarding body, speech, and mind.

Among these, the obscuration of the body is the *skandhamāra*; the obscuration of speech is the *kleśamāra*; and the obscuration of the mind is the *mṛtyumāra*. Furthermore, the external *devaputramāra* is also described in the eighty-sixth verse of the fifth chapter: "Those mantras of a cruel nature that were proclaimed by the Lord of the Three Worlds—all of them never produce fear of the destruction of the faction of Māra for living beings."

"Those who are the authors of the Smṛtis, those who delight in the field of battle, and other Mārakas and Tīrthikas—these [teachings] of theirs are to be applied by the son of the Supreme Jina for the sake of protecting living beings.
(Kālacakratantra 5.86). Therefore, according to the word of the Blessed One, a yogin must not engage in the activity of ignorance through the words of Māra.
Thus, the Blessed One Vajrasattva is the manifestation of the habitual tendencies of the minds of sentient beings;
likewise, the Blessed One is the manifestation for sentient beings as a mass of merit or a mass of evil.
This was stated by the Blessed One in the Jñānapaṭala, in the fourth verse of the *Pañcākārastava*.

Namely: I bow to Vajrasattva, the Lord of the World, who possesses manifold forms and is the progenitor of the three worlds; he is pure consciousness alone, the essence of mantra, surrounded by the thirty [gods], whose nature is both suffering and bliss; he appears in peaceful form to the virtuous, yet his own actions bring a terrible experience to the wicked; whatever karma one performs, its fruit arises for that person according to the rule—[I bow] to him.
Thus.

(Kā0 Ta0 5.247) Therefore, for sentient beings, Vajrasattva and Māra are both manifestations of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of their own minds; it is not that there is a Māra distinct from the Blessed One.

That which is called Kāmadeva—the perishable moment (*kṣara-kṣaṇa*) that generates these aforementioned Māras of ignorance regarding body, speech, and mind—is destroyed by the Tathāgata through the supreme imperishable moment (*paramākṣara-kṣaṇa*). The "shattering of Māra" (*mārabala-bhaṅga*) is the destruction of those forms of ignorance consisting of passion, hatred, and delusion.

In this context, through the cessation of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the perishable, there is the cessation of attachment, aversion, delusion, and anger; from their cessation comes the cessation of ignorance.

Thus, there is the gradual cessation of the twelve links [of dependent origination]. From the cessation of the twelve links comes the cessation of the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*); from the cessation of the wheel of existence, Buddhahood becomes free from obscuration.

Within these systems of the Śrāvaka, Pāramitā, and Mantra vehicles, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, has taught the heart of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara-hṛdaya*) in the *Nāmasaṃgīti* of the Lord Vajradhara.
Not understanding its meaning, false gurus who have strayed from the knowledge of the supreme syllable will come into being in the future;
by those ruined ones, sentient beings are to be destroyed.
Therefore, in the Root Tantra, in the *Praise of the Fivefold Wisdom*, the Blessed One taught the meditation on the five aspects through five verses.

For example, in the chapter [of the aforementioned], in the *Mahoddeśa* titled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of Supreme Unchanging Syllable" (*Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*), verse [X]: "This collection of entities in emptiness, devoid of the form of conceptual construction, is seen like a reflection in a mirror by a young girl. Thus, in terms of supramundane truth, there is the mirror-like knowledge regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Having become equal to all entities, the single entity remains as the unchanging syllable (*akṣara*).
"Arising from the knowledge of the syllables, it is neither annihilated nor eternal.

Thus, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is the Gnosis of Equality (*samatājñāna*). All phonemes, which consist of all conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*), originate from the family of the letter *A*;
having attained the state of the Great Syllable (*mahākṣara-pada*), they are neither conceptualization nor possessors of conceptualization.

Thus, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*); in phenomena that are unarisen and devoid of formative activity (*saṃskāra*), there is no Buddhahood by means of awakening, nor is there a sentient being, nor even a life-principle.

Thus, the aggregate of formative activity (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*); for the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-dharmatā*) transcends [these aggregates], being pure wisdom, indeed stainless.
"Phenomena are luminous by nature and have reached the state of the *dharmadhātu*.
Thus ends the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), which is the wisdom of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*.
Likewise, in the *Laghutantra*, the characteristics of the aggregates of the Tathāgatas, beginning with the wheel symbol, are described in three verses consisting of one hundred and one [syllables].

That is to say: the wheel is the pure [mind] throughout the three realms; bliss is its jewel; passion is its lotus; the sword is the destruction of the afflictions; the vajra is indeed the body of great gnosis, which is beyond being known; the cleaver is the cutting away of ignorance; and those six families produced by these [elements] are likewise to be understood as follows: the aggregates, elements, sense-faculties, and so forth, are of a single flavor like space. That in which the form of birth goes to its end is called "Great Form"; that in which the suffering of saṃsāra goes to its end is called "Great Feeling."

That in which the notion of saṃsāra reaches its end is the notion of Mahāvajra; that in which the increase of saṃsāra reaches its end is indeed the vajra-refinement (*vajrasaṃskāra*). That in which the states beginning with waking reach their end is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); that in which the state of ignorance reaches its end is the very gnosis (*jñāna*) of the Sage. These are Vairocana and the others, the six supreme and excellent Victors, the six families; and the others are the divisions of the six elements: earth, fire, water, wind, space, and peace.

(Kālacakra-tantra 5.101–103) In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated that in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, the Blessed Lord Vajradhara’s supreme unchanging gnosis (*paramākṣarajñāna*), which constitutes the heart of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, was revealed by the Tathāgata through one hundred and sixty-two verses consisting of requests and responses.

In this regard, from “Then the glorious Vajradhara... up to “standing before him in his manifest form,” there are sixteen verses of supplication; from “Then the Blessed Śākyamuni... up to “Excellent, O Blessed One,” there are six verses of response; then, from “Now, beginning with the names... up to “the great Uṣṇīṣa family,” there are two verses surveying the six families; from “This king of mantras... up to “homage to you, Arapacana,” there are three verses on the sequence of awakening through the *Māyājāla*; and from “Thus, the Blessed Buddha... up to “the supreme method of the Mahāyāna.”

Thus, up to this point, there are fourteen verses of praise for the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu; from "The Buddha Mahāvairocana" up to "Vajrāṃśa, the Great Noose," there are twenty-four and a quarter verses of praise for the Wisdom of the Perfectly Pure Dharmadhātu;
from "Vajrabhairava-bhokara" up to "Ghoṣa, the Best among those possessing sound," there are ten and a quarter verses of praise for the Mirror-like Wisdom (ādarśajñāna);
and from "Tathatā, the True Selflessness" up to "Jñānārci, the Radiant One," there are forty-two verses of praise for the Discriminating Wisdom (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna).
From the verse beginning with *iṣṭārthasādhakaḥ* up to *ratnaketumahāmaṇiḥ*, there are twenty-four verses in praise of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
From the verse beginning with *sarvasambuddhaboddhavyaḥ* up to *mañjuśrīḥ śrīmatāmvaraḥ*, there are fifteen verses in praise of the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).
From the verse beginning with *namaste varadavajrāgrya* up to *jñānakāya namo 'stu te*, there are five verses in praise of the wisdom of the five Tathāgatas.

By these one hundred and sixty-two verses, the heart of the Blessed Lord Vajradhara has been extracted and condensed from all the vehicles. It is Samantabhadra, the supreme unchanging great bliss, pervading as far as the limits of the realm of space, shining forth on all sides. It is produced from the accumulation of pure gnosis, possessing a form that is both profound and vast, naturally luminous, and merely beginningless and endless. It is free from the stains of conceptual constructions such as self and other, or subject and object; it is at all times undefiled, knowing the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, and liberated from the latent tendencies of saṃsāra. It is devoid of coming and going, a form beyond conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), the support for various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and mnemonic powers (*dhāraṇī*) that unfold through their own natural flow. Like a precious vase, a wish-fulfilling tree, or a *cintāmaṇi* jewel, it fulfills the hopes of all sentient beings. It is beyond the range even of the Great Sages, yet brings supreme peace to the vast multitude of beings; it is like an illusion, like a dream, like a reflection, and like an echo.

This very knowledge of the yogi, which is worthy of honor in the three worlds, self-cognizable, and the supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*), must not be abandoned by the yogi; such is the injunction of the Tathāgata.
Its cultivation was taught by the Tathāgata in the *Jñānapaṭala* of the *Mūlatantrarāja*, as follows:
"Having cultivated smoke and the other [signs], one should make the mind immovable."
Having purified the central channel, one should meditate on the supreme syllable.
Having established the vajra in the lotus, one should cause the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to enter the drop (*bindu*).
One should place the drops within the wheels (*cakras*), and arrest the vibration (*spanda*) of those drops within the vajra.
The yogi whose *liṅga* is always firm shall always be one whose vital essence flows upward;
through constant application to the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), he is empowered by the penetrations of the vajra.
By means of the twenty-one thousand six hundred supreme unchanging syllables (*paramākṣara*), [he attains this].
"O Great King, in a single moment, one becomes Vajrasattva himself.

This is the *Mahoddeśa* titled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of Supreme Unchanging [Reality] (*paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*). It was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Jñānapaṭala* (Chapter on Knowledge) of the *Tantrarāja*, in the *Pañcākārastava* (Praise in Five Aspects), in the first verse, regarding Nirvāṇa as being without signs (*nirnimitta*), as follows: "That which has no end, beginning, or middle; no abiding, death, or existence; no sound, smell, taste, touch, or form; no mind, no primordial nature (*prakṛti*), no person (*puruṣa*); and neither bondage nor liberation, nor an agent—"

I bow to that seed which is not manifest in time, which is neither of the nature of suffering nor of happiness in all worlds, which is nirvāṇa, signless, devoid of instruments of action, and free from qualities. Thus, clothing is the means (upāya).

In this very context, wisdom (*prajñā*) is described as being without signs (*nirnimittā*) by the fifth verse: “One who is neither one nor not one, yet one; equal and unequal, yet equal; on the right, left, front, back, above, and below, indeed, all around; white, green, and of great universal color; short, long, and protracted; without qualities, yet possessing qualities; woman, man, and neither man nor woman—he who is the sole support of all, the singular, auspicious, and supreme fortune: homage to you, homage to you! Thus it is said.

Sattva is the lotus, which is wisdom; thus Vajrasattva has been described by the Blessed One in the Jñānapaṭala of the King of Tantras: "The lotus of wisdom and the vajra of method are said to be the support and the supported;
their union is the meditative absorption (samāpatti), the yoga of the two, non-dual and immutable."
"I bow to that Kālacakra, the Vajrayoga which is fourfold;
he is the King Pauṇḍarīka himself, who emerged from Kalāpa and holds a lotus.
Thus.

Thus, in the *Vimalaprabhā* commentary on the *Śrī-laghukālacakra-tantra-rāja*, the twelve-thousand-verse [work], the third great chapter entitled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of Supreme Unchanging [Reality]" is concluded.

(4) Now follows the great chapter on "Disciples to be Tamed by Various Means": having prostrated to the five-syllabled Great Void, the six-syllabled Void of the Bindu, and the rest beginning with the vowels and consonants, the number of breaths is here set forth.

The vowels beginning with *Lā* (l, e, ai, o, au), which consist of eight measures (*mātrā*) and pertain to the qualities of the sense objects (*viṣayaguṇa*), are devoid of half-measures; they are mutually divided by their differences, numbering fifty-six (*pada-rasa-śara*), and carry the middle breaths (*madhyamāśvāsa*).

When the second consonant (*lagne dvitīye*) is joined due to the influence of the qualities of the sense objects, they are further divided by mutual difference; then, when conjoined again in the third position, they possess the qualities of the sense objects as protracted (*pluta*) and carry the middle breaths.
[From the *Vimalaprabhā*: "Beginning with *Lā*" and so forth...]

In this context, the eight measures beginning with *ḷ* are devoid of half-measures and pertain to the qualities of the sense objects: *la* pertains to the quality of smell (*gandha*), *u* pertains to the quality of form (*rūpa*), *ṛ* pertains to the quality of taste (*rasa*), *i* pertains to the quality of touch (*sparśa*), *a* pertains to the quality of sound (*śabda*), *aṃ* pertains to the quality of *sattva*, *aḥ* pertains to the quality of *rajas*, and *ā~* pertains to the quality of *tamas*; these are the protracted (*pluta*) vowels, while the unstruck (*anāhata*) half-measure is *ha*.

By this [calculation], they are seven and a half; likewise, the eighth measure is diminished by half a measure. Thus, being mutually distinguished by these divisions, each is divided into seven and a half parts. When all of these are multiplied by the truth of the origin (*samudayasatya*), they become fifty-six and a quarter—[expressed as] "sixty-five with a quarter and six flavors" (*sapādaṣaṭpañcāśad bhavanti sapadarasaśarāḥ*). These are the short and medium breath-flows for a newborn child at the ascendants of Aries and so forth;
thereafter, there is the movement through the mandalas in the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*) for the child born first.
Borṅka also states this: "In the second ascendant, such as Taurus and so forth, when it is even, the breaths are of medium inhalation.

Although here the [breaths] beginning with *la* have been mentioned, nevertheless, while the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs in the spheres of ether and so forth in the left nostril, here again, by the rule of the five qualities beginning with the navel and so forth, the vital breath is grasped through its similarity to ether, earth, and the rest, according to the distinction between short and long [vowels] in the odd and even ascendants.
Furthermore, when joined in the third [channel], the qualities of the *pluta* sphere are carried by the *madhyamā* breath;
thus, if a fool is at the time of transition (*saṃkrānti*), then the vital breath (*prāṇa*), having become *pluta* in the *madhyamā*, circulates through the left and right [channels].
By these aforementioned [rules], the movement of all syllables is to be understood.

Herein is the differentiation of the letter *la*, as follows: *ḷ lu lu li la laṃ laḥ lāṃ l*; likewise *u vḷ vu vū vi va vaṃ vaḥ vāṃ v*; likewise *ṝ ḷ ruri ra raṃ raḥ rāṃ r*; likewise *i yla yu yṛ ya yaṃ yaḥ yāṃ y*; likewise *a al o ar e aṃ aḥ āṃ a*; likewise *aṃ mla mu mṛ mim aṃ maḥ māṃ m*; likewise *a rla ru ṛri ra raṃ raḥ rāṃ r*; likewise *ha hala hu hṛ hi ha ha haḥ hāṃ ha*. Thus, there are fifty-six and a quarter [syllables].

In this way, the long and protracted [vowels] are to be understood according to their mutual distinctions. Now, the measures of the breaths of day and night are stated: Thus, in the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*), there are fifty-six middle breath-measures; the letters beginning with *ka* are three hundred and sixty, clearly divided into nine hundred and thirty, distinguished by the divisions of six measures. In the three ascendants (*lagna*) and three channels (*nāḍī*), there are four thousand five hundred [breaths]; likewise, those belonging to the other day are divided into long [measures] in the three ascendants and three channels.
Regarding the "three signs and three nāḍīs":

there are thirty letters beginning with *ka*, namely the thirty letters starting from *ka* belonging to the six groups *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *pa*, *ta*, and *śa*. These clearly constitute the hundreds [of combinations], for through the mutual conjunction of each individual letter within the thirty divisions, thirty variations arise.
Namely: k-ka, k-kha, k-ga, k-gha, k-ṅa; k-ca, k-cha, k-ja, k-jha, k-ñ-a; k-ṭa, k-ṭha, k-ḍa, k-ḍha, k-ṇa; k-pa, k-ph-a, k-ba, k-bha, k-ma; k-ta, k-tha, k-da, k-dha, k-na; k-śa, k-pa, k-ṣa, k-sa, k-ka.
In this manner, the [consonants] beginning with *kh* should be understood;
thus they become one hundred and eight through the process of manifestation.

// 129 // Furthermore, even when divided by six measures (*mātra*) at the time of night, and likewise when divided by long [measures] at the departure of another night, in the three *lagna*s and three *nāḍī*s— within those three *lagna*s and three *nāḍī*s— the great chapter on the various means for training disciples states that they carry inhalations and exhalations during the time of each day numbering sixty thousand and two hundred (60,200). Having first extracted the zeros, one should join them to the middle channel according to the even and uneven movement.
Furthermore, those nine hundred [syllables], divided by the six measures (*mātra*),
when differentiated by *a*, *i*, *ṛ*, *u*, *la*, and *aṃ*, become one hundred fifty-four (*khakhayugaśara*).
This is the arising from midnight during the three conjunctions (*lagna*) and three dances (*nāṭya*).

"Up to" means as follows: from that point, for six long *mātrās*, the breaths divided by the rising [of the sun] until midday consist of three *lagnas* and three *nāḍīs*, with the number being as previously stated.
Again, for six short *mātrās*, from midday until the time of night—that is, until sunset—for three *lagnas* and three *nāḍīs*, the number is as before.
Thus, in the latter part of the night until midnight, for three *lagnas* and three *nāḍīs*, the number of breaths with their respective *mātrās* is equal to the previous count.

Thus, they carry the inhalations and exhalations every day at the rate of *khakhaṣaṭ-candranetra*—that is, twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths. Within these breaths, one should first extract the zeros (*śūnya*) and join them to the middle channel (*madhyamā*) according to the even and uneven movement.

Here, as previously stated, there are eleven and a quarter [breaths] in each maṇḍala; and those, through the divisions of the rising of the zodiacal signs beginning with Capricorn (*makara*), and through the divisions of the letters beginning with *da* at the end of each maṇḍala, one should join them to the middle channel.
This great proliferation has not been written down here because of its vastness; it is to be understood from the *Paramāvibuddha*, the commentary of sixty thousand verses.

Furthermore, there is no supramundane cause [to be found] by which effort must be exerted, since this [process] proceeds from the beginning of the alphabet up to the number of body hairs and head hairs. || 130 ||

Now, that which is the eighth half-measure, following the seven and a half, is described: The eighth half-measure that occurs externally as a *ghaṭikā* situated beyond the movement of Rāhu is, in one's own body, indeed free from darkness and illuminates all worlds.

That first half-measure dissolves the entire triple world into darkness within the Void; therefore, having pierced through it, the yogi of the Single Yoga of Kālacakra enters that state free from darkness. (131)
Regarding the passage beginning with "external" (*bāhya*) and so forth:

here, in this external world-system, that which arises as the eighth path-measure (*mātrā*), the *ghaṭikā*, occurs after the enjoyment of Rāhu. Here, for each season, Rāhu consumes five channels characterized by the five sense-objects; likewise, he consumes those three characterized by the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Within the wheel of the zodiac signs (*rāśicakra*), he consumes seven and a half [channels] among them.

He is not capable of consuming even half a *nāḍī*; that [time] remains beyond the consumption by Rāhu. That half-breath (*śvāsārdha*) exists within his own body as a staff-like form between the navel and the forehead; because there is no outward exit, it is called "half-breath," and according to the distinction of mantras, it is the "half-mora" (*ardhamātrā*).
Indeed, that [energy], free from darkness and illuminating the entire world, possesses the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) for a fetus six months old;

it causes the entire triple world, including its deep gloom, to dissolve. Therein, at the end of death in the void, having abandoned the fourth state (*turyā*), it enters the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptā*); then, for six months, the fetus, having reached the state of dreaming (*svapna*), enters the latter half of the measure.

Therefore, having differentiated that state of darkness—which does not exist further in the *Vimalaprabhā*—the yogi of Kālacakra, with the movement of the vital breath restrained, enters the heart where darkness has departed and remains in the navel-cakra; thus, having entered the state of the womb, there is the accomplishment of yoga for the yogis. || 131 ||

Now, the loss of the digits (*kalā*) and so forth for children who have been born is described: The supreme digit of the Lord (*vibhu-paramakalā*), which is diminished by the moon and increased by the sun, moves through the four junctions (*sandhyā*) at every watch (*yāma*). By the power of night and day, through the divisions of the half-ascendants (*ardhalagna*), there are thirty-six messengers of Time (*kāladūtī*). There are another thirty-two [messengers] in the division of the two eights (sixteen), and furthermore, others in the eightfold division of the days (*vāra*), yet others indeed in the various locations of the single junctions. *Note: This verse describes the astrological and temporal correspondences of the Kalās within the system of the Kālacakra, correlating them with the movement of the moon and sun, the watches of the day and night, and the divisions of time such as the *tithis*, *vāras*, and *sandhyās*. The "thirty-six" refers to the six *ṛtus* multiplied by the six *cakras* (or the six *kalās* per *cakra*), while the "thirty-two" refers to the sixteen *tithis* and sixteen *vāras*. The "eightfold division of the days" likely refers to the eight *vāras* (days of the week), and the "single junctions" (*naikasandhipradeśe*) may refer to the specific points where these cycles intersect.*
Regarding "The moon," and so forth:

here, as it is externally, so it is internally; the moon’s daily lunar day (*tithi*) consists of sixty *ghaṭikās*, and that [total] minus one *ghaṭikā* pertains to Venus internally. That which is "excessive" is [the portion] of the sun; thus, in the solar course, there are two *nāḍīs* as previously stated in the internal chapter.

"Vibhu" refers to the *bodhicitta*. Its supreme digit (*paramakalā*), characterized by gnosis (*jñāna*), is the waning of the lunar digit; that which is characterized by consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the waning of the solar enjoyment.

This [digit] moves through each watch (*yāma*) within the four junctions (*sandhyā*) here, according to the power of night and day, through the divisions of the inauspicious *lagna*s; these are the thirty-six "messengers of time" (*kāladūtī*s), who are the *ḍākinī*s in the *Tricakrasaṃvara*. Their movement occurs in conjunction with the *kulikā*.

Just as externally there is enjoyment (*bhoga*), dissolution (*laya*), authority (*adhikāra*), and sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) according to the divisions of the twilights and the divisions of the watches (*prahara*) and half-lagnas, so too internally there is [these states] according to the divisions of the rising of the sun and the divisions of the rising of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Here, in the external world of the four continents, where the sun rises, there is enjoyment; where it is midnight, there is dissolution; where it is midday, there is authority; and where it sets, there is sovereignty.

From the entry of night for the *kulikā* until midnight is for the enjoyment of the *yoginīs*; from sunrise until midday is the enjoyment of the monks during the daytime. Therefore, the rule is that the Lord Vajrī is day and Prajñā is night for the sake of enjoyment. Consequently, from sunrise until midday, the food consumed by the monks must be free of meat; from sunset until midnight, the *samaya* rites must be performed by the yogins and yoginīs.
Beyond that, there is the breaking of the vow for both the Śrāvaka and the Mantrin; from its breach comes the loss of supernatural powers and accomplishments.

Thus, just as there is the enjoyment (*bhoga*), dissolution (*laya*), and so forth for the four *yoginīs* according to the division of the twilight periods (*sandhyā*), so too is the movement of the eight cremation-ground *yoginīs* according to the division of the watches (*prahara*). From midnight until midday, they move in direct order (*anuloma*) through the east, south, west, and north. During the four watches from midday until midnight, they likewise move in reverse order (*viloma*) through the directions of Īśāna, Vāyavya, Nairṛtya, and Agneya. Furthermore, according to the division of the half-lagnas, there is a clockwise movement in the Mind-Cakra (*cittacakra*) during the half-lagna of Scorpio and Sagittarius; and for the four [yoginīs], there is a counter-clockwise movement during the half-lagna of Capricorn and Aquarius.

Thus, in the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*), there is a movement through the divisions of Pisces, Aries, Taurus, and the half of Gemini; likewise, in the wheel of body (*kāyacakre*), there is a movement through the divisions of Cancer, Leo, Virgo, and Libra. This is the movement of the thirty-six [deities] according to the divisions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

These are the Kāladūtīs; as it is said in the *Cakrasaṃvara*: "With the central and supreme breath, together with scented water, one should constantly worship Kulikā, and the Dūtīs at specific times."
Here, with supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*) and through the cessation of the channels of feces, urine, moon, and sun, one should worship Kulikā Vajravārāhī;

at the specified times mentioned, one should worship the thirty-six female messengers (*dūtī*) by means of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇasañcāra*), both externally and internally. This is the great chapter on the various means for those to be trained (*vineya*). In the first circle of the navel wheel (*nābhicakra*), there are four petals.

Among those, the eastern petal is the Seat of the Self (ātmapīṭha), the southern is the Seat of the Other (parapīṭha), the western is the Seat of Mantra (mantrapīṭha), and the northern is the Seat of Reality (tattvapīṭha).

Likewise, the mouth-gate is Śūlabheda cremation ground in the east; the right nostril is Śavadahana in the south; the anus-gate is Pūtigandha in the west; and the left nostril is Klinna in the north. Similarly, the left ear is Bālamṛtyu in the northeast; the right ear is Ghorayuddha in the southwest; the right eye is Sarpadaṣṭa in the northwest; and the left eye is Ucchiṣṭa in the southeast.

Thus, regarding the names of the eight channels in the heart-cakra: the eastern channel is Rohiṇī-Pūrṇagiri, known as Piṅgalā; the southern channel is Jālandhara-Jayā; the western channel is Oḍḍiyāṇa-Iḍā; and the northern channel is Arbuda. Likewise, in the intermediate directions: in the northeast is Kuhā-Godāvarī; in the northwest is Alambuṣā-Rāmeśvarī; in the southwest is Pūṣā-Devīkoṭa; and in the southeast is Hastijihvā-Mālavaka.
In this manner, the eight channels in the first circle of the throat-cakra are to be known by the designations of Kṣetra, Upakṣetra, Chandoha, and Upachandoha.

In this way, on the forehead as well, in the first circle, eight channels are to be known by the names *mela*, *upamela*, *śmaśāna*, and *upaśmaśāna*; such is the rule in the *Cakrasaṃvara*. The seed-syllables for these are the semivowels *ya, ra, la, va* in the directions starting from the east in the body wheel (*kāyacakra*), and likewise *vā, lā, rā, yā* in the intermediate directions starting from the northeast (*īśāna*). [The syllables] *ha, hā, haṃ, haḥ* are in the cremation grounds of fire, wind, northeast, and southwest.
Thus, in the speech-chakra (vākcakra), [the vowels] e, ai, ar, and al are in the cardinal directions;
in the intermediate directions, au, āl, ār, ai, a, ā, aṃ, and aḥ are in the cremation grounds of the east, west, north, and south.
In the mind-chakra (cittacakra), i, ṛ, ḷ, and u are in the cardinal directions; in the intermediate directions, ū, ṝ, and ī.
On the petals of the lotus of the womb, *a* and *ā* are in the east and west, and *aṃ* and *aḥ* are in the north and south, belonging to the twelve-armed [deity].

Thus the Blessed One said in the Root Tantra: "The mind, situated in the center of the navel through the union of gnosis and consciousness, is bound by the eight qualities of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), like silkworms by their own cocoons."

Due to the distinction between the three types of cognition—waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—the mind of living beings has three faces; through the time of the fourth state (turyā), it becomes four-faced.
Thus, through the yoga of consciousness, the mind— which consists of five or six objects, which has five faces and six mouths, and which is both non-mind and a different kind of mind— is attained.

The *bindu* is situated in the center of the navel, and the *visarga* is within it; through the union of knowledge (*jñāna*) and realization (*vijñāna*), the *bodhicitta* is established by means of these two enclosures.
"Due to the different movements of the vital breath (prāṇa) during the junctions (sandhyā), the nadir-lagnas, and so forth,
thirty-six female messengers (dūtī) are taught here for the purpose of initiating the ignorant.
Thus, these thirty-six channels (nāḍikā) are the messengers of time (kāladūtī) according to the flow of the vital breath, and they cause the destruction of the body.
Therefore, the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which has entered those [channels] must be restrained.
Now, the thirty-two secret channels (*guhyanaḍī*) that carry the bodhicitta are described, beginning with "twice the kings" (*dviguṇanṛpatayaḥ*).

Here, "twice the kings" refers to the thirty-two [channels] situated in the secret wheel (*guhyacakra*) through the differentiation of gnosis (*jñāna*). Among them, sixteen abide in the white lunar phase (*śuklapakṣa*) through the differentiation of the digits (*kalā*) of passion (*rāga*); sixteen abide in the black lunar phase (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) through the differentiation of dispassion (*virāga*), by way of the waning of the lunar digits as previously described.
For it is said here: "Indivisible, subtle in form, divine, Vāmā, and Vāmanī," and so forth.
There is no [separate] *śmaśāna* or *upaśmaśāna*;
rather, these thirty-two channels (*nāḍīs*) are the substratum (*ādhāra*), and the *ḍākinīs* are the qualities supported therein (*ādheya-dharmin*), due to their conjunction with the *apāna* wind.

By means of these [thirty-two], Heruka or the *Samāja* consists of thirty-three; because it is a secret tantra, its emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*) is twofold, consisting of a wheel of sixty-four yoginīs that causes the flow of the five maṇḍalas.

Furthermore, regarding the eight days of the week, there are again the channels of the days: in the heart-lotus are the eight [goddesses] beginning with Gaurī, and in the forehead are the sixteen beginning with Nairātmyā.

Thus, in the region of the many joints—specifically the three hundred and sixty joint-regions—there are channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) equal in number to the days of a year; the *yoginīs* are the contents (*ādheya*) within them.

In this way, through the distinction between support and supported, there are as many *ḍākinīs* as there are channels among the seventy-two thousand *yoginīs*, according to the movement of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths; such is the non-conceptual word of the Blessed One. 132.
Now the seal (mudrā) of the Blessed One is described:

The mother of the three worlds, Ḍākinī, who possesses the forms of all things and whose breaths are equal to the Vedas and seasons, is the supreme consort of the Lord of Jinas; she exists as her own seal in two ways.

She who resides in the sun has eight divisions on the petals of the cardinal and intermediate directions, ending with the enjoyment of the watches of the night. The remaining others are the goddesses of the wheels, all of whom are extremely terrifying and reside within the outer body. || 133 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "vedavit" and so forth:

here, "the knower of the Vedas" refers to the sixty-four [breaths]. At its end is that which is the lost lunar digit (*candrakalā*) for transmigrating beings; by contrast, the "unlost lunar digit" is the final breath among the sixty-four breaths, characterized as breath, the mother of the three worlds, the *ḍākinī* of universal form, who is devoid of the moon within the Supreme Lord of Jinas—the *bodhicitta*. She is one's own *mudrā*, and she is twofold.

One is the conventional nature, the Great Māyā, the Great Fierce One who effects the destruction of beings; the second is Great Wisdom, the Prajñāpāramitā of the Buddhas’ *bodhicitta*, free from arising and passing away, the Buddha-Māyā, the Great Auspicious One who brings about creation and dissolution. She exists in the *apāna* due to the division of the outflows (*anāśrava*), and she exists in the sun (*arka*). She has eight divisions: she resides in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the nature of passion (*rajas*), and she possesses eight aspects through the division of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, the three qualities (*guṇas*), and the five objects of the senses—thus she consists of eight attributes.
And she is situated upon the eight petals of the lotus within the maṇḍala; this is the visualization.

The remaining others—the previously mentioned wheel-deities—are conceptualized as being entirely outside the body and extremely terrifying; such is the rule for the movement through the channels (nāḍīs). || 133 ||

Now the Ḍākinīs of the planetary movements and enjoyments are described: In Saturn, they are nine and fifteen; in Rāhu, two and a half; in Jupiter, the number of eyes with a half-eye (two and a half); in the Supreme Lord of Jinas, six and a half, born from the mind-vajra. In Mars, they are zero, eight, and one;
in the Sun, Mercury, Venus, and Ketu, they are zero, eight, one, and one with an eye (one and a quarter), born indeed from the pure speech-vajra of the Supreme Sovereign. (134)
Regarding the passage beginning with "manda" and so forth:
here, in the external movement of the sun, a season (*ṛtu*) of the sun occurs every two months; internally, a season of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs every two zodiac signs (*lagna*).
And that [season] arises through the flow of the ten mandalas on the left and right, by way of the distinction between emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).

Therefore, in the case of the dull-witted (*manda*) who possess dull enjoyment (*mandabhoga*), there is an enjoyment of nine *ghaṭikās* in the wheel of signs (*rāśicakra*) during the period of the *ṛtu*; and these are the *ḍākinīs* in the chapter (*paṭala*). Thus, they are called "the fifteen" (*vinākhya*). Regarding the phrase "in the night, the enjoyment of the Preceptor of the Gods (*suraguru*) is the number of eyes and half-eyes," this refers to twenty-two and a half; when unified, these are "six and a half born from the Vedas," which amounts to forty-six and a half.
"O Supreme Lord of Jinas, they arise from the fire-pit" means that they are produced from the *citta-bindu*.
"On earth, [there are] zero, snakes, and moons" is the elaboration (*prapañca*);
the rule is that as many channels (*nāḍīs*) as are obtained by the sixty-fold division of its mandala—generally, one hundred and eighty.

In this system, wherever there is a deficient portion of Mars, the solar motion (*ravikābhoga*) must not be subtracted; rather, one month of lunar motion (*candrabhoga*) is to be added. Here, it is traditionally held that Mars completes its own day in twenty-three months, whereas others claim it is eighteen months; however, that is incorrect. Therefore, the rule here is that the planetary mandala occurs in a hundred years plus eight months and twenty-one days, as is the actual case for the planets. Thus, for Mars, [the calculation] is zero, eight, and one.
For the Sun, Mercury, Earth (Mars), Jupiter, and Ketu, the values are zero, three, one, and one;
thus, from the combined movement of these five planets, there arise one thousand two hundred and twenty—one thousand, two hundred, and twenty.
Indeed, these are the "eight" arising from pure speech (*śuddhavāk*) of the Supreme Lord; the meaning is that they are produced by the bonds of speech. || 134 ||
The seasonal movement of the moon, which consists of sixty-six and three (663), arises from the Body-Vajra; when these are unified as a whole, they become six, six, two, and four (6624) half-nāḍīs.

Likewise, the Ḍākinīs, who are the embodiments of Time, pervade all bodies and are the destroyers of the life-force of living beings; therefore, they should be mastered by blocking them within one's own body at every daily occasion.

That which is the Moon’s monthly consumption—three thousand six hundred *ghaṭikās* of duration—is said to arise from the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*), meaning it arises from the *bindu* of the effect; when unified as a whole, these are four thousand eight hundred and sixty-six, according to the phrase "nine, six, four, two, and yugas. Likewise, half a *nāḍī* is the same number. This is the single total count of the *ḍākinīs*.
Those *ḍākinīs* are the form of Time (*kāla*); pervading all things, they are the slayers of the life-force of gods and other living beings in a single moment.

Furthermore, in the six seasons, there are twenty-nine thousand one hundred and ninety-six; this is the number of ḍākinīs included within the movement of the planets among sentient beings—this is the rule. Therefore, they are to be accomplished by provoking them every day through the cessation of their prāṇa and apāna, and through the cessation of the four drops—this is the rule. || 135 ||

As long as the devotion of the planets, moving through their own and others' courses, proceeds from the movement of inhalation and exhalation, so long does the messenger of Time prevail—she who is the bestower of boons and all-pervading throughout the three realms.

This messenger must be known through the practice of yoga by those whose impurities have been removed, within the subtle movement, the words of the Guru, the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and the immutable (*akṣara*); not otherwise by those with minds of passion.
That which was stated by the second verse beginning with "as far as" (*yāvat*) and so forth is easy to understand. || 136 ||

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the entry of Rāhu into the course of the Moon is now described: The positions of the Sun and Moon are struck by thirst due to their movement in both directions; when Rāhu enters, he devours the remainder of the degrees of the lunar station (*caraṇa*), and Ketu [devours] all the twilights and eight watches (*yāma*).

At every daily time, for living beings, there are twelve-limbed breaths (*śvāsa*) in each single zodiacal sign (*lagna*), and the limb is said to consist of the flow of eighteen hundred breaths. (137)
Regarding the passage beginning with "mārtaṇḍa" and so forth:

here, the eleven instances of the word *mārtaṇḍa* are those previously mentioned in the verse "rasayugaśaśinaḥ"; the twenty-five instances of the word *indu* are those from the verse "bhūtā bhūteṣu" and so forth. When these two groups are combined together, they total thirty-six;
when multiplied by eight qualities (*guṇas*), they become two hundred and eighty-eight.
Thus, struck by thirst,
the twenty-four lunar positions obtained by dividing the twelve lunar mansions (*lagna*) by eight [as] limbs become [the result];
at the entry of Rāhu, Ketu swallows the remainder, the twenty-fifth step.
Internally, the mind is the sense organ that moves through the semen-element (*śukradhātu*);

that which is the "empty limb" refers to all four twilights (*sandhyā*) and eight watches (*prahara*) within the daily time of living beings. These constitute the twelve limbs, meaning the twelve zodiacal signs (*lagna*). In each single sign, there are eighteen hundred breath-flows (*prāṇavāha*), namely two thousand nine hundred; these are said to be "one limb."
Thus, in the external [time], one limb [of the year] consists of eighteen hundred *daṇḍas* in one month; with two months, there is a season (*ṛtu*) consisting of thirty-six hundred [daṇḍas].
In this way, there are six seasons, each consisting of two limbs [of the year], and an eclipse occurs every three seasons by virtue of the movement of the Moon, the Sun, and Rāhu. || 137 ||

In each pair of fortnights, ignorance (*avidyā*) occurs according to the influence of the first nine days, extending up to twelve factors (*dvādaśāṅga*). From that, the days and factors for the [subsequent] seasons follow; the ninth day of the subsequent period is as before.
Thus, through five modes, the season (*ṛtu*) also comes to be, wherein every two months the single digit of the moon reaches its end; that indeed is the first month. (138)

In the first day of each pair of lunar days, there is ignorance (*avidyā*); on the second day, there is formative predisposition (*saṃskāra*). In this sequence, there is aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), and again on the thirteenth day, ignorance; on the fourteenth, formative predisposition. Thus, on the ninth day of the dark fortnight, there is aging and death; again on the tenth, ignorance; on the eleventh, formative predisposition. In this sequence, there is aging and death on the sixth day of the bright fortnight.
Again, ignorance (*avidyā*) occurs on the seventh [lunar day], formative forces (*saṃskāra*) on the eighth, and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) on the third of the dark fortnight;

again, ignorance on the fourth, formative forces on the fifth, and in this sequence, old age and death on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). Thus, it is held that there are five revolutions within a season according to the nature of earth, water, fire, air, and space.
In this way, one fortnight is short (*hrasva*), a month is long (*dīrgha*), and a season is protracted (*pluta*).
The fortnight has the quality of *sattva*, the month has the quality of *rajas*, and the season has the quality of *tamas*;
thus, through these five modes, the season also occurs in its entirety, consisting of two months each.

In whichever month the digit (kalā) of the moon reaches its disappearance, that very first month of the two-month period becomes the third; thus, by the waning of the digit over sixty-four days, [the cycle is completed]. ||138||

In this chapter, the Great Instruction on Training through Various Means: The seizing [of the moon] may also occur by means of the twelvefold dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda) over six months and three seasons. The sixth division of the sun’s seasons enters into the middle of the moon by virtue of the movement of its steps;

therein, within the middle of the limb of contact (sparśāṅga), Rāhu swallows both the moon and the sun along with their steps. Those medicinal herbs which are gazed upon by Rāhu at the time of day or night bestow accomplishment (siddhi).
Through three seasons of six months each, there occurs the grasping by means of the realization of the twelve limbs;
herein, the first season possesses the nature of *sattva*, the second possesses the nature of *rajas*, and the third possesses the nature of *tamas*. By that [third], there is entry into *tamas*.
Likewise, the month is divided according to the six elements, up to the sixth month, which is the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*).
Thus, the seasonal division of the sun, by virtue of its movement through the quarters, enters into the midst of the moon on the new moon day;
therein, at the midpoint of the contact-point, Rāhu swallows both the moon and the sun along with their quarters.
At that time, the medicinal herbs attain perfection during the periods of day and night.
During a solar eclipse at day and a lunar eclipse at night, the trees and other objects mentioned below bear fruit when looked upon by Rāhu at the time of the eclipse.

Herein is the instruction: in every month during the sun's transit through a zodiac sign (*sūryabhoga*), one should add two constellations (*nakṣatra*) and eleven *ghaṭikās*; thus, over six months, there are twelve constellations and sixty-six *ghaṭikās*.

Having subtracted three days and six *ghaṭikās* from the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*), the remainder is thirteen; thus, fifty-three [units] are to be added to the lunar day (*amāvāsyā*) during an eclipse, or the solar day (*ravikā*) is to be subtracted.
Then, having subtracted forty-five *ghaṭikās* from the motion of Rāhu, one should subtract the remaining nakṣatra motion.
When the eclipse of the sun occurs facing eastward, it then occurs at the western tail-motion.
Thus,

it is established that the characteristic of an eclipse for the moon on the full moon day is just as it is externally; likewise, within the self, it should be understood by yogis to occur daily at the sixth ascendant.
This is inaccessible to the ignorant; it cannot be explained by means of the treatises. || 139 ||

Now, the fields (kṣetra) of Maṅgala and the other planets are described: Mars, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon; the Sun, Mercury, and Venus; Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and Jupiter—these are the lords of the fields (kṣetriṇaḥ) in the signs beginning with Aries at every time of day.

For pacification (śānti), the fields are those of the Moon and the Sun; for nourishment (puṣṭi), subjugation (vaśya), and attraction (ākarṣaṇa), they are the fields of Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. In separation (viyoga), this [field] prevails; and if it should occur during death, the field belongs to the one who dies. || 140 ||
"Earth-born" (bhauma), and so forth: here, the planets beginning with Mars are the lords of the signs starting from Aries;

Mars is the lord of Aries, Venus of Taurus, Mercury of Gemini, the Moon of Cancer, the Sun of Leo, Mercury again of Virgo, Venus of Libra, Mars of Scorpio, Jupiter—called "the Counselor" (mantrī)—of Sagittarius, Saturn—called "the Scavenger" (ākī)—of Capricorn, Saturn again—called "the Slow" (manda)—of Aquarius, and Jupiter—called "the Counselor"—of Pisces.
The meaning is that at the time of the rising of each of the twelve signs every day, those born under them are the enjoyers [of the results] at all times.

Here, in the rite of pacification (*śānti*), there are the two signs of Cancer and Leo belonging to the Moon and Sun; for nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the two signs of Gemini and Virgo belonging to Mercury; for subjugation (*avaśya*), the two signs of Taurus and Libra belonging to Venus; for attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), the two signs of Aries and Scorpio belonging to Mars; for eradication (*uccāṭana*), the two signs of Sagittarius and Pisces belonging to Saturn; and for killing (*māraṇa*), the two signs of Capricorn and Aquarius belonging to Saturn.

If, by virtue of the enjoyment of a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), a planet should be situated in its own field (*svakṣetra*) at this [time], then that sign (*rāśi*), presided over by another planet at no other time, becomes the giver of those results in the previously mentioned rites; such is the rule. || 140 ||

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*) and subjugation (*vaśya*), the pacification (*śānti*) and other rites are now described according to the divisions of the Blessed One’s faces: for pacification, the first face is white; for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), it resembles white gold during the watch of the hands (*hastayāma*); for immobilization (*stambhana*), it is like gold and the sun during the watch of fire (*agniyāma*); and for delusion (*mohana*), it is red during the watch of the ocean (*abdhi*).

In the fifth [watch] during attraction, it should be like the sun and clouds; in the sixth watch during subjugation, it has a black face; for killing on a mountain, it is dark-white; and here, at the end of the night during expulsion, it is "ho."
Regarding "In [the rite of] pacification," and so forth:

here, at the beginning of pacification, during the first watch (prahara) from sunrise, by virtue of the movement of the twilight [deities], the Lord becomes the leader in the east with a white face. Therefore, for the purpose of pacification, one should accomplish the fruit within a single watch through the mantras and meditations previously established in the east. "Resembling white gold" refers to the second watch; by virtue of the movement [of the deities], the west, north, and east become the leaders. Through that mixture, one should accomplish the rite of enrichment (pauṣṭika).

The *pota* with the western face is the leader for one *prahara* from midday; by means of that, during the third *prahara*, the fire-watch (*agniyāma*), it grants success in the matter of paralyzing (*stambhana*).
In the fourth *prahara*, the leader is yellowish-red, like gold and the sun, a mixture of yellow and red; by means of that, one should perform enchantment (*mohana*).
Thus, in the fifth *prahara*, the leader will have a red face for the purpose of summoning (*ākṛṣṭi*).

In the sixth [watch], one should accomplish subjugation (*vaśya*) by means of the leader who is a mixture of red and black; likewise, for killing (*māraṇa*), [one uses] the black-faced [deity] during the seventh watch, that is, at midnight. For driving away (*uccāṭana*), [one uses] the white [deity] during the final watch, from the end of the night until sunrise.

Thus, when the Blessed One Kālacakra has eight faces through the division of the watches (*prahara*), he then possesses four feet through the division of the four twilights (*saṃdhyā*). He is established as having sixteen arms through the division of the half-watches (*ardhaprahara*).
Such is the rule regarding the division of the arms: there are eight activities during the day through the division of the half-watches, and likewise at night.

There are four activities through the division of the four twilights: pacification (*śāntika*) at the morning twilight, immobilization (*stambhana*) at midday, summoning (*ākṛṣṭi*) when the sun has set, and killing (*māraṇa*) at midnight.

In this case as well, for the eight-faced [deity], the wisdom consort has two arms; this is the rule of meditation for the performance of rites: the two front and back sandhyās constitute the two arms, from midday until midnight constitutes the two arms, and the entire day and night constitutes the face. 141.
From this verse onwards, the second part is easily understood:

Earth, water, fire, and wind are not the moon, sun, gods, or the living soul (jīva) that experiences; rather, it is their *jīva* that is the experiencer. Yet, under the influence of inauspicious fruits [of karma], one thinks, "I am the experiencer.

Having seen [this state] and being attached to suffering, one should pray to the planets, serpents, and gods, as well as the host of spirits, for liberation—that grace by which mastery over the mind arises; yet even he does not grant peace. (142)

Now, the characteristics of the breath of a newborn infant are described: The primary breath (ādiśvāsa) is devoid of qualities; yet, by the power of the three qualities (guṇas), it also becomes threefold. These are called the lunar dates (tithis); they too become tripled by the power of the qualities of the objects (viṣayas). Thus, they become the number of the "ocean of elements" (fourteen). Again, when multiplied by the four divisions of the wheels (cāras), they become the number of breaths in half a nāḍī. Furthermore, when doubled, they become the number of breaths in one ghaṭikā. || 143 ||
Regarding "Āditya" and so forth:

the first lack of trust (*aviśvāsa*) that arises here in the infant is of the nature of non-qualities (*aguṇātmā*), being devoid of qualities such as *sattva* and the like, as well as odors and so forth;
its activity proceeds from there by the power of the threefold qualities, specifically by the power of *sattva*, as stated in the chapter [and] verse...

The second major section, the "Great Instruction on Training through Various Means," has emerged as the first breath; the third [breath] arises from the power of *rajas*, and the fourth from the power of *tamas*.
Among these, the first is not grasped as a quality (*guṇa*);
therefore, it is counted as the third along with them because of its all-pervasive nature.

Furthermore, those [fifteen] which have the nature of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* each become fivefold through the distinction of the five qualities of the objects (*viṣaya-guṇa*); thus they are called "the lunar days" (*tithi*), making fifteen. These, again, are tripled by the distinction of body, speech, and mind, resulting in the number "ocean of elements" (*bhūtābdhi*), which is forty-five.

Moreover, these are multiplied by the divisions of the movements (*cāra*) of the Moon and the Sun; for the movements of the Moon and Sun are fourfold, according to the distinctions of fast, slow, retrograde, and direct motion, as well as the increase and decrease of wealth, and the increase and decrease of debt.

Multiplied by those four, the number of breaths (*nāḍī*) is one hundred and eighty; when that number of breaths is doubled again, it becomes the number of breaths in a *ghaṭikā*, which is three hundred and sixty. This, by virtue of being the nature of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), is one channel (*ekanāḍī*) flowing through one mandala for the child [in the womb], whether on the left or the right;
from that come the second and the third. || 143 ||

This time-measure (kālanāḍī) is increased by two, three, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and ten; therefore, through the various divisions of the squares, this time-measure proceeds along a twofold path, filling the three worlds on all sides and bestowing the fruit of equal happiness, arising from the movement of the moon and sun, as long as four times three fire [twelve] prevails, fixed as the knife with a shell in hand. 144.

By the verse beginning with "dvitryandhīṣu" and so forth, this *kālanāḍī*—the central channel (*madhyamā*) that flows through the ten mandalas—is increased on the left and right; it extends for sixty mandalas within a single day and night.

Therefore, according to the previously mentioned divisions such as the *gaṃ-prabhṛti* [groups], the letters of the *kakārādi* class, and the zodiacal signs beginning with Aries (*meṣa*), the *kālanāḍī* proceeds everywhere along various paths.

Filling the body known as the "three worlds," filling the seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*), and bestowing the fruit of equal bliss, that [energy] proceeds from the movement of the moon and sun—that is, from the movement of *lalanā* and *rasanā*. Through the flow of the five mandalas, it is the differentiation of the time-channels (*kālanāḍī*) resulting from the exhalation of breath;
this is the second differentiation, which develops for the sake of producing the embryo through the differentiation of the groups of time-channels during conception.
In that regard, there is one [channel] for each of the groups: the central *avadhūtī* among the six wheels constitutes two groups;
the four channels of the *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus constitute four groups;
the first circle at the navel consists of three groups, namely the nine heart-channels; the second circle at the navel consists of eight [channels]; and the ninth is the place of the moon's birth.
The group of four is sixteen; these are on the forehead, outside the circumference of the lunar mansion (*rāśi*) of the navel-cakra.
The group of five is twenty-five; these are the lunar stations (*candrapada*) on the forehead.

The group of six is thirty-six; in their midst, at the throat, are thirty-two. The birth-places of the four—Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus—are at the navel, outside the circumference of the lunar stations.

The square of seven is forty-nine; in the second circle of the throat, there are forty-eight signs (*rāśipada*). One is the Sun’s place of birth, and in the navel, the square of eight is sixty-four; in the navel-wheel (*nābhicakra*), there are sixty channels carrying the circles, plus four, which are the empty channels (*śūnyanāḍī*).
The square of nine is eighty-one, and the square of ten is one hundred.
This [number] of one hundred and eighty, when doubled due to the external division because of its nature as *rajas*, is to be known as existing in the locations of the three hundred and sixty joints.

Just as it is in the throat, so it is in the secret wheel (*guhyacakra*); just as it is in the forehead, so it is in the *vajra*; just as it is in the *uṣṇīṣa*, so it is in the tip of the *vajramaṇi*—thus there are four. This is the pervasion of the body.
As for "the Vedas, twice, and fire," this refers to twenty-four fortnights and three hundred and sixty days.

Thus, the division of the *nāḍīs* is established according to the distinctions of time, year, solstice, season, ascendant (*lagna*), fortnight, and day; the second rule concerns the divisions of twilight, half-watch (*praharārdha*), and watch (*prahara*) through the distinction of gnosis (*jñāna*).
In this way, by union with that, the Goddess arises as the determined Katikā holding a shell in her hand;
here, the Blessed One [is established] through the purification of the year, and the Goddess through the purification of each day.
The meaning is that the knife is day and the skull-cup is night. || 144 ||

Now the wheels of the *ka*-group are described: the eight wheels, numbering four [in each], by virtue of the objects and qualities, perform protection for the Lord through the divisions of body, speech, and mind; these eight goddesses, Dhūmā and the rest, bestow the fruit of equal bliss.

Thus the Sun is the Lord, whose universal form is embraced by the supreme digit of the Moon; he is the Goddess among the Buddhas and gods, the one to be venerated by Rāhu, the Moon, and the Sun, who are the objects and the subjects. || 145 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with *cakrāṇi*:

here, there are thirty consonants starting with *ka*, and fifteen vowels starting with *a*. These forty-five are the objects (*viṣaya*). Since there are five qualities (*guṇa*) and three [states], there are fifteen [consonants]—namely, those beginning with *ṅa* joined with the five vowels in both short and long forms, as well as those joined with the nasal bindu and the visarga.
Thus, there are thirty ten-spoked wheels, with the letters beginning with *la* and ending with *sa* following one another on the [outer] wheels,

and those beginning with *a* and ending with *ka* on the six-spoked wheels; these wheels, numbering fifty-four, perform the protection of the Lord Kālacakra— the Great Bliss— through the divisions of body, speech, and mind, by virtue of the qualities of the sense objects,
as do the eight goddesses beginning with Dhūmā, who possess the fruit of equal bliss.

Here the *ṅa*-wheel is described: on the exterior of all wheels, within the body, at the tip of the hair (*lomāgra*), there is *ṅa* above; *ṅi* in the east; *ṅa* in the south; *ṅa* in the north; *ṅla* on the western spoke; *la* in the northwest; *ṅa* in the northeast; *ṅa* in the southwest; *ṅī* in the southeast; and *ṅā* in the underworld (*pātāla*).

Thus, in the element of hair (*loma-dhātu*)—namely, in the skin and flesh—is the *ca*-group; in the blood is the *ṭa*-group; in the fluids (*rasa*) is the *pa*-group; in the bones is the *ta*-group; and in the marrow (*majjā*) is the *śa*-group in reverse order.

Thus, there are thirty wheels with ten spokes each, ending with the marrow; then [there are] six-spoked [wheels]: *la* in the eastern spoke, *laḥ* in the south, *laṃ* in the north, *lā* in the west, *lāḥ* below, and *lāṃ* above. In the channels (*nāḍī*) of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, it is thus: *va*, *ra*, *ya*, *ha*.
Likewise, in the *rajas* element: *al* in the east, *alaḥ* in the south, *alaṃ* in the north, *ālu* in the west, *ālaḥ* below, and *ālaṃ* above;

thus, *o*, *ar*, *e*, and *a* constitute the protection in the *śukradhātu*. In the *tamas* element: *ḷ* in the east, *ḷḥ* in the south, *laṃ* in the north, *‘lla* in the west, *lūḥ* below, and *lṛ* above.
Thus, *e*, *vaṃ*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *i*—these are the nine constituents (*dhātavaḥ*) beginning with the body hair and ending with semen;
thereafter is the consciousness constituent (*vijñānadhātu*) in the center of the moon, surrounded by the voids such as smoke and so forth—this is the meaning.

In that context, "smoke and so forth" refers to the void of the five objects and the void of the three qualities (*triguṇa*); thereafter is the vision of the digit and the drop (*kalābindu*), and thereafter is the vision of the image (*bimba*)—this is the meaning.

Thus, the Lord of the Sun is the sixteenth digit of the supreme moon; embraced by her, he is at all times the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*) because he possesses every aspect. Regarding the term "deities" (*deva*), it refers to the *dhātus*; regarding "Buddhas," it refers to the *skandhas*. Of what kind are they? They are the "immortals" (*amara*), being free from birth, old age, and death. And he is the object of worship even for Rāhu, the Moon, and the Sun—the objects of sense and the subjects of sense. Thus, the Blessed One is the Great Immutable Bliss (*mahākṣarasukha*), the Wheel of Time (*kālacakra*). || 145 ||
From here on, the four verses are easy to understand:

those *ḍākinīs* who are the subtle forms of the Lord, whose domain consists of excellent qualities, who are internal yet possess external seals (*mudrās*), who cause supreme terror in the three realms, and who are born from the mind of wrath— [as described] in the chapter, verse...

The Great Chapter on the Disciples through Various Means: The sense-faculties of the Lord, as well as the speech of body, speech, and mind existing within the threefold existence—these are the Vajra-Ḍākas, embraced by the qualities of their respective objects, such as Maṅgalā and the others. (146)

Form, sound, taste, smell, and likewise touch, smoke, dust, and the mind—these six qualities of the objects of sense, which manifest in succession and are likewise embraced by Rāhu, are situated in the form of a wheel within the six-petalled [lotus] as eightfold, due to their slow and various movements such as swift, retrograde, and so forth. || 147 ||

The primary breath has eight divisions, situated within the qualities of the uneven [channels], and is obstructed by the ḍākinīs, such as Dhūmā and the others, on all sides; it wanders through the six realms of existence by virtue of the threefold movement.
In its center is Kālacakra, embraced by the throbbing digit of nectar, who is the pure body (śuddhakāya); he is that very Kālacakra who, having cut off the breath, enters the body of the Victor. 148.

At the conclusion of the cessation of breath, this threefold movement becomes sixfold; when the *bindu* is completely obstructed, the supreme bliss of the All-Pervading Lord (*paramavibhu*) persists for infinite time.

Having abandoned the pleasures of *saṃsāra*, the yogi should cultivate the supreme bliss of the Guru—the conduct in the form of passion (*śṛṅgāra*), which is most terrifying and causes dissatisfaction among the *yoginīs*. (149)

Now, the entry of the planetary movements into the vajra-breath is described: the entire movement of the host of planets is led into the breath of the Lord through the conjunction of time. When the breath has entered zero, zero, zero, zero, two, three, fire (three), and ocean (four), and is impelled into the universal void, then by these years, in the external state of the supreme Lord—which consists of emanation and withdrawal—the movement of the Lord of Jinas situated within the breath must be known according to its own respective measures. || 150 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "of the Lord" (*bhartuḥ*) and so forth:

according to the principle that "as it is externally, so it is internally," the external [measure] consists of *śakti*, breaths (*śvāsa*), and years. When the end of the eon (*yugānta*) occurs by means of those years—specifically 43,200,000 years of breaths belonging to the *śakti* (calculated as zero, zero, zero, zero, two eyes, fire, and oceans)—the same applies to all sentient beings.
At the end of these breaths, one breath is a year; externally, in the world-system, one breath in the middle [channel] is the year in which the Kali age departs and the Kṛta age enters.
Thus, by means of the four ages (*caturyuga*), there is the flow of the ten mandala channels of the *śakti*;
each individual mandala consists of four hundred thousand years plus thirty-two thousand.
When this has been done, there are four mandalas in the left channel—namely space, air, fire, and water.

In that same [cycle], during the *tretā* [age], there is one mandala in the left channel characterized by earth; then follows the entry into the central channel (*madhyamā*) for one hundred and thirty-five thousand [breaths] of the five mandalas, which constitutes the time of the central channel.
Then follows the movement to the right, where the earth mandala and the water mandala occur during the *tretā*.
Then, in the Dvāpara age, there is the mandala of fire and wind; in the Kali age, according to the Vimalaprabhā, there is the mandala of space and gnosis.
Thereafter, the season becomes complete.
Then, at the end of the intermediate breaths, one additional breath brings about universal illumination.
If by that mere breath he remains in the waking state, that breath occurs during the sleeping state of all sentient beings;
thus, with forty-two million three hundred and twenty thousand breaths, one season of the planets occurs within the inner self.
At the end of the mandala of emptiness in the central channel, there is entry into the mandala of gnosis; therefore, it is called "the graspable" (grāhya).
Thus it should be understood that the feet of the Lord of Jinas, according to their respective measures, are situated within the movement of the breath; this is the rule. || 150 ||

From here onwards, the fourteen verses are easy to understand. At the end of the Yuga, when the Sun enters zero (0) by virtue of its own daily motion, the remainder of the Moon’s transit through Revatī on the day marked by zero, sky (0), mother (3), sky (0), ocean (4), ocean (4), and moon (1)—namely, 004401 days—there occurs the entry of Rāhu. O Lord, the entry of Mantrin (Ketu) occurs after 006040 days, calculated from the days traversed by its own motion. || 151 ||

O King, on the day when the sky is [counted as] zero, zero, and eight (008), there is the entry of Maṅgala; the entry of the Sun and others occurs on days numbered by zero, zero, zero, zero, two, three, and four (0000234).

On the day when [the count is] zero, zero, zero, zero, four, ocean (4), and serpent (8) (000048), there is the entry of the Moon; at that time, O King, the destruction of the world occurs according to its own measure. 152.
