This movement of the channels (nāḍī-saṃcāra) arises, and from that, the moon and sun emerge; [the numbers] one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, and eight increased by nine become the secret channels known as the apertures (randhra), or the ten channels (daśamī nāḍī) exist; furthermore, on the upper path, that subtle channel (sūkṣma-nāḍī) becomes divided into groups, and the wheel-channels (cakra-nāḍī) come to possess qualities and objects. || 153 ||

In the crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), the heart region, the head at the lunar station, the throat region at the solar movement, and the navel, there are indeed channel-wheels (cakranāḍyaḥ) numbering four, eight, seven, and sixteen respectively, which are not distinct from the movements of the moon;

these are thirty-two and twice that [sixty-four], and when mixed with all the stations of the sun, they are likewise not distinct as one hundred and eighty-one. These are the joints and channels located in the hands and feet, which are of two kinds. || 154 ||

In the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), at the region of the heart, in the movement of the moon and sun, and in the throat-cakra, there remain eighty-one; those which are the final ten are the manifest planets, gentle and fierce.

Of these, the initial and final portions situated in the feet of the Lord are consumed by the *kāla-nāḍī*; and the Mother of the Three Worlds, the *Ḍākinī* with the adamantine body (*vajradehā*), also consumes [them] until the end of the day. (155)

The Great Chapter on Training through Various Means: That which was initially of the nature of emptiness, having entered into the qualities of the objects, became their very essence; then, having entered again into the elements and aggregates, and likewise equally into the sense-faculties such as the eyes, and having entered into the states of waking, dreaming, and so forth, that Vidyā—the Mother of the Buddhas—struck by the equilibrium of supreme bliss and abiding in the state of the vajra-word, is to be sought by the yogin. 156.

Through the power of the body of the Lord, the excellent form arises; through the power of his speech, yogins possess the divine eye and ear, and that which resides in the hearts of others is known through his mind.

Through the power of the body of wisdom, there is the recollection of previous births within the three realms of existence; through the power of the speech of wisdom, there arises at all times the all-pervading supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) equal to space. || 157 ||

From the nature of wisdom and gnosis (*prajñājñāna*), there arises equal bliss that is forever unstruck (*anāhata*); that which is invisible even to the eye becomes visible through the power of the divine eye, and through the power of the divine ear, the sound of bliss from the heart is heard as uttered by living beings; likewise, O Lord of Men, everything such as touch and so forth comes to be through the yoga of body, speech, and mind. (158)

Those channels within the *apāna* that follow the threefold path, which carry urine, feces, and semen—through them flows the ninefold movement of the *prāṇa*. The final [channel] is the "Buddha's Mouth" (*buddhavaktra*).

It is twofold in the ears, nose, and eyes; it exists in the uvula together with the tongue; and it is at the *bindu* and the aperture of the *uṣṇīṣa*. This tenth [channel] is sealed for the ignorant. (159)

When the *prāṇa* and *apāna* are restrained, the agitated moon enters the solar disc; when the lotus is awakened by the vajra, that [moon] melts again by the radiance of the solar disc. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) and primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) become one with the wind when the moon and sun are restrained. In this way, in this way, and likewise in this way—thus it becomes threefold; there is nothing else whatsoever. (160)
When the orbs of the moon and sun are swallowed within the sky, there is neither day nor night;
that twilight state exists at all times within the center of the body for yogins who have attained the station of nectar.

Just as the moon, waning during its fortnight, enters into a state of equal flavor with the solar orb while remaining in the sky, so too, when the fire of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is extinguished, [the yogin] clearly becomes wrathful within the body at the time of attaining perfection.

When the disks of the moon and sun have vanished, when the vital breath is always restrained in both paths, when the lotus is awakened by the vajra, when the great solar disk has entered the molten moon, when existence and non-existence have become one, when the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) has reached the threefold state of existence within the Stainless Radiance (*vimalaprabhā*), and when that gnosis is fully awakened—at that time, the yogi proceeds to the supreme state, wherein there is no duality whatsoever. (162)

The wrathful Buddhas together with their goddesses, as well as Rasakuliśa, Bhūmigarbha, and the others, indeed become manifest in the sky; at the time of accomplishment, the yogins become joyful of heart.

At dawn, at midnight, and on a moonlit night, there occurs for him the attainment of his desired goal, and by the power of the yoga of time, an excellent rain of jewels or flowers falls upon the surface of the earth.

The body is pure, its atoms destroyed; it arises equal to space, fully endowed with the [thirty-two] marks and so forth. The entire three worlds appear as pure as a dream, free from the afflictions of the ocean of existence.
Speech is uninterrupted on all sides, reaching the hearts of others through various languages. The mind is full of true bliss; embraced by the innate (*sahaja*), it does not waver at any time. (164)

Now the dissolution of the world-system is described: Having drawn the atoms from the earth, one should send them to water, fire, and wind; from the water-element, earth, fire, and wind [to] water; and from fire, the atoms of earth, water, and wind [to] fire. Having drawn [them] from wind into wind, [one sends] earth, water, and fire from wind [to] the void. And those who have gone to another field, struck by the karma-wind due to the power of the threefold existence, are driven by the karma-wind. (165)
"Of the earth," and so forth.
Here, the Dharma teaching of the Blessed Buddha is twofold: one is by way of worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), and the second is from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Regarding these, he states the worldly convention: "The cognition born of the senses, being without [conceptual] form, directly perceives the accumulation of atoms."
"The Vaibhāṣika doctrine is considered the ocean of the Kashmiri school's thought.

Thus, all non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthikas) are proponents of the accumulation of atoms; therefore, the arising and passing away of external Buddha-fields and world-systems should be understood [in that same manner].
And that [wind] exists for as long as there is a multitude of sentient beings, serving as the cause for their enjoyment of the fruits of virtuous and non-virtuous actions; this is the rule.

Therefore, at the time of the dissolution of the world-system, this wind of karma is that by which the world-system was previously produced, and its nature is twofold: one is immovable within space like the stars, such that neither the world-system nor the Buddha-field moves in any direction; the second has a rotating nature, like the wheel of the zodiac in space.
Thus, among those things contained within the world-system (*lokadhātu*), the nature of stationary objects is immobility, while the nature of living beings is mobility;
this is due to the wind of karma (*karmavāta*) according to the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

In this way, there is the dissolution of bodies composed of atoms; therefore, at the time of the dissolution of the world-system and the dissolution of the Buddha-fields—characterized by the cycles of evolution and devolution, and subject to the laws of arising and passing away.

In that regard, at the time of the destruction of the world-system (*lokadhātu*), from the earth—that is, from the earth—the atoms (*paramāṇu*) which exist through the conjunction of the elements such as water are drawn away from that mass of earth-atoms; having separated the earth-atoms individually, he casts them into the element of water, into the mass of water-atoms. Likewise, drawing them from the element of water, he casts them into fire; drawing them from fire, he casts them into wind; drawing them from wind, he causes them to move individually into space. In this manner occurs the withdrawal of the world-system.

Furthermore, there is a certain deity in Pātāla named Kālāgni; that which is Kālāgni burns the world-system and reduces it to ashes. That very [deity] is a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu-saṃcaya*). Because it consumes other phenomena, it is devoid of atoms; thus, it burns nothing and consumes nothing.

When the destruction of stationary things has occurred in this way, those vital breaths (*prāṇa*) characterized by consciousness go to another field, another world-system, which has been produced by the wind of karma for their enjoyment.

In this way, there are infinite winds of karma that produce world-systems and produce buddha-fields; just as the vital breaths of living beings individually produce bodies and, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), produce the growth of stationary things, so it is in conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). 165.

Now, the movement of those joined with the winds of karma is described: having beheld the entire Buddha-field as being without karma, all the Buddhas are in the pure atoms; the Bodhisattvas are enveloped by the atoms of both [families] in the equality of the two; the Vajra-sons are each enveloped by the atoms of the two families according to the power of their respective families; and [the elements] from earth up to space, belonging to all the families, have entered the immovable [atoms] and so forth. || 166 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "the Buddha-field," it was stated here in the *Bhadracaryā* recitation by the Blessed One as follows: "Upon a single atom, there sit Buddhas and sons of the Buddhas, equal in number to all atoms" (*Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra*). According to this statement, the conventional dwelling of the Buddhas is not devoid of a support; that is, it is not without a basis. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no dwelling whatsoever, because of their nature of being free from obscurations (*nirāvaraṇadharma*).
It is stated in the *Dharmodgata-parivarta* of the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "The going or coming of the Buddhas has not occurred anywhere, nor will it occur, nor does it exist.

Therefore, within that single-flavored supreme pure atom—the perfected elixir (*siddharasa*) which is the basis that penetrates all elements—all Buddhas are collectively characterized by emptiness and are free from obscuration.

Thus, the entire Buddha-field is without karma, free from the winds of karma; having liberated the inhabitants of the three worlds by means of the gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*), all those Buddhas dwell together within the pure atom (*śuddhāṇu*). "In the pure atom of the equal flavor of both" means that having transformed the ordinary essence into the perfected essence, the transmigrating bodhicitta has been rendered immutable. They are "enveloped by the Bodhisattvas," meaning they are the Vajra-sons endowed with only slight residual obscurations through the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhicitta*).
"Each and every atom" means they abide in the nature of both wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*); that is to say, they abide in the [ten] stages beginning with *Acalā*.

Thus, the atoms of the stages and so forth—beginning with those free from passion (*rāga*)—are the entirety [of reality] directly realized; the meaning is that these infinite [realities] have entered into the stage of *Acalā* and the others.
Here, by the word "atom" (*aṇu*), the stages beginning with *Acalā* are meant, not [physical] atoms (*paramāṇu*).
By the term "pure atom" (śuddhāṇu), the twelve stages that serve as the foundation are meant; the meaning is: due to the destruction of all obscurations. || 166 ||
Vajrasattva dwells together with them in the sky for as long as the duration of the world lasts, maintaining the subtle atom whose nature consists of earth, fire, water, wind, and space.

Churning all the individual atoms within the *Jñānapaṭala* of the *Vimalaprabhā*, until they attain oneness, there occurs again the mutual conjunction of these [elements], wherein the primary state becomes a minor state. (167)
"With them, Vajrasattva dwells in the sky until the time of dissolution.

Here, "until" means as long as the accumulations of merit and wisdom have not been achieved by sentient beings, so long the appearance of a Buddha is not seen by them; therefore, he dwells in the sky, meaning he has entered the *dharmakāya*.
Now, the arising of the world-system is described: "until the time of dissolution."
"Saṃvarta is declared to be dissolution (*bhaṅga*).

This term does not exist here [in that sense], because *varta* refers to the proceeding of dharma and adharma by way of their purified forms; for that reason, the wind of karma (*karmavāta*) becomes threefold: the sustaining (*sandhāraṇa*), the churning (*manthāna*), and the structural (*saṃsthāna*).

Their "supporter" (saṃdhāraṇa) sustains the aggregate of atoms beginning with earth; just as rain and wind sustain the aggregate of water atoms, so the "churner" (manthāna) churns the aggregate of atoms from earth up to the essence (rasa), until the elements attain solidity like salt.
In this way, their mutual conjunction occurs; when one is primary, the others are secondary.
Therefore, among solid substances (*kaṭhinadharma*), the earth atom (*bhūmiparamāṇu*) is primary, while the others are merely minor;
likewise, in water there is water, in fire there is fire, in that which is characterized by motion there is air, and in taste everything is the same, being devoid of its own specific qualities. 167.

The great all-encompassing wind arranges the entire buddha-field; furthermore, within each individual world-system there is a great Cakravāla mountain range on all sides, and in its center arises a world-system whose nature is that of the great land of karma. The remaining [worlds] are of the nature of enjoyment, providing the pleasures of the sensory objects and filled with every kind of jewel. || 168 ||
Then he constructs the entire Buddha-field by means of the "great wind of all forms," which refers to the ten winds beginning with prāṇa and apāna;
just as there are causes for the decay and growth of those things dependent upon the external world, so too are there [causes] for the prāṇas and other winds within the body.
Furthermore, regarding the destruction of each individual world and the surrounding Great Cakravāla:

just as there is hair and skin on each individual body of sentient beings, so too within that Buddha-field there exists one world-system characterized by the nature of karma, just as the single avadhūtī is among all the channels,
while the remaining world-systems are like the other channels, characterized by the nature of enjoyment.

Those world-systems, which produce sensory pleasure, are filled with all kinds of jewels like the channels of the body; just as the channels are filled with blood, so too does the Buddha-field, together with the world-system, come into being, just as the arising of the body is accompanied by seventy-two thousand channels. || 168 ||

Now, the characteristics of Mount Meru and the other mountains within the world-system are described: In the east, the lord of all mountains is pure sapphire; in the south, it is ruby; in the west, it is yellow karketana; and in the north, it is moonstone, white as the moon.
In the center, it is dark blue; and within that is the great maṇḍala. At its core, first is the nature of mind, doubled [in size], and then from the center [proceeds] the nature of speech. (169)

"East," and so forth: here, "east" refers to that which faces Pūrvavideha, being pure sapphire (*śuddhendranīla*); because its nature consists of the wind element (*vāyudharma*), it is the lord of all mountains—this is the meaning.
[The letters] *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* are the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*).
In the east and the south is the ruby (*padmarāga*); because its nature is the Dharma, it is the syllable *ra*, the great instruction on the various means for training disciples.
In the west is Karketanapīta, because its nature consists of the syllable *la*;
and in the north is Candrakānta, white as the moon, because its nature consists of the syllable *va*.
In this way, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* are to be understood in the four continents.

In the center it is dark blue, because its nature consists of the *dharmas* of the syllable *ha* representing emptiness; the great maṇḍala placed within that is its "womb" (*garbha*), as was previously stated at the beginning.
First is the mind-maṇḍala, which has the nature of mind;
in the middle, twice that size, is the speech and body maṇḍala. || 169 ||

Twice that [measurement] multiplied by ten, a thousand yojanas, is outside that in the form of a wheel; then, by the seasons, it is the nature of the world-system (*lokadhātu*) consisting of six wheels and six families, situated within the wind-circle (*anilavalaya*). The mandala has four hundred thousand [yojanas], and the peak has eight pillars; it is surrounded by sixteen [spokes] in the form of a womb (*yonirūpa*). || 170 ||

At the position of the *kaṇikā* of Mount Meru is the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*); at the position of the heart is the mandala of mind (*cittamaṇḍala*); at the position of the throat is the mandala of speech (*vāṅmaṇḍala*); and on the forehead is the mandala of body (*kāyamaṇḍala*). Outside of that, all the mandalas abide as the nature of the world-system (*lokadhātu*), measuring five hundred thousand *yojanas*. Thus, fifty thousand *yojanas* above Mount Meru is the mandala of body, speech, and mind.
In the heart is the Kālacakra and the characteristics of the mudrās;

outside of that, through the six seasons— that is, by means of the purification of the six seasons— is the nature of the world-realm (*lokadhātu*), which has the nature of the six seasons, consisting of fifty thousand [spokes] in the form of the six wheels.

"By the six wheels and the six families," as previously stated by people numbering two hundred thousand [verses], "situated within the circle of wind" means the mandala reaching to the end of the wind-mandala;

in the center, the foundation is pure with sixteen spokes and pillars. By those pillars, the wheel of knowledge (*jñānacakra*) is surrounded in the center; having the form of a womb (*yoni*), it generates all accomplishments—thus is the formation of Meru. || 170 ||

From the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) to the middle of the *ūrṇā* [hair-tuft] of the Lord of Jinas is one and a half solar digits (*sārdhasūryāṅgula*). From there, the lotus of the throat is likewise; from that, the heart; and from there, the lotuses of the navel and the secret place are thus.

The feet, the lower part, the knees, thighs, and buttocks are measured by the mantras, the principles (*tattva*), the Vedas, and half-vedas, respectively, with one and a half solar digits; the arms, forearms, and hands are measured by zero, eyes, kings, and suns [i.e., 0, 2, 16, and 12 digits]. (171)

One hundred and twenty-one human years constitute one unit of measurement for mortals; by nine such units, the height from the feet to the crown of the head of the Lord of Jinas is established. From the feet up to the end of the forehead is four and a half *vedas* (four and a quarter *yugas*) plus one *veda*; from the forehead down to the end of the nose is one *veda* plus a *veda*; from the nose down to the throat is another *veda*; and from the center of the lotus at the base of the throat downward is likewise measured. || 172 ||

Therefore, O Lord of Men, it becomes the heart, the navel, and the secret place, together with the suns [the cakras], in sequence; the secret lotus is at the root of the navel, and the vajra of the Sage is above that. The *ūrṇā* is indeed at the *uṣṇīṣa*.

That which generates the imperishable bliss within the middle of the secret lotus, which is the abiding of the seminal drop (*śukrabindu*), is this glorious Vajra-ground in the wheels of body, speech, and mind, by virtue of the two families.
Regarding "from the uṣṇīṣa" and so forth:

here, from the uṣṇīṣa of the Blessed Lord, the Master of Jinas, upwards to the middle of the ūrṇā—that is, the middle of the eyebrows—it measures one and a half suns (sūrya), which is a measurement of twelve and a half finger-breadths (aṅgula).
From that point, the throat-lotus likewise measures twelve and a half finger-breadths.
The *hṛvaya* (heart) is likewise twelve and a half finger-breadths from there;

thus, from the navel to the secret place (*guhya*), it is likewise twelve and a half finger-breadths. Therefore, the navel-lotus is twelve and a half finger-breadths, and similarly, the secret-lotus is twelve and a half finger-breadths.
Then, from the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) down to the secret lotus, the body measures sixty-two and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The feet below [the knees] are fourteen finger-breadths by means of the mantras;
the knees are twenty-five, as they are the *tattvas*; and the thighs are likewise.
The height of the feet is four and a half finger-breadths according to the Vedas;
likewise, the knee-joint and the buttocks are each four finger-breadths;
thus, from the buttocks down to the end of the feet, the measurement is sixty-two and a half finger-breadths.
Likewise, the Buddha-body consists of one hundred and twenty-five [units],
with the thighs measuring twelve and a half units;
the arms, forearms, and hands measure twenty, twenty, and twelve units respectively, ending at the middle finger.

With one [finger], the joint of the forearm (karopabāhu) and the joint of the upper arm (bāhūpabāhu) likewise measure sixty-two and a half finger-breadths; as it is on the left, so it is on the right,
and everywhere the measurement of the body is one hundred and twenty-five [finger-breadths], forming a square.

That same [measurement] for beings is four cubits for men, which is ninety-six finger-breadths; from top to bottom it is eighty-four. Thus it is established by the Vedas that men are not endowed with the [major] marks. By four [parts] is the measurement of the *uṣṇīṣa*;
the height of the head is four and a half; the forehead is four; by the word "and" (*ca*), the nose is four; from the base of the nose down to the chin is four and a half; the neck is four.

Therefore, O Lord of Men, the secret place (guhya) is located at the navel; by means of the six suns [the channels], the secret lotus is in the root of the navel, while the vajra of the Sage is above that, at the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa).
The ūrṇā [hair-tuft] is in the middle of the secret lotus; it is the producer of the immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*), wherein the semen-drop (*śukabindu*) resides.

This is the glorious *Śrī-vajrabhūmi*: according to the sequence of the two lineages (*ubhayakula*), the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*) is the forehead and the navel; the speech-wheel (*vākcakra*) is the throat and the heart; and the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*) is the secret place and the crown of the head. (171–173)

Now the purification of the body-maṇḍala is described: the practitioner [should know] twenty-five [units], and twice that for the wheels of mind, speech, and body; half of the mind [wheel], six and a half [units], and the innate [wheel] located at the heart is one finger-breadth; the wheel of gnosis [is] from three [units]; one should make the doors from the eighth part of the maṇḍalas, consisting of a jeweled arrangement; through the coming and going, the wheels of body, speech, and mind below and above should also be double [that]. || 174 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "sārdhārka" (and a half sun):

here, within this body, the heart is located between the secret place and the *ūrṇā* (the hair-treasure between the eyebrows); that itself is the mind wheel (*cittacakra*). From the middle of the navel to the throat is twelve and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). From the boundary of the navel to the throat is twenty-five finger-breadths; this is the speech wheel (*vākcakra*). Likewise, from the secret lotus to the end of the *ūrṇā* is fifty finger-breadths; this is the body wheel (*kāyacakra*) on the vajra-ground.
"Half of the mind" means that the wisdom wheel (*jñānacakra*), which is contained within the mind wheel, measuring six and a quarter finger-breadths, is to be purified.
The ablative "from three" (*tribhyaḥ*) is used in the sense of the locative;

one should construct doors in the three circles. The doors of the mind (*cittadvārāṇi*) are the four states beginning with waking; the doors of speech (*vāgdvārāṇi*) are the openings of the mouth, anus, and nostrils; and the doors of the body (*kāyadvārāṇi*) are the openings of the eyes and ears—thus there are twelve doors.
The remainder is as previously described.

Thus, through the distinction between the going and coming of the *bodhicitta*, the wheel of body, speech, and mind becomes double in both the downward and upward directions; that is to say, it measures one hundred finger-breadths. || 174 ||

[Regarding] the Vajra [section], Chapter [XV], Verse [175]: Even though [the Buddha] stands upon Mount Meru, he is half a finger-breadth; for the Lord of Jinas, there are exactly one thousand yojanas. Thus, the measure of his body is half the extent of the divine mountain.

Above that, and below that, there is indeed a peak in the form of a vajra, consisting of three parts. Likewise, below are earth, water, fire, and wind, along with the vajra-garland together with its flames.
Thus, even in the mandala situated on Meru, one *yava* and a half-finger-breadth (*ardhāṅgula*) corresponds to exactly one thousand *yojanas* in the mortal world;
likewise, up to the rim of the wind-circle, it amounts to four hundred thousand *yojanas* within four cubits (*hasta*).
Thus, the measurement of the body is such that the extent of the divine mountain (Meru) is equal to a single *adhamātra* as previously stated.

Above that and below that, there is indeed a peak shaped like a thunderbolt consisting of three parts; outside of Meru are the circle of earth, the circle of water, the circle of fire, and the circle of air; in the lower part, there is a garland of blazing vajras on the exterior of the vajra-circle.

The heart-cakra of the Lord of Jinas consists of one and a half suns [digits] at the center of the lotuses of the navel and throat; the speech-cakra and body-cakra extend upward from the tip of the jewel of the vajra to the limit of the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*).

O King, the *niryūha* (architrave) becomes the glorious cheek, and above the forehead it extends to the limit of the *uṣṇīṣa*. By the practitioners, the circle of earth, water, fire, and wind, together with its radiance, becomes the garland of vajras. (176)
The single verse beginning with "sārdham" (and so forth) [or "hṛccakram" and so forth] is easily understood. || 176 ||

The Buddha-body exists above and below; this wheel of body, speech, and mind is equal in its horizontal dimensions. By the power of the movement of the winds, the wheel becomes eight-spoked through three [units] and six [units] respectively, measured by the six and a half finger-breadths of the Lord of Jinas.
One should fashion the glorious cremation ground as circular, with eight gates and the nails of one’s own palms. 177.
The Buddha-body is both vertical and horizontal, equal and square; the wheel of body, speech, and mind is square.

Horizontally, by virtue of the movement of the winds on all sides, and internally by virtue of the movement of the wind-circle, the movement of the winds—such as the *samāna* and others—extends from the tip of the fingernails of the left hand to the tip of the fingernails of the right hand.
Therefore, it is a fixed rule that the mandala of the body is four cubits in extent and square.

Or else, the enclosure (*saṃvara*) may consist of three wheels, or the enclosure-maṇḍala may consist of six wheels; it is circular with eight gates, each wheel having six spokes, six feet, and six finger-breadths. The previously mentioned circular [mandala] of the Lord of Jinas also has eight gates. One should fashion the glorious cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*) using the nails of one's own palms. In that case, the rule is that within the horizontal maṇḍala, there are again eight gates starting from the mouth above and below, which are the cremation grounds. || 177 ||

Now the maṇḍala of the purity of the body of the Bhagavatī is described: "From the upper and lower [faces] and from the secret place, the maṇḍala of the Bhagavatī arises with the measure of two oceans; from the center of the half-lotus within, there is also a row of three, and then the six wheels.

From the upper and lower [faces] and from the secret place, the maṇḍala of the Bhagavatī arises with the measure of two oceans, meaning it consists of forty-two finger-breadths (aṅgulas). Having excluded the two—the *ūrṇā* and the secret lotus—from among those forty-two finger-breadths, there is the element of passion (*rajo-dhātu*).
Therefore...
The maṇḍala of the Bhagavatī consists of half a lotus with six wheels in equal proportions;
here, the door is dissimilar to the wheel, being one-fifth of the wheel. Why is that which [is prescribed] in the *Catuṣpīṭha* and other texts one-fifth of the wheel?
"In this context, at the time of birth, the mother's womb measures twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); the eighth division out of ninety-six divisions is [the opening].

Thus, there are four doors for women in the four directions. The Blessed One has shown to children the expansion of the womb as a mandala-palace, the fetal body as a host of deities, and the manifestation of birth in the form of deities;
however, according to the principle that "the door is one-fifth [of the height] by the division from the secret place to the crown," [the measurement is determined]."
Thus, the body of sentient beings has the form of the characteristics of a mandala; however, a stūpa is neither wisdom nor method, for it is fixed as being neuter. || 178 ||

Externally, below Mount Meru in the abode of the earth's surface, the eight siddhis are situated: in the east, the sword, mercury, the nectar-fruit pill, and collyrium and gorocana; in the south, the auspicious sandals and the inexhaustible vessel; in the southeast corner of the entire circle of treasures, the sacrificial thread; and in the center, the Vedic chant of the teacher of the gods. || 179 ||

Externally, below Mount Meru, in the abode of the earth’s surface, the eight siddhis are situated: the sword in the east, the mercury (rasendra) in the northeast, the fruit of immortality in the north, the pill (gulikā) in the northwest, the ointment in the west, the yellow pigment (rocanā) in the southwest, the sandals in the south, and the inexhaustible treasure in the southeast;

in the center of the mandala is the sacred thread. This is the rule: the sound of the Veda is that very [sound] of Kālacakra, the teacher of gods and men—the unstruck resonance (*anāhatadhvani*) which awakens the gods and others. || 179 ||
Now the characteristics of the purity of the vajras are stated:

on the jewel [crown], the uṣṇīṣa, the forehead, the throat, the heart, and reaching the navel and the secret place, the vajras are respectively one, two, four, six, eight, nine, and twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length;

their middle, upper, and lower thirds are respectively closed, gaping, and [the latter] for peaceful and wrathful rites. The bell is likewise in three parts, with its upper part equal to the vajra, having a cow’s mouth and the form of a lotus. || 180 ||

"Jewel," and so forth: here, through the purification of the *vajramaṇi*, the *vajra* is one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*); through the purification of the *uṣṇīṣa*-wheel, it is two finger-breadths; through the purification of the forehead, four finger-breadths; through the purification of the throat, five finger-breadths; through the purification of the heart, eight finger-breadths; through the purification of the navel, nine finger-breadths; and through the purification of the secret place, twelve finger-breadths.

For the *kṛtsnas* of air, fire, water, and earth, and for the gods and asuras of the desire realm, respectively, the yogi should fashion vajra ornaments: one finger-breadth for the ear-rings, two fingers for the thumb-vajra, four fingers on the forehead for the sake of the vajra-garland, five fingers on the neck, eight fingers on the shoulder for the sake of the vajra-garland, nine fingers for the heart-protruding vajra, and twelve fingers for the *ullāla*-vajra. These are to be made by the yogi for the purpose of vajra-adornment.

Their characteristics are as follows: [the bell] is divided into three parts—upper, middle, and lower. That same [bell] is called *ullālava-jra* when it is closed (*mukulita*) for peaceful rites; it is called *vikarāla* when it is opened like a blooming flower (*vikasita-śuka*) for wrathful rites. The bell is likewise divided into three parts, with the cloth and the face being equal in the middle and upper sections.
For peaceful rites, it should have a cow-face (*gomukha*).
With faces blooming like lotuses, they are together with the fierce and formidable vajra in the wrathful [mudrā]. || 180 ||

The width [of the lotus] is three parts; the central boss (*varaṭaka*) together with its face is one-third of that; the petal is one-third of that, and the filament (*śūka*) is equal in width. In each cardinal and intermediate direction, the circular base of the filaments is one-fourth [of the total].

Outside, the filament is three parts; below and above, there is a connection shaped like the thorn of a jujube fruit (*badarī*). The faces of the bells (*ghaṇṭāvaktra*) are likewise, as are the petals, the vajra, the cow-mouth (*gomukha*), and so forth. || 181 ||

Here, the width of the prongs (*śūka*) of the vajra is one-third of the width of the vajra; in the center of the vajra is the four-faced hub (*varaṭaka*), which is one-third of that third part. Likewise, above and below the hub are eight petals according to the measurement of the hub. The prong is equal in width to the vajra, being one-third [of it].
In the middle of the *viśi*, in the four cardinal directions or the intermediate directions, the circle of the prongs is one-fourth of the third part of the vajra.

Externally, three parts of the parrots [on the bell] are below and two parts are above; at the top, like the thorns of a jujube tree, there is a connection through the middle with the mixed [colors]. Thus, while it is closed in the *vikarāla* (scattered) state, an opening must be made at the top. Regarding the faces on the bell, it is the same: just as there are four faces on the cloth for the purification of body, speech, mind, and gnosis-bindu through abiding in loving-kindness and so forth, likewise, by means of the quality of passion (*rajas*) in Prajñā and the qualities of emptiness and so forth, the four faces must be made for the purification of the four doors of liberation. This is one logical conclusion.
"The second day, however, is the Lord Vajrī"—thus, *kāli* is the consonantal property (*vyañjanadharma*) and is not to be pronounced because of the absence of vowels;
therefore, there is an absence of a face on the central hub of the vajra.

"Night is proclaimed as Prajñā"—thus, *āli* is the vowel property (*svaradharma*); because its nature is that of pronunciation, the Blessed Lady has one face. Thus, the [single-faced] nature of the vajra-bell is established. || 181 ||

Now the characteristics of the *caitya* are described: The measurement of the *caitya* above the supreme Lord of Jinas is by means of the parts ending with the hair-tuft (*ūrṇā*) of the secret lotus; the height of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is half of that. It is as level as the earth, and its divisions in the cardinal directions are made by three parts each.

The protrusion at the end is one and a half parts; the lotus is a circle reaching to the heart according to the measurement of the pedestal. From the edge of the lotus, it is reduced by one part and is level with the chest; the neck is one part of the division of the directions. (182)

Regarding the passage beginning with "guhya" and so forth: "by means of the secret, the navel, and the end of the spine" refers to the measurement of the caitya from top to bottom as fifty finger-breadths (aṅgulas). "The height of the pedestal (pīṭha) is half of that" means it is twenty-five [finger-breadths]; like the earth, it is square and perfectly level in its horizontal division.

"Three parts plus a third part" means eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas) together with a third of a finger-breadth; the projection of the lotus upon its pedestal is one and a half finger-breadths, and by that same measurement, there is also the projection of the circle located at the heart.

Thus, the heart-region becomes a circle according to the measurement of the pedestal (pīṭha), and the lotus is a circle three parts less than the end of the lotus; the chest is a circle equal to that [lotus] minus one and a half finger-breadths (aṅgula).
Its neck is made with its own twelfth part, measuring eight finger-breadths across (horizontally) and three parts thereof, and four finger-breadths in height (vertically). || 182 ||

The face [of the lotus] is made with half-portions of the pedestal (pīṭha), as level as the earth; from one-third of that, the secret lotus (guhyābja) measures four parts, and above it, the measurement of the pedestal should also be perfectly level with four and a half suns (twelve and a half parts).

From the pedestal to the boundary of the lotus and so forth, then up to the heart-reaching circle, then from there to the base of the neck, and finally from there to the edge of the face—thus, the ocean (four parts) is divided into three sections by four and three-and-a-half [parts].

The mouth [of the pedestal] is by half the measure of the pedestal, that is, by twelve and a half [units] according to the horizontal division; it is square, just like the neck, and as level as the earth. Thus, one-third of that mouth/neck consists of four parts of the directions; there is a protrusion of half a finger for the neck, and a protrusion of three-quarters of a finger for the parts of the directions belonging to the mouth. From the secret lotus, upwards by twelve and a half fingers—that is, by twelve and a half units—the measurement of the pedestal is also to be square and perfectly level from the base of the pedestal.
From the *pīṭha* (the seat) and the lotus, up to the "moon" (*soma*)—that is, as far as the station of the *avadhūtī* at the navel-lotus—it measures twelve and a half *mānas*.

From there, up to the end of the circle located at the heart, it is another twelve and a half *mānas*. From there, to the root of the throat, it is twelve and a half *mānas*. From that station of the *saṃbhoga-cakra*, up to the mouth, and thus up to the station of the row of umbrellas (*chatrāvalī*), the throat is four finger-widths (*aṅgulas*). From the chin to the station of the mouth, it is four and a half *aṅgulas*. Likewise, the station of the beautiful nose is four *aṅgulas*. Thus, at the station of the head, there is the row of umbrellas.
In this manner, the ocean also [extends] for three and a half yugas from the neck to the mouth, which constitutes the third region (Trikhaṇḍa). || 183 ||

From the pedestal and the Vedas [the height] to the heart is a lotus; the measurement to the neck is likewise, and above that, the measurement for the eight faces with a half-unit added becomes the size. Above that is the series of parasols, O Lord of Men, from the limit of the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft on the forehead, then to the head, and finally to the *uṣṇīṣa*. This indeed is the world-system, the body of all the Victors, having the nature of the wheel and the shrine. || 184 ||
"From the pedestal" means above the pedestal;

"the lotus-seat's height is by the Vedas" means the lotus is four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula). Likewise, the circle reaching to the heart is four finger-breadths. The measurement of the neck is likewise [four]; the measurement of the face is with four and a half [finger-breadths], meaning from the chin to the end of the mouth is four and a half, and to the end of the nose is four. Thence is the place of the *ūrṇā* between the eyebrows;
above that, starting from the forehead, there is the row of parasols (*chatramālā*), O King!

From the *ūrṇā* (the hair-tuft between the eyebrows) to the edge of the *chatrāvalī* (the series of parasols), on the forehead and the crown of the head, there is a section [measuring] twelve and a half finger-widths (*aṅgula*); this is the fixed rule. Thus, the world-system of Sumeru is the entire body of the Jina; Mount Meru is the nature of the stūpa, the Buddha-image is the nature of form (*rūpa*), and the emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) consists of the thirty-two marks of a great man.

In this regard, the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) are as follows: the Tathāgata has palms and soles marked with wheels; his soles are well-placed with wheels having a thousand spokes, complete with hubs; he touches the earth with the entire surface of his soles, which rise when the sole is raised and sink when it is lowered; his palms and soles are webbed, like those of a royal swan, with hands and feet joined by a network; they are exceedingly soft, like those of a newborn infant; and he has seven protuberances (*utsada*), namely, on the two feet, the two hands, the two shoulders, and the neck.
The fingers and toes of the hands and feet are long, rounded, and extended, with well-formed joints beginning from the thumbs and big toes.

His hands and feet are long; his shanks are broad and straight; his knees, fingers, and toes are prominent; the hairs on his body point upward and curl to the right; his calves are like those of an antelope; his private organ is concealed in a sheath, like that of an elephant whose privities are covered by a sheath; his complexion is smooth and lustrous like gold; his skin is golden-hued; at each pore there is a single hair that does not collect dust or dirt; between his eyebrows, above the *ūrṇā*, there is a circle consisting of thirty-two extremely fine white hairs, as white as cotton fibers and curled to the right.

The upper half of his body is like that of a lion; he has broad shoulders and massive, well-rounded neck. In his major and minor limbs, there are the "summits of taste" (*rasarasāgra*); these are the vessels (*śirā*) through which the essence of flavors flows, and because they are untainted by wind, bile, or phlegm, the Great Man is "well-proportioned like a banyan tree" (*nyagrodhaparimaṇḍala*). His head is crowned with the *uṣṇīṣa* curl, which is elevated all around like a parasol. With the tip of his tongue, he touches the hairline at the base of his ears, and he can cover his forehead with his tongue as far as the hairline.
He possesses the voice of Brahmā; it is heard by an infinite assembly both externally and internally, even by all sentient beings.
His jaw is like that of a lion; his teeth are forty in number, white, even, and free from all defects.
His eyes are "deep-blue" (*abhinīla*): that which is blue in the eyes is deep-blue, that which is red is deep-red, and that which is white is deep-white.
The eyelashes are like those of a bull; the eyes have their bases above and below.
The body possesses all colors because it perceives the various colors of sentient beings.

Thus, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, beginning from the soles of the feet up to the *uṣṇīṣa*, are described in the *Dharmasaṃgraha* (*Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya*, p. 334); therefore, they are not indicated here by this commentary.
Thus is the arising of the world-system;
thus is it equal to the emanation-body of a Buddha;
thus is the mandala of dust for the sake of sentient beings attaining merit.
Just as Mount Meru is, so too is the caitya;
it has been manifested in the mortal world for the purpose of circumambulating the caitya clockwise like the sun and other celestial bodies, and for the purpose of venerating it.
Just as the Buddha is, so should an image of the Buddha be made, for the purpose of performing worship and other such rites.
Thus, relative truth has been shown here for the sake of attaining merit;
the eighty secondary characteristics (*vyañjana*) have not been stated here for fear of excessive wordiness, as they are stated everywhere else.

Now, the nature of the various elements within the world-system is described: earth would be the element of gold, water also silver, fire the element of copper, wind iron, space tin, and this serpent [the wind] is the nature of the mixed elements.
Earth is yellow gemstone, and water is white; fire is red gemstone, and wind is black; likewise, that which arises from mixed minerals is green.
(185) Regarding the verse beginning with "earth" (*pṛthvī*):

here, earth is the gold mineral; thus gold has the nature of earth and is yellow. Silver has the nature of water and is white. Copper has the nature of fire and is red. Iron has the nature of wind and is black. Tin and lead are mixed.
Mercury and iron have the characteristic of space and the characteristic of the element of gnosis;
thus [there are] the six metals, such as gold and so forth, as well as the precious jewels.

Yellow gem is of the nature of earth; white, of the nature of water; red, of the nature of fire; black, of the nature of air; dark (śyāma), of the nature of space; and blue, of the nature of the gnosis-element (jñānadhātu), because it arises from that [element].

||185 || The earth produces saline [taste], water produces sweet, fire produces pungent, wind produces bitter, and the mixed [elements] produce sour, astringent, and other tastes; furthermore, these originate from the soil and stones of the field.
There are six kinds of medicinal herbs possessing supreme essences, other minerals, and various types of excellent gems; likewise, the waters on earth are perfectly capable of removing all diseases.

Thus, there are six tastes: the saline taste has the nature of earth, the sweet has the nature of water, the pungent has the nature of fire, the bitter has the nature of air, the astringent has the nature of ether, and the sour has the nature of consciousness.
In this way, the source of fields and stones is earth and the other elements.
Thus, there are six categories: medicinal herbs, tastes, supreme tastes (which are the perfected elixirs),
metals, other [substances], and the lords of gems— these are the six.

Thus, there are various tactile sensations on the earth that remove all diseases; likewise, waters such as mountain-streams constitute six types [of remedies]. This is correct. Now, the qualities of the jewel-gems are described: the earth removes colic and also removes poison; the water-element [removes] fire; the wind [removes] paralysis; and space also removes the onset of malignant glances. Knowledge removes everything. Likewise, the jewel situated upon the bodies of kings—indeed, all [these things] possess an inconceivable nature, such as water, taste, gems, touch, mantras, and medicinal herbs. (187)

In this world, a gem or jewel born of the earth-nature (*pṛthvījāti*) becomes a remover of pain from spears; one born of the water-nature (*toyajāti*) becomes a remover of poison and a remover of possession by spirits (*bhūtāveśa*); one born of the fire-nature (*agnijāti*) becomes a remover of paralysis (*stambhana*); one born of the wind-nature (*vāyujāti*) becomes a remover of minor rains and falling [debris]; and one born of the void-nature (*śūnyajāti*) becomes a remover of all defects.
Just as a jewel or gem is so, even an ordinary stone born upon the heads of frogs and the like is a remover of defects when placed upon the limbs of kings.
Thus have been described all those things of inconceivable nature which possess the qualities of earth and the other elements.
Thus is the perfection of the Buddha-field.

|| 187 || The Blessed One, whose nature is the wheel of gnosis, enters the Buddha-field from all sides; furthermore, the activity of sentient beings occurs by the power of the fruit through the conjunction of all causal conditions.

By means of those months, there is the formation of the twelvefold [year] according to the movement of its own days; herein is the formation of Meru, with a stūpa-like form and a vertical peak, a mandala consisting of the vajra of the King (Kālacakra) within its womb. || 188 ||

The Great Chapter on Disciples to be Tamed by Various Means: Externally, there are the wheels of luminaries; upon the surface of the earth are humans in the land of karma; in the lands of enjoyment consisting of the six continents are others, such as the gods, who subsist on the essence of the nectar of fruits.

Mounted upon the eight peaks are the Lord of Gods (Indra), Fire (Agni), Kāla, the Daitya, the Ocean, Wind (Vāyu), Yakṣa, and Rudra, along with their retinues; and above them is Viṣṇu himself, whose face is the ocean.
The two verses following this one are easy to understand. (188–189)

Now, the nature of the zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn is described: Consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the element of space (*śūnyadhātu*) are Capricorn (*makara*); here, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra*) and wind (*vāyu*) are Aquarius (*kumbha*). Mind (*manas*) is Aries (*meṣa*), and the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra*) is Taurus (*vṛṣa*); the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā*) and fire (*agni*) arise as Gemini (*mithuna*). Water (*toya*), form (*rūpa*), earth (*kṣiti*), and the syllable (*akṣara*) are the innate (*sahajā*) signs beginning with Cancer (*karkaṭa*). Their symbols are the vajra and so forth; *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *pa*, *ta*, and *śa* are their presiding deities, both long and short. (190) "Consciousness," and so forth.

Here, Capricorn (makara) has the nature of the aggregate of consciousness and the element of space; Aquarius (kumbha) has the nature of the aggregate of formations and the element of wind; Pisces (mīna) has the nature of the aggregate of sensation and the element of fire; Aries (meṣa) has the nature of the aggregate of perception and the element of water; Taurus (vṛṣa) has the nature of the aggregate of form and the element of earth; Gemini (mithuna) has the nature of the aggregate of cognition and the element of cognition. Thus, Cancer and the other signs have natures beginning with and ending with the "innate" (sahaja). In reverse order, the symbols of these [signs] beginning with Capricorn are the vajra, sword, jewel, lotus, wheel, and flaying knife; for Cancer and the others, they follow the order of emanation and are thus the reverse of those.

The *kavarga* and so forth—*ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *pa*, *ta*, and *śa*—belong to Capricorn (*makara*) and the other signs; *ka*, *na*, *ma*, *ṇa*, *tra*, *ṅa*, and so on, belong to Cancer (*karkaṭa*) and the others, as stated in the chapter on the World-Sphere (*lokadhātu*). Thus, the consonants beginning with *ka* are one hundred and eighty in number, distinguished by the long vowels and divided by the short vowels, and likewise [distinguished] by the short vowels. || 190 ||

Now, the birth signs of the planets are stated: In Aries, Gemini, and Cancer are the Moon, Venus, and the Sun; in Leo, Virgo, and Libra are Mars, Jupiter, and Rāhu; in Scorpio, Sagittarius, and the beginning and end of Capricorn are Mercury, Saturn, and Ketu.
Thus, O King, from the elements of earth and so forth, there is a universal mutual conjunction; this world, filled with all jewels, becomes the form of the karma of sentient beings.
(191) "In Aries," and so forth.

Here, according to their respective order: in Aries and Gemini, the Moon and Venus; in Cancer, the Sun; in Leo, Mars; in Virgo, Jupiter; in Libra, Rāhu; in Scorpio, Mercury; in Sagittarius, Saturn at its beginning and Ketu at its end;
likewise, Agastya in Aquarius; and Dhruva in Taurus.

Thus, according to the previously stated sequence, regarding the element of earth: in the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said that the mutual conjunction of the collection of atoms from all sides results in a state of predominance or a state of scarcity due to the nature of aggregation; thus, the form of the karma of sentient beings becomes this world-receptacle filled with all jewels, which belongs to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. || 199 ||

Now, the power of the karma of sentient beings is described, as follows: Those wish-fulfilling trees on the earth that exist with the most excellent essences and subtle atoms, and other medicinal herbs which are sovereigns of taste and remove all diseases—sentient beings do not see them;
they see only common grasses, shrubs, water, dust, stones, and iron. Pretas see [water] as a great fire, and humans who have gone to hell see everywhere cutting and tearing. (192)

Those wish-fulfilling trees on earth, as well as the medicinal herbs and other divine substances that exist through subtle particles—possessing the highest of essences and the sovereign elixirs that destroy all diseases—the virtuous do not see them due to the power of their lack of merit;
instead, they see only common grass, water, dust, stones, and iron.
The hungry ghosts (pretas), however, see the water in rivers and other sources as having the form of blazing fire.
Beings in the hell realms, by the power of their evil karma, experience cutting, splitting, impalement on stakes, and so forth.

Now, the emanation of the Buddha is described: for the sake of their liberation, the Lord of Jinas, together with his sons, having entered the land of karma and performed the descent into the womb, having generated supreme awakening through great compassion, having struck down the Māras and afflictions, and having turned the wheel of Dharma in his abode upon the surface of the earth, the Blessed One remains that very same pure body, manifesting again as an emanation-illusion.
Regarding the phrase "of these":

for the sake of the liberation of these sentient beings, at the time of the arising of merit, the Lord of Jinas together with his sons—the Bodhisattvas—the Buddha, the Blessed One, entered the field of action (*karmabhūmi*). Having performed the descent into the womb (*garbhādhāna*) for the purpose of training sentient beings, and having generated the spirit of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) through supreme compassion, he overthrew Māra and the afflictions (*kleśa*). Then, having turned the Wheel of Dharma in the abode upon the surface of the earth, the Blessed One, whose body is pure (*śuddhakāya*), returned once more to his original state, just as he had come.
Thus, the illusory emanation of a Buddha appears to sentient beings in the form of nirvāṇa through the power of merit or the power of demerit; this is the rule. || 193 ||

Therefore, though born from that [source], he is not destroyed; though he has entered the three realms of existence, the Victor’s pure body never abandons the welfare of sentient beings. The Lord of Victors is not bound by karma. Thus, I am Lokeśvara, stationed in the world-abode, in the realm of karma, as the sun who bestows the path upon sentient beings and removes the fear of hell; never is there another god [who does so]. (194)

Those for whom there is an assault upon the Dharma, and for whom the continuity of their own bodies and those of others [is the goal]; who believe that heaven comes from a son born of an ignoble woman, and death from the *agnihotra* sacrifice when a kinsman has passed away; who hold that the great instruction for those to be trained through various means consists of the slaughter of animals in sacrifice, entry into the heavenly world by dying in battle, and the attainment of the supreme state by casting the body into a sacred ford (*tīrtha*)—such doctrines do not bestow true happiness. (195)

"Who is your mother? Who is your father? Where are your excellent sons and daughters, your brothers, wives, and sisters? Who is your master, your circle of friends, or anyone who can remove the fear of death, apart from the path of reality?
Therefore, O Sun, at my command, establish a single uniform practice among the sages, so that these seers here, presided over by me within the center of the wheel, may attain liberation."
If suffering arises in the body from the stroke of a staff, the fault lies with the staff; this staff was not sent by the hand, for here the entire fault lies with the hand.
This hand was not sent by the mind, but rather by the great fire of wicked anger; therefore, the Bodhisattva has slain this fire of anger as if it were an enemy of the world.

From passion, hatred, and other faults arise the transgressions of the foremost gods and men through attachment to their own beloved wives and others; for the sake of uprooting that [passion], she was given as a gift of desire to all the sons of the Conquerors.

Therefore, this devotion to giving, which yields the fruit of equal happiness and constitutes this accumulation of merit, has arisen as a protector from the fear of saṃsāra for all people at all times, like a kinsman to the three worlds. (198)
By that very passion through which beings have gone to destruction, the Protectors are liberated; what beings strive to protect at every moment, the Protectors give away.

That bliss residing in their own hearts which beings seek to liberate, the Victors protect; therefore, this conduct of the Supreme Victors would be difficult even for gods, nāgas, and asuras to perform. (199)

Earth, water, fire, air, ether, the qualities, mind, intellect, ego, and the individual soul; form and the other [objects], the eyes and the other [senses]—the objects and the subjects; and the five organs of action: among these, which is the eldest by caste? And who is the youngest among those that pervade even the bodies of beasts and men? For you, being the eldest by caste, have become a teacher of kings and men, yet remain proud with the conceit of your lineage.
The seven verses following this one are easy to understand. || 194–200 ||

Now the characteristics of the great essences (*mahārasa*) and so forth are described: Tāpya (cinnabar), earth, water, pure *tutthaka* (blue vitriol), fire, wind, and the mixed element; and indeed, *capala*, *śaśaka*, and *hiṅgula* as the seventh.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*: *kākṣī*, *kāsīsa*, and *gandha*; equal [parts of] sky, mountain, fire, and water; *śilājatu*, *alaktaka*, *gaurī*, and that which has gone to earth—the salt born of the ocean, *saindhava*, and black *colla*. (201)

"tāpyam" and so forth. Here, *mākṣika* is a great essence (*mahārasa*) whose nature is earth; by the word "and" (*ca*), it is also a great essence. *Vimalā* has the nature of water; *tutthaka* has the nature of fire; *capala* has the nature of wind; *rasaka* has the nature of space (*śūnya*); and *śaśaka* and *hiṅgula* have the nature of the element of gnosis (*jñāna*). Thus, there are seven great essences.

Then there are the six secondary minerals (*uparasa*): *kākṣika* is of the nature of the gnosis-element (*jñānadhātu*); *kāsīsa* is of the nature of space; *gandhaka* is of the nature of air; *manaḥśilā* is of the nature of fire; *tālaka* is of the nature of water; and *gairikā* is of the nature of earth—these are the six secondary minerals. Then there are the five salts: *gatam*, *sāmudram*, *saindhavam*, *kṛṣṇalavaṇam*, and *cullikālavaṇam*, which are of the nature of earth and the other elements respectively. || 201 ||

These are the sources of the earth and so forth: again, *navasāra*, *yavakṣāra*, *sajja*, *saubhāgya*, and the various kinds of glass (*kāca*); they have the natures of ether, wind, fire, water, and earth.
Earth is stone and water; moon-water is water; fire-water is fire; wind is the nature of the void (*śūnya*); and the other, poison-water, is the *kartarī* (scissors) of triple nature. (202)
Then there are five alkalis (*kṣāra*): *navasāra*, *yavakṣāra*, *sarjikākṣāra*, *ṭaṅgaṇakṣāra*, and *kācalavaṇakṣāra*, which possess the natures of space and the other elements respectively.

Then there are five waters: *śailodaka*, which has the nature of earth; *candrodaka*, which has the nature of water; *uṣṇodaka*, which has the nature of fire; *viṣodaka*, which has the nature of air; and *kartaryudaka*, which has the nature of space. And that *kartarī* (scissors/water) is threefold: the *sparśakartarī*, the *chāyākartarī*, and the *śabdakartarī*, because it cuts the practitioner. || 202 ||
The earth element is yellow *musta*; water, fire, and wind are *śaktuka*, black *śṛṅgī*, and that called "void," *kālakūṭa*; thus the secondary poison (*upaviṣa*) is to be known as fivefold.

Stones that have the form of living beings, resembling various fruits, and having the form of skulls, conchs, and so forth—their metals are six, or likewise those born from ore (*ghanaja*), and *devakānta* is fourfold. (203)

Then there are five poisons: *pota-musta* has the nature of the earth element; *śaktuka* has the nature of the water element; *śṛṅga* has the nature of fire; *kṛṣṇaviṣa* has the nature of wind; and *kālakūṭa* has the nature of emptiness.
Another secondary poison (*upaviṣa*) should be understood as being fivefold:
*vajrī* has the nature of earth; *arka* has the nature of water; *dhuttūraka* has the nature of fire; *lāṅgalī* has the nature of wind; and *karavīra* has the nature of emptiness.

On this earth, the field-stones (*kṣetrapāṣāṇa*) exist in the form of various living beings, with the shapes of various fruits, and in various forms such as conch shells; they are of six kinds. From those elements, in the chapter [on the] great instruction on those to be trained by various means (*nānopāyavineyamahoddeśa*), there arise six kinds of metals. From them, gold arises.
In this way, other forms also arise. Solid gold (*ghanana*) is likewise fourfold:
yellow gold has the nature of earth; white [gold] has the nature of water; red [gold] has the nature of fire; and black [gold] has the nature of air.
Thus is *devaloha*;

thus is *ayaskāntaloha*. Likewise, *bhrāmaka* has the nature of air (*vāyu*), *cumbaka* has the nature of earth (*pṛthvī*), *kaṭuka* has the nature of fire (*agni*), and *drāvaka* has the nature of water (*toya*).

The natures of those fluxing agents are diverse. Some are fluxers of diamond exclusively; others are fluxers of mica. Likewise, some are fluxers of gold, and similarly, there are fluxers of silver, copper, and iron.
Those are the enjoyments of the outcastes; one should not cast iron upon them. || 203 ||

In this world, mercury is of two kinds: perfected (siddha) and unperfected (asiddha); it is either penetrative (vedhaka) or non-penetrative (avedhaka). The perfected mercury is a penetrator of metal, and furthermore, when consumed, it is a penetrator of the body. That mercury which is non-penetrative becomes effective when it has been processed by heating (jārita), fluxed (sārita), and applied as a penetration (vedha) or secondary penetration (anuvedha) to metal, thereby removing all diseases, provided that base metals (pūtiloha) have been discarded.
In that regard, mercury (rasa) is of two kinds: perfected (siddha) and unperfected (asiddha).
That which penetrates (vedhaka) iron and other metals is the perfected [mercury], residing in subterranean pits and such places.

That which does not penetrate is the quicksilver (pārada); it becomes the "born" (sūtaka) mercury when it has been digested by the metal and processed with the seed (bīja). Having been reprocessed (pratisārita) and followed through (anusārita), it effects penetration and subsequent penetration into the metal.
When consumed, it becomes a destroyer of all poisons.
"Excluding base metals" means that gold and the other [precious metals] must be digested without using lead or tin.
This is the rule regarding the digestion of mercury and the other [metals].

Having purified all these substances—mākṣika and the others—according to the procedure described in the treatises on alchemy (*rasavāda*), they should then be employed in the aforementioned operations; otherwise, the impure metallic and semi-metallic substances (*rasoparasa*) cause the loss of the material. Likewise, those that are "enemies" to gold and silver must not be added into the midst of gold and silver; rather, for the purpose of working with gold and silver, their "friends" should be used. However, in the process of killing (alloying) iron, the "enemies" should be used, according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures.
Likewise, impure copper or even iron (tīkṣṇa) should not be added to gold or silver.
Lead and tin (nāga and vaṅga) that have not been killed should not be used anywhere. For the smelting of metals, one should kill the metal so that it is rendered non-revivable (nirutthāna).
Copper and other metals should be processed by adding a great mineral (mahārasa), a minor mineral (uparasa), or an enemy (śatru) for the purpose of maintaining the life [of the metal];
however, for the work of the seed (bīja), silver and gold are the friends. ||204||

Now the nature of *rasa* (mercury) is described: Having first entered the fire, it moves with the nature of smoke; when heated, it gradually becomes capable through sound alone, and then through leaping (*utpluta*). Furthermore, it is indeed trembling (*sakampa*) and motionless (*niṣkampa*). The piercing by sound (*śabdavedhī*) and leaping (*plutivedhī*) do not prevail; rather, there is piercing by thread (*sūtravedhī*), which is trembling and motionless. The piercing by spear (*kuntavedhī*) is threefold here, and it is further refined (*sārita*) by means of various *sāraṇā* processes. (205)
And: "There is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "previously" (*pūrvam*) and so forth:

here, previously, that which moves by means of the intrinsic nature of smoke while situated in fire is [first] "melted" (*jārita*); having gradually become fluid, it moves as a child (*bāla*) by leaping (*plutena*), as a youth (*kumārabhūta*) it moves with trembling (*prakampena*), and as an adult (*proḍha*) it moves without trembling; when it becomes a piercing and subsequently piercing agent (*vedhānuvedhī*), it is an elder (*vṛddha*).
In this case, the piercing of the metal is neither "childish" (bāla) nor "leaping" (pluti); rather, Kumāra says that one should cause it to move slightly by means of leaf-coating and mild fire.

Thus: the "childish" piercing is done with leaf-coating, the "youthful" with a blind crucible (andhamūṣā), the "adolescent" with the piercing of a spear (kuntavedha), and the "mature" piercing is performed according to one's desire.

Thus, the *vedhī* (piercing), *śabda* (sounding), and *plutī* (leaping) [types of mercury] arise; furthermore, that which was previously the *ghūmagāmī* (smoke-going) and *patravedhī* (leaf-piercing) becomes *sakampa* (trembling) when acting as a *kuntavedhī* (needle-piercer).

That [mercury], having been processed (*sārita*) by the three types of *sāraṇā* to be described hereafter, becomes "grown" (*vṛddha*) and pierces metal according to one's desire. This is the rule regarding the qualities of mercury. || 205 ||

Now the quality of medicinal herbs is described: By the power of divine herbs, one who has been processed becomes strong and can digest all metals; for in the absence of these, who on the surface of the earth could effect its binding? When bound, it grants the power of moving through the air (*khecaratva*); likewise, when consumed, it brings about death. Yet, in the absence of knowledge, mercury (*rasendra*) goes to destruction. Therefore, this [mercury] should be mastered with great effort by kings. (206)
"Divya" and so forth.

Here, in this entire science of alchemy (*rasaśāstra*), mercury (*rasa*) digests (*jarati*) mica (*abhraka*) without a mouth (*nirmukha*) through contact with diamonds (*vajra*) and *vaikrāntaka* gems, and through conjunction with divine herbs (*divyauṣadhi*). Therefore, there are stones that dissolve mica-cloth; by contact with them—that is, with the *viḍa*—and by the power of the divine herbs, which are the medicinal herbs of mercury to be described hereafter, [mercury] becomes powerful, having digested all metals such as mica and the rest.
Which one is it?
In the absence of those divine herbs, whoever performs the binding (*bandha*) of this *sūtaka* (mercury) while it resides upon the surface of the earth,
there shall be the removal of poverty and passion once it is bound;
for men, it grants the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*), and even death itself goes to destruction when [the mercury] is consumed by its power.
Therefore, in the absence of knowledge, this mercury (rasendra) must be mastered by kings for the purpose of removing diseases; such is the rule. || 206 ||

Their wealth is manifold, and its expenditure occurs through their devotion to song and instrumental music; yet that which is neither burnt, nor spent for the sake of the king’s service, nor given for the sake of dharma is lost.
He who expends wealth for the cause of sin incurs the bondage of that very sin; therefore, a bodhisattva expends all his wealth for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings. (207)
And it is also easy to understand through a different arrangement [of the words]. || 207 ||

In this chapter, the Great Instruction on the Various Means for Training Disciples, the characteristics of the divine medicinal herbs are now described: That herb which, by mere application as an ointment, suddenly removes the blackness (*kālikā*) from a copper leaf—those fortunate ones behold it upon the earth, for it removes all diseases and acts as a digestive agent (*jāraṇī*) for the class of metals.

The binding (*bandha*) of mercury with other [herbs] occurs only after a fixed period of a year; however, through this [divine herb], that binding occurs by means of sweating (*sveda*) following a single thousandfold penetration (*sāhasravedha*). (208)
"By means of renunciations (*saṃnyāsa*) and yogas, the mercury becomes superior through application," and so forth.

Here, that divine herb which is equal to the Great Mercury (*mahārasa*), which when merely smeared onto a copper leaf removes its blackness (*kālikā*) instantly upon being cast into fire—blessed ones behold it on the earth as the remover of all diseases, a digestive agent (*jāraṇī*) for the metallic series when consumed, and for the binding of mercury. Whereas the binding of this mercury by other herbs occurs only after a fixed period of years—that is, twelve years—it becomes a superior binding through sweating and the yogas of renunciation.
The rule is that there is no piercing beyond one thousand [finger-breadths] in measurement. || 208 ||
The alkaline group and the sour group are always combined with all medicinal herbs having extremely pungent tastes using fermented rice-water (*kāñjika*) for the purpose of grinding and heating.

Furthermore, for the whitening of white substances, seeds are sown with flowers; purification by means of pairs [of substances], along with *saubhāgya*, glass, rat, horse, donkey, and poison, results in softness through the sprinkling of oil.

Having been purified sevenfold with *rambhā*, *citra*, ashes, horses, elephants, humans, water, and all alkaline salts as well as pungent substances, one should again purify those [substances] by their color and taste.
Repeatedly heating them with the fire, one should again saturate and dry them a hundred times; thus is the conch powder, this sulphur, saturated and processed in a hundred *puṭas*.

This *viḍa* salt serves for the liquefaction of metals; one-eighth part of it, subjected to *dolāsveda* (swinging-furnace heating) for eight nights according to the *Rasahṛdaya*, will cause even iron to melt completely. From the decoction, a potent and powerful impurity arises; once the metal has been rubbed and melted, it becomes liquid. With the body of the sun and moon (*raviśaśivapuṣā*), one should color all the metals. || 211 ||

That [mercury], pervasive and well-purified, flows when treated with equal parts of *nāgaraṅga* and rice-foam; thus, for one who performs the daily rites of the *sūtaka* (mercury) according to the procedures to be described, there occurs a binding [of the mercury] which, over time, attains a manifest state of heavy density, free from all defects. This [remedy] removes disease and death, and always dispels the suffering of total poverty in the excellent body. (212)
From this meter, the subsequent four meters are easy to understand.

Now, for the sake of preserving the mercury (*rasa*), the worship of Jambhala is described: In the hand-offering (*hastārgha*), there is a golden lotus with eight petals; in the center of the pericarp (*kaṇikā*) is a vajra made of pure sapphire (*indranīla*).

On the southeast petal is a beautiful ruby (*padmarāga*); on the southwest, a topaz (*karketana*); on the northwest, iron; on the northeast, copper and silver; on the western petal, gold; and in the pericarp, the medicinal paste (*piṣṭī*) produced from a layer of gold.
"Half a cubit," and so forth.
Here, in a golden lotus of eight petals measuring one span (vitasti)—that is, half a cubit—one should fasten the seed-syllable (*bīja*) with pure gold in the pericarp at the center of the womb.
On the eastern petal is sapphire (*indranīla*); on the southern petal, ruby (*padmarāga*); on the western [petal], yellow karketana gem; and on the northern [petal], moonstone (*candrakānta*).
Then, one should fix a sharp [metal] in the southeast, copper in the southwest, gold in the northwest, and silver in the northeast.
One should place a paste of gold and mica upon the diamond in the center. || 213 ||

Upon her head, two cubits high, is Jambhala made of gold, holding a mongoose and granting boons; and within the center, on the petals, are the eight goddesses, golden or silver, holding lotuses and granting boons.

On their crowns is the Buddha Ratneśa, with a jewel and granting boons. Likewise, for the Yakṣiṇīs, there are the eight syllables beginning with *haṃ* and *ha*, short and long, in the cardinal and intermediate directions on the petals, in due order.

Upon that plaster, one should fashion a two-armed Jambhala out of gold, holding a mongoose in his left hand and displaying the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*) with his right; he should be four finger-widths in height, measured by the standard of a crown (*uṣṇīṣa*).
Likewise, on the petals are the eight Yakṣiṇīs, holding lotuses and gestures of granting boons, made either of gold or silver.
In this regard, if Jambhala is made of silver, then the Yakṣiṇīs are made of gold; if Jambhala is made of gold, then the Yakṣiṇīs are made of silver.
Thus, when there is a golden lotus, then there is a silver basin; when there is a silver lotus within the womb, then it becomes a golden basin for the pouring of water.
On the crown [of the head] is the Buddha Ratneśa, with his hand holding a jewel and a varada-mudrā, and likewise for the Yakṣiṇīs.
In this way, Jambhala is accompanied by Prajñā, together with Vasudhārā, like Halāhala.
Their seed-syllables are in the pericarp: *haṃ* and *hā* for Jambhala and Vasudhārā;

likewise, *hoṃ* in the eastern goddess [Tārā], *hīḥ* in the southeast [Pāṇḍarā], *haṃ* in the south [Māmakī], *hrīḥ* in the southwest [Locanā], *hu* in the north [Vajradhātvīśvarī], *hūḥ* in the northeast [Vasudhārā], *ahalṛ* in the west, and *ahalu* in the northwest.
Tārā is Sparśavajrā, Pāṇḍarā is Rasavajrā, Māmakī is Rūpavajrā, Locanā is Gandhavajrā, and Vajradhātvīśvarī is Vasudhārā.
For the sake of the substance, all the elements (dhātus), together with their presiding deities, must be marked with the seal of the Great Jewel; this is the rule. || 214 ||

Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers at the three junctions of every day, one should offer water to the Lord of Waters (Jalendra) in the moon-shaped sacrificial pit (*indukuṇḍa*) with this mantra: "Oṃ... [name]... svāhā" at the beginning, and "jaṃ bhaḥ" in the middle. O King, with a joyful mind, for the sake of protecting the mercury, by means of such a protective rite, neither the Lord of Beings (*bhūtanātha*) nor the Lord of Serpents (*ahinātha*) shall steal the mercury. || 215 ||
Bho. Hā! Ca. Hi!
Ca. Hūṃ!
ca. hai | ca. huṃ | ca. hnaḥ |
[In the *Ca-la-paṭala*, verse:
The Great Chapter on the Various Means for Training Disciples. Then, one should worship daily at the three junctions of the day with perfumes, incenses, flowers, and so forth, in a silver vessel.
Thereafter, one hundred and eight handfuls of water should be offered with this mantra: *oṃ jambhalajalendrāya svāhā*.
With a joyful mind, the speaker should offer water to the deity for the sake of protecting the *rasa*.
By this protective rite, neither the Lord of Beings (*bhūtanātha*), nor the Lord of Serpents (*ahinātha*), nor the King of Nagas (*nāgarāja*) shall take away the *rasa*.
Likewise, other Daityas who steal the *rasa* shall not take it away by the command of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (*vajradhara*) through the protection of Jambhala. || 215 ||

Now, the digestion of mercury by means of juices (*rasajāraṇa*) is described: One should grind the mercury for ten days with the desired groups of alkaline and acidic substances and then subject it to sweating while placed in a paste. Having caused it to fall [into a crucible], one should again add [the juice] at all times. Furthermore, if the mercury dies within that falling-paste, it will digest even that; having consumed its own source there, that mercury then consumes another and every other source. (216)
"Desired," and so forth.
Here, first, having added salt to the desired powder, one should grind the mercury with the acid of citron and other fruits for ten days and subject it to heating (*sveda*).
Then, having taken the primary mercury and dried the remaining water, one should filter the mercury contained within the paste and cast it back into that very same mercury at all times.

Whatever paste (kalka) arises from the mercury that has been rubbed, all of that must be subjected to the *pātana* process again for the purpose of capturing the mercury. If, when the mercury has been made to fall, it does not actually descend, then the mercury is dead within that very paste; having been blown with a blowpipe (*saṃdhmāta*), one should digest even that [paste] along with another metal to be grasped. Therein, the mercury, having been dried and having consumed its own source (*svayoni*), consumes yet another source of all the metals. || 216 ||

Now, the digestion (*jāraṇā*) of all mixed metals is described: Lead, steel, copper, and another [metal] produced from a plate or from a mine—purified and equal in quantity—is smelted together with tin equal to that used for silver-work; at the beginning, one should take a sixtyth part as a dose, and once it is melted, one should increase it by a single increment up to a quarter-part, for beyond that, more should not be given. || 217 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "nāgam" (lead):
here, the metals indeed digest one another; therefore, one should cause them to be mixed.
