Lead (*nāga*), steel (*tīkṣṇa*), copper (*āra*), *paṭalaja* (copper from the *paṭala* ore), *abhra-phaloha* (mica-metal), or *kṣetraja* (field-born metal)—that is, various mineral ores—should be purified in place of steel and the other metals.

These five metals, taken in equal proportions and smelted together, become *saṃkaraloha* (mixed metal). In the work of gold-making (*hemakārya*) or alchemy (*rasāyanakārya*), lead (*nāga*) must not be added; one should instead prepare a mixture of four metals.

For the work of silver (*tārakārya*), one should digest white mica-metal (*śvetābhrakaloha*) and tin (*vaṅga*) along with the two [other] metals to produce silver. For the work of silver, [these are used].
Having thus performed the mixing and purified the mercury, among the various vessels for calcination, the boat-vessel (*naukāyantra*) is the best; one should cast the mercury into that boat-vessel.
Then, taking a thirtieth part from the mercury, one should grind it with the base mercury and an iron [powder] amounting to a sixtieth part of the base mercury upon a stone mortar.

Having thus given a morsel (*grāsa*) equal to one-sixtieth [of the mercury] at the beginning, then having placed a cloth-net over the liquid in an earthen boat-vessel, and having applied the aforementioned [mixture] on top and added *kāñjika* (sour gruel), one should place the boat over a fire of powdered husks and cow-dung.
Once the *kāñjika* has been purified, *kāñjika* should be added again continuously;
in this way, the mercury consumes the morsel in one or two days.

Then, once it has been digested, another double portion should be given by that same sequence; again, having ascertained it is digested according to the *Vimalaprabhā*, if the paste of what was strained through a cloth is not seen on the cloth, then it is said to be "melted" (*jārita*).

In this way, one should increase the morsel (*grāsa*) until it consumes a quarter-part (*pādāṃśa*) of the morsel; beyond that, one should not increase it—nothing more should be given—this is the prohibition.
Above that, the previously mentioned seed (*bīja*) [is to be used] by this method. || 217 ||
Doubled by one fortnight, this [mercury] digests again; thus purified, it likewise digests when doubled, tripled, or eightfold. Once digested, it is processed with *viḍa* salts.

Even the heating in the *cakra* vessel is effective for undigested mercury for up to eight nights. Indeed, when touched by divine herbs, it digests while situated in the peacock-feather tube (*śikhigata*); for in this case, the iron becomes mouthless (*nirmukha*). || 298 ||

This mercury digests [the impurities] twofold in one fortnight; thus the seed is purified. In this manner, the seed digests [the impurities] two, three, or eightfold; then, once it has been processed (*jārita*), it is further treated with the aforementioned *viḍa* salts.

If it then becomes undigested (*ajīrṇa*), then when it is undigested, "wheel-sweating" (*cakrasveda*) should be performed: having placed the mercury in a crucible shaped like a cow's udder, one should bury it in the ground until it is no longer visible for a depth of three finger-breadths.
Then, having dug a circular pit outside of that, one should fill it with powdered dried cow-dung and apply fire.

By means of that *cakrasveda* for eight days, the mercury (*rasa*), together with the fluxing agent (*viḍa*), abandons the defect of indigestion (*ajīrṇadoṣa*) within the crucible; thereafter, it should again be placed in the *naukāyantra*.
In this manner, beginning from one year up to twelve years, one should digest all the metals and other substances in order to achieve *vedha* and *anuveḍha*.

Then, by the power of merit, when divine medicinal herbs (*divyauṣadhi*)—both liquefiers (*drāvaka*) and digesters (*jāraka*)—are encountered, then, through the powder of the touch-liquefier (*sparśadrāvaka*) and the aforementioned fluxing agents and divine medicinal herbs, even the mica-metal (*abhrakaloha*) situated in the fire is digested without opening [the crucible]; thereby, the mercury becomes exceedingly powerful. || 298 ||

From mica, strength becomes eightfold in iron; that [strength] is also eightfold in the liquefaction [of iron]; from that, it is eightfold again in the seed (bīja); and from that, it is indeed eightfold in the diamond-gem (vajraratna).
Thus, one should digest the metals, gems, and fierce mercury in the midst of fire until a vortex occurs; thereafter, it becomes capable of piercing many hundreds of thousands of times.
When the iron has been digested by abhraka, its strength becomes eightfold;
when the liquid (druti) is swallowed, its strength also becomes eightfold; from that, when the seed (bīja) is digested, the strength of the liquid becomes eightfold;
and when the diamond jewel (vajra-ratna), sapphire (indranīla), and so forth are digested, its strength again becomes eightfold—such is the rule regarding strength.

In this manner, one should digest iron and other metals in the midst of fire until they undergo transformation; once they become capable of entering [the body] by the millions, no further process such as their killing (māraṇa) need be performed. || 219 ||

In the absence of *sparśauṣadhi*, when [the mercury] has become firm through rubbing with excellent *viḍa* salts and by means of sudation, it remains motionless; from that point, the *sāraṇā* process, which is equal to the gold, should be performed.

Furthermore, another [process] two or three times [the amount] should be done by casting [the mercury] into the juice of quicksilver-gold (*drutakanaka*) extracted from oil. For the sake of the substance, eight parts of lead (*nāga*) should be diligently cast into the juice of quicksilver-gold.

[Chapter on] Various Means for Training Disciples, verses 217–222: In the absence of the medicinal herbs for touch (*sparśauṣadhi*), one should proceed with the excellent *viḍa* salts mentioned previously, using massages and fomentations until [the mercury] becomes truly motionless. Then, the extraction (*sāraṇā*) is equal to gold. Here, if the mercury that has been processed (*jārita*) does not move after being placed upon glowing coals, then that which is motionless should be cast into a crucible shaped like a cow’s teat (*gostanākāramūṣā*), and castor oil (*eraṇḍataila*) should be poured over it until the mercury sinks.

Then, having melted mercury equal in weight to the gold, one should add lead amounting to one-eighth part for the sake of the substance and cast it over the mercury; by that, it becomes processed (*sārita*).
Again, by this same sequence, with twice the amount of gold, it becomes re-processed (*pratisārita*); with three times the amount, it becomes post-processed (*anusārita*).
Thus, processed in these three ways, it becomes penetrative (*vedhī*), reaching up to a thousandfold [purity] according to the strength of the metal.

Then, having melted the mica, powdered the mercury, and wrapped it with beeswax, one should cast it into that [melted substance] along with dead lead and tin; by this, [the mercury] undergoes transmutation and becomes a penetrator (*vedhin*), whether into silver or gold—this is the rule for *jāraṇā*. || 220 ||

Now the process of binding [the mercury] through renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is described: Having killed gold with sharp iron, copper, *phaṇida*, *arada*, realgar, and sulfur; and having likewise killed the "king of colors" (mercury), tin, and lead with orpiment and *tāpya*; then, for the purpose of making gold and silver, one should mix equal parts of alkalis, poison (*viṣa*), salt, minor metals (*uparasas*), and mercury equal in weight to the base metal; having saturated these with bile and acids for ten days, they should be cast into the midst of stones. || 221 ||

Indeed, when heated for six months in the interior of the earth by one possessing the crest-lock (*śikhin*), that mercury becomes a penetrator (*vedhin*) at all times for copper drawn from a smelting pit; furthermore, with a sixteenth part [of it], it turns copper into silver equal to gold—this is the auspicious gold that destroys the suffering of disputants. For pure copper, when pierced with an eighth part of *tāra* (silver), it likewise becomes silver. ||222||
Regarding the passage beginning with "hemam" and so forth:

here, one should kill gold (hemam) by means of a nāga through the process of re-coating (prativāpa); one should kill steel (tīkṣṇa) by means of cinnabar (darada) through the application of *puṭa* (sealed heating); one should kill lead (ahinaga) in realgar (manaḥśilā);
and for the purpose of gold-work, one should kill copper (tāmram) by means of sulfur (gandhaka).

For the purpose of transmuting silver, one should fix silver with white honey; one should fix tin with talaka; and one should also fix the metal produced from clouds, namely white mica-iron, with honey.

Then, one should take four alkalies equal in weight to mercury (amṛtaloha); in the absence of all these, three or two [alkalies] and an equal amount of viḍa salt; salts in equal amounts; and the secondary minerals (uparasas) possessing the nature of enemies [of mercury]. Mercury (sūtaka) should be equal in weight to the metals. Having combined everything and ground it for ten days with the bile of fish and the like, and with acidic juices such as those of the citron (bījapūraka), one should place all those stone fragments into a crucible (saṃpuṭa). Then, having buried it in the ground, it should be heated by fire on top for six months at all times. Thereafter, it becomes bound (baddha).

Then, after six months, there occurs the piercing (*vedha*) of that copper by a sixteenth part. Furthermore, when that very same pierced copper is made into silver with an equal portion of gold, one should open it with a *puṭa* (sealing) process;
this becomes auspicious gold, which destroys the suffering of disputants.

Now, if there is a binding by means of the deposition of *tāra* and so forth, then the pure *tāna* becomes pierced *tāra*, provided that one-eighth part is given to the *tāra*; such is the rule for the binding of the deposition.

Next, the *golaka*-binding as taught in the *Ādibuddha* is described: here, in the work of gold-making, one should dissolve some *mantra* consisting of yellow *abhraka* and so forth; or, for the purpose of *tāra*, one may use white *abhraka* in its entirety or half.
Then, for the work of gold, one should grind it with lead; for silver, with tin. Then, one should wrap that in a gold leaf for the purpose of gold, and in a silver leaf for the purpose of silver.
Likewise, having ground realgar (*manaḥśilā*) upon a gold leaf with cow’s urine, one should apply a coating with it;

then, externally, with cinnabar (*darada*), and then one should wrap it with potter’s clay (*kumbhakāramṛttikā*). When it is dry, one should wrap it again with cow-dung; then, having dried it again in intense sunlight, one should apply a mild firing (*mṛdupuṭa*) using a fire of dried cow-dung (*gokarṣāgni*).

Then, having removed the ash from the crucible, one should blow the clay ball with intense coals until the great essence (*mahārasa*), the secondary essence (*uparasa*), gold, lead, and the paste (*piṣṭī*) become of one flavor (*samarasībhavanti*).

Then, once it has cooled, one should break the ball; whatever paste is found in the middle along with the gold, by means of which the binding of the ball (*golakabandha*) was formed—that very thing, when added in a sixty-fourth part to copper, becomes gold or silver as before. This is the "binding of the ball" according to the *Mūlatantra*. (221–222)

Now the binding of the metals of the field (*kṣetraloha*) is described: Those stones on the earth that resemble fruits or bodies, having forms such as conch-shells or skulls—one should place their source-matter (*yoni*) into them along with ghee and honey and heat them with intense winds.

Having purified them through repeated sprinklings (*niṣeka*), and again with the group of *ṭaṅgaṇa* alkalis, one should identify the metal-source and cause it to be digested (*jāraṇa*) by the alchemist (*vādī*) even in a double amount of mercury. || 223 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "pāṣāṇa" (stone) and so forth:

here on this earth, there are stones that take the forms of various living beings and the forms of various fruits and the like. Their very source (*yoni*) consists of the flesh of those living beings for [stones resembling] living beings, and the powder of fruits for [stones resembling] fruits; for conch-shells, *takārā*, and so forth, it is the powder of conch-shells and the like. Having added their powder along with ghee, honey, and *ṭaṅgaṇa* (borax) to make pills, one should blow [the crucible] intensely with a cloth for dropping metal (*lohapātana-vastreṇa*) until the metal falls out.
Then, having poured [the liquid] back and extracted it again, one should add *ṭaṅgaṇa* once more and purify it until it becomes completely pure.

Having performed purification in this manner, the wise one should take that base metal— either iron or copper— and perform a binary alloy (*dvandva*) with gold, or that very metal should be digested (*jāraṇīya*) twice its weight by means of mercury.
First, having caused the mica (*abhraka*) to be digested, whether it be *saṃmukha* or *nirmukha*, thereafter other metals and so forth should be caused to be digested.
In this manner, one should digest *mākṣika*, copper, or gold; or *tutthaka*, copper, or gold; or *rājāvartaka*, copper, or gold; or *śaśaka*, copper, or gold.

Just as iron is caused to fall [as a flux] from field-stones here, so too should one purify *mākṣika* and the others, as well as *vimalā* and the others; then they become effective for the previous operations. Otherwise, they destroy the substance.
Now, first of all, the means of livelihood for practitioners is described, by which that which has been consumed is digested without difficulty.

Here, through the application of leaf-coating with processed mercury (*jārita-rasa*), base gold (*hermāddhaka*) becomes pure gold; however, when not processed, it remains as *kumāra* or *bāla*. In this context, one part out of three is said to be the measure for two parts of gold.

In this process, first one should form a leaf of copper with salt and sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and subject it to *niṣeka* until it becomes a powder; then, having added water to remove the defect of the salt, one should dry it;
thereafter, having added rock salt (*saindhava*) in a sixteenth part, one should grind it with the acid of *bījapura* and other fruits and cook it in a *puṭa*.
In this manner, having repeatedly added rock salt (*saindhava*), one should cook it in a sealed crucible (*puṭa*) seven or eight times, until it becomes somewhat dark, resembling the dust of bricks.
Then, having made pills with honey, clarified butter, and borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), one should cause the metal to fall as before;
thus, one obtains half a *mātra* free from impurities.

Again, having made that same leaf-cup, one should apply sulphur (gandhaka) and cinnabar (darada) to the foot of the [mercury] and kill it with *puṭa* applications. Then, taking that powder together with mercury in an eighth part, adding sulphur twice the amount of mercury and cinnabar half the amount of mercury, one should grind it with acid. Again, one should heat it in a shallow pan (*kharpara*) and grind it once more for seven days.

One should place that very [substance] mixed together into a vessel fashioned by a potter (as stated in verses 221–224 of the *Nānopāyavineyamahoddeśa*). One should seal the mouth of the vessel with clay from a potter;
an external coating should also be applied to the vessel, one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) high, and the size of a coconut; it should not be made larger in width.
Then one should dry it in the sun,
smear it again on top with cow-dung, and dry it once more until the cow-dung has become completely dry;
thereafter, one should cook it by means of a *puṭa*.

In this way, by embracing that copper powder, the mercury dies and the copper becomes free of defects due to their mutual union. Then, having added a quarter-part of gold to silver and having added twice as much copper as the gold, one should heat it in an iron crucible until everything becomes a uniform liquid (samarasa).

Then, once it has cooled, one should remove the crucible lid, add again a quarter-part of gold and twice as much copper, and heat it as before. Then, once it has cooled, one should remove the crucible lid; by means of half the amount of gold, it becomes pure gold, being purified by two *puṭas*.
Now another application is described: one should cause this powder to permeate gold in double or triple proportion.

Having made a paste with that [powder] as a quarter part in mercury, having placed it inside a crucible, having applied sulphur powder on top, and having provided a lid over that, one should blow charcoal fires upon it for a mere moment.
Then, once it has cooled, one should repeatedly apply an equal amount of sulphur to the paste and burn it eight times.
Then the mercury embraces the gold and does not release it;

thereafter, having added a seed (bīja) equal to one-fourth part of the silver (tāra), and having added that same amount of copper equal to the silver, one should blow it in an iron crucible (abhramūṣā).
Then, when it has become cold, having removed the crucible lid, one should fashion that mass into a leaf or a thin plate.
One should have a leaf-ointment prepared from that flour;
for the purpose of causing it to penetrate, one should apply it on top with the juice of betel leaves,
and then place it upon the surface of a furnace.
Having applied clay over [the crucible] to the thickness of a finger, one should perform the cooking of the house (i.e., smelting) with fire for three days;

then, having removed it and added a quarter-part of seed-metal again, one should take out that leaf, which then becomes a plate; by means of this, superior gold is produced—thus it was spoken by the Blessed Buddha, and no further detail has been written here. || 223 ||

Now, the elixir for those seeking a healthy body is described: After purifying the digestive tract with a decoction of the three fruits (triphalā), one should take ghee and honey combined with the powders of the herbs, which have been processed with mercury and cow’s milk, along with boiled water. For seven days, one should consume this with fresh *śāli* rice, avoiding vegetables, sour foods, salt, fish, and meat. Within half a month, men [attain the desired result]. 224.
"Seven days," and so forth:
here, whoever consumes bound mercury must first perform a purification of the digestive tract;
that is, one should administer a purgative using water boiled with equal parts of the three myrobalans (triphalā).

A diet of *śāli* rice, free from salt and sourness, should be taken with milk as the wholesome regimen (*pathya*). Then, one should consume that very same [preparation] in a dose of one *akṣa* daily, consisting of iron powder processed with *nirguṇḍī*, along with sharp metallic powders (*tīkṣṇacūrṇa*) processed with *nirguṇḍī*, combined with ghee and honey, together with mercury (*sūtaka*) that has been well-purified and is equal in quantity to the other ingredients. This should be eaten every day; the wholesome regimen consists of fresh cow's milk from a cow that has recently calved, while the food previously consumed should be old and aged.

In this way, purification of the internal organs occurs within half a fortnight; one should then consume the essence [of mercury], avoiding rice and similar grains, and abstaining from vegetables, sour foods, salt, fish, oil, and fire. || 224 ||

Having understood this, one who pierces a thousand [leaves] should consume it for a hundred times a hundred crores [of days], until finally, at the time of each day, only the portion of a mustard seed—and ultimately the portion of a black mustard—is to be taken.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said: "The temple of knowledge, a dwelling on the earth, arises free from cold, wind, and heat; within six months, this middling [practice] produces a divine body, free from wrinkles and grey hair. (225)

Having understood that one who pierces a thousand [times] should eat a hundredth part of a hundred [i.e., one-tenth of a grain]; one who pierces a hundred thousand (lakṣavedhī) should eat as much as can be consumed by piercing ten million (koṭivedha); and one who pierces a thousand [times] should eat a measure of barley (*yava*) every day;
one who pierces a hundred thousand (*lakṣavedhī*) should eat a measure of mustard seed (*sarṣapa*); and one who pierces ten million (*koṭivedhī*) should eat a measure of black mustard (*rājikā*).
Thus, the final portion of *rājikā* (mustard seed) should be understood here as being for the consumption of mercury; it is a palace within the earth, or a palace free from cold, wind, and heat.

In this way, the middling mercury, having performed a thousand-fold transmutation (*sahasravedhī*), makes one free from wrinkles and grey hair within six months by consuming it. Otherwise, the perfected mercury (*siddharasa*) acts by being taken daily, even in a single dose. || 225 ||

Now, the remedy for indigestion caused by mercury (rasa) is stated: one should drink a decoction of *karkoṭī*, *devadālī*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *bṛhatī*, nimba, and *kirātatikta* for three days during indigestion, and furthermore, one should perform fasting (*laṅghana*).

Likewise, [this applies] when [mercury] has entered *candrodaka* and so forth, or into fire, poisonous water, the juice of *śailabhallātaka*, *durgandhā*, *bhūmiśaila*, or other preparations of poisonous meat; thus [should act] the practitioner of mantras (*mantrī*). ||226||
Regarding "karkoṭī" and so forth:

here, when indigestion of the *rasa* occurs, then *bandhakarkoṭī*, *devadālī*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *bṛhatī*, neem leaves (*nimbapatra*), and *kirātatikta*—these [eight] remaining ingredients are boiled in water; this decoction, or *kvātha*, is called a *kvathana*.
That very thing is indeed the drink for indigestion.
One should observe fasting for three days until extreme hunger occurs; thereafter, wholesome food (pathya) must be consumed.
Likewise, when the moon-water (candrodaka) has been drunk, one should fast for three days, and thereafter consume wholesome food.
By that [method], one should bathe daily in fire and water; by that same [method], eating and drinking are prescribed. For six months or up to one year, one should consume milk and rice;
this regimen is beneficial even for poison-water, mountain-water, and bhallātaka-water.
One should drink only a measure equal to a seed-corn (akṣamātra) of these;
more than that would cause death.

This same rule applies to the consumption of foul-smelling substances, the eating of earth or stones, poisonous meat, and other preparations such as shoots and sprouts, including wholesome foods and the like. || 226 ||

Now, the characteristics of the elixir herbs (*rasāyana-auṣadhī*) are described: That herb which, when eaten, causes intense fainting like poison—one should grind that entire herb into a fine powder and consume it in small quantities along with ghee and honey. Likewise, those beings who eat it—whether humans or animals—do not find success through such an herb; rather, that herb which bestows death and causes supreme terror to [ordinary] practitioners (*yogins*) shall be nectar (*amṛta*) for [true] practitioners. || 227 ||

Because the leaf of the *mātṛkā* is extremely indistinct, it is being re-extracted here and there with the assistance of the Tibetan text [chapter, verse]: The Great Chapter on the Various Means for Training Disciples (*Nānopāya-vineya-mahoddeśa*). Regarding the passage beginning with "that which is consumed" (*yā bhuktā*), etc.:

here, among the creepers such as *challa* and *pallava*, that which is consumed produces an intense swoon like poison. Having taken the five parts (*pañcāṅga*) of that medicinal plant, one should have them made into a fine powder.
One should consume that very powder in a small quantity every day together with ghee and honey; the remainder is as before, according to the previous rule.
Among those beings who consume it, that herb which does not cause fainting is the one that grants success (*siddhi*) for those beings;
however, that which bestows death and causes supreme terror is the one that grants success for yogins, by means of the power of mantra and meditation. || 227 ||

Now another elixir is described: having ground equal parts of *daṇḍotpala* with the juice of its own petals, along with *śāliparṇī*, *abjasāri*, and mercury (*rasa*), together with sulfur (*gandhaka*), for three days in a beautiful vessel made of iron;

he who consumes it at every daily occasion for six months in a dose of one *ṭaṅka* (one-fourth of a *karṣa*), being freed from diseases such as leprosy, and having overcome wrinkles and graying hair, will possess the appearance of a sixteen-year-old. || 228 ||
"Equal," and so forth:

here, one should grind equal parts of sulfur and the juice of *daṇḍotpala* with either the juice of *śāliparṇī* or the juice of *utpalasārī* in an iron magnet vessel using an iron ball for three days;
having thus ground it, one should consume it every day.
"Of the measure of a ṭaṅka-pāda" means one should consume one *māṣa*;
he is liberated from diseases such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair, and here he becomes sixteen—that is, like a sixteen-year-old. || 228 ||
Now, the perfected medicinal herb for the killing of mercury (rasa-māraṇa) is described: *vokkāṇākāśaśaktu* (the flour of *vokkāṇa* and *ākāśa*) kills even volatile mercury; likewise, *kīracañcu*.

Having combined equal parts of the fruit-born gold killed by another herb and *kānta* iron, one should prepare a pill (*golaka*) with six *palas* of the aforementioned *kānta* vessel, using the decoction of *sajīva* (a living plant) from which the juice has been removed, along with *mastaka* (curd-whey); this removes wrinkles and grey hair. || 229 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "vokkāṇa" and so forth:
here, he who desires the contraction and the killing of mercury must seek out these medicinal herbs— namely, *vokkāṇa*, which is asafoetida (*hiṅgu*),
by means of which [mercury], when smeared with a blue thread, becomes white.
By that [substance], when the crucible is smeared, the mercury dies;
"ākāśa" means "ambar" (cloth), which is the excrement of the *bhairuṇḍa* bird, and that is of two kinds: *chatrāmbara* and *śikhāmbara*.
If, when thrown into the midst of fire, smoke issues forth after spreading a cloth over its head, and that cloth pierces through [the flame] in the shape of a crest (*śikhā*), that is the best.
That which resides in the smoke in the shape of an umbrella is the middle one; by that, there is the contraction-bond (*saṃkocabandha*).
Likewise is the *śāktuka* poison, and likewise the *koracañcu*, the parrot-beak (*śukatuṇḍaka*), which causes the flow of blood and is well-known in the world as a blood-extractor.

There is another variety of cinnabar described in the *Vimalaprabhā* [of the *Jñānavajrasamuccaya*]: "In this way, he who places his foot upon a lotus with a water-jar (*kaṃpadma*) shall see the stars in the sky by day;

if he does not see these, then—under the pretext of another medicinal herb—he should digest mercury killed [by processing], along with equal parts of red copper (*aruṇa-tāmra*), brass (*phalaja*, i.e., *akala-loha*), gold, and magnetite (*ayaskānta-loha*)."
When the liquid is four palas, it should be joined with two palas— which is half of that— making six palas in total;
the remaining procedure is according to the method taught in the Adhyātmapaṭala.

Now, the nature of the mercury capable of piercing a thousand [atoms] and so forth is described: through six months, two months, one month, fifteen days, ten days, seven nights, three nights, one night, and even in a single moment, accomplishment arises in the body by its power.

For men—whether inferior or superior—there is the common, the middling, and the supreme accomplishment of knowledge, which is free from dissolution, according to the force of their own past virtuous deeds accumulated over many births. || 230 ||
"Within six months," and so forth:
if it is consumed here according to the previously mentioned procedure, that which possesses the power of a thousandfold penetration (*sahasravedhī*) performs the supreme task within six months;
thereafter, by its power, accomplishment (*siddhi*) occurs in the body within six months.

By the power of piercing ten thousand [leagues] in two months; by the power of piercing one hundred thousand [leagues] in one month [along with ten days for the king]; by the power of piercing thirty-four hundred thousand [leagues] in sixteen days; by the power of piercing six million [leagues] in seven days; by the power of piercing eighty million [leagues] in three days; and by the power of piercing ten million [leagues] in a single day—this is instantaneous accomplishment (*siddhi*) in a single moment.

This is the common accomplishment of mercury and so forth; it is middling, consisting of the accomplishment of the sword and so forth, the accomplishment of the *vidyādhara*, the accomplishment of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), and the accomplishment of the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*).
Of these two, the supreme accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others is the attainment of supreme gnosis through the cultivation of the image of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, whatever accomplishment arises for individuals by the power of their own performed merit, therein lies the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*), which results from the penetration [of that merit] over many lifetimes. || 230 ||

Now, the examination of treasures for those seeking wealth is described: A lamp of human affection reveals a treasure from a sword; a creeper serves as the wick for a lotus-fiber lamp. At the time of daily recitation, where there is no conflict with animals, one should perform the mantra-recitation of the Lord of Beings at that daily hour until a sign appears in the excavation; from that, the attainment of wealth occurs for the practitioners of mantra. || 239 ||
With the verse beginning "Sword-sun" (*khaḍgāditya*) and so forth:

here on this earth, whatever creepers, trees, or other entities appear, there a substance exists; and furthermore, wherever a constant horizontal opposition appears—a quarrel for the sake of one's own place—there a substance is found. Having made a wick from a red lotus fiber above a fine steel sword or above a knife, having soaked it with human fat, and having consecrated it with the mantra of the Lord of Spirits as described in the chapter on mantra-attainment, one should gaze upon the ground.
If the tongue of fire falls downward, then treasure exists; if it does not fall, then there is none.

Thus, if it should fall, one should perform the recitation of the mantra of the Lord of Spirits at that place during the three junctions of the day until a vision appears; thereafter, the practitioners shall attain the success of the subterranean treasure.
Otherwise, it becomes a source of affliction; wealth guarded by the asuras cannot be recovered by anyone. || 231 ||

Since there is no further folio of the *Mātṛkā*, the text from the commentary on the verses up to "or the *kulataru* of the three powers" is extracted from the Tibetan translation and rendered into Sanskrit in this chapter [verse]: In the *Mahoddeśa on the Various Means for Training Disciples*: First, the six *yakṣiṇīs* whose mantras originate from the six wombs (*ṣaḍyonimantra*) and who are empowered by the Vajra of the Lord of Jinas are to be accomplished; having accomplished them, one must then accomplish the *kṣetravādās* upon the surface of the earth.

Having accomplished the nāginīs, you must accomplish the medicinal herbs that have the essence of the fruit of immortality; having accomplished the ḍākinīs, you must accomplish the asuras who cause supreme terror. || 232 ||

Having accomplished the *nāgas* and so forth, the excellent gods and humans are to be accomplished by the yogi; having accomplished the *dhūmas* and so forth, the middling ones who cause fear of death are to be accomplished; having accomplished the *prāṇas* and so forth, the drops (*bindus*) that have melted from the moon are to be accomplished; and having accomplished true bliss, the all-pervading body of the coemergent Victor (*sahajajina*) is to be accomplished. || 233 ||

That which bestows death upon sentient beings is the nectar (*amṛta*) presided over by all; it is the desired accomplishment (*siddhi*) reached through perfected mantras, and that which is to be reached through meditation within the abode of the three worlds.

That gnosis (*jñāna*), which is difficult to obtain yet easily accessible when presided over by bliss, resides precisely in the vajra and the lotus. Thus, may that Vajrin grant equal bliss to all living beings at all times. (234)
Therefore, the three stanzas following this one are easy to understand. (232–234)

Now, the division of the *kula* as taught in the *Kulāgama* is stated: Rāhu and Agni, the Moon and the Sun; Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Space—this group of four is consumed. The other group of five is the collection of planets. From this [group of] six, the four continents arise from Meru in the directions. The five sense objects are said to be external. Likewise, within the center of the body, there is this supreme triadic sequence of the qualities (*guṇas*), beginning with *sattva*. || 235 ||

By the words "Rāhu" and so forth, here the *Kulāgama* is indicated: having purified externally and within the body the sequence of four, five, six, four, five, and three [units] starting from the western house, then follows the worship of the deities.
Now, externally, these are Rāhu, Kālāgni, the Moon, and the Sun.
The union of these is a group of four, meaning the four seats (*catuṣpīṭha*).
Then, for the purpose of filling the world-system, there is a group of five beginning with earth and ending with taste (*rasa*).
Then, excluding the other group of four consisting of the host of planets, there are Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and Ketu.
The group of these [elements] is sixfold; then, from Meru, there are four continents in the four directions, which is a group of four;
and the five objects of sense, beginning with smell, are a group of five.

The qualities beginning with *sattva* are likewise a triad; just as the qualities beginning with *sattva* form a triad externally in the *pīṭhas* and so forth, so too should it be understood within the body.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*), bliss (*ānanda*), blood (*rakta*), and nectar (*amṛta*) constitute a tetrad in the lotuses and so forth; from that [tetrad] comes the pentad of bone and the rest, and from that, the hexad of the eyes and so forth.

19, 5, 10, 15, 20, 20, 25, 10, 15, 20, 20, 225, 30, 146. In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the knowledge [chapter]: "The two hands, the feet, the group of four, the five belonging to the hands and feet, and the 'all-three' of those fingers—the entire sequence here is to be understood in this family. (236)

Here, for the sake of the arising of the body, [the yogis] declare that the *ālayavijñāna* is Rāhu within the mother’s womb; *ānanda* is Kālāgni; "blood" is the fire-particle (tejas) which is Sūrya; and "nectar" is the semen which is Candra. These four constitute the tetrad of causes for the initial arising of the Body-family (*kāyakula*).
From that tetrad arises the pentad beginning with bone:
bone is earth, bile is water, blood is fire, flesh and skin are wind, and marrow is space; thus the entire pentad is produced.
Then, the group of six beginning with the eye consists of:
the eye is Bhīma, the ear is Budha, the tongue is Bṛhaspati, the nose is Śukra, the organ of action is Śanaiścara, and the mental organ is Ketu;
likewise, the group of four consisting of the hands and feet is as follows: the left hand is Pūrvadvīpa, and the right hand is Dakṣiṇa.
The right foot is the southern continent, the left foot is the western continent, and [the other two feet] are the northern continent—this is the group of four;
and the fingers constitute the group of five.
Here, by way of the qualities of earth and the other elements, the thumb is smell, the index finger is taste, the middle finger is form, the ring finger is touch, and the little finger is sound.

Regarding those five fingers, it is said that there are three joints each: the first joint is the quality of *sattva*, the middle joint is the quality of *rajas*, and the final joint is the quality of *tamas*.
At the end of *tamas* is the primary joint of the nail; thus, it is appropriate to understand that this entire sequence exists here within this *kula*. || 236 ||

Now, the divisions of the *pīṭhas* and so forth are described: the mountains (*bhūbhṛt*) are the divisions of the principles (*tattva*); the suns (*bhānu*) are sixty, being the number of the *rasas* (six) multiplied by the *rasas*; the Viśatis are twenty; all these, when added together, amount to sixty-four, three, nine, and five—the number of breath-movements (*prāṇacāra*). Furthermore, that movement of the planets is said to be the "movement of the Yoginīs" (*yoginīcāra*), which is distinct from the others. || 237 ||
"Mountains," and so forth:
here, by virtue of the four quarters, there are four divisions;
likewise, these are the divisions of the seats (pīṭhas).

"Bhūbhṛt" refers to sixteen divisions of the principles (*tattva*), which amount to twenty-five in total. Where there is one, there are five multiplied by the flavors (*rasa*); thus, six multiplied by six makes thirty-six. These are the divisions of Mars and the other [planets] according to their six movements. In the fourth [category], there are twelve divisions for the Sun; there are twelve divisions for the joints of the hands and feet; and externally, there is the Moon with its twelve zodiacal signs (*rāśi*) divisions.
In the fifth [chapter], there are twenty [divisions] according to the number of fingers;
likewise, there are sixty divisions according to the finger-joints.
These divisions pertain to men and gods as well, meaning they apply to those with complete bodies, not to those with pure (vimala) bodies.
All those, when added together, are said to be "the number of the moon in the hollow of the *vaṭa* tree," which is one hundred and sixty-nine.
All those, when added together, are thus [one hundred and sixty-nine]. By those totals, there would be "three times nine," which is twenty-seven;
furthermore, the divisions of Śiva and Śakti, by way of the relationship between the support (*ādhāra*) and the supported (*ādheya*), should be understood as fifty-four.

In this family, the movement of the planets within the life-channel (*prāṇanāḍī*) and the movement of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*)—whatever movement these possess—is described by others who delight in external words as the "movement of the Yoginīs.

Thus it is stated in the *Mūlasūtra*, in the chapter on the "Great Summary of the Disciples through Various Means": "That which is Power (*śakti*) is the Blessed One (*bhagā*), endowed with a threefold motion, consisting of three syllables and three natures; therein resides the illustrious Oḍḍiyāna, together with the excellent jar (*kalasa*), situated in the center and exceedingly radiant."

In the very corner to its right is the manifest abode of the glorious Jālandhara-pīṭha; to the left is the glorious Pūrṇa-pīṭha; and in front of it is Kāmarūpa, which strikes fear into the ignorant. Thus pervading is the Pīṭha, the terrifying mother Vyāpinī, the power (śakti) of Rudra. In its center is the Liṅga, which bestows supreme bliss; within that is the Bindu containing the Nāda, eternally blissful and exceedingly tranquil. She who, through the sixfold meditations, sustains that which is perceived as the three desires, I bow to her named Kubjikā, whose body is as fleeting as a flash of lightning.
Thus, it is appropriate that the innate, flowing power (*śakti*) of all sentient beings is called *bhaga*;
this is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of *bhaga*.
Now, regarding the *Kulasūtra*, it is the cause for the formation of the body.
Namely: Kū is in Kāmarūpa; Puligatapulikā is at Jālapīṭha; Agnijihvā is in Oḍra; and at Śrīmadhyapīṭha there are the eight Devaśṛṅgas located on the threefold path.

There are five Siddhis, and likewise five goddesses accompanied by Ḍa, Ra, La, Ka, and Sa. From those [arise] the three Śaktis. Therefore, I bow to the Mother named Kubjikā, the Tree of the Family (Kulataru).
In the Vimalaprabhā, it is said: "Thus, this supreme secret is not known by the Bhakṣyas, the Daityas, the Mārakāyikas, and the Kolis; such is the rule of the Kulasūtra. (237)

Now, the compendium of the Buddhas' Dharma is stated: Furthermore, this pair of gnosis and space, as well as the three jewels of the vehicles, the afflictions, the Māras, the abodes, the fixed [stages], the two feet, the outflows, the fearlessnesses, the truths, and then the four applications of mindfulness and right efforts—these, ending with the means of attraction, are to be meditated upon by yogins through the vajras of the Lord of Jinas. || 238 ||

"The two spaces of gnosis" refers to gnosis as the apprehending mind (*citta*) and the apprehended empty image; these two are wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*), not the union of the female and male organs.
By performing this for the benefit of sentient beings, one becomes a teacher of the three vehicles and a knower of the compendium of the Dharma.
Here, the three vehicles are the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Samyaksambuddha vehicle.
That by which one goes is the "vehicle" (*yāna*), which is indeed the Three Jewels: the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha.

These are the three roots—the teacher, the teaching, and the requester—namely: the arousal of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), the purity of intention (*āśaya*), and the abandonment of the notions of "I" and "mine" (*ahaṅkāra-mamakāra*).
Likewise, taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Saṅgha—this is the going for refuge.
The afflictions (kleśas) of sentient beings are fourfold: attachment, aversion, delusion, and pride;
these are the four Māras, namely the Māra of the aggregates (skandhamāra), the Māra of afflictions (kleśamāra), the Māra of death (mṛtyumāra), and the Māra of the son of a god (devaputramāra).

The destroyers of these [afflictions] are the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) of the Buddhas— namely, loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)— as well as the four liberations (*vimokṣa*)— namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*),
and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*)— and the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): desire (*chanda*), energy (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*).

Sentient beings have four outflows (*āsrava*), namely: the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), and the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*).

The Buddhas have four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), namely: the ground of self-confidence in ascending to all dharmas; the ground of self-confidence in teaching all dharmas; the ground of self-confidence in leading others onto the unobstructed path to nirvāṇa; and the ground of self-confidence in the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows and its abandonment. There are four truths (*satya*), namely: the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), the truth of the origin (*samudaya-satya*), the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*), and the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

The four reliances (*pratiśaraṇa*) are as follows: reliance on the meaning, not reliance on the letter; reliance on gnosis (*jñāna*), not reliance on consciousness (*vijñāna*); reliance on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), not reliance on the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*); and reliance on the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), not reliance on the person (*pudgala*). The four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are: mindfulness of the body, mindfulness of feelings, mindfulness of the mind, and mindfulness of phenomena.
The four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*) are: generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and consistency of purpose.

Here, by the word "meaning" (*artha*), the great meaning (*mahārtha*) is intended—the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*)—and its practice (*caryā*) and the state of having the same purpose (*samānārthatā*);

this is giving through the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*). There are four gifts of Dharma: (1) all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; (2) all conditioned phenomena are suffering; (3) all phenomena (*dharma*) are selfless; and (4) nirvāṇa is peace.
There are four right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*): (1) the arousal of desire for the non-arising of unarisen faults; [and so forth]. Chapter on the [Four] Abandonments, Verse...

The Great Chapter on Training through Various Means: the antidote for the roots of non-virtue is their production; the generation of unarisen virtues; and the dedication of arisen roots of virtue toward Buddhahood.

These four types are, by means of the vajra of the supreme Victor, to be cultivated through the purification of body, speech, mind, and gnosis—that is, through the purification of the Nirmāṇa, Dharma, Sambhoga, and Svābhāvika bodies—for the sake of worldly accomplishment as the forms of the deities. || 238 ||

The five superknowledges (*abhijñā*) are the powers of the Supreme Victor; the five views are the five eyes. Thus, the aggregates (*skandha*), the faculties (*indriya*), and the mindfulnesses (*smṛti*)—these six—and the sevenfold worship of the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), as well as the sevenfold eightfold path, are the excellent refuges. The eight formless liberations (*vimokṣa*) are the eight [realms]; the ninefold scripture is that which is called the "openings. Furthermore, the stages (*bhūmi*) are equal in measure to the directions. || 239 ||

Thus, the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā) of the bodhisattvas are: the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, recollection of former abodes, and the supernormal power of moving through space—these are the five powers (pañca balāni): the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom;
likewise, these are the five faculties (pañcendriyāṇi).

Sentient beings have five views: the view of a self-existent body (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), the view of grasping at extremes (antagrāha-dṛṣṭi), false view (mithyā-dṛṣṭi), the view of adhering to [wrong] views (dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa-dṛṣṭi), and the view of adhering to [wrong] conduct and observances (śīla-vrata-parāmarśa-dṛṣṭi).
Buddhas have five eyes: the flesh eye (māṃsa-cakṣus), the divine eye (divya-cakṣus), the Buddha-eye (buddha-cakṣus), the wisdom eye (prajñā-cakṣus), and the knowledge eye (jñāna-cakṣus).

The supramundane Buddhas have five aggregates (skandhas): the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīla-skandha), the aggregate of meditative concentration (samādhi-skandha), the aggregate of wisdom (prajñā-skandha), the aggregate of liberation (vimukti-skandha), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha).

The worldly elements (*dhātu*) such as form and so forth; the sense faculties (*indriya*) such as the eye and so forth; the objects (*viṣaya*) such as odor and so forth; the organs of action (*karmendriya*) such as the anus and so forth; and the activities of the organs of action such as speaking and so forth—this pentad, together with the *dharmadhātu*, constitutes the entire hexad.

These are the six recollections (*anusmṛti*): recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of renunciation (*tyāga*), recollection of ethical discipline (*śīla*), and recollection of the deities (*devatā*).

The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are: the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasambodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of energy (*vīryasambodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prītisambodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*prasrabdhisambodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*), and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣāsambodhyaṅga*).

The sevenfold worship (*saptavidhā pūjā*) consists of: salutation (*vandanā*), offering (*pūjanā*), confession (*deśanā*), rejoicing (*anumodanā*), entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇā*), supplication (*yācanā*), and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

The eightfold path (*aṣṭāṅgika mārgaḥ*) consists of: right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), right speech (*samyagvāk*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).

The eight meditative liberations (*dhyāna-vimokṣa*): one perceives form as empty; one perceives internal form while external form is empty; one perceives the image (*bimba*) in all its aspects as "empty," perceiving it as empty of being produced by views of the beautiful or the ugly; one perceives the sphere of infinite space as empty; one perceives the sphere of infinite consciousness as empty; within the image in all its aspects, one perceives the sphere of nothingness as empty; one perceives the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as empty; and one perceives the cessation of perception and feeling as empty—this is in the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*).

The ninefold teaching of the compilers consists of the eight form-possessing [categories]—the four great elements, visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility—as well as sound; namely: Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Nidāna, Vṛtta, Jātaka, Vaipulya, and Adbhuta, for the purpose of collecting the Dharma.

The ten powers of the Buddhas, the ten masteries that are manifest, the twelvefold dependent origination, the cessation regarding form and so forth, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the thirty-two marks of the supreme Victor, and the eighty minor signs—all this, the sovereign supreme state, is to be meditated upon by the mantra-practitioner within his own body. The ten sets of ten, beginning with the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*), are taught in the *Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*aṣṭādaśāveṇikabuddhadharma*) are taught here;

and for the monks, there are the twelve ascetic virtues (*dvādaśadhūtaguṇa*): namely, being an alms-collector (*piṇḍapātika*), wearing the three robes (*traicīvarika*), eating only after the midday meal (*paścātkhalubhaktika*), sitting in one posture (*naiṣadyika*), accepting whatever seat is offered (*yathāsaṃstarika*), eating at a single sitting (*ekāsanika*), dwelling in the open air (*abhyavakāśika*), dwelling at the foot of a tree (*vṛkṣamūlika*), dwelling in the forest (*āraṇyavāsika*), dwelling in a cemetery (*śmaśānika*), wearing robes made of rags from a dust heap (*pāṃśukulika*), and possessing few possessions (*nāmantika*).

Having thus understood the compendium of all phenomena (sarvadharmasaṃgraha) at the beginning, the practitioner, together with the preceptor, must then meditate upon the supreme state of the Lord (vibhuḥ), which is neuter, within his own body; this is the meaning. || 240 ||

One is the nature of the moon; two are the eyes of Yama (Kāla) and the two solstices (pakṣa-ayana); three are the worlds, the times (kāla), and the qualities (guṇa); four are said to be the fires (agni), the oceans, the Vedas, and the arrows; five invariably arise as the elements (bhūta) and the senses (indriya); six are the tastes (rasa) and the seasons (ṛtu); seven are the days of the week (vāra), the mountains (adri), and the sages (muni); likewise, eight are the Nāgas and the Vasus. ||241||

The channels (nāḍīs), the apertures (randhras), the planets (grahas), the treasures (nidhis), the nine, the directions (diks), the lords of the ten, the sun (sūrya), the bodiless one (anaṅga), Manu, the worlds (bhuvanas), the lunar days (tithis), and the kings (nṛpas)—these twelve increase by one [respectively];

the faults (doṣas) are eighteen; these excellent and complete Jinas are twenty-four; the principles (tattvas) and limbs (aṅgas) are twenty-five; "the twice-born" (dvijaka) becomes thirty-two; and the three gods (trideva). 242.
From here on, the two verses that clarify the designations for the numbers beginning with one and the moon and so forth are easy to understand. ||241-242||

Indeed, in all the kings of tantras, the vajra-word was concealed by the Vajrin; however, it has been declared in its entirety, directly, in the *Ādibuddha* for the sake of the liberation of living beings.

Therefore, O Sucandra, this glorious *Tantra-Ādibuddha*, the supreme designation of the Lord of Victors, is the most excellent of tantras—entire, without omission, and transcending both the mundane and the supramundane. (243)
Regarding the passage beginning with "In all," etc.:

here, in this entire *Yoginīyogatantrarāja*, the "adamantine state" (*kuliśapada*), which is the bliss of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣarasukha*), has indeed been concealed by the Vajrī, namely Śākyamuni.
"Vajra" refers to the indestructible gnosis (*abhedyajñāna*) and the inconceivable mind-vajra; that in whom this exists is the "Vajrī. By him, the Vajrī...

For what reason? Because in the Noble Land (Āryaviṣaya), due to the pride of scholarship among Buddhists, those Buddhist scholars who—without having served their gurus—look at a book and say, "We have understood the vajra-word," will not go to Rākṣasa due to that egoism. Because of the absence of the tradition of consecration (*sekasaṃpradāya*), this [teaching] was concealed.

That very same thing, which is the entire *Mahoddeśa* on various means for training disciples, has been spoken directly in the *Ādibuddha* for the sake of liberation for those born in the land of Sambhala whose minds are free from egoism.

The *Tantrōttara* is indeed the complete and unimpaired *Tantrarāja*. It is superior to the *Lokatanttra*, which is the *Kriyātantra*, and to the *Lokōttara*, which is the *Yōgatantra*; it is superior to both.
It is the designation—that is, the expressive term—for the co-emergent (*sahaja*) Gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*) of the glorious *Adibuddha*, the Supreme Lord of Jinas, which is supramundane. (243)

I bow to that which has no end, beginning, or middle; no state of existence, death, or birth; no sound, smell, taste, touch, or form; no mind, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), or person (*puruṣa*); no bondage or liberation, no agent, no seed, no manifest time, and no inherent nature of suffering or happiness in any world; it is Nirvāṇa, signless, devoid of instruments of action, and free from qualities. (244)

I pay homage to Kālacakra—the weapon of Viśva and the others, the incomparable Puruṣa, all-pervading, free from conceptual proliferation, immutable, with ears, nose, mouth, eyes, and head, with hands and feet everywhere, the end of beings and the lord of beings, the bearer of the boon for the three worlds, the cause of causes, the primordial knowledge, attainable through yoga, and the state of supreme bliss. (245)

Regarding the passage beginning with "of whom" (*yasya*) and so forth: here, the fivefold great emptiness is the *vajra*. Its cessation of consciousness (*vijñāna-nirodha*) is the first emptiness. From the words "of whom there is no end, beginning, or middle," up to "I bow to that which is devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇaṃ taṃ namasye*), [it is shown that] because it transcends the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-dharmatātīta*), as stated in the *Nāmasaṃgīti* (8.23): "The wisdom that bears the form of non-duality," it transcends the nature of consciousness; therefore, even for those born in its family, it transcends the elements such as space, the sense faculties, and so forth. Consequently, upon the cessation of mental formations (*saṃskāra-nirodha*), there is the second emptiness.
The passage beginning with "Kālaṃ viśvāvivajram" and ending with "kālacakraṃ namasya" is easily understood. || 244-245 ||

I bow to the Creator in the form of Śakti, resembling lightning and fire, possessing the brilliance of the twelve suns; I bow to that white Visarga, which is knowledge with the luster of a thunderbolt, leading to the supreme state, the Lord of the three worlds, flowing from the moon, established at the peak of the world, the nectar that destroys death and crushes the fear of existence, existing in the form of a drop (bindu). || 246 ||

I bow to Vajrasattva, the Lord of the World, who is the universal form, the progenitor of the three worlds; he is pure consciousness in the form of mantra, surrounded by the thirty gods, whose nature is both suffering and bliss, appearing peaceful to the virtuous and experiencing the results of their good deeds, yet appearing terrible to the wicked and experiencing the results of their cruel actions—he who, according to the law, brings about whatever fruit corresponds to whatever karma one performs within one's own mind. 247.
One and yet not one, both one and many; equal and unequal, yet equal; on the right, left, front, back, above, below, and all around; white, green, and of every color, yet of a single form;

in the *Vimalaprabhā*, short, long, and protracted, yet devoid of qualities, yet possessing qualities; female, male, and neither male nor female; the sole support of all, the auspicious and supreme *bhaga*—homage to you, homage to you, homage to you! 248.

From the statement, "In this way, those other conditioned factors [are empty]," one should understand that the elements and faculties, such as wind and so forth, are free from obscuration by means of the second emptiness.

Then, the third emptiness is the cessation of feeling (*vedanā-nirodha*), beginning with the words "the creator" and ending with "I bow to that emission" (*visarga*); because of the statement "that feeling is other," the elements such as fire (*tejo-dhātu*), the sense faculties (*indriya*), and so forth, are unobscured—this is the third emptiness. Then, the fourth emptiness is the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā-nirodha*), beginning with the words "white" and ending with "I bow to the form of the drop" (*bindu-rūpa*); because of the statement "that perception is other," the elements such as water (*toya-dhātu*), the sense faculties, and so forth, are unobscured—this is the fourth emptiness.

Then, from "the fifth void is the cessation of form, mere consciousness," and so forth, up to "I bow to Vajrasattva"—because of the statement "the other is its form"—there is the state of being free from obscuration for the elements such as earth, the sense faculties, and those belonging to their respective families; the detailed explanation of this has been stated in the first chapter on the world-system (*lokadhātu*), and therefore it is not elaborated upon here.

The five-syllabled Great Void (*pañcākṣaro mahāśūnyaḥ*) [is taught in *Nāmasaṃgīti* 10.2], and from that, the six-syllabled Bindu-Void (*binduśūnyaḥ ṣaḍakṣaraḥ*) [in *Nāmasaṃgīti* 10.2]. This Dharma has as its support the characteristic of the Buddha-image, which exists throughout the three realms and the three times.
Its cessation consists of the thirty-six elements, beginning with the six aggregates; the thirty-seven [factors] include fluxing gnosis (*kṣarajñāna*).
The state of these being free from obscuration is called the Dharmakāya and the Source of Dharma (*dharmodaya*).

The fourth is the Vajra, the five-syllabled; the emanation from that which is not a womb is the Nirmāṇakāya, the sound that displays various miraculous powers and teaches the Dharma is the Saṃbhogakāya.
Here, by means of the statement beginning with "neither one nor many, yet one, even, and uneven," the Madhyamaka tenet is established:

that which is the support of all is the One; all is the great imperishable bliss (*mahākṣarasukha*), and its support is the One characterized as space (*ākāśa*), who is the Sublime Lord (*subhaga*) whose nature consists of qualities such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
"Varabhaga" means the supreme among the elements (*dhātu*);
for that reason, "namaste śirasā namaḥ" means let there be salutation with the head; "te" means to you, O Mañjuśrī. (246–248)

I am that very one who, having dispelled all impurities in the world of mortals, am the illustrious Guru, the bearer of the Vajra. It is no wonder that through an offense against him, living beings surely fall into hell;

yet when I am pleased, it is by his satisfaction that I am pleased. When I am enraged, he is indeed great with the fire of my wrath; for sentient beings, that very anger is liberation, bestowing the fruit of equal bliss—he is to be revered and worshipped by his own sons.

Who is more sinful than he who does not worship the lotus feet of the venerable Guru at the three times of day? Who is ignorant? He who does not create a maṇḍala with various kinds of flowers at the three times of day.

Who goes swiftly to the Avīci hell? He who causes distress to the Guru, who is equal in both pleasure and pain. Who attains wisdom and knowledge? He who, remaining undeluded, never abandons the feet of the excellent Guru. || 250 ||

Who is lost? He who, even when the breath has entered the *trinaḍī*, is killed for an infinite time. Who is a hero? He who would kill the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the downward breath (*apāna*) on both even and uneven paths.

Who is a donor? He who gives his own body, children, wife, and everything to the venerable Guru. Who is base? He who is deceitful and whose mind is drawn away by the impurities of his own heart; he is a rogue. (251)
In the chapter [on] the Great Chapter on the Disciples through Various Means (ślokas 248–258):
O Lord of Men, the glorious Adibuddha, the King of Tantras, speaks from that multicolored throne in the glorious Dharmacakra, which is saluted by the best of gods, upon which the Buddha is seated.

O Sūrya, that which was spoken by the Teacher of the Gods for the sake of sentient beings during the awakening regarding the questions of Candra—that very same [teaching] has now been declared by me to you in this *Kalāpa*, for it is indeed a concise tantra. (252)

"O Holder of the Vajra, although the *Kālacakra* has been spoken by me according to what was taught by the Buddha in the composition of the *Sragdharā* meter, you must indeed give its teaching. O Puṇḍarīka, may beings who have entered the threefold existence become like Saraha, the sage of our lineage, through having obtained the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*) by the grace of *Kālacakra*. (253)
O Lord of Men, through the single yoga of Kālacakra, you have been born in this lineage of Brahmā as Sūrya; I am Mañjughoṣa, the King Yaśas.

My beloved is Śrītārā, the white lotus (Pauṇḍarīka), the Lord of the World who is a treasury of all virtues, marked by the lotus. Behold the entire existence of yourself and others, as it truly is, within the stalk of the blue water-lily. 254.

Having observed the entire existence of himself and others within the stalk of the blue lotus exactly as it is, the Sun, together with the lords of sages, bows his crowned head at the lotus feet of Kalkin;

and with both hands, he pays homage and says to the assembly of sages: "May the Sole Teacher, having rescued us from the terrible suffering of saṃsāra, establish us upon the path of knowledge through supreme compassion. (255)

Though old, you are a youth; though the son of all the Jinas, you are the Primordial Buddha from the beginning. Though associated with women, you are a celibate; out of supreme compassion, you are the friend of the world. Though gentle, you are the wielder of the excellent vajra; you are the remover of the fear of death and the constant slayer of Māra. Though liberated, you enter this worldly existence for the sake of maturing the world; you are Yaśas. (256)

I am Sūrya, born into the lineage of Brahmā and bowed at the soles of your feet by the community of sages; for the sake of the liberation of sentient beings, I have manifested the entire Kālacakra upon the earth.
You are Arka (the Sun) in the Kalkī clan, bowed to by kings, O Śrī-Yaśaḥ-Śrīkalāpa; terrified of this fierce saṃsāra, I have come to your lotus-feet for refuge. || 257 ||

On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, when the night has passed and the day has not yet begun, the Sun, having attained the perfection of the mudrā and accompanied by the jewel-like people, is presided over by the Lord of the Universe.

As described in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "For the sake of the liberation of sentient beings, may the Mind-Vajra, which pervades all the earth, proceed for the sake of sentient beings alone—pervading the threefold existence—through the power of Kālacakra, just as it is for me. (258)

Having taught the meaning of the tantra out of supreme compassion for the sake of all sentient beings, the treasury of excellent qualities bestows this command upon his son Puṇḍarīka: "O friend of the world, you must first compose a commentary on this entire King of Tantras, present here in its book-form in its complete and unimpaired state; thereafter, you may indeed proceed at your own will to the supreme state. (259)

May all those Bodhisattvas above, those wrathful kings who cause supreme terror to the Daityas standing on the side of Māra and who, together with their consorts, are situated in every direction and sub-direction within the world of mortals;
and may those lords of serpents in the netherworld who always bind the inauspicious state of the planets—may they all protect the world of ignorance from every side at this daily hour. (260)

For the sake of the liberation of sentient beings, I have taught this most concise *Śrī Kālacakra Tantra* in its entirety, spoken by the Lord of Victors (*Jinapati*), with Vajrasattva as its presiding deity;

it is the single union of wisdom and means, the Lord of Victors through the thunderbolt [of the mind], the reality of sixteen aspects. By that merit, may sentient beings attain the supreme immutable bliss. Homage be to him! (269)
Now, the qualities and other attributes of the teacher of Kālacakra, beginning with "So 'ham," and so forth, are all easily understood. (249–261)

Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Great Instruction on Training through Various Means, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghu-kālacakra-tantra-rāja* following the *Mūla-tantra*. By him who was prophesied by the Perfect Buddha and established the assembly of the most excellent sages on the path of the Buddha, the *Kālacakra* was taught with supreme compassion after bestowing the initiation of wisdom.

Having extracted this chapter on arrows from the *Ādibuddha* tantra, Mañjuvajra—the King Śrī Kalkin—taught it here. I am his son, the King Yaśas, in this *Śrī Kalāpa*. [Chapter, verses 258–261] This is the Great Chapter on those to be trained by various means, composed with a joyful mind at the request of the illustrious Yaśas, who was prophesied by the Perfect Buddha, as a commentary upon the *Tantrarāja* seeking the clear vajra words of the glorious *Mūlatantra*.

By whatever vast, pure merit has been acquired by Puṇḍarīka through this gift, may the entire world become a fully awakened Buddha, having attained the path of the Vajrī. This commentary on the Chapter on Knowledge (Jñānapaṭala) is completed. The Vimalaprabhā commentary is finished.
Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; thus speaks the Great Śramaṇa.

This is the religious gift of the venerable [monk], a follower of the excellent Mahāyāna. Whatever merit there is herein, may it, preceded by his preceptors, teachers, mother, and father, be for the attainment of the fruit of supreme knowledge by the entire mass of sentient beings.

In the year 39 of the illustrious Harivarmadeva, the Great King of Kings, on the twenty-ninth day of Āṣāḍha according to the solar reckoning; in the eleventh day having passed, on the seventh day of the dark fortnight of Māgha in the year of Harivarma.
Having purified the *mṛtapātra* by inspection,
one should take the little finger and ask this as follows:
"In the north-eastern direction, in the waters of the Vegavatī river,
your death shall occur after seven years."
